overview.what_it_does: Dixon Technologies is an Indian contract manufacturer of electronics and appliances — it builds products in its own factories that are sold under other companies' brand names (management calls itself 'the brand behind brands'), for customers such as Motorola, Xiaomi, Nokia, Samsung, Bosch, Dell, Acer, Lenovo, Airtel and Nokia's telecom arm. It works both as a pure assembler to a customer's design (EMS) and as an ODM/JDM player where Dixon does the design itself and the brand simply puts its name on it, so revenue comes from the price of each unit shipped on large volumes at thin single-digit margins rather than from any brand of its own. Operations are essentially all in India — plants in Noida, Dehradun, Tirupati, Chennai and elsewhere — serving mainly the Indian domestic market, with a growing slice of exports and help from government production-linked incentive (PLI/ECMS) schemes. Full-year FY26 revenue was about INR 48,893 crore with EBITDA of roughly INR 1,887 crore and PAT of about INR 845 crore; the business runs on negative working capital and high return ratios (ROCE ~45%, ROE ~28-32%), and it is now pushing into making the components inside its own products — display modules, camera modules, enclosures — through joint ventures and subsidiaries.

parts.name: Mobile and EMS division
parts.what: Assembles smartphones and feature phones (Motorola, Xiaomi, Nokia/HMD, Itel and others, partly via ODM partners like Longcheer and Compal and the Ismartu subsidiary for Africa exports); by far the biggest part of the company — INR 9,485 crore of the INR 10,520 crore total revenue in the March 2026 quarter, up from INR 1,305 crore in the June 2022 quarter.

parts.name: Consumer electronics (LED TVs and refrigerators)
parts.what: Makes LED televisions — including large-screen, mini-LED, Google TV and Samsung Tizen models, plus interactive panels and digital signage — and more recently refrigerators; roughly INR 567 crore of quarterly revenue by end-2025, and management says Dixon has India's largest TV capacity, serving over a third of the country's requirement.

parts.name: Home appliances
parts.what: Designs and builds washing machines (semi-automatic, fully automatic and now front-loading) for brands such as Bosch, Lloyd and Croma, and has added robotic vacuum cleaners for Eureka Forbes; a smaller but relatively high-margin line at about INR 329-355 crore a quarter and margins above 11%.

parts.name: Lighting
parts.what: Produces LED bulbs, battens, downlighters and streetlights as India's largest lighting ODM, with capacity described as covering a large share of national demand; a modest and pressured line at roughly INR 227-231 crore a quarter, facing weak demand and price competition.

parts.name: Telecom and networking products
parts.what: Builds routers, ONTs/GPON set-top boxes, 5G fixed wireless access devices for Nokia and Airtel and, more recently, complex backhaul microwave radios; a fast-growing segment (INR 418 crore in the June 2024 quarter) that management expects to grow at high double digits and is shifting from pure assembly to joint design work.

parts.name: IT hardware products (laptops, tablets, desktops)
parts.what: Manufactures notebooks, all-in-ones, tablets and now desktops for Acer, Lenovo and other top global PC brands from a dedicated Chennai plant and a 60:40 JV with Taiwan's Inventec; still small but management guides to roughly 3x revenue growth in FY27 and calls it a future pillar, with a possible move into servers and data-centre hardware.

parts.name: Security surveillance systems
parts.what: A 50%-owned business making CCTV cameras and recorders, with capacity being expanded from 10 million to 14 million units a year; INR 131 crore of revenue in the June 2022 quarter, and it is not broken out separately in the later calls.

parts.name: Components and backward integration
parts.what: A newer effort to make the parts that go into its own products — camera and fingerprint modules through subsidiary Q Tech (expanding from about 70 million to 180-190 million units a year), display modules via a 74:26 JV with HKC, plus SSDs, enclosures and optical transceivers under the government ECMS scheme; largely captive today but positioned by management as the main route to higher margins and a competitive moat.

overview.what_it_does: Aarti Drugs is an Indian pharmaceutical manufacturer that makes bulk drug ingredients (APIs — the active chemical inside a medicine), specialty chemicals and intermediates, and finished formulations such as tablets. It mainly sells business-to-business — to other drug companies and customers who turn its APIs into medicines — with roughly 63% of standalone sales in India and 37% exported, and exports increasingly going to strictly regulated markets (73% of exports in FY26 versus 66% in FY25). It makes money by producing large volumes of chemicals at its plants in Tarapur (Maharashtra) and a newer greenfield site at Sayakha (Gujarat), so profits swing with product prices, raw-material and energy costs, and how fully the plants are running. Consolidated revenue was about INR 2,568 crores in FY26 (INR 721 crores in the March 2026 quarter alone), of which the API and specialty chemicals business ("standalone") is about 88%.

parts.name: API business (standalone)
parts.what: The core business: manufacturing active pharmaceutical ingredients across therapy areas — antibiotics (about 35-38% of API sales, the biggest and the one whose weak demand has repeatedly dragged results), anti-protozoal (~20%), antidiabetic such as metformin (~15-17%), anti-inflammatory (~12%) and antifungal (~10-12%).

parts.name: Specialty Chemicals and Intermediates
parts.what: A smaller but higher-margin chemicals arm (about INR 57 crores in the June 2022 quarter) that makes intermediates and specialty products, including salicylic acid at Tarapur, which management calls a laggard that was shut down in FY26 pending new equipment.

parts.name: Formulation segment (Pinnacle Life Science)
parts.what: The finished-dosage arm run as a subsidiary under its own Managing Director, contributing roughly 12-14% of consolidated revenue (INR 330.5 crores in FY26, up 16%), with about two-thirds of its sales exported; it does contract manufacturing for the domestic market and owns its own dossiers/IP abroad, out-licensing to local marketing partners.

parts.name: Oncology formulations
parts.what: A newer push within formulations with a dedicated US FDA-approved plant — still pre-revenue as of Feb 2026 with the first product due to launch that quarter, but management expects it to generate about 40% of formulation revenue within three years.

parts.name: Backward integration (Sayakha methylamines plant)
parts.what: A captive plant, started September 2025, that makes the methylamine raw material for its own metformin (antidiabetic) production instead of buying it outside; it hit about 1,000 tonnes/month in March 2026 at just over 40% utilisation, with management targeting over 70% within a year to cut costs and improve margins.

overview.what_it_does: Aarti Industries is an Indian speciality-chemicals maker that runs chemical plants (Vapi, Jhagadia, Dahej SEZ and a new greenfield site called Zone IV) and turns basic petrochemical feedstocks — mainly benzene and toluene, plus inputs like aniline, methanol and sulphur — into a wide range of intermediate chemicals such as nitrochlorobenzene, nitrotoluene, dichlorobenzene, MMA and hydrogenated/ethylated derivatives. It sells these in bulk to industrial customers who use them to make agrochemicals (crop protection), pharmaceuticals, polymers, dyes and pigments, paints and additives, and fuel/energy products; roughly 65% of FY26 revenue came from exports (up from about 50% in FY23). It makes money on the spread between raw-material cost and selling price on large volumes, with cost inflation largely passed through to customers, plus multi-year contracts with global chemical and agrochemical majors that give committed volumes and margins (including a $150 million supply deal running to March 2030). FY26 revenue was about Rs. 9,018 crore with EBITDA of Rs. 1,172 crore and profit after tax of Rs. 419 crore; a separate pharma business was demerged and listed as Aarti Pharmalabs in December 2022.

parts.name: Energy applications (led by MMA)
parts.what: Supplies chemicals used in fuel/energy applications where it says it holds a market-leading global position — the single biggest piece at roughly 40% of revenue, with capacity being expanded from about 290 KT to 360 KT, though margins swing with crude, gasoline and naphtha cracks.

parts.name: Agrochemicals
parts.what: Makes intermediates that go into crop-protection products; volumes have been steady and it is a focus for long-term contracts, but pricing has been squeezed by Chinese oversupply.

parts.name: Pharmaceuticals
parts.what: Supplies intermediates into pharma end-uses; described as stable but smaller since the separate pharma manufacturing arm was demerged into Aarti Pharmalabs in 2022.

parts.name: Polymers
parts.what: Products like PDCB/DCB and PDA/MPDA feeding polymer makers, currently in a strong growth phase on EV-related demand (PPS), though MPDA is under heavy Chinese competition; DCB capacity is being debottlenecked from 120 to 140 KTPA.

parts.name: Dyes, pigments and paints
parts.what: An older end-market for its benzene-chain products; demand was weak in FY23 and is described in recent calls as broadly stable rather than a growth driver.

parts.name: Benzene and Toluene value chains (core integrated chemistry)
parts.what: The backbone of the company — NCB, nitrotoluene, chlorotoluene, hydrogenation and ethylation chains where it calls itself the 'go-to integrated player', with production tracked quarterly in tonnes and about 78% of sales described as value-added products.

parts.name: Long-term contracts / custom manufacturing
parts.what: Multi-year dedicated supply arrangements with global chemical and agrochemical companies, sometimes with capex built specifically for the customer (e.g. Rs. 200-250 crore backward-integration project on a 15-year contract), giving visible volumes and margins.

parts.name: R&D and Advanced Materials (future growth)
parts.what: A 250+ scientist/engineer R&D team with 50+ products in the pipeline, now steering the company toward higher-value 'advanced materials' and sunrise areas like circularity, renewables and battery chemistries — a stated strategy rather than a large revenue contributor today.

parts.name: Joint ventures (Augene/Superform with UPL, and RESL)
parts.what: A 50-50 JV with UPL for downstream amine derivatives used in agrochemicals, paints and coatings (about Rs. 150 crore invested by each side, commissioning around H1 FY27, targeting Rs. 400-500 crore of peak annual revenue), plus a separate JV with RESL on circularity initiatives.

parts.name: Zone IV greenfield site
parts.what: A new manufacturing site with multipurpose plants, chlorotoluene and PEDA blocks being commissioned in phases using in-house technology — the main capex project, with total FY26 capex of Rs. 1,125 crore falling to a guided Rs. 700-800 crore in FY27.

overview.what_it_does: Aarti Pharmalabs is an Indian pharmaceutical chemicals maker that manufactures and sells bulk drug ingredients rather than finished medicines — active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), chemical intermediates, and caffeine-type 'Xanthine' derivatives — plus contract manufacturing and development services (CDMO/CMO) for other drug companies. Its customers are pharmaceutical companies (including regulated markets such as the US and Europe, plus 'rest of world' and non-regulated markets) and, for Xanthine, beverage makers who buy caffeine — beverage customers were 63%–74% of Xanthine volumes in recent quarters. It makes money by selling these chemicals in bulk, with roughly half of Xanthine sales exported and half local; standalone revenue was Rs.1,798 crore in FY2026 with EBITDA of Rs.406 crore and profit after tax of Rs.176 crore. It operates plants in India — Tarapur in Maharashtra (including a US FDA-approved API facility, Unit-4) and Vapi, with a new greenfield site at Atali in Gujarat ramping up — and has been investing about Rs.400 crore a year in expansion.

parts.name: Xanthine Derivatives
parts.what: Makes caffeine and related xanthine chemicals sold mainly to beverage companies and some pharma buyers; it is the single biggest segment at roughly 43%–49% of quarterly revenue, with capacity being expanded from 4,000 tonnes a year originally to 5,000, then 6,000, and targeted at 9,000 tonnes per annum, though Chinese competition keeps pushing spot prices down.

parts.name: API and Intermediates
parts.what: Produces active pharmaceutical ingredients and chemical building blocks — including oncology, steroid, anticoagulant (Apixaban) and diabetes (gliflozin) products — sold mostly into regulated markets (about 52%–53% of the segment), and it ranged from roughly 42% of revenue in earlier quarters down to 28% in Q4 FY2026 as pricing pressure hit.

parts.name: CDMO/CMO
parts.what: Develops and manufactures molecules on contract for other pharma companies using largely the same plants as the API business; it grew from about 6% of revenue in mid-2023 to a record 29% (Rs.155 crore) in Q4 FY2026 with 21 customers and 54 active projects (35 commercial), is described by management as the higher-margin business, and is expected to lead growth with 40%–50% sales growth guided for FY2027.

overview.what_it_does: ABB India makes and sells the electrical and automation equipment that powers and runs factories, buildings and infrastructure — everything management describes as "substation to socket" electrical gear (switchgear, compact substations, low- and medium-voltage power distribution, UPS), plus motors, generators and drives, process control/SCADA systems, and industrial robots. Its customers are industrial and infrastructure buyers across roughly 23 market segments — data centres, railways and metros, renewables, buildings and infrastructure, metals and mining, energy and petrochemicals, automotive, electronics, food and beverage — sold both directly (about 59% of business) and through 750-plus channel partners, integrators and OEMs (about 41%), with an added stream of after-sales service. It earns money by booking orders into a backlog and converting them into revenue: CY2025 orders were about ₹14,115 crore, revenue about ₹13,203 crore, profit before tax ₹2,230 crore (16.9% margin) and profit after tax ₹1,669 crore, with a closing backlog of ₹10,471 crore and return on capital employed of 21%. It is overwhelmingly an India business — manufacturing here for over 75 years from 5 factory locations (Nashik, Faridabad, Baroda and two Bengaluru campuses) housing 25 shop floors, served by 28 sales offices — with exports to about 30 countries making up roughly 10% of the portfolio.

parts.name: Electrification
parts.what: Sells the full chain of electrical distribution products from substation to socket — low- and medium-voltage switchgear, compact substations, smart power products, UPS and installation products for cities, buildings, data centres and infrastructure; management calls it part of the core that makes up a major share of revenue, and it is the business most cited in data-centre and building/infrastructure wins.

parts.name: Electrification Distribution Solutions
parts.what: A distribution-focused unit within Electrification that got its own president by 2025-26, supplying power-distribution platforms such as the new ARTU Formula low-voltage switchgear platform that partners use to build value-added solutions.

parts.name: Motion
parts.what: ABB's energy-efficiency core — electric motors, generators, drives and mechanical power transmission products plus related services, used in HVAC and cooling, water and process plants, metals electric powertrains, rail propulsion and now locally built wind power converters; described alongside Electrification as a major part of the revenue stream.

parts.name: Process Automation
parts.what: Process control systems and integrated electrification-plus-digital solutions for process and hybrid industries — SCADA, remote terminal units, leak detection, city gas distribution monitoring, petrochemical and energy projects — typically larger, longer-cycle project work.

parts.name: Robotics & Discrete Automation
parts.what: Industrial robots and factory/machine automation, historically driven by automotive but increasingly sold into FMCG and food & beverage end-of-line packaging and palletising, and electronics and mobile-phone assembly.

parts.name: Automation (combined)
parts.what: By the 2025-26 calls, Process Automation and Robotics & Discrete Automation are presented together under a single Automation head, so ABB India describes itself simply as an electrification, motion and automation company.

parts.name: Divisions and market segments (how the parts are organised)
parts.what: The business areas are split into distinct divisions with their own business models — 20 in 2022, 19 in 2024, 18 in 2025 and 16 by early 2026 — all pointed at the same 23 market segments, a spread management says smooths out the cyclicality of any single end market.

parts.name: Exports
parts.what: Shipments from Indian plants to about 30-plus countries; growing (up 45% in Q2 2022, 23% in Q1 2024) but still only around 10% of the portfolio because domestic growth is much stronger.

parts.name: Services
parts.what: After-sales service and support attached to the installed base, delivered increasingly through channel partners close to the customer; grew 14% in the Q2 2022 quarter.

overview.what_it_does: Abbott India Limited sells branded prescription medicines, vaccines and over-the-counter health products in India. Its customers are reached through doctors who prescribe its brands and retail pharmacies (increasingly including online pharmacy and retail-chain channels), with management also pushing into government/public-market channels such as ESIC and state and central immunisation programmes. It makes money by selling branded formulations — mega-brands like Thyronorm, Duphaston, Duphalac, Cremaffin, Udiliv, Digene and Influvac — where it invests in disease awareness, free/subsidised diagnostic testing (25 lakh thyroid tests a year, FibroScan for liver) and patient-adherence programmes to expand the category rather than just fight for brand share. It operates only in India (about 70% of sales from metros and class-one towns, now expanding into class two/three and 'extra urban' areas), is the only multinational in the top 10 of the Indian pharmaceutical market, and grew top line 14.1% last year (7.6% volume, rest price) with a stated goal of becoming a $1 billion business by 2025. About 26% of sales by value come from price-controlled NLEM products.

parts.name: Women's Health
parts.what: Sells women's health medicines led by the long-standing brand Duphaston (plus newer launches Femoston for post-menopausal problems, Preservgest for pregnancy maintenance and Riligol, a heat-stable carbetocin for postpartum bleeding marketed with Ferring); the portfolio grew over 23% and Duphaston, after 60 years as the only brand, now faces about 41 competitors — it has lost share in gynaecology but held share in IVF and still grows.

parts.name: Gastroenterology (GI)
parts.what: The company's strongest growth driver at about 27% growth, with market leadership and brands including Udiliv (chronic liver disease), Duphalac and Cremaffin/Cremaffin Plus (constipation), Digene and the new Digeraft and Digecaine antacids, plus second-line 'hidden gems' Creon, Ganaton, Librax and Heptral; management is adding headcount and launching another business unit inside GI.

parts.name: Metabolics
parts.what: Mainly hypothyroidism treatment through Thyronorm, where Abbott is market leader with roughly 53% share and is still gaining share against about 11 competitors, supported by the MITA ('Making India Thyroid Aware') campaign and ~25 lakh thyroid tests a year; the full 12.5–150 mg range sits under NLEM price control.

parts.name: Vaccines
parts.what: Four products — Influvac for influenza (a 100-crore-plus brand within a roughly 200-crore vaccine business), Enteroshield for typhoid, Rotasure for rotavirus, and the newly launched Havshield for Hepatitis A which should cross $1 million in its first year; growth focus is shifting to adult vaccination, which management sees as the bigger opportunity versus pediatric.

parts.name: Over-the-counter (OTC) / direct-to-consumer
parts.what: A consumer-facing portfolio covering antacids, laxatives and some pain products, sold with heavy digital and direct-to-consumer marketing as media habits move online.

parts.name: Top 10 brands and the 'next 10'
parts.what: The top 10 brands are each $15 million-plus and, with the top 20 brands, contribute roughly 90–93% of the business, while a 'next 10' tier of $5–15 million brands (Arachitol, Creon, Ganaton, Prothiadin, Zolfresh) is expected to grow into that top tier.

parts.name: New product introductions
parts.what: About 35 products launched in the last three years with roughly 75 planned over the next five, coming from lifecycle extensions of mega-brands, molecules going off patent (management cites 500-plus loss-of-exclusivity opportunities in branded generics), and adjacent therapy areas.

overview.what_it_does: Aditya Birla Capital is an Indian financial services group that sells a broad range of money products to Indian customers — loans to individuals, small businesses (MSMEs) and larger corporates, home loans, mutual funds, life insurance and health insurance — all under one roof through what management calls a "One ABC, One P&L" approach. Its customers are retail consumers, SMEs/MSMEs and corporate/mid-market borrowers, reached through an "omnichannel" network of 1,712 branches (as of September 2025), virtual relationship managers, bank partnerships, and its own digital platforms. It makes money mainly from interest spreads on its lending books (NBFC net interest margin about 6.1%, housing finance similar), from fees on managing mutual fund assets, and from insurance premiums; the parent also collects dividends from subsidiaries such as the asset management company. It operates only in India, backed by the Aditya Birla Group (ABG) parentage, and by Q3 FY26 was earning roughly 983 crore rupees of quarterly consolidated profit on about 14,181 crore rupees of quarterly revenue.

parts.name: NBFC business (Aditya Birla Finance / lending)
parts.what: The largest business — a non-bank lender making secured and unsecured business loans to SMEs/MSMEs, personal and consumer loans, and corporate & mid-market loans, with a loan book that grew from about 86,000 crore rupees in June 2023 to about 1.48 lakh crore rupees by December 2025 and delivered 772 crore rupees of quarterly profit; roughly 73% of the book is secured and business loans to MSMEs are about 56% of it.

parts.name: HFC business (Aditya Birla Housing Finance / ABHFL)
parts.what: The home-loan arm, described as a "full-stack" lender across prime, affordable housing and construction finance, growing fastest in the group — the book grew about 48% a year over three years to 42,204 crore rupees with best-in-class bad loans (gross stage 3 of 0.54%), and in Feb 2026 Advent International agreed to put in 2,750 crore rupees for about 14.3% of it, valuing it at 19,250 crore rupees.

parts.name: Asset management business (Aditya Birla Sun Life AMC)
parts.what: Runs mutual funds — equity, debt, passive/index and alternate funds — for investors, with average assets under management growing from about 2.97 trillion rupees in mid-2023 to over 4.25 trillion rupees by September 2025 and quarterly profit of roughly 241–242 crore rupees; it is also the source of the parent's dividend income (311 crore rupees in Q2 FY26).

parts.name: Life insurance business
parts.what: Sells individual and group life insurance policies, distributed heavily through bank partnerships (Bank of Maharashtra, IDFC First Bank, Axis Bank), described as among the fastest-growing private life insurers with individual first-year premium up 19% year-on-year in FY26 and a new-business (VNB) margin of 14.2% in Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Health insurance business (ABHI)
parts.what: A standalone health insurer using a "Health First" model, repeatedly called the fastest-growing standalone health insurer in India, with premiums up 31–39% year-on-year and a combined ratio (claims plus costs versus premiums) of about 111–112%, meaning the underwriting itself still runs at a loss.

parts.name: ABCD (D2C digital platform)
parts.what: A consumer app launched April 2024 offering 26+ products — payments, loans, insurance, investments — that acts as the group's customer-acquisition engine, with more than 7.6 million customers acquired by late 2025 against a stated goal of 30 million in three years.

parts.name: Udyog Plus (B2B MSME platform)
parts.what: A paperless digital platform for small businesses offering loans plus business services and supply-chain finance, tied into the wider Aditya Birla Group ecosystem; it reached about 4,400 crore rupees of loans and now sources roughly 32% of the unsecured business-loan book.

parts.name: Omnichannel branch network / One ABC locations
parts.what: The physical distribution layer — 1,712 branches across all businesses as of September 2025, including 1,028 "co-located" branches at 260 One ABC locations where a customer can access several of the group's products in one place, with a push into tier 3 and tier 4 towns.

overview.what_it_does: Allied Blenders and Distillers (ABD) is an Indian alcoholic-spirits company that makes and sells branded liquor — mainly whisky, plus brandy, rum, vodka and gin — under the "IMFL" (Indian-made foreign liquor) label, with 17 brands including its 35-year-old flagship Officer's Choice, ICONiQ White, Sterling Reserve and Kyron. Management describes it as India's third-largest spirits company by annual sales volume (31.7 million cases in FY24, 9 million cases in a single quarter by FY27), and says whisky is about 97% of its portfolio. Because liquor is a state subject in India, ABD must produce and sell within each state, so it runs 32 bottling units plus its own distillery and sells to whichever wholesaler the state allows (government-run or private), which then supplies roughly 79,000 retail outlets and on-premise venues — over 90% width of distribution; it also supplies the defence forces (CSD and paramilitary) and exports. Revenue comes from selling cases of liquor at a margin — FY26 consolidated income from operations was Rs 3,949 crore with a 14.4% EBITDA margin — and management is pushing two profit levers: shifting mix toward pricier "Prestige & Above" brands, and backward integration (its own PET bottle plant, malt distillery and ENA distillation) to cut input costs.

parts.name: Prestige & Above (P&A)
parts.what: The premium end of the mainstream portfolio — brands like ICONiQ White, Officer's Choice Blue, Sterling Reserve B7 and Srishti — and the main growth engine: 47.2% of volume and 57.3% of value in FY26, up from about 25% of the mix back in FY18, with ICONiQ White alone at 10.7 million cases in FY26 and called the world's fastest-growing millionaire whisky brand.

parts.name: Mass Premium and others
parts.what: The affordable, high-volume end led by Officer's Choice whisky — roughly flat to slightly declining in recent quarters, but management calls it the leader in India's Mass Premium whisky category, with gross margins over 40%, and describes it as the key cash-flow and profit generator that funds everything else.

parts.name: ABD Maestro (Super-Premium to Luxury)
parts.what: A newer, deliberately "asset-light build, buy and partner" platform launched to enter the top-end market, with 10 brands across whisky, gin, vodka and rum (including Arthaus and Zoya gin) built in its first year FY26; still small in revenue terms, with the current focus on widening distribution to over 5,500 premium touch points, duty-free and six international markets.

parts.name: International business / exports
parts.what: Selling its Indian brands abroad — expanded from 14 countries in mid-2024 to 39 countries by Q1 FY27, making it one of India's leading spirits exporters by volume, with Officer's Choice as India's No.1 exported whisky; management calls it asset-light, higher-margin than the domestic business and lighter on working capital per case, targeting 1 million cases in Africa by FY28.

parts.name: Manufacturing and backward integration
parts.what: Its own production base — 32 bottling units, a distillery in Telangana (its largest market) and an R&D/blending centre in Aurangabad — now being expanded with a Rs 115 crore PET bottle plant (commissioned 2025, already EBITDA-accretive, 600 million bottles a year), a malt distillery and ENA distillation capacity; not a separate revenue line but management's stated route to roughly 300 basis points of EBITDA margin gain by FY28 and another 100 bps by FY29.

overview.what_it_does: Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail Limited (ABFRL) is an Indian clothing company that designs, sources and sells apparel and related fashion products — western wear, Indian ethnic and wedding wear, and luxury goods — to retail shoppers in India, from metros down to Tier-3 and Tier-4 towns. It makes money mainly by selling through its own branded stores and department-store format (about 1,273 stores covering roughly 7.9 million sq ft as of March 2026), plus e-commerce, its own online platforms, and wholesale/multi-brand and departmental-store counters. Revenue for FY26 was INR8,177 crores, up 11%, with EBITDA of about INR903 crores (11% margin), though the company was still loss-making at the bottom line (FY26 loss of INR235 crores adjusted) as it invests in newer businesses. The business it reports today is smaller than earlier years because in FY25-26 it split off its Madura lifestyle brands (Louis Philippe-type menswear, youth western wear, innerwear and sportswear) into a separately listed company, Aditya Birla Lifestyle Brands Limited; the earlier calls (FY23, FY24) describe the combined group, which had revenue of INR13,996 crores in FY24.

parts.name: Pantaloons segment (including OWND!)
parts.what: A chain of large value-and-'masstige' family fashion department stores selling mostly its own private-label clothing, and the single biggest piece of today's ABFRL — about INR1,048 crores of revenue in Q4 FY26 (19% growth) at a 15.5% EBITDA margin; it is being repositioned away from value-led fashion towards a more premium proposition, and includes the newer OWND! store format, which grew to 79 stores.

parts.name: Ethnic business — designer-led
parts.what: Indian ethnic and occasion wear sold under partnerships with and stakes in leading designers — Sabyasachi, Tarun Tahiliani, Shantanu & Nikhil, House of Masaba — plus the craft-led premium brand Jaypore (44 stores); management calls it a strong, profitable business growing over 30% year-on-year with strong double-digit margins.

parts.name: Ethnic business — premium ethnic (Tasva and TCNS/W)
parts.what: Mass-premium ethnic wear: Tasva, a fast-expanding men's wedding-wear brand now at 94 stores, and TCNS (the W group of women's brands, acquired in FY24), which was cut back from about 650 to 480 stores to fix profitability and has more than halved its cash losses; together with the designer brands, the whole ethnic portfolio is INR2,227 crores of FY26 revenue across 680-plus stores at a 10.8% EBITDA margin, and management calls it a key strategic pillar.

parts.name: Luxury retail — The Collective and international mono-brands
parts.what: Multi-brand luxury stores (The Collective) and single-brand stores for international luxury labels, at 49 stores and growing about 16% year-on-year with improving profitability; it also opened Galeries Lafayette, described as India's first flagship luxury department store, in November 2025.

parts.name: TMRW (digital-first brands)
parts.what: A house of online-native fashion brands, including the associate brand Wrogn, run on data-science and technology capabilities; it is at roughly an INR1,100 crore annual revenue run rate, grew 29-45% year-on-year in recent quarters, has 90-plus stores, and is still the loss-making part of the group — management repeatedly quotes margins 'excluding TMRW' to show the rest is close to breakeven.

parts.name: Madura Lifestyle Brands (demerged into Aditya Birla Lifestyle Brands Ltd)
parts.what: The group's original core — leading branded western wear, sold across 2,500-plus stores plus wholesale and e-commerce, generating INR6,560 crores of revenue and INR1,284 crores of EBITDA in FY24 — which the board approved separating in April 2024 into a separately listed company, so it is no longer part of ABFRL's reported results in the FY26 calls.

parts.name: Youth western wear, innerwear, athleisure and Reebok (pre-demerger)
parts.what: Younger and activewear brands described in the earlier calls — American Eagle and Forever 21, an innerwear and active-athleisure business sold through 29,000-plus trade outlets, and the Reebok India business taken over from October 2022 (160-plus stores and 900-plus points of sale) — which contributed a growing minority of group sales before moving with the lifestyle demerger.

overview.what_it_does: ABLBL (Aditya Birla Lifestyle Brands Limited) is an Indian branded-apparel company that sells western-style clothing, innerwear and sportswear to everyday Indian shoppers under names like Louis Philippe, Van Heusen, Allen Solly, Peter England, Reebok and American Eagle. It makes money by selling this merchandise through its own network of 3,348 stores covering 4.9 million square feet across nearly 800 Indian cities and towns, plus wholesale trade channels (multi-brand outlets and department stores, roughly a 60-40 split), e-commerce, and a small contract-manufacturing business that exports garments to other brands worldwide. Growth comes from two levers management repeats constantly: opening more stores (300+ added in FY26) and getting more sales out of existing ones (like-to-like growth). It became a separately listed company on 1 May 2025 after being demerged, and in FY26 posted revenue of INR 8,396 crore, EBITDA of INR 1,429 crore (17% margin) and reported profit of INR 171 crore, with net debt of INR 726 crore and a maiden dividend of 50 paise per share.

parts.name: Lifestyle Brands
parts.what: The core and by far the largest part — the four established menswear/apparel brands Louis Philippe, Van Heusen, Allen Solly and Peter England (management calls them the 'Power brands'), which brought in INR 7,154 crore of FY26 revenue (roughly 85% of the company) at a ~19.6% EBITDA margin and grew high-single-digit for the year.

parts.name: Emerging Businesses
parts.what: The smaller, faster-growing portfolio of Reebok, American Eagle and Van Heusen Innerwear, spanning 390+ stores and growing 18% in Q4 FY26; it is currently loss-light but improving fast, and management expects it to be about one-fourth of the whole company in 4-5 years.

parts.name: Reebok
parts.what: The sportswear brand inside Emerging Businesses, acquired at some point before these calls with 100 stores and since expanded to 210+ stores with sales more than doubled; it grew 20%+ in Q3 and 30% in Q4 FY26 and management plans another 40-50 stores a year.

parts.name: American Eagle
parts.what: A casual/denim brand in the Emerging portfolio that management describes as steadily and profitably growing, with double-digit like-to-like growth in recent quarters; no separate revenue figure is given in the calls.

parts.name: Van Heusen Innerwear
parts.what: The innerwear line inside Emerging Businesses, which had been loss-making but cut losses sharply and returned to double-digit growth, with management targeting a break-even quarter by Q4 of the current fiscal year.

parts.name: Peter England Red
parts.what: A small-town store format under the Peter England brand that management says returned to significant double-digit growth on the back of strong small-town demand.

parts.name: Contract manufacturing / exports
parts.what: A side business that manufactures garments for other brands around the world and shows up in the 'others' line of the Lifestyle Brands channel mix (about INR 127 crore in a quarter); it had a good year after a new large factory added capacity.

parts.name: Forever 21
parts.what: A brand that was closed during FY25 and is repeatedly cited only as a drag on the prior-year comparison base for Emerging Businesses — excluding it, Q3 FY26 segment growth was 19% rather than 13%.

overview.what_it_does: Aditya Birla Real Estate Limited (ABREL, NSE code ABREL, BSE 500040) is the Aditya Birla group company that was called Century Textiles and Industries until it was renamed; it develops and sells residential apartments in India under its Birla Estates brand, in projects such as Birla Niyaara (Worli, Mumbai), Birla Trimaya/Evara (Bengaluru), Birla Arika and Birla Pravaah (Gurugram/NCR), Birla Taranya (Thane) and Birla Punya/Evam (Pune). It buys or ties up land, gets approvals (RERA and others), builds and sells homes mostly to individual buyers in the premium, luxury and ultra-luxury end of the market, booking 'presales' when flats are sold and taking in cash as 'collections' over the construction period. It operates in four main city markets — MMR (Mumbai region), NCR, Bengaluru and Pune — and reported FY26 presales of INR 8,136 crores, collections of INR 3,341 crores and 5.5 million square feet sold. In the earlier years covered by these calls the same company also ran two manufacturing businesses — pulp and paper, and textiles — which no longer feature in the FY26 calls, where management discusses real estate only.

parts.name: Real Estate (Birla Estates)
parts.what: Buys land, builds and sells residential projects in Mumbai/MMR, NCR, Bengaluru and Pune; it was a small part of the company in FY23 (segment revenue INR 33 crores in Q1 FY23 against a group turnover of INR 1,172 crores) and by FY26 is effectively the whole company, delivering FY26 presales of INR 8,136 crores and a stated development pipeline that was INR 54,000 crores of gross development value as of mid-2024.

parts.name: Business development (land acquisition / tie-ups)
parts.what: The team that adds new projects by buying or tying up land parcels — e.g. 13.27 acres in Gurugram (GDV INR 5,300 crores) and 16.5 acres in Manjri, Pune (GDV INR 2,500 crores) in Q1 FY25 — with management saying it added roughly INR 25,000 crores of projects in FY25 and targeting INR 10,000–15,000 crores in FY26; this is how the future sales pipeline is refilled.

parts.name: Society redevelopment
parts.what: A newer way of sourcing projects in Mumbai, where the company partners with existing housing societies to rebuild their land; management announced its first such project in Khar with GDV potential of INR 1,700 crores and says talks with several more societies are in progress, describing it as a future growth contributor rather than a large business today.

parts.name: Pulp & Paper
parts.what: A manufacturing business making writing and printing paper, paperboard and tissue, sold in India (including government tenders) and exported; it was the largest revenue line in the earlier calls — INR 857 crores of net sales with 15.6% EBITDA margin in Q1 FY23 and INR 786 crores with 8.3% margin in Q1 FY25 — but it is not discussed at all in the FY26 calls.

parts.name: Textiles
parts.what: Made apparel fabrics and bed linen, selling domestically and exporting bed linen mainly to the US; it was the smallest line (INR 268 crores of sales and just INR 1 crore of EBITDA in Q1 FY23) and by the July 2024 call the company was reporting 'continuing operations' without it, with no mention in the FY26 calls.

overview.what_it_does: Aditya Birla Sun Life AMC (ABSLAMC) is an Indian asset management company — a fund house that manages other people's money for a fee. It runs mutual fund schemes (equity, debt/fixed income, hybrid and passive/index funds) sold to ordinary retail savers, wealthy individuals and institutions, gathered largely through monthly SIP plans and a distributor network reaching 19,000+ pin codes across India, including smaller 'B30' towns. Its earnings scale with the size of the assets it manages: overall average AUM including alternate assets was about Rs. 6.28 lakh crore in the June 2026 quarter (up 42% year-on-year) with closing total AUM crossing Rs. 10 lakh crore, versus Rs. 2.93 lakh crore back in June 2022. It operates almost entirely in India (part of Aditya Birla Capital, listed on BSE/NSE, 30+ years old), with a small offshore arm out of GIFT City aimed at NRI and foreign investors.

parts.name: Mutual fund business
parts.what: The core business — equity, debt and hybrid schemes sold to retail and institutional investors; mutual fund quarterly average AUM was about Rs. 4.28 lakh crore in Q1 FY27, and this is what management spends most of each call discussing.

parts.name: Equity mutual funds
parts.what: The higher-value slice of the mutual fund book (flagship schemes like Flexi Cap, Balanced Advantage, Multi Asset Allocation, Mid Cap, Small Cap, Multi-Cap, GenNext); equity QAAUM was roughly Rs. 1.99 lakh crore, about 46.5% of the mutual fund mix, up from 41% in mid-2022.

parts.name: SIP book
parts.what: Monthly recurring investments that management calls the 'cornerstone' of the franchise because they make customer money sticky — about Rs. 1,085 crore of SIP contribution in June 2026 from 40 lakh SIP accounts, up from Rs. 898 crore a month in June 2022, though it dipped slightly in the latest quarter.

parts.name: Alternate business (PMS and AIF)
parts.what: Portfolio Management Services and Alternative Investment Funds for wealthy and institutional clients, plus credit offerings — a key growth focus, with assets tripling from Rs. 11,300 crore in Q4 FY25 to Rs. 32,570 crore in Q4 FY26, helped by the ESIC mandate.

parts.name: Passive business
parts.what: Index-linked and ETF-type products that track markets rather than pick stocks; described as growing progressively through new launches and scaling existing products, but treated as a smaller supporting line.

parts.name: Offshore / GIFT City business
parts.what: Funds set up in GIFT City to bring NRI and foreign money into India and give Indian investors global exposure (Global Emerging Market Fund, India ESG Engagement Fund, Global Blue-Chip Fund, Flexi Cap for inward remittance); still small — the Global Emerging Market Fund was around Rs. 400 crore when first mentioned.

parts.name: Institutional / retirement mandates
parts.what: Large government-linked money-management mandates won recently — ESIC, and then EPFO at roughly Rs. 6.08 lakh crore, which alone pushed closing total AUM past Rs. 10 lakh crore in the June 2026 quarter.

parts.name: Distribution and digital platform
parts.what: Not a revenue line but the engine management repeatedly flags — distributors, banking-channel recommendation lists, virtual relationship managers, and investor/partner apps, a GenAI chatbot and WhatsApp servicing that support 1.11 crore investor folios.

overview.what_it_does: ACC Ltd. makes and sells cement in India — it digs limestone, burns it into clinker at kiln plants, then grinds that clinker (often blended with fly ash) into bagged and bulk cement sold under the ACC and Adani Cement brands. It sells through two channels the management always splits out: "trade" (a dealer/retail network serving home-builders, about 74% of volumes by Q4 FY26) and "non-trade" (bulk supply to infrastructure and institutional projects), with demand driven by housing, infrastructure spending and rural construction. Money is made on the spread between the price realised per tonne or per bag and the cost per tonne of fuel, power, raw material and freight — so nearly every call is about price realisation, premium-product mix and cutting cost per tonne (targeting roughly INR3,650–4,000/tonne against INR4,400 achieved in FY26). It operates only in India, plant-by-plant across regions (Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, West Bengal, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Maharashtra, Gujarat and the South), and since 2022 has been part of the Adani Group's cement business alongside parent Ambuja Cements — the calls are held jointly, and ACC is now being merged into Ambuja under a "One Cement Platform".

parts.name: Cement (grey cement — trade and non-trade)
parts.what: The core and essentially the whole business: bagged cement sold to dealers and homebuilders plus bulk cement sold to infrastructure and institutional buyers, with the group's combined capacity at 109 million tonnes and FY26 sales of 73.7 million tonnes, and trade pricing running up to INR31 per bag above non-trade.

parts.name: Premium cement products (ACC Gold, Ambuja Kawach)
parts.what: Higher-priced branded cement grades pushed as a margin lever — management calls them "blockbuster" super-premium products and says they made up 35–36% of trade sales, up 31% year-on-year, among the highest in the industry.

parts.name: Clinker manufacturing and grinding units
parts.what: The upstream half of the operation — large kiln/clinker lines (Bhatapara, Jodhpur, Maratha, Ametha) feeding a wider spread of smaller grinding units near markets under a "hub and spoke" model, which management says cuts lead distance and freight; roughly 7 million tonnes of clinker and 10.7 million tonnes of grinding capacity were added in FY26.

parts.name: Captive and green power (waste heat recovery plus renewables)
parts.what: Power generated for its own plants from waste heat recovery systems (grown from ~40 MW at Adani takeover toward 218 MW) and ~900 MW of solar/renewables, described purely as a cost lever — green power reached 32–37% of the mix, and surplus that cannot yet be consumed on site is being sold into the market meanwhile.

parts.name: Alternative fuels and waste co-processing (Geoclean / AFR)
parts.what: Burning industrial and municipal waste as substitute kiln fuel, presented as both an ESG and a fuel-cost initiative, with the AFR share of the fuel mix rising to 9.5% against a 30% thermal-substitution goal.

parts.name: Ready-mix concrete (RMC)
parts.what: A smaller downstream line supplying ready-mixed concrete, including a green variant called ECOMaxX; the calls note it is growing but give no revenue or volume figures, so it is clearly secondary to cement.

parts.name: Captive limestone and coal mining
parts.what: Securing its own raw material and fuel — 70 million tonnes of new limestone reserves added in one quarter and active bidding for government coal-mine auctions — done to lower input costs rather than sold as a business in its own right.

overview.what_it_does: Action Construction Equipment (ACE) is an Indian manufacturer that builds and sells heavy machinery — cranes, construction equipment, material-handling equipment like forklifts, and farm tractors and implements — from its plants at Dudhola, Palwal in Haryana. It makes money by selling these machines in volume (2,863 units in one quarter of FY25, for example), mostly to Indian buyers in infrastructure, construction, manufacturing, logistics and farming, with government infrastructure spending on roads and railways cited as the main demand driver. Revenue is overwhelmingly domestic: in the June 2026 quarter exports were about 3% of sales (Middle East, notably Saudi Arabia, plus African markets) and defence supplies to the Indian armed forces about 5%. Quarterly standalone revenue has grown from roughly INR 501 crore (Jun 2022) to INR 836 crore (Jun 2026), with EBITDA margins rising from about 9% to about 20%, and the business is seasonal — 40-45% of the year's revenue in the first half, 55-60% in the second.

parts.name: Cranes
parts.what: The core and largest business, making pick-and-carry cranes and tower cranes where management claims market leadership; it is being extended into heavier truck, crawler and rough-terrain cranes through a joint venture with Japan's KATO Works starting end-July 2026.

parts.name: Construction Equipment
parts.what: Backhoe loaders and similar site machinery — a smaller line (about INR 52 crore in the Jun 2022 quarter at roughly 4.5% margins) that management has since grouped with cranes and material handling and targeted for 15%+ annual growth.

parts.name: Material Handling (later called 'Metal Handling')
parts.what: Forklifts and related lifting/handling equipment for factories and logistics (about INR 38 crore in the Jun 2022 quarter at ~11% margins), and the line behind the custom-built forklift orders for the Indian armed forces.

parts.name: Agri Equipment
parts.what: Tractors and farm implements, the smallest and lowest-margin division — roughly 8% of revenue (INR 61 crore in Q2 FY25, INR 42.67 crore in Q1 FY27) with margins in the low single digits, and demand tied to the monsoon and crop cycle.

parts.name: Defence business
parts.what: Sales of backhoe loaders, 4x4 multipurpose tractors, forklifts and rough-terrain forklifts to India's Ministry of Defence; around 5% of revenue in the June 2026 quarter, in line with the stated goal of 5-10% of overall revenue, and boosted by a single order of over INR 400 crore.

parts.name: Exports and overseas projects
parts.what: About 3% of revenue in the June 2026 quarter (Middle East and Africa), and including a roughly INR 200 crore (US$24.98 million) contract to design and set up a tractor, backhoe and farm-implement assembly plant for the Government of Ghana, funded by an India Exim Bank credit line and intended to open West African markets.

overview.what_it_does: Archean Chemical Industries (ACI) is an Indian manufacturer of "marine chemicals" — it pumps natural brine from its own reserves in the Great Rann of Kutch, Gujarat, and separates it at its Hajipir plant into three saleable products: elemental bromine, A-grade industrial salt and sulphate of potash (a specialty fertilizer). It sells these in bulk to industrial buyers — chemical, pharma, agrochemical, flame-retardant, water-treatment and oil & gas companies, plus large trading houses such as Japan's Sojitz — with the bulk of volumes historically exported to China, Japan, South Korea, the Middle East and Europe, shipped out through the nearby Jakhau Jetty and Mundra Port (77% of Q3 FY23 revenue was exports; the company cited 52 customers at that time). Money is made on tonnage: roughly 4.2 million tons of industrial salt and about 3,700 tons of bromine per quarter in FY26, at prices that swing with global demand, so profits move with commodity pricing, monsoon/logistics disruptions and freight and fuel costs. More recently it has been moving downstream into bromine-based derivative chemicals and oilfield drilling chemicals, and has made outside bets on silicon-carbide semiconductors and zinc-bromide batteries.

parts.name: Elemental bromine
parts.what: Bromine extracted from the company's brine and sold to pharma, agrochemical, flame-retardant, water-treatment and oil & gas users — management calls it the leadership position in India's merchant bromine sales and India's largest bromine exporter; capacity was raised from 10,000 to 28,500 tons a year with expansion toward 42,000 tons, and it ran at about half of revenue in FY23 but roughly 24%–32% of standalone sales by FY26 as salt grew faster.

parts.name: Industrial salt
parts.what: A-grade salt that comes out of the same brine process, sold almost entirely overseas to makers of caustic soda and soda ash (feeding chlorine and PVC chains), with Sojitz Corporation a major customer; it is now the biggest revenue line at roughly 67%–70% of standalone sales, running above 1 million tons a quarter and 4.2 million tons in FY26, though prices have been under pressure (down ~10% year-on-year in Q4 FY26).

parts.name: Sulphate of Potash (SOP)
parts.what: A specialty fertilizer for chloride-sensitive crops that ACI says it is one of very few producers to make from natural sea brine (a low-cost, chemical-free route, REACH-certified for Europe); it has been dogged by feedstock and technical problems for years and remains tiny — 644 tons and about ₹3.5 crores of revenue in FY26 — with management still expecting meaningful volumes only from the second half of FY27.

parts.name: Bromine derivatives (Acume Chemicals Private Limited)
parts.what: A wholly owned downstream subsidiary at Jhagadia, Gujarat (about ₹250 crores of capex) that turns the company's own bromine into higher-value products — flame retardants, clear brine fluids, bromine catalysts, PTA-synthesis chemicals, calcium bromide, NPBR, PBR-3 and zinc bromide; it is scaling fast (revenue up nearly 300% in FY26) but still runs at only about 45% capacity utilisation across roughly 40 reactors, so margins are thin.

parts.name: Idealis Mudchemie (formerly Oren Hydrocarbons)
parts.what: An acquired business, taken over through an NCLT order in July 2024, that makes specialty drilling-mud chemicals and clear brine fluids for oil and gas drilling customers; three plants have been commissioned over the past year and it is still in customer trials, with the Gujarat plant awaiting state approvals.

parts.name: Semiconductors (SiCSem Private Limited and the Clas-SIC Wafer Fab stake)
parts.what: A diversification into silicon-carbide chips: ACI is putting GBP 15 million into a 21.33% stake in UK wafer foundry Clas-SIC Wafer Fab to secure technology exclusivity in India, and its subsidiary SiCSem is building a project in Odisha that broke ground in November 2025 and signed a fiscal support agreement with the Government of India in May 2026 — pre-revenue, with commercialisation described as a 2-3 year road map.

parts.name: Energy storage (Offgrid Energy Labs)
parts.what: A roughly USD 12 million investment for a 21% stake in a US-registered developer of zinc-bromide "ZincGel" batteries, pitched as a natural outlet for the company's own bromine, starting with a pilot plant in the UK and an intended gigafactory in India — also pre-revenue, on a stated 2-year path to commercialisation.

overview.what_it_does: ACME Solar Holdings is an Indian renewable-power producer that builds and then owns electricity-generating plants — mainly solar, plus some wind and, more recently, large battery storage — and sells the power they produce. It is "fully integrated," meaning it designs, engineers and constructs its own plants in-house (it does no third-party EPC work) and then runs them for the 25-year life of the contract. Most of its money comes from selling electricity at a fixed, pre-agreed tariff under long-term 25-year power purchase agreements, overwhelmingly with central government off-takers such as SECI, NHPC and REMC/Indian Railways (about 86% central off-takers), which makes revenue highly predictable; a newer slice comes from batteries sold on merchant and short-term terms. It operates entirely in India, with the bulk of its generating capacity in high-sunlight states, Rajasthan alone accounting for 2,250 MW of the operating fleet. Scale as of FY26: revenue of about INR 2,507 crore with ~90% EBITDA margin and PAT of INR 498 crore, roughly 2,990 MW of operating generation capacity and a total portfolio of 8,071 MW.

parts.name: Solar (utility-scale)
parts.what: Large ground-mounted solar farms selling power under 25-year PPAs — historically 100% of the portfolio and still the core of it, including one of India's largest plants at 1,800 MWp.

parts.name: Wind
parts.what: A small and newer addition, with the first 50 MW wind project commissioned in Q1 FY26 and 72 MW more in Q3 FY26 — used mostly as a component inside hybrid/FDRE projects rather than as a standalone business.

parts.name: FDRE / Hybrid / Round-the-Clock (RTC)
parts.what: Contracts that promise firm, dispatchable power around the clock by combining solar, wind and batteries — the main area of new order wins (e.g., 250 MW FDRE with NHPC at Rs 4.33/unit, 130 MW RTC for Indian Railways at Rs 4.35/unit), and management says the company captured a large share of this segment.

parts.name: Battery Energy Storage (BESS)
parts.what: Batteries that buy cheap off-peak power and sell it at peak, both bundled inside FDRE projects and as standalone contracts (first was 550 MWh with NHPC); about 2.3 GWh was commissioned by May 2026 earning roughly INR 2.2 crore a day on merchant/short-term sales, with a total portfolio requirement of around 17 GWh — the fastest-growing part of the business.

parts.name: In-house EPC and O&M (the "integrated" model)
parts.what: Not a separate revenue business — the company does its own design, engineering, construction and 25-year operation solely for its own plants, which management says lets it control cost, timing and technology and stay competitive on tariffs.

parts.name: Land, grid connectivity and financing
parts.what: A supporting activity management stresses heavily: securing grid connectivity and land in the best solar/wind zones (Rajasthan, Gujarat) before bidding, then borrowing long-term against the completed assets and refinancing to cut interest cost — the operational fleet's average debt cost fell to about 8.4%.

overview.what_it_does: Adani Energy Solutions (formerly Adani Transmission) is an Indian electric utility that builds and operates the wires that carry electricity, plus the meters and supply arrangements around them. It runs India's largest private-sector power transmission network — about 28,000 circuit kilometres of high-voltage lines won mostly through competitive government bidding — and gets paid a fixed tariff for keeping those lines available (99.7% availability, which also earns bonus incentive income), plus it sells electricity directly to households and businesses as the licensed distribution utility for Mumbai and Mundra under regulator-set tariffs. It also installs and operates smart electricity meters for state distribution companies under long-term contracts, and from FY27 runs a fourth 'energy solutions' business supplying mainly green power to large commercial and industrial customers. It operates entirely in India, spends very heavily on building assets (about Rs 22,000 crore of capex planned for FY27), and earns returns on that invested capital over long contract or regulatory periods.

parts.name: Transmission
parts.what: Builds and operates high-voltage lines and substations won through competitive bidding, earning availability-linked tariffs; it is the biggest business — about 28,000 circuit km, roughly 29% share of projects put out to bidding, a capex pipeline that grew from Rs 17,000 crore to Rs 55,000 crore, and about Rs 15,500 crore of the Rs 22,000 crore FY27 capex, including the Rs 25,000 crore Bhadla-Fatehpur HVDC project and the completed Mumbai HVDC.

parts.name: Distribution (AEML - Mumbai and Mundra)
parts.what: Sells and delivers electricity to end customers as the licensed utility in Mumbai (since 2018) and Mundra (since 2020) under regulator-set tariffs on a regulated asset base that has grown from about Rs 5,400 crore to over Rs 10,500 crore, with distribution losses cut from 8.5% to 4.2% and supply reliability above 99.9%; a steady, cash-generating business with about Rs 2,350 crore of FY27 capex.

parts.name: Smart metering
parts.what: Installs and runs smart electricity meters for other distribution companies under long-term contracts — 13.4 million installed against an order book of 24.6 million, rising to about 47 million with the IntelliSmart acquisition — and management sees it as a perpetual business rather than one that ends with the concession; about Rs 3,900 crore of FY27 capex.

parts.name: Energy Solutions / C&I
parts.what: The newest vertical, scaled up from FY27, which ties up long-term power supply (about 5,000 MW, mostly green) and sells it to commercial and industrial customers such as data centres, plus a lower-margin services arm that manages energy assets other companies have built; still small (around 350 MW of C&I customers contracted) but flagged as a major growth driver.

overview.what_it_does: Adani Enterprises (AEL) is an Indian holding-and-incubator company: it builds large infrastructure and resource businesses from scratch, scales them up, and then spins them off as separate listed companies — management says this playbook already produced Adani Ports, Adani Transmission, Adani Green Energy, Adani Total Gas and Adani Wilmar, and is described as 'build, stabilize, scale and unlock'. Its money today comes from two kinds of activity: older 'established' businesses that sell services and commodities — running coal and iron-ore mines under contract for their owners, and importing/trading coal and other natural resources for Indian industrial, retail and public-sector customers — and newer 'incubating' infrastructure it owns and operates, mainly airports, toll/annuity roads, solar-and-wind equipment manufacturing, a copper smelter and data centres. Almost all operations are in India (Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Maharashtra, Gujarat/Mundra, plus 8 airports), with one coal mine in Australia (Carmichael). For FY26 the whole company reported total income of about INR 1,02,943 crores and EBITDA of about INR 16,464 crores, with roughly 80% of EBITDA now coming from core infrastructure and services.

parts.name: Airports (Adani Airport Holdings)
parts.what: Operates 8 Indian airports — including Mumbai and the new greenfield Navi Mumbai airport opened in December 2025 — earning regulated 'aero' charges plus retail, cargo, ground-handling and advertising income; it is now the single biggest earner, with FY26 income of INR 13,081 crores, EBITDA of INR 5,394 crores, 95.3 million passengers, and about 23% of India's passenger traffic and 29% of its air cargo.

parts.name: Adani New Industries Ltd (ANIL) / green hydrogen ecosystem
parts.what: Makes and sells solar modules (plus its own ingots, wafers and cells) and wind turbines, and is building toward green hydrogen and downstream products like ammonia and methanol; module sales run over 1 GW a quarter, Adani Solar is called a top-10 global solar manufacturer with 15+ GW cumulative shipments, and the announced ambition was USD 50 billion of investment over a decade with TotalEnergies taking a 25% stake.

parts.name: Mining services (MDO — Mine Developer and Operator)
parts.what: Develops and runs coal and iron-ore mines on contract for their owners — handling approvals, land, infrastructure, mining, washing and transport to the customer's plant — with 18 contracts covering 145 million tonnes of peak annual capacity, of which only 7 are operating (about 50 MMT), producing FY26 revenue of INR 4,536 crores and EBITDA of INR 1,986 crores.

parts.name: Integrated Resource Management (IRM)
parts.what: Buys and sells coal and other natural resources to a mix of retail and public-sector Indian customers, including through an online trading portal; management calls it India's number one player, with FY26 volume of 44.6 million tonnes, revenue of INR 29,112 crores and EBITDA of INR 2,767 crores.

parts.name: Commercial mining
parts.what: Mines coal it owns itself, principally the Carmichael mine in Australia (11.2 million tonnes in FY24), plus domestic coal and bauxite blocks still in the project stage; FY26 earnings here fell on heavy Australian rain and a non-cash currency mark-to-market of roughly INR 600 crores.

parts.name: Roads (Adani Road Transport)
parts.what: Builds and operates highway and expressway concessions under BOT/HAM contracts, now 9 operational projects plus the completed 1,000-plus-crore-scale Ganga Expressway — an asset of roughly INR 18,000 crores on a 27-year concession where AEL takes traffic risk.

parts.name: Metals / primary industries (Kutch Copper, PVC)
parts.what: A new 0.5 million tonne greenfield copper refinery at Mundra that shipped its first output in March 2024, alongside a planned PVC project — both still early and yet to contribute much profit.

parts.name: Data centres (AdaniConneX)
parts.what: Builds and runs full-service data centres, an incubating business with an INR 5,000 crore capex plan flagged for FY25 and a new 358 MW hyperscale order signed in Q4 FY26 with about a 40-month build timeline.

parts.name: Aerospace, Technology & Defence
parts.what: A newly forming business with announced tie-ups on regional civilian transport aircraft (Embraer) and helicopters (Leonardo); management declined to give revenue or investment figures and said it will only report it as a proper segment from the second half of FY27.

parts.name: Adani Capability Center (GCC)
parts.what: An in-house global capability centre set up within AEL for shared corporate/technology work, including artificial intelligence and a shift to an 'agentic workforce' model; no financial figures were given.

overview.what_it_does: Adani Green Energy Limited (AGEL) builds and runs large-scale renewable power plants in India — solar farms, wind farms and combined solar-wind 'hybrid' plants — and sells the electricity they generate. Most of that power goes out under long-term power purchase agreements to government-backed buyers such as state distribution companies (management said about 87% of its portfolio was 'sovereign' in FY24), with the rest sold to commercial and industrial customers or on the open 'merchant' market when a plant is running ahead of its contracted start date. Essentially all revenue is 'revenue from power supply' — INR 11,602 crores for FY26, up 22% year on year — and because a built plant costs little to run, EBITDA margins are extremely high, around 91%-94%. The company has grown operating capacity from 8.3 GW in mid-2023 to over 20 GW by mid-2026, is targeting 50 GW by 2030, and is now adding battery and pumped-hydro storage so it can supply power at night and when the grid needs it.

parts.name: Solar
parts.what: Ground-mounted solar plants that generate power during daylight hours; it is the largest technology in the portfolio, with capacity utilisation around 28% overall (higher, ~32%, at the Khavda site) and a build cost management quotes at about INR 4.5 crores per MW.

parts.name: Wind
parts.what: Wind farms that generate at higher utilisation than solar (38.7% CUF in Q1 FY24) and, importantly, produce more in the evening — management notes wind fetched far better merchant prices (Rs 5.70/unit) than solar (Rs 2.20/unit) in Q1 FY26; wind costs more to build, roughly INR 6.5 crores per MW.

parts.name: Hybrid (solar-wind)
parts.what: Plants combining solar and wind on one site and one grid connection, which lifts utilisation sharply (47.2% CUF in Q1 FY24) and gives steadier output through the day; hybrid made up the bulk of the 2.5 GW added in the year to June 2023.

parts.name: Khavda, Gujarat mega-site
parts.what: A single 30 GW renewable complex described by management as the world's largest renewable energy installation and the engine of growth — 5.6 GW operational by June 2025 and over 10 GW by mid-2026 — prized for its exceptional sunlight and wind, though limited transmission lines out of the site have caused curtailment costing roughly 5%-7% of EBITDA.

parts.name: Battery Energy Storage (BESS)
parts.what: A newer business, big enough to have its own CEO (Rajat Seksaria), that stores surplus daytime generation in batteries at Khavda and releases it in the evening — 3.5 GWh installed by June 2026 against a 10+ GWh target for the year — with returns management says are similar to or slightly better than solar and wind, and which also acts as a hedge against grid curtailment.

parts.name: Pumped hydro storage
parts.what: A second, longer-duration storage technology still at an early stage, with the first 500 MW project at Chitravathi in Andhra Pradesh due to be commissioned in FY27.

parts.name: Offtake mix: sovereign PPAs, C&I and merchant
parts.what: How the power is sold — long-term contracts with state distribution companies form the bulk and are the low-risk core, while capacity previously labelled 'merchant' (sold at volatile spot prices) has been re-contracted on an arm's-length basis to group company Adani Energy Solutions, about 4 GW, and now shows up as commercial and industrial (C&I) business; only plants running ahead of their PPA start date are still sold at market prices.

parts.name: 25% stake in Mundra Solar Energy (associate)
parts.what: A minority holding in a 2 GW solar module manufacturing unit set up under a manufacturing-linked PPA; it contributes only associate income — about INR 111 crores in Q1 FY26 — and is a small side item, not part of the core power business.

overview.what_it_does: Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Limited (APSEZ) runs commercial seaports and the transport services around them. Its customers are shipping lines, exporters and importers whose cargo — containers, coal, fertiliser, agricultural goods, LPG and other bulk items — is loaded and unloaded at its terminals; it earns money mainly by charging per tonne of cargo handled, so revenue tracks both volume and the mix of cargo and customers (management tracks a 'port revenue per ton' figure). Its main base is India, where it operates a network of ports along the west coast (Mundra, Hazira), east coast (Dhamra, Gangavaram, Krishnapatnam), and south (Vizhinjam, Ennore, Kattupalli); it has also expanded overseas with terminals and marine operations in Israel (Haifa), Sri Lanka (Colombo), Tanzania, Australia (NQXT) and elsewhere. Alongside the ports it runs an inland logistics business (trains, warehouses, trucking, freight forwarding), a marine services fleet of tugs and vessels, and a special economic zone / land-and-port-services operation. In FY26 it handled 500 million metric tons of cargo in total (451 million in domestic ports, about a 27% share of the Indian market), with revenue growing 25% and net debt at 1.9x EBITDA.

parts.name: Ports business (domestic)
parts.what: The core operation — Indian seaport terminals that load and unload ships, by far the biggest part: in Q3 FY23 it was about Rs.3,936 crore of Rs.4,786 crore total revenue and Rs.2,737 crore of Rs.3,011 crore total EBITDA, running at roughly 70-72% EBITDA margins and 23% return on capital employed in FY26.

parts.name: International ports
parts.what: Overseas terminals and concessions — Haifa in Israel, the CWIT terminal in Colombo, Tanzania, and the NQXT terminal in Australia — a smaller but fast-growing piece, with revenue up 34% and EBITDA up 180% in FY26 as Colombo ramped up.

parts.name: Logistics
parts.what: Moves cargo inland and around the ports via rail rakes, inland container depots, warehousing, agri silos, trucking and freight forwarding — described as the 'second business pillar', around Rs.490 crore of quarterly revenue in Q3 FY23, growing 55% in FY26, with lower margins than ports (roughly 29% EBITDA margin) and return on capital employed rising from 6% to 10%.

parts.name: Marine services
parts.what: The 'third business pillar' — a fleet of tugs and support vessels (136 vessels at its FY26 peak, including deployments in Mexico and Sri Lanka) that assist ships in and out of berths; small but growing very fast, with revenue up 134% and EBITDA up 125% in FY26.

parts.name: SEZ and O&M
parts.what: Leases land in its special economic zone and operates port facilities for third parties under management contracts (for example an O&M contract for a container facility at Kolkata's Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port) — the smallest piece, about Rs.360 crore of revenue and Rs.132 crore of EBITDA in Q3 FY23.

overview.what_it_does: Adani Power Limited is an Indian electricity generator that runs a fleet of large coal-fired (thermal) power plants — sites named on the calls include Mundra, Udupi, Raipur, Raigarh, Mahan, Godda, Korba, Dahanu, Tuticorin, Butibori/Vidarbha and Churk — totalling about 18.15 GW of installed capacity as of December 2025. It sells that power mainly to state electricity distribution companies (DISCOMs) such as Maharashtra's, plus a cross-border customer in Bangladesh supplied from the Godda plant, under long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs), and sells whatever capacity is not contracted into the merchant and short-term markets at prevailing market prices. Under the PPAs it earns fixed capacity charges simply for keeping plants available (management notes fuel cost is largely a pass-through), while merchant sales earn whatever the market clears at — Q1 FY27 realisation was INR 5.93/unit under PPAs versus INR 7.04/unit merchant. Revenue for the first quarter of FY27 was INR 17,936 crore with profit after tax of INR 4,867 crore, and the company is building toward a 45 GW portfolio, largely across central and eastern Indian states.

parts.name: Power sales under long-term PPAs (contracted capacity)
parts.what: Electricity sold to state DISCOMs and the Bangladesh offtaker under multi-year contracts that pay fixed capacity charges for availability with fuel costs passed through; management says over 90% of the 18.15 GW operating fleet is now tied up this way, and PPA volumes were 25 of 29 billion units sold in Q1 FY27 — this is the core, most stable earnings stream.

parts.name: Merchant and short-term / bilateral sales
parts.what: Untied capacity sold into the day-ahead, short-term and bilateral markets at market prices, which boosts profit when demand and tariffs are high but swings with weather and renewable output; it has shrunk from 6 billion units in Q1 FY26 to 4 billion in Q1 FY27 as more capacity moved into PPAs.

parts.name: Capacity expansion programme (greenfield and brownfield projects)
parts.what: A roughly 24 GW pipeline of new coal units — Mahan Phase-II, Raipur Phase-II, Raigarh Phase-II, Korba Phase-II, Mirzapur, a 3,200 MW Assam project won on a DBFOO basis — with all boiler-turbine-generator equipment already ordered and 56% of the new capacity pre-sold under long-term PPAs; management says these new PPAs carry higher capacity charges than legacy ones and are the main driver of future earnings growth.

parts.name: Acquisitions of distressed / operating power assets
parts.what: Buying existing plants cheaply, often out of insolvency, and turning them around — Mahan, Coastal Energen (renamed Moxie/Tuticorin), Korba (ex-Lanco Amarkantak), Dahanu, the Vidarbha/Butibori plant restarted from a multi-year shutdown, and in 2026 Jaiprakash Associates' assets including the 180 MW Churk plant plus minority stakes in Jaiprakash Power Ventures and Prayagraj Power; this has been a steady source of added capacity and volume growth.

parts.name: Fuel security / captive coal mining
parts.what: Securing coal near its plants, including acquiring Stratatech Mineral Resources (the Dhirauli mine next to the Mahan plant) which is expected to supply 5 million tonnes of coal for Mahan's untied capacity — a supporting activity rather than a revenue line, aimed at protecting cost advantage.

parts.name: One-time / prior-period regulatory income
parts.what: Past regulatory claims for things like domestic coal shortfall, carrying cost and late payment surcharge that get recognised in lumps — INR 2,781 crore in Q2 FY24 and INR 9,227 crore in 9M FY24, now shrinking to INR 1,353 crore in 9M FY26 as the old disputes are settled; meaningful to reported profit but explicitly not part of recurring earnings.

parts.name: New areas: international hydropower and nuclear
parts.what: Early-stage diversification the CEO flagged in July 2026 — hydropower projects abroad and preparing for nuclear opportunities — with no capacity, revenue or timeline given on the calls.

overview.what_it_does: Advanced Enzyme Technologies makes and sells enzymes — biological ingredients that speed up chemical reactions — plus related products like probiotics, and it sells them mostly to other businesses rather than to consumers. Its customers are pharmaceutical, nutraceutical/supplement, food-processing, animal-feed and industrial companies, who buy the enzymes as inputs into their own products; the calls describe demand coming from global pharma, nutraceutical and biotech sectors shifting toward wider enzyme use, and management pitches the company as offering integrated end-to-end capabilities and customized solutions. It earns money by manufacturing and selling these enzyme formulations at high margins (EBITDA margin roughly 26%–33% and PAT margin roughly 15%–25% across the period), with revenue of INR 7,458 million in FY26, up 17%, and a small direct-to-consumer (B2C) piece worth under USD 1 million a quarter. It operates from India — head office in Thane, Maharashtra and a factory at Nashik, with a new Nashik R&D centre coming up — and sells both domestically and internationally, with the Americas/USA its key export market; subsidiaries include evoxx, JC Biotech and SciTech, and it files product dossiers with the US FDA and Europe's EFSA.

parts.name: Human Nutrition / Human Healthcare
parts.what: Enzymes and related products sold into human pharma, nutraceutical/nutrition, probiotics and biocatalysis uses in India and abroad — consistently the biggest segment at roughly 56%–67% of revenue (INR 1,281 million, 63% of revenue, in Q4 FY26), and management calls it the flagship division.

parts.name: Animal Nutrition / Animal Healthcare
parts.what: Enzyme products for animal feed and animal health, contributing around 11%–14% of revenue (INR 250 million in Q4 FY26), and one of the faster-growing pieces recently with growth driven mainly by Asia.

parts.name: Bio-processing (split into food and non-food)
parts.what: Enzymes used in industrial processing — a food business (the larger, faster-growing half) and a smaller non-food business — together about 13%–16% of revenue.

parts.name: Specialized Manufacturing
parts.what: A smaller contract/specialised production line that has swung around a lot (52% decline in Q1 FY23) but grew 23% in FY26, making up roughly 5%–9% of revenue.

parts.name: Anti-inflammatory enzyme (largest single product)
parts.what: The company's biggest individual product, with quarterly sales of roughly INR 280–350 million — about 18% of total revenue — and approval for it was filed in Europe two years before FY26 and awaited during FY26.

parts.name: B2C segment
parts.what: A small direct-to-consumer business selling around USD 0.95–1.14 million a quarter, i.e. a minor slice of the total.

parts.name: Subsidiaries (JC Biotech, evoxx, SciTech)
parts.what: Separately-reported group companies whose numbers management discloses each quarter — JC Biotech at roughly INR 150–170 million of quarterly revenue, evoxx (loss-making in FY25, profitable again by Q3 FY26) at roughly INR 47–87 million, and SciTech around INR 66–111 million.

overview.what_it_does: Aegis Logistics is an Indian company that owns and operates port-side storage terminals for bulk liquids (chemicals, petroleum products) and gases (mainly LPG, and now ammonia), and also buys and resells LPG in India. It makes money three ways: charging fees to store and move other people's cargo through its tanks and jetties (terminalling/throughput), importing and reselling LPG in bulk and in cylinders to industrial, commercial, household and auto-fuel customers, and trading/sourcing LPG cargoes. Its customers include state oil companies (IOC, HPCL, BPCL), large private conglomerates, industrial users, hotels/restaurants/small industry, and households. It operates only in India, from terminals at Mumbai, JNPT, Kandla, Pipavav, Kochi, Mangalore and Haldia, with FY26 revenue of INR8,333 crores, normalized EBITDA of INR1,599 crores and profit after tax of INR1,107 crores.
