parts.name: Liquid Terminal Division (Liquids)
parts.what: Rents out tank storage at ports for chemicals and petroleum products — including specialized heated storage up to 230°C — earning steady fee income; it is the smaller but far higher-margin half, with FY26 revenue of INR644 crores and EBITDA of INR472 crores (roughly 73% margins), on close to 2 million kilolitres of capacity being built out across the coastline.

parts.name: Gas / LPG Division — Logistics (terminal throughput)
parts.what: Imports and handles LPG through cryogenic and static tanks, jetties, rail gantries, truck bays and pipeline links for oil marketing companies and other customers, charging a throughput fee; volumes hit a record 5.15 million tons in FY26, up 14%.

parts.name: Gas / LPG Division — Distribution
parts.what: Buys LPG and sells it on its own account to bulk industrial users, to hotels/restaurants/small industry under the 'Aegis Pure Gas' brand, to households under the 'Aegis Chhota Sikander' brand, and as auto gas at fuel stations — the fastest-growing piece, with volumes up 45% to 7.54 lakh tons in FY26 (Q4 alone up 71%).

parts.name: Gas / LPG Division — Sourcing
parts.what: Buys and resells LPG cargoes, which drives most of the group's headline revenue but carries thin margins; FY26 sourcing sales were 6.07 lakh metric tons, up 2%, and the LPG segment as a whole booked INR7,689 crores of revenue and INR1,131 crores of EBITDA.

parts.name: Aegis Vopak Terminals Limited (AVTL) — joint venture / listed subsidiary
parts.what: A tie-up with global tank-storage operator Vopak that holds much of the liquid and LPG terminal infrastructure, was IPO'd (proceeds used to pay down debt), acquired 75% of Hindustan Aegis LPG at Haldia to enter the East Coast, and holds the 15-year take-or-pay petroleum contract at Pipavav for over 0.5 million tons a year.

parts.name: Ammonia terminals (new energy)
parts.what: A newly launched line building India's first independent ammonia terminal at Pipavav (36,000 tons, backed by a 15-year take-or-pay deal with Hindustan Zinc), plus an MoU with L&T for a green ammonia terminal at Kandla — small today but positioned as the next growth leg, with management aiming to be vertically integrated in ammonia as it is in LPG.

parts.name: Expansion pipeline / capex program
parts.what: Not a segment but central to the story: roughly USD1.2 billion of cumulative capex by FY27 and a USD5 billion roadmap to 2030, including a non-binding MoU for about INR20,000 crores at the proposed Vadhavan port, funded from about INR6,000 crores of cash and prudent debt.

overview.what_it_does: Aequs is an Indian precision manufacturing company that makes complex, high-precision metal and plastic parts and assemblies to other companies' designs, rather than selling its own branded products. Its customers are global aerospace OEMs and Tier-1 suppliers such as Airbus, Boeing, Collins, Safran, SAAB and Honeywell, plus consumer companies including toy brands (Mattel, and formerly Hasbro), a large consumer electronics brand, and cookware partner Tramontina. It earns money by being paid per part shipped under long-qualification, multi-year programmes, running an unusually vertically integrated chain in-house — forging, machining, molding, stamping, surface treatment and assembly — so it captures more of the value per part; roughly 93–94% of sales are US-dollar-linked exports or deemed exports. Operations run from three integrated manufacturing clusters in Karnataka, India (Belagavi, Hubballi, Koppal, 2.22 million sq ft, much of it inside a special economic zone), plus units in Cholet, France and Paris, Texas, USA, with FY26 revenue of INR 12,304 million (up 33%) but a full-year loss of INR 1,133 million.

parts.name: Aerospace
parts.what: Makes critical aircraft parts for aerostructures, actuation, engines, landing gear and interiors — 5,654 part numbers as of March 2026 — and is the mature, profitable engine of the company at INR 10,464 million of FY26 revenue (roughly 85% of the total), 20% segment ROCE and a USD 889 million order book.

parts.name: Consumer
parts.what: Applies the same precision capabilities to components and products for consumer electronics, toys and cookware; it grew 84% to INR 1,840 million in FY26 (about 15% of revenue) but is still loss-making (EBITDA loss of INR 783 million) because new capacity is running at only 23% utilisation, with management targeting EBITDA break-even by Q4 FY27.

parts.name: Consumer electronics (within Consumer)
parts.what: Newly industrialised stamping, precision machining and injection-molding programmes for a large global electronics brand — the main destination for recent capex, approved for MeitY PLI incentives with the first eligible year being FY27.

parts.name: Toys (within Consumer)
parts.what: Precision molded/assembled toy manufacturing, entered around 2016-17 to target an USD 80 billion global market; Mattel began shipping in Q3 FY26 under a long-term agreement, while Hasbro has told Aequs it will stop placing purchase orders.

parts.name: Cookware (within Consumer)
parts.what: A joint venture with Brazilian multinational Tramontina aimed at the global cookware market.

parts.name: Joint ventures
parts.what: Partnerships that fill in specific process capabilities — Magellan Aerospace (Canada) for surface treatment and Aubert & Duval (France) for forging — which management says deliver strong margins and add about INR 1,162 million of revenue on top of the consolidated figure in FY26.

parts.name: Defence / UAVs
parts.what: A newer venture with Accel India and Vagus Defense to design and manufacture unmanned aerial vehicles, mainly for Indian defence needs; the calls describe it as an early-stage strategic priority rather than a revenue contributor.

parts.name: New capacity build-out
parts.what: Signed MoUs to invest INR 1,900 crore over 10 years in a new vertically integrated aero-engine and landing-gear ecosystem at Hosur, Tamil Nadu (250 acres), and INR 2,856 crore over five years across the existing Belagavi and Hubballi clusters in Karnataka.

overview.what_it_does: Aether Industries makes specialty chemicals — complex, small-volume "advanced intermediates" that other companies use as ingredients — at its plants in Sachin GIDC, Surat, Gujarat, India (Sites 1 to 5, plus a large R&D centre and one of the world's biggest pilot plants). It sells to industrial customers rather than consumers: pharmaceutical and agrochemical companies (about 45-46% of sales in FY26), oil & gas / oilfield services (~22%), materials science (~17-18%), and more recently semiconductor and battery makers, with named clients including Baker Hughes, H.B. Fuller and Otsuka Chemical. It earns money three ways — selling its own catalogue of chemicals, manufacturing products exclusively under contract for a single customer, and doing paid research plus manufacturing for clients — and stresses that many of its products are made in India for the first time, replacing imports, at prices around $30-40 per kilo. Roughly 36-42% of revenue is exported (Europe, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, USA) and the rest sold in India; management is also spending heavily on new plants, R&D labs and captive solar power (16 MW and a further 15 MW) to cut electricity costs.

parts.name: Large Scale Manufacturing
parts.what: Aether's own catalogue of chemical products made in bulk and sold to many customers — historically the biggest driver at about 66% of sales in Q1 FY25, easing to roughly 41-43% by FY26 as the other models grew, with pricing swinging on things like Chinese dumping (FY25) and later a conflict-driven supply shock that pushed prices up over 20% year-on-year in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Contract / Exclusive Manufacturing (CEM)
parts.what: Making specific products exclusively for one customer under a multi-year agreement — the fastest-growing leg, rising from about 18% of sales in Q1 FY25 to roughly 43% in Q3 FY26, anchored by a multi-year deal to make six products for Baker Hughes globally out of Site 4 (Site 4 sales grew from INR 50 crores to INR 220 crores, about 21% of total sales in FY26) plus a contract with Otsuka Chemical worth INR 35-40 crores in FY26.

parts.name: Contract Research and Manufacturing Services (CRAMS)
parts.what: Paid R&D and process development for multinational innovator companies that can later turn into manufacturing orders — the smallest slice at around 8-14% of sales, but management says inquiries keep rising and expects CRAMS and CEM together to reach over 70% of sales in coming years; current focus is on non-pharma, non-agro work in oil & gas and materials science.

parts.name: Sustainability and Renewables segment
parts.what: A newer segment launched in FY25 covering Converge polyols (a polymer ingredient containing up to 40% carbon dioxide by weight, developed with Saudi Aramco Technologies and first sold to H.B. Fuller), technology with Novoloop to turn post-consumer plastic waste back into virgin monomers, and organic electrolyte additives for lithium-ion batteries supplied to a major global battery producer — small today but described as high-margin with strong order visibility for FY27.

parts.name: Electronic / semiconductor chemicals
parts.what: A recent extension out of Site 5 supplying chemicals to the semiconductor industry with customer bases in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan; validation batches have been dispatched and management says the opportunity could triple by 2030, so it is still at an early, pre-revenue-scale stage.

overview.what_it_does: Afcons Infrastructure is a Mumbai-based construction contractor, founded in 1959 and listed in India in 2024, that builds large, technically difficult infrastructure — metros, bridges, tunnels, roads, railways, ports and jetties, dams and water systems, and oil-and-gas facilities. Its customers are mainly governments and government agencies in India (central and state) plus overseas clients, and it wins work by bidding for contracts, so revenue comes from executing a backlog of construction orders over several years rather than from selling a product. Management runs it as a single construction business split into five verticals, tracking an 'unexecuted order book' (about INR 32,600–35,300 crores across FY25–FY26) that converts into revenue (INR 12,322 crores in FY26) at an EBITDA margin they describe as 11–14%, among the better in the industry. It works across India and internationally — Africa (a EUR 100 million+ road in Uganda), the Middle East, and a first entry into Europe via Croatian road and rail tenders — with a stated goal of taking overseas work to about 30% of the order book; earnings swing quarter to quarter with the mix of work executed, client payment delays and project timing, and FY26 included a loss-making fourth quarter.

parts.name: Urban infrastructure
parts.what: Elevated and underground metro rail plus bridges in cities — examples given include the Bangalore double-decker metro and flyover corridor, Agra and Kanpur metros, and two packages of the Delhi–Meerut RRTS; management flags metro bidding as increasingly competitive and aggressive.

parts.name: Surface transport
parts.what: Roads and railways, such as the Nagpur–Mumbai Samruddhi Mahamarg package with India's widest road tunnels, the Udhampur–Srinagar–Baramulla rail link, and new road/rail wins in Uganda and Croatia; it is a core segment for both domestic and overseas order intake.

parts.name: Hydro and underground
parts.what: Tunnels (including NATM and tunnel-boring-machine work), dams and barrages — the calls treat this as the company's technical showcase, citing 13 complex tunnels in the Katra–Laole section and national records of 740 and 777 metres of TBM tunnelling in a month.

parts.name: Marine and industrial
parts.what: Ports, jetties, wharves, LNG tanks and industrial/energy facilities such as the commissioned HRRL crude oil terminal at Mundra; the calls note two domestic marine contracts worth about INR 1,400 crores in one quarter and an Engineering News-Record ranking of 8th globally among international marine and port contractors.

parts.name: Oil and gas
parts.what: The fifth vertical listed by management, covering oil-and-gas related construction, described alongside industrial and energy infrastructure but given the least detail in these calls.

parts.name: Water (newer addition)
parts.what: Water supply and distribution work entered in FY25, including a 3.35 km water tunnel in Raigad and the CIDCO water supply project (first 5.5 km TBM drive completed a month early), plus Jal Jeevan Mission projects in Uttar Pradesh that management says it remains cautious about.

parts.name: Order book / order inflow
parts.what: Not a product line but how management frames the business: a pending order book of roughly INR 32,600–35,300 crores, FY26 new orders of INR 4,125 crores (plus about INR 3,800 crores of variations), an addressable pipeline of about INR 3.8 trillion, and FY27 order-booking guidance of INR 30,000 crores.

overview.what_it_does: Affle 3i (formerly Affle (India) Limited) is a digital advertising technology company that runs what management calls an AI-powered "Consumer Platform Stack" — software that places ads inside mobile apps and on devices (as opposed to browser/cookie-based web ads) and uses its own data, algorithms and patented targeting to turn those ad impressions into actual users who install, sign up or buy. Its customers are advertisers and brands across verticals such as gaming, fintech, quick commerce, edtech, hospitality and travel, OTT, FMCG and D2C retail, with about 75% of revenue coming from direct customers. It is paid almost entirely on an ROI-linked "CPCU" (cost per converted user) basis — the advertiser pays a fixed rate per consumer conversion delivered, so revenue is essentially conversions multiplied by the CPCU rate (Q4 FY2026: 120.3 million conversions at INR 60.0 each), and its main cost is buying ad inventory and data, at roughly 61-63% of revenue. It is anchored in India and other global emerging markets (~72-74% of revenue) with the rest from developed markets like the US, and delivered FY2026 revenue of INR 27.1 billion, EBITDA of INR 6.1 billion and PAT of INR 4.55 billion.

parts.name: CPCU business (Cost Per Converted User)
parts.what: The core, ROI-linked model where advertisers pay per consumer conversion delivered rather than per impression — it is effectively the whole company, with CPCU revenue of INR 7.21 billion out of INR 7.24 billion total revenue in Q4 FY2026, growing at ~20% y-o-y.

parts.name: Non-CPCU business
parts.what: A small remainder that management describes as an entry point for certain customers and partners doing "top-of-the-funnel" tech enablement on the platform, intended to pull them into the deeper-funnel CPCU model later.

parts.name: India & Global Emerging Markets
parts.what: The company's anchor geography — India, Indonesia, Africa, LATAM and similar markets where digital's share of total ad spend is still low — contributing 71.6%-73.9% of revenue in recent quarters and growing around 20% y-o-y.

parts.name: Developed Markets
parts.what: The US and other developed-market entities, contributing roughly 26-28% of revenue and growing 17-37% y-o-y in the quarters discussed, with a dedicated North America CEO hired in FY2026 to accelerate it.

parts.name: Consumer Platform Stack (incl. Newton, Niko, OpticksAI)
parts.what: The unified technology layer behind the revenue — Newton is the campaign platform, Niko is an agentic AI engine that automates bidding, targeting and budget decisions in a self-service mode, and OpticksAI adds creative optimization; the stack is backed by an IP portfolio of 18 granted and 21 pending patents covering fraud detection, precision targeting and AI-native ads.

parts.name: Inorganic growth / acquisitions
parts.what: An ongoing strategy of buying and integrating ad-tech businesses (e.g. Jampp, consolidated into a single cash-generating unit by FY2025), with the Board approving an ~INR 11 billion warrant issue to promoter Affle Holdings in FY2026 to fund further deals.

overview.what_it_does: Dr. Agarwal's Health Care runs a chain of eye-care hospitals and clinics — it treats eye problems, with cataract surgery as by far the biggest procedure, alongside refractive (SMILE/LASIK-type), retinal and corneal work, plus routine eye check-ups and consultations. Its customers are ordinary walk-in patients: management says nearly 10,000 people a day enter its facilities, and roughly 62% pay out of their own pocket, 27% via insurance/TPA and about 12% through government schemes. It earns money mainly by charging for surgeries (over 65% of revenue), plus consultations and diagnostics, and by selling spectacles/optical products and pharmacy items at its centres. It operates a 'hub-and-spoke', asset-light network — 269 facilities as of March 2026 across 14 Indian states and 5 union territories in 155 cities, plus 19 facilities in Africa — with the South of India its largest market at 61% of revenue; FY26 revenue crossed INR 2,080 crores with EBITDA of INR 614 crores and profit after tax of INR 168 crores.

parts.name: Surgical services
parts.what: Eye operations — cataract (about 75% of surgery volumes), refractive (~5%), retinal and corneal transplants — and this is the main pillar of the business at over 65% of group revenue, with 3.23 lakh surgeries done in FY26.

parts.name: Diagnosis, consultations and non-surgical treatments
parts.what: Eye examinations, doctor consultations and treatments that don't involve surgery, contributing about 14% of total revenue and acting as the feeder that converts walk-ins into surgeries.

parts.name: Sale of optical products and pharmacy
parts.what: Selling spectacles, lenses and eye-related medicines to patients at its centres, worth about 21% of total revenue.

parts.name: Tertiary hospitals (hubs)
parts.what: The largest, most fully-equipped hospitals that handle complex and high-end procedures such as robotic 'Femto' cataract surgery — 28 of these as of December 2024, and the anchor of each regional cluster.

parts.name: Secondary centres / day-care surgical centres (spokes)
parts.what: Mid-sized centres where routine day-care eye surgeries are performed close to where patients live — 132 as of December 2024 and the bulk of the network's new greenfield openings.

parts.name: Primary centres / eye clinics (spokes)
parts.what: The smallest format — clinics for check-ups, consultations and optical sales that feed surgical cases up to the bigger centres — 61 as of December 2024, with more added every quarter.

parts.name: India operations (South, West, North regions)
parts.what: The core of the company at roughly 90% of group revenue, led by the Southern region (61% of revenue, 182 facilities in FY26), then West (16%) and North (8.3%), including a recent entry into Delhi NCR.

parts.name: International / Africa operations
parts.what: A smaller overseas eye-care network of 19 facilities in Africa, making up about 7% of total facilities and roughly a tenth of group revenue, with management's stated focus increasingly on India.

overview.what_it_does: Ahluwalia Contracts (India) Limited is an Indian construction contractor — management describes it as being "only in buildings and factories," not roads or other civil infrastructure. It is hired by clients to build structures: hospitals, railway station redevelopments (CSMT Mumbai), government complexes (Central Vista), commercial and institutional buildings, industrial parks and residential towers for private developers such as DLF, Signature Global, SmartWorld and Emaar. It makes money by winning contracts through competitive bidding (it talks about being "L1," i.e. lowest bidder), building up an order book, and then billing clients as work is executed — FY26 turnover was INR4,565 crores on a closing order book of INR21,096 crores, with EBITDA margins running around 9-10% and PAT margin near 5-6%. Work is spread across India (in FY23 split roughly East 38%, North 34%, West 18%, South 5%, plus about 6% in Nepal), with NCR/Delhi alone around 44% of the order book by FY26, which is why Delhi pollution shutdowns, monsoons, elections and labour shortages repeatedly hit quarterly execution.

parts.name: Government / public-sector projects
parts.what: Building work for government and public bodies — hospitals, railway station redevelopment, airports, Central Vista — which was about 81.5% of the order book in FY23; management says competition here is intense and rates are worse than private work.

parts.name: Private-sector projects
parts.what: Building work for private clients and developers, about 18.5% of the order book in FY23, but the stated focus area from FY25 onward because there are few capable contractors, competition is lower and the rates are "far better than the government projects."

parts.name: Hospitals / healthcare buildings
parts.what: The single largest end-use category in the FY23 order-book split at about 32%, including projects like Tata Memorial Hospital.

parts.name: Residential buildings
parts.what: Apartment and housing construction for developers (DLF, Signature Global, SmartWorld, Emaar), about 13% of the FY23 order book; repeatedly described as "not a focus area," and by FY26 management said it had deliberately slowed down bidding for further residential work, especially in NCR.

parts.name: Commercial buildings
parts.what: Offices and similar commercial structures, roughly 8% of the FY23 order book, and one of the categories management says it is now steering toward.

parts.name: Institutional buildings
parts.what: Education and other institutional structures, plus airports and hotels — not given a separate percentage, but named from FY23 onward as a growth area on the private side and, by FY26, the stated focus alongside commercial work.

parts.name: Large marquee / design-build projects
parts.what: A handful of very big, named jobs that drive revenue in any given year — CSMT (targeted at INR300-350 crores in FY26 and ~INR700 crores the next year), Central Vista (INR2,600 crores, awarded January 2026), and the Gem & Jewellery Park / IJPM (starting Q1 FY27 at an expected 20-25% of project value in that year).

parts.name: Mechanization / equipment capex
parts.what: Not a revenue line but a stated strategic shift: because individual orders are bigger, buildings more complex, timelines squeezed and labour chronically short, the company has been investing heavily in machinery — which has raised depreciation and held back return ratios, with management arguing the margin payoff comes over the next couple of years.

parts.name: Real estate inventory
parts.what: A small legacy holding of INR59.73 crores mentioned once in the FY23 balance-sheet data points; never discussed as an operating business.

overview.what_it_does: AIA Engineering is an Ahmedabad (Gujarat, India) based manufacturer of high-chrome wear parts used inside the huge grinding mills that crush rock and other hard material — mainly 'grinding media' (the hard-metal balls that do the grinding) and 'mill linings' (the replaceable plates that protect the inside of the mill), plus related castings and newer 'discharge system' designs. Its customers are mostly global mining companies (especially copper and gold mines) and, in the non-mining part, cement plants and similar industries, with most output exported from India to markets such as North and South America; management notes the plants are in India but has announced plans for facilities in Ghana and China. It earns money by selling consumables that wear out and must be repeatedly replaced, priced largely on a cost-plus basis so raw material and ocean freight are passed through to the customer — realisation ran about INR165 per kg in FY26 on 258,000 tons of sales, giving roughly INR4,355 crores of revenue and INR1,270 crores of profit. Growth comes from persuading mines to switch from cheaper forged steel balls to AIA's high-chrome solution by showing hard savings — more throughput, better ore recovery, lower power and reagent costs — and the company also earns sizeable non-operating income from a large cash pile (about INR4,300 crores net cash), export incentives and rupee-related foreign exchange gains.

parts.name: Mining
parts.what: Supplies high-chrome grinding media and liners to metal mines (chiefly copper and gold); this is the bigger and strategically central half — roughly 160,000 of 258,000 tons sold in FY26 — and management sizes the addressable gold-and-copper market at 800,000 to 1 million tons.

parts.name: Non-mining
parts.what: The same wear parts sold to cement and other industrial users, around 98,000 tons in FY26 (about 25,000 of the 70,000-ton March-2026 quarter); management describes it as steady but cyclical quarter to quarter, with no structural change.

parts.name: High chrome grinding media
parts.what: The core product — the grinding balls themselves — accounting for the largest share of installed capacity (314,000 tons of the 436,000-ton total after the Bangalore subsidiary Welcast Steels was shut, removing 24,000 tons); an 80,000-ton new grinding media plant was built out over FY23–FY25.

parts.name: Mill lining (metal, and composite/rubber)
parts.what: Replaceable mill liners, expanded via a 50,000-ton metal liner plant commissioned in 2022 and a roughly INR65 crore, 20,000-ton composite and rubber liner line at Kerala GIDC, so AIA can offer a full suite rather than just metal; management calls it the key lever for winning larger combined orders and reported a first big lining 'proof of concept' win at a marquee South American mine in 2026.

parts.name: New generation discharge system
parts.what: The newest piece of the lining solution — redesigned linings at the discharge end of the mill that lifted throughput and cut power for a large South American customer after two years of trials; small in revenue today but presented as the proof that AIA sells engineered solutions, not just castings.

parts.name: Castings / other non-grinding media
parts.what: Other cast wear products making up the remaining 120,000 tons of capacity; a heavier casting mix in the March 2026 quarter was one reason realisation jumped to about INR178 per kg that quarter.

parts.name: Treasury and other income
parts.what: Not a business line as such, but a meaningful earnings contributor — roughly INR474 crores in FY26 from interest on the cash pile (about INR67 crores in Q4), export benefits like RoDTEP and duty drawback, and foreign exchange gains from a weakening rupee.

overview.what_it_does: Ajanta Pharma is an Indian drug maker that manufactures and sells prescription medicines, mostly generic versions of established drugs sold under its own brand names. It earns money four ways: selling branded medicines to doctors and pharmacies in India through a field force of about 3,750 medical representatives; selling branded generics in Asia (Middle East, South-East Asia, Central Asia) and Africa (West and East Africa); selling plain generic pills in the United States under approved ANDA filings to distributors; and supplying anti-malarial drugs to aid agencies in Africa through tenders. Its therapy focus is chronic, doctor-prescribed areas — cardiology, ophthalmology, dermatology and pain, with gynaecology and nephrology being added. In FY2026 the company crossed Rs. 5,453 crores of revenue with net profit above Rs. 1,000 crores, gross margins around 78%, and it spends roughly 5% of revenue on R&D.

parts.name: India branded business
parts.what: Sells its own branded medicines to Indian doctors and chemists through a large sales force; contributed 30% of total revenue in FY2026 (Rs. 1,654 crores, up 14%), with cardiology 36%, ophthalmology 31%, dermatology 23% and pain 10% of India branded sales, and the company ranked 24th in the Indian pharma market.

parts.name: Trade generics (part of India business)
parts.what: A smaller unbranded/generic-counter channel inside India; recorded Rs. 188 crores in FY2026 versus Rs. 179 crores the year before — a modest slice of the India total.

parts.name: Asia branded generics
parts.what: Branded medicines sold in the Middle East, South-East Asia and Central Asia, largely chronic therapies with 15 new launches in FY2026; sales were Rs. 1,175 crores in FY2026, down 1%, hurt by Middle East supply-chain and logistics disruptions.

parts.name: Africa branded generics
parts.what: Branded medicines sold in West and East Africa; sales rose 15% to Rs. 861 crores in FY2026 with 8 new launches, and together with Asia this branded generic block made up 38% of company revenue.

parts.name: US generics
parts.what: Plain (unbranded) generic products sold to US distributors, which requires filing ANDAs with the US FDA; the fastest-growing part of the company, up 49% to Rs. 1,557 crores in FY2026 on the back of 8 new launches, lifting it to 29% of total revenue.

parts.name: Africa institution business
parts.what: Anti-malarial medicines supplied in bulk to government and aid procurement agencies in Africa; small and lumpy at roughly 3% of revenue (Rs. 160 crores in FY2026), and management repeatedly calls it unpredictable because it depends on donor funding and order flow.

overview.what_it_does: Akums is an Indian pharmaceutical manufacturer whose main business is contract development and manufacturing (CDMO): other pharma companies hire it to develop and make finished medicines — tablets, capsules, liquids, injections, creams, eye drops, nasal sprays, gummies and more — which those clients then sell under their own brands. Management calls it the largest India-focused CDMO with over 30% market share, serving 1,500+ clients a year including 26 of India's top 30 pharma companies, and it earns money largely on a cost-plus basis, so its billing rises and falls with raw-material (API) prices while profit tracks volumes and product mix. Alongside this it sells its own branded medicines in India (through Akumentis) and in about 65 export markets (through Unosource), sells unbranded trade generics through distributors, and makes bulk drug ingredients (APIs, mostly cephalosporins). Manufacturing and R&D are based in India (units including Baddi and a planned Jammu expansion, 11+ formulation plants, ~49 billion units of annual capacity, four R&D centres), with FY26 revenue of Rs 4,359 crore and a growing regulated-market push into Europe and a Zambia partnership.

parts.name: CDMO (contract development and manufacturing)
parts.what: Develops and manufactures finished dosage medicines for other pharma companies to sell under their brands; by far the biggest piece — about three-fourths of revenue at listing and Rs 3,485 crore of FY26's Rs 4,359 crore, with Rs 467 crore of EBITDA, and the segment management treats as its core growth engine including new European supplies from FY28.

parts.name: Domestic branded formulation (Akumentis)
parts.what: Akums' own branded medicines sold in India through a field force of 1,500+ reps across roughly 140 brands, focused on gynaecology, cardio-diabetics, orthopaedics and paediatrics with ~70% chronic/sub-chronic sales; roughly Rs 446 crore of FY26 revenue and Rs 90 crore EBITDA, so a small but profitable second leg.

parts.name: International branded formulation / exports (Unosource)
parts.what: Sells Akums-branded generics in about 65 overseas countries across CNS, anti-infectives, analgesics and gynaecology, backed by 700+ product dossiers and regular new approvals; small in size (about Rs 50 crore in the December 2025 quarter) but described as a focus segment for the group.

parts.name: Trade generics
parts.what: Unbranded generic medicines sold through distributors in India; a loss-making segment management has deliberately been shrinking for years (about Rs 25 crore of quarterly revenue, down 18% year-on-year), which finally turned EBITDA-positive in the March 2026 quarter and is expected to stay small and profit-focused.

parts.name: API (active pharmaceutical ingredients)
parts.what: Makes bulk drug ingredients — around 85% cephalosporins, plus respiratory, CNS and anti-diabetic molecules — with 737 MT of capacity; contributes over 5% of revenue and has been loss-making throughout the period on falling cephalosporin prices, with management cutting losses through cost control and shifting toward higher-margin non-cephalosporin products and regulated markets.

overview.what_it_does: Alivus Life Sciences (formerly Glenmark Life Sciences, renamed after Nirma became its promoter in 2024) is an Indian company that manufactures active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) — the chemical raw materials that go into finished medicines — and sells them in bulk to drug makers rather than to patients. Its customers are generic pharma companies across India, Europe, Japan, Latin America, the US and other regulated markets, plus its former parent Glenmark Pharma, and it had about 900 customers and 176 unique molecules as of FY26. It makes money by selling these APIs (mostly for chronic conditions like heart and central-nervous-system disease, which are about two-thirds of revenue) and, to a smaller extent, by making molecules to order for other companies under contract (CDMO). Manufacturing sits at plants in Dahej, Ankleshwar and Solapur in India, with a new R&D centre being built at Taloja; FY26 revenue was Rs. 2,552 crores with EBITDA margins of 33.6% and no net debt.

parts.name: Generic API business
parts.what: The core business — making and selling off-patent APIs to pharma customers worldwide, backed by 611 DMF/CEP regulatory filings as of March 2026; it is the overwhelming majority of revenue (roughly Rs. 535 crores of Rs. 588 crores in the Q1 FY25 quarter management broke out).

parts.name: Non-GPL (external) business
parts.what: API sales to outside customers across Europe, Japan, LATAM, India and rest-of-world — the growth engine management keeps pointing to, up from 59% of total revenue in FY22 to 71% in FY26 and growing 13% in FY26.

parts.name: GPL business
parts.what: API supply to Glenmark Pharma, the former parent — a large but flat and lumpy captive customer (it fell 41% year-on-year in one 2022 quarter and rebounded 18% quarter-on-quarter in mid-2024); management is deliberately reducing dependence on it, now down to about 29% of revenue.

parts.name: CDMO
parts.what: Contract development and manufacturing — making molecules to a customer's own specification instead of a catalogue product; small (about Rs. 43 crores in the Q1 FY25 quarter, roughly 7% of that quarter's sales) and volatile, but it doubled quarter-on-quarter in Q3 FY26 as new projects started and is credited as one of the main drivers of the recent margin improvement.

parts.name: High-potency API portfolio (including oncology)
parts.what: A pipeline of more complex, harder-to-make APIs such as cancer drugs, built in dedicated facilities — 28 products in development as of March 2026 (12 validated, 7 in advanced stages), described as addressing a $70 billion market and intended as the company's future higher-margin growth layer rather than a current revenue line.

overview.what_it_does: Alkem Laboratories is a Mumbai-headquartered Indian drugmaker that makes and sells prescription medicines — mostly generic pills and injections sold under its own brand names — to doctors, chemists and distributors. Its biggest business by far is India, where it is one of the top five pharma companies and is best known as a leader in anti-infectives (antibiotics) and gastro medicines, while pushing harder into long-term 'chronic' therapies like diabetes, heart, respiratory and skin. It earns money by manufacturing (and in some cases outsourcing production of) these medicines and selling volume through a large field force of medical representatives, plus a growing export business selling generic drugs in the US and other countries such as Australia. In FY26 total revenue was about INR 14,712 crore, roughly two-thirds from India (INR 9,851 crore) and the rest from international markets, with an EBITDA margin of about 20%.

parts.name: India / domestic branded generics
parts.what: Sells branded generic prescription medicines in India through doctors and pharmacies; the core of the company at about INR 9,851 crore in FY26 (growing ~10%), and management repeatedly calls domestic its 'top most priority'.

parts.name: Acute therapies (anti-infectives, gastrointestinal, pain, vitamins & minerals)
parts.what: The traditional strength — Alkem says it holds the leadership position in anti-infectives and, per IQVIA data, grows faster than the Indian pharma market in anti-infectives, vitamins/minerals, pain and GI.

parts.name: Chronic business
parts.what: Long-term-treatment medicines (antidiabetic, cardiac, respiratory, dermatology) that management describes as the key growth driver, consistently outperforming the market and gaining ranks; in Q4 FY26 chronic grew 16.1% versus the market's 13.6%.

parts.name: Trade generics
parts.what: Unbranded generics sold through the trade channel, largely made by outside manufacturers rather than in-house; management says it earns a decent return on capital but less than the branded generic business.

parts.name: GLP-1 / semaglutide
parts.what: A newly launched diabetes/weight drug launched on day one of patent expiry in March 2026, already at roughly 11% unit market share and called out by the MD as doing 'extremely well'.

parts.name: US business
parts.what: Sells generic drugs in the United States via ANDA filings and approvals from the US FDA (with plants at St. Louis, Indore and a Taloja bio-equivalence centre subject to FDA inspection); it went through years of heavy price erosion before stabilising and returning to double-digit growth.

parts.name: Non-US international
parts.what: Sales across other geographies including Australia; together with the US, total international sales grew about 22-26% recently and crossed INR 4,000 crore for the first time in FY24.

parts.name: Biosimilars and Enzene (bio-CDMO)
parts.what: Complex biological medicines sold in India (a portfolio of seven products by FY24) plus contract development and manufacturing for other drug companies through subsidiary Enzene, including a new US plant; management calls it a future growth engine targeted at 25% EBITDA margins in 4-5 years.

parts.name: Alkem MedTech
parts.what: A newly acquired medical-devices arm (announced February 2026) focused on orthopaedic implants and cardiology, run as a separate company with its own CEO; management targets roughly INR 1,000 crore of revenue in 3-5 years with INR 200-300 crore of further investment.

parts.name: Alkem Wellness
parts.what: A consumer/wellness business carved out as a separate entity, which management said in Q3 FY26 is facing headwinds while the core prescription business grows strongly.

parts.name: R&D
parts.what: Spending on new product development and clinical trials, including for biosimilars, running at roughly 4-5% of revenue and expensed through the P&L each year.

overview.what_it_does: Alkyl Amines Chemicals is an Indian chemical maker that produces aliphatic amines — mainly methylamines and ethylamines — plus amine derivatives and specialty chemicals such as acetonitrile. It sells these as bulk industrial inputs to other manufacturers, chiefly pharmaceutical (API) makers and agrochemical companies, with a newer product aimed at dyes, pigments and electronics; management notes it is usually only a small 'C item' in a customer's total input cost. It makes money on volume and on the spread between selling prices and raw material costs (ammonia, methanol and other alcohols, plus coal that generates about 80% of its power/fuel cost as steam), passing raw material increases through to customers where it can. It runs three plants in India (including a site at Kurkumbh) at roughly 60%–85% utilisation, selling largely into the domestic Indian market — where it competes with Balaji, RCF, the newly entered Aarti Drugs and aggressive Chinese imports — with some direct exports including to the US.

parts.name: Methylamines
parts.what: Its larger, more export- and competition-exposed amines line; management sizes the total Indian market across the four producers at roughly 80,000–90,000 tons against installed capacity of over 150,000 tons, so it describes methylamines as a 'long' (oversupplied) item, and it was the part most hurt by US-related trade disruption and Chinese pricing in FY26.

parts.name: Ethylamines
parts.what: A mainly domestic-focused amines line in an Indian market of about 30,000–35,000 tons, less affected by global disruption because competition is local, though selling prices fell enough in H1 FY26 to squeeze contribution per kg; a high-capacity new ethylamine plant was commissioned around May–June 2023.

parts.name: Acetonitrile
parts.what: A specialty solvent sold mainly to pharma, made via the acetic acid route (versus imports made as an acrylonitrile by-product), addressing an Indian market of roughly 30,000–35,000 tons where imports had been about 40%; an anti-dumping duty effective end-June 2025 is expected to lift its volumes and prices from around Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Amine derivatives and new import-substitute products
parts.what: R&D-developed products, largely import substitutes for the same pharma and agro customers, run partly on capacity freed up by the ethylamine expansion; management in 2022 put 25,000–30,000 tons of new capacity at Rs. 600–800 crore of eventual annual sales potential.

parts.name: New Kurkumbh project
parts.what: A roughly Rs. 120 crore plant for a product going mainly into dyes and pigments, electronics and other uses, with no other Indian producer; mechanical completion slipped to about end-June 2026 with commissioning shortly after, and management expects about 1.5x sales-to-asset turnover.

overview.what_it_does: Amber Enterprises India Limited is an Indian contract manufacturer that builds finished products and components for other companies' brands rather than selling under its own name — management calls itself a "one stop solution provider" and an ODM/OEM player, and its customers are appliance brands, electronics and telecom companies, automotive and defence firms, and railway/metro rolling-stock makers. It started as a maker of room air conditioners and AC components for India's AC brands, and has since diversified into electronics manufacturing services (assembled circuit boards and bare printed circuit boards), railway and metro sub-systems, and most recently mobile phone assembly for Oppo/OnePlus/Realme. It earns money by manufacturing to customer order, passing raw-material cost changes through to customers (with a roughly one-quarter lag), and it grows both by winning more of each customer's spend and by buying or partnering into new product areas (IL JIN and Ever, Ascent Circuits, Sidwal, Resojet, Yujin, Power-One, Unitronics, Shogini). Operations are almost entirely in India — plants in Punjab, Haryana (Faridabad), Noida, Pune, Hosur and Sri City in the south — with consolidated revenue of INR12,186 crores in FY26, up 22%, and operating EBITDA of INR970 crores.

parts.name: Consumer Durable division
parts.what: Makes complete room air conditioners for brands plus AC components, non-AC components (telecom, smart meter, IT server, refrigerator, microwave, washing machine, water purifier and auto parts) and, through the Resojet JV, fully automatic washing machines; it is by far the largest part at INR8,383 crores of FY26 revenue (about two-thirds of the group), growing 14% in FY26 with roughly 6-8% operating margins.

parts.name: Electronics / EMS division (IL JIN, Ever, Ascent Circuits, Shogini, Ascent-K, Power-One, Unitronics)
parts.what: Assembles printed circuit boards (PCBA) for appliances, consumer electronics, hearables/wearables, telecom, smart meters, automotive and defence, and now also manufactures the bare PCBs themselves; it is the fastest-growing part at INR3,268 crores in FY26 (up 49%, with EBITDA up 89%) and management guides to about 40% further growth in FY27.

parts.name: Railway Sub-system and Defense division (Sidwal, Yujin JV)
parts.what: Supplies equipment that goes inside trains and metro coaches — air conditioning/HVAC, pantry units, doors and gangways, plus couplers, gears and pantographs — to railway and metro projects and defence customers; smallest of the three divisions, it grew 19% in FY26 and sits on an order book of over INR2,600 crores with 30-35% growth guided for FY27 and FY28.

parts.name: Mobile phone manufacturing (Oppo collaboration)
parts.what: A brand-new, asset-light arrangement signed June 2026 to assemble phones for Oppo, OnePlus and Realme in a facility subleased from Oppo India, starting with roughly 8 million units in year one and 13-15 million in year two, at thin industry-standard margins of about 1.5-2% EBITDA; trial production is only due in Q4 FY27, so it contributes nothing yet.

overview.what_it_does: Ambuja Cements is an Indian cement maker — part of the Adani group since 2022 — that produces and sells cement and clinker across India, and calls itself the world's ninth largest building material solutions company. It makes money by mining limestone, firing it into clinker at large kiln plants, grinding it (mostly with fly ash into 'blended' cement) at grinding units near its markets, and selling bags and bulk cement through two channels: 'trade' (dealers and retailers serving individual home builders, about 74% of sales by Q4 FY26) and 'non-trade' (direct bulk sales to infrastructure and construction projects). Profit comes from the gap between selling price per tonne and cost per tonne, so management talks constantly about realisation per bag, cost per tonne (about INR4,400 for FY26, targeted lower), fuel, power and freight. It operates plants and grinding units across Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab, Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, Bihar, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh and the southern states, with FY26 sales of 73.7 million tonnes, capacity of 109 million tonnes, EBITDA of about INR6,539 crores and PAT of about INR2,647 crores, and it says it is debt-free.

parts.name: Cement (Ambuja standalone)
parts.what: The core business — making and selling grey cement under the Ambuja brand; it is the parent company and the largest single piece, with standalone quarterly revenue of about INR4,218 crores as far back as Q3 FY23.

parts.name: ACC Limited (listed subsidiary)
parts.what: A separately listed cement company Ambuja controls and reports alongside itself; together the two form the bulk of 'Adani Cement', and ACC is now proposed to be merged into Ambuja under the 'One Cement Platform'.

parts.name: Sanghi Industries
parts.what: An acquired cement company (Gujarat-based) folded into the group and amalgamated with Ambuja in FY26; part of roughly 19 million tonnes of acquired capacity that was running well below par — cement utilisation about 57% in Q4 FY26 — and is being turned around.

parts.name: Penna Cement
parts.what: An acquisition completed to strengthen the group in southern India (consolidated from August 2025, amalgamated with Ambuja in FY26); like Sanghi it is a fixer-upper, at about 46% cement utilisation in Q4 FY26 and needing heavy maintenance capex.

parts.name: Orient Cement
parts.what: Another acquired cement business, consolidated for 11 months of FY26 and still in the process of being merged into Ambuja; management credits the acquired assets collectively with utilisation rising from 37% to 58% year-on-year in Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Premium cement products
parts.what: Higher-priced branded cements such as Ambuja Kawach and ACC Gold, sold through the trade channel at better realisation; these grew to about 35-36% of trade sales volumes by FY26, up from 24% in Q1 FY25, and are management's main lever on price.

parts.name: Blended cement
parts.what: Cement mixed with fly ash and other additives rather than pure clinker — about 86% of sales volumes; it is both a cost lever (lower clinker factor, 65% by Q4 FY26) and a green lever.

parts.name: Ready-mix concrete (RMC)
parts.what: A smaller downstream business selling ready-mixed concrete, including a green product line called ECOMaxX; the calls describe it as growing but give no size figures.

parts.name: Captive and green power
parts.what: Waste heat recovery systems and renewable energy plants (about 900 MW built, heading to 1,122 MW by FY27) that supply the plants' own electricity; green power was about 32-37% of the power mix, and surplus power is currently being sold into the market until approvals allow captive use.

parts.name: Alternative fuels and waste (Geoclean / AFR)
parts.what: Burning industrial and municipal waste as substitute kiln fuel — around 9% of the fuel mix, with a target of 30% thermal substitution — which cuts fuel cost and supports the sustainability story.

parts.name: Logistics and distribution
parts.what: Not a revenue line but a major cost centre management runs like a business unit — own GPWIS rail rakes, hub-and-spoke grinding units, shorter lead distances and direct-from-plant dispatches, with freight running around INR1,300 per tonne.

overview.what_it_does: Anand Rathi Wealth is an Indian wealth-management firm (a "non-bank wealth solution company") that helps rich families — high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth individuals with roughly ₹5 crore to ₹50 crore to invest — put their money into financial products and manage it over the long term. It does not manufacture most of what it sells: it is an AMFI-registered mutual fund distributor that places clients into regular-plan equity and debt mutual funds and into structured products/market-linked debentures (sourced both from group NBFC Anand Rathi Global Finance and from third parties), earning distribution commissions and recurring trail fees on the assets it looks after. The work is done face-to-face by a large in-house team of relationship managers (about 360 as of mid-2024), and management stresses very low client and RM attrition as the engine of growth. It operates mainly in India, with total assets under management crossing ₹1 lakh crore (₹1,06,300 crore as of June 2026) across ~13,900 client families, FY26 revenue of ₹1,198 crore and profit of ₹386 crore; it has recently started operations in the UK.

parts.name: Private Wealth / Wealth Management (flagship business)
parts.what: The core business: relationship managers advise HNI and ultra-HNI families and place their money in equity and debt mutual funds and structured products, and it is overwhelmingly the largest part — it accounts for essentially all of the ~₹1 lakh crore AUM and ~13,941 client families, with mutual fund distribution alone bringing in ₹494 crore of FY26 revenue.

parts.name: Digital Wealth Management (DWM), a B2B2C business
parts.what: A technology-led offering for the smaller "mass affluent" segment, delivering wealth solutions through a mix of technology and human contact; it is small — ₹2,526 crore of AUM and 7,320 clients as of June 2026, with revenue of only about ₹7 crore in a quarter.

parts.name: Omni Financial Advisors (OFA), a SaaS platform
parts.what: A subscription software platform sold to independent mutual fund distributors so they can service their own retail clients; it had 6,890 subscribers and ₹1.66 lakh crore of assets sitting on the platform as of June 2026, but is tiny financially (revenue of about ₹1.84 crore in a quarter).

parts.name: Platinum and Gold client segments
parts.what: An internal way of grading clients by size, with Platinum being the largest accounts — launched about two and a half years ago and grown from 40–45 clients to roughly 230, with management aiming for 400–500.

parts.name: Stake in Anand Rathi Global Finance Limited (ARGFL)
parts.what: A roughly 8% shareholding in the group's unlisted NBFC, which issues the market-linked debentures the wealth business distributes; it is a passive holding rather than an operating line, though revaluing it produced fair-value gains in FY26.

parts.name: UK operations
parts.what: A newly started overseas operation announced in the July 2026 call, with no revenue contribution yet.

overview.what_it_does: Anant Raj Limited is a family-run Indian property developer (in the construction business since 1969, now run by the fourth generation of the Sarin family) that buys land, builds on it, and sells or leases the finished space. Most of its money still comes from selling homes — group housing towers, independent floors, villas and plots — built mainly on its large land bank in Sector 63A, Gurugram, Haryana, plus lower-cost government-linked affordable housing in places like Neemrana and Tirupati; it also owns roughly 5 million square feet of completed commercial buildings that it leases out. Since about 2020 it has added a second business: converting its own ready land and buildings at Manesar, Panchkula and Rai (Sonipat) into data centres that rent out computing capacity and power to customers, and from October 2024 its own 'Ashok Cloud' service sold to businesses. Operations are concentrated in the Delhi-NCR region (Haryana, with a first Delhi project started in 2025); revenue rose from about ₹1,004 crore in FY23 to about ₹2,100 crore in FY25, and management says the company is now effectively net debt-free with surplus cash after a ₹1,100 crore QIP fundraise.

parts.name: Real estate – residential (group housing, independent floors, villas and plots)
parts.what: Builds and sells homes, mostly on its Gurugram Sector 63A land where it holds around 200 acres (about 97 acres left to develop, good for roughly 4.5 million sq ft), with 2.6 million sq ft of launches planned in FY26 and projects like Ashok Estates, Estate Residences and The Estate One — this is the company's main cash earner and by far the largest share of revenue.

parts.name: Birla Navya (JV with Birla Estates)
parts.what: A roughly 43-acre joint-venture housing project in Gurugram with Birla Estates (owned by Century Textiles), where phases have been launched and about 228 units of Phase I had been handed over by late 2024.

parts.name: Affordable / low-cost housing
parts.what: Applies for land from state governments and builds low-cost housing — the completed Neemrana project was described as a very good cash earner and the formula is being repeated elsewhere, such as Tirupati, though it is a smaller line than the Gurugram residential business.

parts.name: Commercial (leasing and new commercial development)
parts.what: Owns about 5 million sq ft of ready commercial buildings that it leases out with facilities, and has started two new projects — Ashok Towers in Sector 63A and a first 7 lakh sq ft Delhi development combining commercial, service apartments and a hotel, with Phase 1 due by FY28.

parts.name: Data centre business
parts.what: Runs co-location data centres on land and buildings it already owned — 21 MW at Manesar plus 7 MW at Panchkula delivered (28 MW total, showcased in August 2025), 35 MW more under construction targeting 63 MW by December 2026, and a 20 MW first phase at Rai, Sonipat out of a planned 200 MW there; it contributed ₹58.4 crore of the ₹1,223 crore H1 FY26 revenue, so it is still small in the numbers but is management's main growth focus.

parts.name: Cloud services – 'Ashok Cloud'
parts.what: A newer add-on launched in October 2024 (following a March 2024 agreement with partner TCIL) selling infrastructure-as-a-service to business customers on its own servers, described as a sovereign Indian cloud, with plans to extend into platform- and software-as-a-service; management said adding servers can lift revenue per megawatt several times over plain co-location.

overview.what_it_does: Angel One is an Indian digital stockbroker: it runs a mobile and web app (its "Super App") through which retail customers in India buy and sell shares and equity derivatives (futures and options) on the NSE and BSE, and it also acts as their depository participant for holding shares in demat form. Its customers are everyday retail investors — increasingly young, first-time and from beyond the big metros — with over 38 million registered users by Q1 FY'27 and a client base that grew from about 22 million in early 2024. It earns money mainly from charges on the orders its clients place (431 million orders in the Q4 FY'26 quarter alone, roughly 7.4 million a day), plus interest on money it lends clients to trade (an average client funding/MTF book of ₹61.4 billion), commissions from distributing mutual funds and other products, interest on personal loans it arranges, and fees from its newer wealth and asset-management arms. It operates only in India, is regulated by SEBI (and RBI on the credit side), and reported Q1 FY'27 revenue of ₹14.3 billion with profit after tax of ₹2.3 billion.

parts.name: Broking (Direct Business)
parts.what: The core business — executing customers' share and derivatives trades through the app; management calls it the "gateway product" that brings most clients in, and it holds roughly 20% of India's retail equity turnover, 22.2% of equity derivatives turnover, 17.4% of cash equity turnover and 16.7% demat market share.

parts.name: Assisted Business (channel partners)
parts.what: A network of independent partners/sub-brokers who bring in and service clients, supported by the company's dedicated NXT partner app; it sits alongside the direct app-based channel as a second route to customers.

parts.name: Client funding / Margin Trading Facility (MTF)
parts.what: Lending clients money against securities so they can trade larger positions, earning interest on the balance; the company raised ₹15 billion of capital in FY'24 partly to fund this book, which reached a lifetime-best average of ₹61.4 billion.

parts.name: Mutual fund distribution (SIPs)
parts.what: Selling and servicing mutual fund investments, especially monthly systematic investment plans, inside the same app — described as a high-engagement product where Angel One is the country's second-largest source of new SIP registrations (about 1.4 million unique SIPs in one quarter of FY'24).

parts.name: Credit / loans (New Business)
parts.what: Personal and other loans offered to existing clients through the platform; still small but scaling in a "calibrated" way, with ₹27.1 billion of lifetime cumulative disbursements and ₹6.1 billion disbursed in the Q4 FY'26 quarter, against a client base management says already borrows over ₹1 trillion a year elsewhere.

parts.name: Wealth management (Ionic Wealth)
parts.what: A separate, tech-led advisory business launched in FY'24 for ultra-high-net-worth and high-net-worth families that is being extended to retail; its assets under management crossed ₹100 billion (up 23% quarter-on-quarter), across a client base of 1,900-plus of whom over 45% are from non-metro cities.

parts.name: Asset management (Angel One Asset Management Company)
parts.what: Its own in-house fund house, set up with a hired leadership team and regulatory approval and now launching its own schemes — the newest and smallest of the businesses.

parts.name: Technology / AI platform (Super App, Ask Angel)
parts.what: Not a revenue line but the backbone management emphasises most: a single app covering onboarding/KYC, trading, option strategies, mutual funds, credit and wealth, now with an AI assistant "Ask Angel" serving over 1.1 million users, which they say lowers cost-to-serve and drives cross-selling across all the other parts.

overview.what_it_does: The Anup Engineering Limited is an Indian fabricator of large custom-built process equipment — mainly heat exchangers, plus pressure vessels, reactors, columns, silos and centrifuges — that it builds to order for plants in oil & gas, refining, petrochemicals, fertilizers, hydrogen and, more recently, nuclear and thermal power. It sells to refiners, EPC contractors and technology licensors (for example a Graham Corporation tie-up in the US where Anup is the exclusive manufacturer, and licensed designs from Lummus and Brembana & Rolle on which it pays royalties), winning work order-by-order and recognising revenue as each project is executed, so results depend on the pending order book (about INR 770 crores entering FY27) and an inquiry pipeline of roughly INR 1,100–1,200 crores. Money is made on the margin between the contract price and steel, labour and subcontracting costs, with FY26 consolidated revenue of INR 822.3 crores and EBITDA of INR 174.2 crores (about 21%). It manufactures from three locations — Ahmedabad and Kheda in Gujarat and Mabel Engineers in Tamil Nadu, plus a design office at Vadodara — and ships slightly over half its revenue as exports, to the Middle East, Europe and the US.

parts.name: Heat exchangers
parts.what: Its core product and the biggest revenue line — around 56–57% of revenue in FY26 (72% in H1 FY25) — including specialised and licensed proprietary designs such as helical and EMBaffle exchangers, focused mainly at the Ahmedabad plant.

parts.name: Vessels, reactors and columns
parts.what: Large pressure vessels, reactors and distillation columns at about 35% of FY26 revenue, made largely at the Kheda plant, which management says is the proof that the Kheda investment is paying off.

parts.name: Silos, centrifuges and other products
parts.what: A smaller catch-all bucket that rose to about 7% of revenue, into which management has been adding first-time products such as skids, air heaters, low-pressure feed water heaters for NTPC thermal projects and precision machined turbine-frame components for GE.

parts.name: Ahmedabad (Odhav) plant
parts.what: The original and largest works, delivering INR 540 crores of FY26 revenue (66% of the 9-month total), and the site of the heat-exchanger focus, a 150-tonne bay and clean room for exotic materials.

parts.name: Kheda plant
parts.what: The new Gujarat facility built in phases from FY23 onward; after Phase 2 it has 20,000 square metres of fabrication area and about 8,000 tonnes a year of capacity, capable of INR 400–450 crores of revenue, and it contributed INR 239 crores in FY26.

parts.name: Mabel Engineers (Tamil Nadu subsidiary)
parts.what: A 100%-owned acquired unit doing silos and site-fabrication work; still small at INR 43 crores of FY26 revenue and behind management's earlier INR 100 crore ambition because site projects ran long.

parts.name: Anup Technical Services
parts.what: A young services vertical that had over 10 orders executed in FY26 — small today, but management calls it potentially highly profitable and wants to grow it into a sizeable business.

parts.name: Vadodara design office
parts.what: An in-house engineering and design centre that removes a bottleneck in design work as volumes grow and has begun taking on small paid work of its own.

overview.what_it_does: Anupam Rasayan is an Indian specialty chemicals maker that manufactures complex, multi-step chemical molecules to order for large global companies — it does not sell branded consumer products but supplies intermediates and key starting materials that its customers use in crop-protection products, medicines, personal care items and high-performance materials. Most sales come from long-term contracts and LOIs signed with a handful of multinational customers (the top 10 customers were about 77% of revenue in Q1 FY25), priced on a cost-plus basis where raw material, freight, energy and other costs are passed through, which is how management says it keeps EBITDA margins in a roughly 22%-28% band. Its plants are in Gujarat (Sachin and Jhagadia, near Surat), and about 58% of 9MFY26 revenue was exported, with Japan alone around 17% of a recent quarter and the US growing after buying Jayhawk Fine Chemicals. Consolidated revenue was INR 1,730 crores for the nine months to December 2025 (up 84% year-on-year), and the group also owns fluorine chemicals maker Tanfac, has completed the Jayhawk purchase, and has agreed to buy a controlling-sized stake in Bliss GVS Pharma.

parts.name: Agrochemicals (Agro)
parts.what: Custom-manufactured intermediates and molecules for global crop-protection companies; historically the core of the business at 76% of standalone revenue in FY22, deliberately reduced to 55% by FY26, and it went through a sharp downturn in FY25 on customer channel-inventory destocking before recovering during FY26.

parts.name: Pharma
parts.what: Key starting materials and intermediates for blockbuster drugs such as Atorvastatin, Sitagliptin, Dapagliflozin and Vonoprazan, pitched as import substitution; the fastest-growing part, up 15-fold from INR 21 crores in FY22 to INR 339 crores in FY26 standalone and 19% of 9MFY26 sales, with 30+ more molecules in R&D and pilot.

parts.name: Polymer / Performance Materials (incl. high-performance materials, electronic materials, defence, semiconductors, EV)
parts.what: Advanced materials including fluoropolymers and electronic chemicals sold into defence, electronics, semiconductor, automotive and EV applications; contributed 17% of 9MFY26 revenue, grew 245% year-on-year in that period, and standalone high-performance materials revenue tripled from INR 97 crores in FY22 to INR 305 crores in FY26, with 35+ molecules under development.

parts.name: Personal Care
parts.what: A smaller fourth vertical management lists as part of the diversified revenue mix alongside Agro, Pharma and Performance Materials, but which the calls do not size separately.

parts.name: Fluorination chemistry / Tanfac Industries
parts.what: A controlling stake bought in 2022 in a fluorine chemicals company that supplies hydrofluoric acid and potassium fluoride — the starting raw materials for Anupam's fluorination products — giving backward integration, supply security and cost stability; Tanfac's numbers are consolidated into group results and it is now adding its own new products and customers.

parts.name: Jayhawk Fine Chemicals (US)
parts.what: A US specialty chemicals business bought outright from the CABB Group and completed in FY26, giving Anupam onshore American manufacturing and advanced custom-synthesis capability; it has pro forma annual revenue of about US$76 million but only 1 month and 2 days of it was consolidated in FY26, so the full contribution shows from FY27.

parts.name: Bliss GVS Pharma (announced, not yet closed)
parts.what: An agreed purchase of a 43.3%-48.2% equity stake plus an open offer for up to 26% more, funded partly by INR 300 crores of non-convertible debentures, intended to become a dedicated formulations and pharma CDMO/CMO platform sitting alongside the core specialty chemicals business.

parts.name: Captive renewable power
parts.what: Not a revenue line but a cost lever management repeatedly highlights — a 12.5 MW solar plant plus later solar/wind additions saving roughly INR 14-15 crores a year in energy costs and targeted at 65% green electricity and energy net-zero by 2027.

overview.what_it_does: Alembic Pharmaceuticals (NSE: APLLTD, BSE: 533573) is an India-based drug maker headquartered in Vadodara, Gujarat, that manufactures and sells finished medicines plus the active chemical ingredients that go into medicines. It earns money three ways: selling branded prescription medicines (and animal health products) to doctors and chemists in India; selling generic copies of off-patent drugs, mainly in the US but also in Europe and other rest-of-world markets; and selling bulk active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) to other drug companies, largely in regulated markets. The business runs on a pipeline model — it spends heavily on R&D (roughly INR 475-800 crores a year, about 8-12% of sales) to file ANDAs with the US FDA (270 cumulative filings by Q3 FY26) and launch a stream of new products each year, while running FDA-inspected plants for oral solids, injectables and oncology. Consolidated revenue was about INR 6,229 crores in FY24 and grew to roughly INR 7,300+ crores by FY26 (quarterly run-rate around INR 1,850 crores), with gross margins management targets at 70-75%.

parts.name: India Branded Business (branded formulations)
parts.what: Branded prescription medicines sold to Indian doctors through a field sales force, spanning specialty therapies (gynaecology, gastroenterology, antidiabetic, cardiology, ophthalmology) and acute/anti-infective and respiratory products; it is one of the largest single pieces at about INR 2,200 crores in FY24 and INR 652 crores in the December 2025 quarter, though growth has lagged the overall Indian market at 4-7%.

parts.name: Animal Healthcare (veterinary)
parts.what: Medicines for animals sold within the India business, repeatedly called out by management as a strong and consistent growth driver (roughly 35% growth in one early quarter) even when other India segments were flat.

parts.name: US Generics
parts.what: Generic versions of off-patent drugs sold to US buyers and distributors, historically the company's biggest single territory at roughly $47-56 million a quarter (about INR 367 crores in Q1 FY23), driven by 15-25 new product launches a year and constantly squeezed by price erosion.

parts.name: Ex-US Generics (Europe, Canada and rest-of-world)
parts.what: The same generic formulations sold outside the US, reusing the same product dossiers filed for the US; smaller than the US at around INR 182 crores in Q1 FY23 but the fastest-growing part lately — up 23% in FY24, 36% in ROW markets in Q3 FY26, and 20% for full-year FY26.

parts.name: API business
parts.what: Bulk active pharmaceutical ingredients sold to other pharma companies, mostly into regulated markets, at roughly INR 233 crores a quarter in FY23; volumes have held up but pricing has been a persistent headwind, with management guiding to high-single to low-double-digit growth for FY27.

parts.name: US Branded business (new)
parts.what: A newly started, deliberately small specialty push into selling its own branded drug in the US, beginning with Pivya (an in-licensed first-line oral antibiotic for uncomplicated urinary tract infections in women) launched in Q4 FY26; it currently costs money rather than making it, with management framing it as a multi-year build rather than a quick scale-up.

parts.name: R&D and manufacturing platform
parts.what: The engine behind everything else — INR 600-800 crores of annual R&D aimed at complex areas (injectables, peptides, oral solids, oncology, drug discovery) and early-entry First-to-File / Day-1 / NCE-1 launches, supported by newer plants (Karakhadi injectables, an oncology facility, Indore) whose rising utilisation management says is the main lever on margins.

overview.what_it_does: Apollo Tyres is an Indian company, headquartered in Kochi, that manufactures and sells tyres — mainly truck and bus radial tyres (TBR), passenger car radial tyres (PCR) and farm tyres. It sells them three ways: to vehicle makers fitting new vehicles (OEM customers like Mahindra, Maruti Suzuki, Toyota, VW, Skoda, BMW, MINI, Genesis and KIA), to the much larger replacement market of existing vehicle owners buying through dealers, and as exports to overseas markets. It makes money on the spread between tyre selling prices and raw-material costs (natural rubber being the biggest swing factor), so management talks constantly about passing on cost increases through price hikes and about shifting mix toward premium, higher-priced products. It runs two reported businesses — India Operations and Europe Operations — with plants in India (including Chennai and an Andhra Pradesh plant) and in Europe (Hungary, plus a plant at Enschede being shut), and consolidated revenue of roughly INR 73–77 billion per quarter by FY26 with EBITDA margins around 14–15%.

parts.name: India Operations (standalone)
parts.what: The core business — making and selling Apollo-brand truck/bus, passenger car and farm tyres in India plus exports — and by far the bigger piece, at INR 52.4 billion of the INR 73.4 billion consolidated revenue in the March 2026 quarter, at about 14.6% EBITDA margin.

parts.name: Europe Operations
parts.what: Tyres sold in European markets, led by the premium Vredestein brand and weighted toward high-performance passenger car tyres (UHP mix 52% of the quarter), running at roughly EUR 170–180 million of revenue a quarter with margins in the mid-teens to ~18%; demand there has been flat to muted while India grows.

parts.name: Replacement channel
parts.what: Selling tyres to owners of vehicles already on the road, through dealers — described by management as the core, most profitable channel, with the TBR and PCR replacement segments repeatedly called out as the growth engine in India.

parts.name: OEM channel
parts.what: Supplying tyres as original fitment to vehicle manufacturers; smaller and more volatile than replacement (it dragged growth down in FY25 when truck OEM demand fell), but strategically important because premium approvals — a 'marquee German passenger car manufacturer', BMW, MINI, Genesis, KIA — validate product quality and help premiumise the brand.

parts.name: Exports
parts.what: Tyres shipped from India to overseas markets; a swing factor that grew 20%+ year-on-year in mid-2024 but was knocked back to mid-single-digit growth by FY26 due to freight rates, shipping disruptions and West Asia geopolitics.

parts.name: Product categories: TBR, PCR and farm
parts.what: The three product lines management reports on — truck and bus radials, passenger car radials, and agricultural/farm tyres (the 'Virat' farm range was launched in India) — with the current INR 5,800 crore Andhra Pradesh plant expansion aimed at adding PCR and TBR capacity over FY27–29.

parts.name: Brands (Apollo and Vredestein)
parts.what: Apollo is the mainstream brand, Vredestein the premium European brand (backed by a Formula-race-winner ambassador) that hit its highest-ever volumes in the December 2025 quarter; brand spend is significant, including sponsorship of the Indian cricket team jersey, which temporarily squeezed India margins.

parts.name: Adjacencies (e.g. Trumigo)
parts.what: Occasional side ventures meant to support the core tyre business — Trumigo was a doorstep car-servicing business intended to connect with car tyre customers, but it was shut down in 2024 after financial performance fell well short of expectations.

overview.what_it_does: Aptus Value Housing Finance India Limited is an Indian lending company that gives small home loans and small business loans to low- and middle-income, mostly self-employed customers in Tier 2, 3 and 4 towns — people the calls describe as 'underserved and unserved' and who have little access to regular mortgage credit. It makes money on the spread between what it charges borrowers (high rates — management cites about 21% on small business loans, with home loan rates cut 50-75 bps on new loans in FY26) and what it pays to borrow from banks, the National Housing Bank, NCD investors (including IFC, insurers and mutual funds) and securitisation, with cost of funds down to about 8.1% and spreads around 9% by March 2026. It lends through its own physical branch network — 211 branches in mid-2022 growing to 339 by March 2026 — backed increasingly by digital/referral sourcing and 'connector' partners, and the loan book (AUM) grew from about Rs. 5,519 crores in June 2022 to Rs. 13,107 crores in March 2026, earning roughly 8% return on assets and over 20% return on equity. It started in and is still concentrated in the southern states (Tamil Nadu, where it has operated 15-16 years, plus Karnataka, Telangana and others) and is now expanding into Maharashtra and Odisha.

parts.name: Housing Loans (home loans)
parts.what: Loans to buy or build a house for low- and middle-income households in small towns; management calls this the core affordable-housing business and, alongside small business loans, one of the two things it is 'growing disbursements and loan book' in — it is the segment where it cut lending rates by 50-75 bps on new loans in FY26 to attract better-quality borrowers.

parts.name: Quasi home loans
parts.what: Loans that sit next to the plain home loan (referred to on calls as 'quasi home loans' and, by one analyst, alongside LAP) at higher yields than home loans; the company says it did not cut rates here and is raising average ticket size by about Rs. 1 lakh a year like its other products.

parts.name: Small Business Loans / SME
parts.what: Loans to small self-employed businesses at a yield of around 21%, which management says is at or below what rivals in that segment charge; it is described as the second growth engine beside housing and as a reason Aptus's returns look higher than peers', though management flagged a slight uptick in SME NPAs in Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Small-ticket loans below Rs. 7 lakhs (discontinued)
parts.what: A sub-segment of lending the company deliberately stopped sanctioning during FY26 to move upmarket to better-quality customers — it was about 17.5% of lending in April 2024 and was still roughly 10-11% of the loan book in December 2025, running down over time, and dropping it temporarily slowed disbursement growth in the first half of FY26.

parts.name: NBFC arm (group entity)
parts.what: The calls refer to consolidated results and to 'the NPA of NBFC' rising slightly in FY26, indicating lending is done through more than one group entity, but the calls give no further detail on its size or products.

parts.name: Branch network and sourcing channels
parts.what: The delivery engine rather than a product: 339 branches as of March 2026 with about 60 more planned in FY27, supported by digital channels (customer referral app, construction ecosystem app, social media) that contributed roughly 18% of business in Q1 FY25, plus a newer 'connector' partner channel described as still nascent.

parts.name: Borrowing and liquidity function
parts.what: How the lending is funded — roughly 58% from banks, 15% NCDs, 19% securitisation including direct assignment, and about 9% from NHB as of March 2026, with Rs. 2,057 crores of liquidity including Rs. 1,505 crores of undrawn bank sanctions; ratings were upgraded to AA- by CARE and ICRA back in 2022, which management says helped lower funding costs.

overview.what_it_does: Arvind Fashions Limited (part of India's Lalbhai Group) is a branded clothing company that sells apparel and related products to Indian consumers under a portfolio of five brands it owns or licenses — U.S. Polo Assn., Tommy Hilfiger, Calvin Klein, Arrow and Flying Machine. It makes money by designing/sourcing the product (sourcing is predominantly India-based) and selling it at retail prices through its own stores (EBOs), its own websites/apps and online marketplaces, and by wholesaling to multi-brand outlets and department stores. The mix is mainly menswear — shirts, polos, denim, t-shirts, blazers — plus growing 'adjacent' categories like footwear, innerwear, accessories and kidswear, which management says are now about 24% of the business. Full-year net sales value was about INR 4,620 crores in FY25 and grew 14% in FY26 (Q4 FY26 alone was INR 1,365 crores), with the company operating in India and steadily shifting sales toward direct-to-consumer channels (62% of sales in Q1 FY27, targeting 65%).

parts.name: U.S. Polo Assn. (USPA)
parts.what: A licensed American sportswear brand that management repeatedly calls its largest and 'marquee' brand — it 'led the pack' with the highest-ever growth in Q4 FY26 and Q1 FY27, and its adjacent categories (footwear, innerwear, etc.) alone were over 25% of its revenue by FY24.

parts.name: PVH brands — Tommy Hilfiger and Calvin Klein
