parts.what: Handles payments, collections and liquidity management for government departments and agencies; described as having moved from a deposit-gathering business to a solutions business, with mandates signed across the Indian Army, Navy, Police and Forest Department.

parts.name: Digital Banking platforms ('open' by Axis, NEO, Adi)
parts.what: The bank's mobile and platform channels, treated as a distinct source of growth rather than just a channel — 'open' by Axis carried 33% deposit and 74% loan growth in FY24, NEO for Business serves 3.1 lakh MSME customers, and the bank now runs GenAI tools (Adi, AXIOM) that management expects to show bottom-line impact over the next 18–24 months.

parts.name: Citibank India Consumer Business (acquired)
parts.what: A consumer banking portfolio bought from Citibank N.A. and Citicorp Finance India in FY23, bringing deposits, retail assets, wealth clients and about 1,600 corporate salary relationships; intangibles of Rs 8,714 crore were fully written off in FY23, and a related tax benefit of Rs 2,193 crore was recognised in FY26.

parts.name: Domestic subsidiaries
parts.what: Separate group companies whose profits are counted in consolidated results — annualised profit after tax of about Rs 1,082 crore in Q1 FY23, up 10% YoY; the calls refer to marketing the group jointly as 'One Axis' but do not name each subsidiary.

overview.what_it_does: AXISCADES Technologies is a Bengaluru-listed engineering research & development (ER&D) services company that sells outsourced design, engineering and embedded-electronics work — and, increasingly, actual manufactured hardware — to large global equipment makers, mainly in aerospace, defence, energy, heavy engineering and automotive. It earns money by billing clients for engineering projects and staffing (its long-standing base, where several customers have been with it over a decade), and from defence 'production' orders where it builds and delivers physical products, which the company says are lumpier because of long government procurement cycles. Revenue grew from about Rs 194 crore in the September 2022 quarter to Rs 1,159 crore for full-year FY26 (12.4% growth, 15.3% EBITDA margin). It operates out of India (Bengaluru head office, plus new campuses at Devanahalli and a missile complex in Hyderabad), Germany (automotive, via an acquired business), the US (a new Silicon Valley deep-tech subsidiary) and Vietnam, and in FY26 began selling off its lower-margin engineering-services lines to concentrate on aerospace, defence, space, electronics and AI under a stated 'Power 930' target of Rs 9,000 crore of revenue by FY2030.

parts.name: Engineering Design Services / engineering services
parts.what: The original core: outsourced design and engineering projects for aerospace, industrial, energy and automotive clients — still the single largest line in FY25 at about Rs 181 crore of the Rs 264 crore quarterly revenue, but management signed away 'Phase 1' of it (heavy engineering, energy and automotive) in FY26 and plans further divestment in H1 FY27.

parts.name: Aerospace
parts.what: Engineering and R&D work for global aircraft makers and their suppliers — historically one of the two founding verticals, contributing about 29% of revenue (Rs 76 crore) in the September 2024 quarter, growing 19% year-on-year, and now being extended into actual aerospace manufacturing and MRO through new campuses and a pending acquisition.

parts.name: Defence
parts.what: Design plus serial production of defence hardware for government-linked customers; described as roughly 32% of revenue (Rs 84 crore) in the September 2024 quarter with Rs 121 crore of order intake that quarter, and management repeatedly warns quarterly results here swing widely because of procurement cycles, budgets and geopolitics.

parts.name: Products & Solutions / embedded electronics (Mistral Solutions)
parts.what: System engineering, product design and embedded electronics — brought in via the Rs 292 crore phased acquisition of Mistral Solutions, serving product solutions, homeland security and defence customers; it grew 129.5% year-on-year in the September 2022 quarter off a small base and is treated as a key cross-selling engine.

parts.name: Automotive (including the German business)
parts.what: Embedded, mechanical and hardware engineering for tier-1 automotive suppliers and OEMs, built up through a long-term tier-1 contract and the acquisition of add solutions GmbH in Germany (wiring systems, testing, automation); it went from a growth story in FY23 to the main drag on FY25 margins amid a German auto downturn, and was part of the FY26 divestment.

parts.name: Energy
parts.what: Engineering services for global energy clients, one of the fastest-growing verticals early on (up 58.5% year-on-year in the September 2022 quarter) and counted with aerospace and defence as roughly 65% of revenue in FY25 — but sold as part of the FY26 Phase 1 engineering-services divestment.

parts.name: Heavy Engineering
parts.what: The other founding vertical, doing engineering work for heavy industrial clients (up 16.2% year-on-year in the September 2022 quarter on new service offerings); also included in the FY26 divestment of Phase 1 engineering services.

parts.name: Space Division
parts.what: A newly created unit as of FY26, running a space situational awareness initiative with a partner called Aldoria and evaluating tie-ups to manufacture space buses and payloads at the Devanahalli campus, where infrastructure is already being built — no revenue figures given.

parts.name: Xida Inc. (deep tech, electronics and AI)
parts.what: A newly created American-led, Silicon Valley-headquartered subsidiary into which the existing ES AI business and AI team are being moved so it starts with revenue and customers; aimed at hardware, electronics and AI around data centres, generative AI and physical AI, with two further acquisitions under evaluation.

parts.name: Manufacturing, testing and MRO capacity
parts.what: Not a revenue line yet but repeatedly flagged as the growth engine: the Devanahalli campuses and the Missile Atmanirbhar Complex (MAC) in Hyderabad go operational through FY27, and an aerospace manufacturing acquisition is meant to start high-value manufacturing in Q3 FY27.

overview.what_it_does: Azad Engineering makes extremely complex, life-critical rotating metal parts — mainly airfoils, blades and nozzle vane segments — that go inside gas, steam and nuclear turbines and inside aircraft and fighter-jet engines, plus precision assemblies for oil and gas; these are 3D-shaped parts made from exotic alloys that run at extreme heat and pressure, not ordinary machined components. It does not sell to end users but supplies global original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) such as GE Vernova, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Siemens, Baker Hughes, Rolls-Royce (defence and civil), Safran and Pratt & Whitney, competing head-on with suppliers from the US, Europe, China and Japan. Money comes from manufacturing and shipping these components under long-term, multi-year contracts and purchase agreements that it can only win after years — sometimes a decade — of qualification, audits and certification, which makes the business sticky and high-margin; the order book was over INR 6,000 crores in FY25 and over INR 6,500 crores by Q3 FY26. It manufactures out of Hyderabad, Telangana, India, including several new 'lean' plants dedicated to individual customers, and sells into global markets; FY26 revenue was INR 590 crores with EBITDA margin near 36.9% and PAT margin 22.4%.

parts.name: Energy and Oil & Gas
parts.what: Critical rotating components and airfoils for gas, steam and nuclear turbines plus complex precision assemblies for oil and gas — the original business and still the dominant one, at INR 97 crores or 77.7% of Q4 FY25 revenue, and management says it continued to contribute the majority of revenue through FY26.

parts.name: Aerospace and Defence (A&D)
parts.what: Mission- and life-critical rotating parts for aircraft and military jet engines, entered more recently on the back of the energy experience — INR 25 crores or 19.8% of Q4 FY25 revenue, described as the 'next big leap' with a steadily rising share, anchored by Rolls-Royce and newer engagements with Safran and Pratt & Whitney.

parts.name: Dedicated customer facilities (mega-factory vision)
parts.what: Separate lean manufacturing plants built for one marquee customer each — Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (7,200 sq m), GE Vernova (7,600 sq m), Siemens and, from April 2026, Baker Hughes — described as the deepest form of customer integration; four such plants exist since listing, with the infrastructure build-out about 70%–80% complete and full utilisation expected by FY28.

parts.name: Subsidiaries: Azad Prime and Azad VTC
parts.what: In-house 'special processes' operations that bring work previously sent to outside vendors inside the group, cutting dependence on external suppliers and saving cost; management expected them to begin contributing from FY26.

overview.what_it_does: Bajaj Auto is an Indian vehicle maker, based in Pune, that designs and manufactures motorcycles, electric scooters and three-wheelers (auto-rickshaws used as passenger taxis and small cargo carriers). It sells them to retail buyers through a dealer network in India and exports them to emerging markets across Latin America, Africa and Asia — exports alone were about 40% of revenue and USD 2.2 billion in FY26. Money comes from selling vehicles (plus spare parts), with a deliberate tilt toward higher-priced 125cc-and-above bikes, premium brands like KTM and Triumph, and newer 'green' products (electric and CNG), which management says lifts both revenue and margins. In FY26 the company reported record revenue of over INR 58,000 crore, EBITDA above INR 12,000 crore at a 20.5% margin, and profit of about INR 9,800 crore.

parts.name: Exports business unit
parts.what: Ships motorcycles and three-wheelers to overseas emerging markets — Nigeria and Africa, Latin America (Mexico, Brazil, where it also manufactures locally), and Asia (Sri Lanka, Philippines, Nepal) — and is the single largest piece at roughly 40% of company revenue, about 7,32,000 units and USD 735 million in the June 2026 quarter.

parts.name: Domestic motorcycles business unit
parts.what: Sells Bajaj-branded bikes in India — mainly the Pulsar sports range (125cc to 400cc), the Boxer/commuter end, and the CNG-petrol Freedom 125 — and accounts for about 25% of company revenue, with management focused on the faster-growing 125cc-plus half of the market where its 125cc share is around 25%.

parts.name: Commercial vehicles / three-wheelers
parts.what: Makes petrol/CNG and electric three-wheeler autos and cargo carriers for drivers and fleet operators; it is the company's most dominant position, with roughly 78% share of the conventional Indian three-wheeler market, about 35% of the electric auto market, and record export volumes of 100,000 units in a quarter.

parts.name: Chetak (electric scooters)
parts.what: The company's electric scooter brand, sold through 500-plus exclusive Chetak stores and shared motorcycle dealerships in 850+ cities; it crossed 5 lakh units and about INR 4,000 crore of revenue in FY26 with roughly 23% market share, and has just begun exporting.

parts.name: Pro-biking (KTM and Triumph)
parts.what: The premium motorcycle arm, building and selling KTM bikes (in partnership with KTM Austria) and Triumph models like the Speed 400 through dedicated and joint showrooms; combined domestic volumes reached about 40,000–43,000 units a quarter, growing 40–50% year on year, and these bikes are also exported from India.

parts.name: Electric mobility (EV two-wheelers and three-wheelers together)
parts.what: Management groups its electric scooters and electric autos as one growth story, saying they now make up about 30% of domestic revenue and earn double-digit EBITDA margins; the broader 'green' portfolio including CNG was cited at 44% of domestic revenue.

parts.name: Spare parts
parts.what: Sale of replacement parts to the installed base of vehicles, mentioned as one of the three drivers (alongside domestic and export vehicle sales) of record quarterly revenue.

overview.what_it_does: Bajaj Electricals is an India-based, Mumbai-headquartered maker and seller of branded electrical goods for homes, sold under the Bajaj name (plus Morphy Richards) and, on the lighting side, to institutional and outdoor buyers as well. It earns money by manufacturing/sourcing and selling household products — fans, kitchen and small appliances such as mixers and induction cooktops, geysers, room heaters and summer cooling products — and lighting products including ceiling and outdoor lights, mainly by shipping stock to a deep network of distributors and dealers ('primary sales') who then sell through to retailers and consumers ('secondaries'), so quarterly results swing with channel inventory, the festive season (Diwali) and the summer season. It was historically also an EPC (engineering-procurement-construction) contractor, but that business was demerged in September 2023 into a separate listed entity, Bajel Projects Limited, leaving Bajaj Electricals a pure consumer company with two verticals: Consumer Products and Lighting Solutions. The company says it has been debt-free since March 2022, runs on negative working capital, and ended FY26 with about INR 934 crore of cash; it recently began extending the lighting business into adjacent electrical categories — switchgear, solar solutions and wires.

parts.name: Consumer Products
parts.what: Fans, kitchen and small domestic appliances (mixers, induction cooktops), water heaters/geysers, room heaters and summer cooling products sold through distributors and retail; it is the larger of the two verticals and the main revenue driver, but also the volatile one — it grew ~58% year-on-year in Q1 FY23 and about 7.4% on a 3-year CAGR then, while in Q3 FY26 revenue fell 25% and EBIT went negative as management deliberately cut shipments to clear elevated channel inventory.

parts.name: Lighting Solutions (earlier called the Illumination business)
parts.what: Lighting products including ceiling and outdoor lights, plus newly added adjacent categories — switchgear (entered Q2 FY26), solar solutions (Q3 FY26) and wires (launched Q4 FY26); management describes it as the consistent performer, growing 9% in Q3 FY26 and 16% in Q4 FY26, with annual revenue up 9.5% in FY26 and a record annual EBIT margin of about 8.5% (versus roughly 2% EBIT in the year-ago quarter), and it is run separately under its own COO, Rajesh Naik.

parts.name: EPC (demerged — no longer part of the company)
parts.what: An engineering, procurement and construction project business (power transmission/infrastructure-type contracting) that had a large pending order book and contributed to over INR 2,000 crore of debt five years earlier; it was brought back to breakeven around FY23 and then demerged in September 2023 into a separate company, Bajel Projects Limited, so it no longer forms part of Bajaj Electricals' results.

overview.what_it_does: Bajaj Finserv Limited (BFS) is an Indian holding company that owns and runs a group of financial-services businesses, selling insurance, loans and other money products to Indian retail customers, small and large businesses, and government-sponsored schemes. It does not really sell anything itself; its income is the consolidated income of its subsidiaries — premiums and investment income from its general (non-life) and life insurance arms, and interest income from its lending arms — with the parent company's own standalone results described as small and only discussed 'where material'. Its consolidated total income was about INR 38,508 crore in the March 2026 quarter with consolidated profit after tax of about INR 2,539 crore. It operates in India, with premium accounted under Indian GAAP for the insurers and Ind AS at group level; a long-running joint venture with Germany's Allianz SE ended when Bajaj bought out Allianz's 23% stake in January 2026 and the insurers bought back the residual 3% in March 2026, making both insurance businesses 100% Bajaj-owned.

parts.name: Bajaj General Insurance Limited (earlier Bajaj Allianz General Insurance, 'BAGIC')
parts.what: The non-life insurer, selling motor, retail and group health, crop, commercial lines (fire, marine, engineering, liability) and travel insurance through bancassurance and agency channels; it is one of the two core businesses the call spends most time on, ranked first among private players on premium in Q3 FY26 with quarterly gross written premium of about INR 7,389 crore, investment assets of roughly INR 35,500–36,400 crore, and a combined ratio management repeatedly claims is among the best in the multi-line market.

parts.name: Bajaj Life Insurance Limited (earlier Bajaj Allianz Life Insurance, 'BALIC')
parts.what: The life insurer, selling savings and protection policies — par, non-par savings, term, annuity and unit-linked (ULIP) plans — to individuals; it is the other core business, with gross written premium of about INR 9,237 crore in the March 2025 quarter and value of new business of INR 549 crore, and from FY25 has been running a 'Bajaj Life 2.0' strategy shifting from fast growth to 'sustainable and profitable growth'.

parts.name: Bajaj Finance Limited (BFL)
parts.what: The group's lending business and, on the numbers given, the largest profit contributor — total income of about INR 11,917 crore and profit after tax of INR 4,480 crore in the March 2025 quarter at roughly 19% return on equity — though it holds its own separate earnings call, so BFS management takes only 'high-level' questions on it.

parts.name: Bajaj Housing Finance Limited (BHFL)
parts.what: A home-loan/housing finance subsidiary described as another 'material' subsidiary that, like Bajaj Finance, reports on its own call, so the BFS call gives it almost no separate detail.

parts.name: Bajaj Finserv Direct Limited
parts.what: One of the group's 'emerging companies', run by its own MD/CEO who joins the call from FY25 onwards; the excerpts name it as part of the emerging-business grouping but give no size figures.

parts.name: Bajaj Finserv Health Limited
parts.what: Another 'emerging company' in the group with its own MD/CEO on the calls from FY25; the excerpts identify it as a health-related venture within the group but provide no financial detail.

parts.name: Bajaj Finserv Asset Management Limited (Bajaj Finserv AMC)
parts.what: The group's asset-management (fund) arm, the newest of the 'emerging companies' — its MD appears on the calls from FY26 — again with no size disclosed in these excerpts.

parts.name: Bajaj Finserv Limited standalone (the parent)
parts.what: The listed holding entity itself, which prepares the group's Ind AS accounts and holds the stakes in the operating companies (for example 77.33% of each insurer after the Allianz buyout); its standalone results are discussed only 'where material', implying they are small next to the subsidiaries.

overview.what_it_does: Bajaj Housing Finance is an Indian housing finance company (an HFC regulated by the Reserve Bank of India) that lends money against property. Its main product is home loans to individual borrowers, alongside loans against property, lease rental discounting to owners of commercial real estate, and construction/developer finance to builders — with home loans the dominant piece at roughly 54-57% of the loan book. It makes money on the gap between what it charges borrowers and what it pays to raise funds — portfolio yield around 9.1-9.9% against a cost of funds of 7.3-7.9%, leaving a gross spread of about 1.7-1.9% and a net interest margin near 3.8-4.1% — topped up by fee income and income from assigning (selling down) loans; it borrows from banks, the money market (NCDs and commercial paper) and National Housing Bank refinance rather than taking deposits. It operates only in India, through 226 branches across 182 locations as of March 2026, with assets under management of over Rs. 1,40,000 crore, growing about 23% a year, and very low bad loans (gross NPA 27 bps, net NPA 11 bps).

parts.name: Home Loans (HL)
parts.what: Loans to individuals to buy homes — the company's largest and defining business at about 54-57% of AUM (management calls prime housing a 'scale builder'), growing roughly 18-24% year on year.

parts.name: Loan Against Property (LAP)
parts.what: Loans given to borrowers who pledge property they already own as security — a smaller but steady slice at roughly 10-11% of AUM, growing 24-32% in recent quarters.

parts.name: Lease Rental Discounting (LRD)
parts.what: Lending against the rental income streams of commercial properties, including large 'marquee' and REIT-linked transactions — the second-biggest product at about 20-22% of AUM and the fastest grower recently (up 44% in Q4 FY26).

parts.name: Developer Finance / Construction Finance (DF)
parts.what: Construction funding to real estate developers for their projects, at roughly 11-12% of AUM; growth slowed to 13-18% lately because funded projects were repaying cash back faster.

parts.name: Sambhav Loans SBU (Near Prime and Affordable)
parts.what: A separate business unit set up about 18 months before Feb 2026 to reach lower-ticket, higher-yield customers — 'Near Prime' at Rs. 40-60 lakh ticket sizes with 9-11% yields in the top 36 markets, and 'Affordable' at Rs. 15-35 lakh with 11-13% yields in outskirts, tier-4 and rural areas — currently disbursing Rs. 325-350 crore a month with a target of Rs. 600 crore-plus monthly in 12-15 months.

parts.name: Other loans
parts.what: A small residual category of about 1.7% of the portfolio that management does not break out further.

overview.what_it_does: Bajaj Finance Limited (BFL) is an Indian non-bank lender, headquartered in Pune, that makes loans to ordinary consumers and small businesses across India — everything from financing a shopper's purchase of consumer durables at the point of sale, to personal loans, home loans, gold loans, small-business (MSME) loans and vehicle finance. It reaches customers through a very large physical and digital footprint: roughly 4,200 locations, a customer franchise that grew from 66 million in late 2022 to 119.3 million by March 2026, and the Bajaj Finserv app (about 67 million customers as of early 2025), with management running what it calls 32 different lines of business. It earns money mainly on the spread between what it charges borrowers and its cost of funds (7.41% in Q4 FY26), plus fee and distribution income; it funds itself with market borrowings and customer deposits (INR 68,533 crore, 16% of consolidated borrowings in Q4 FY26). Assets under management grew from about INR 2.31 lakh crore in Q3 FY23 to roughly INR 5.10 lakh crore in Q4 FY26 (22.4% growth), with FY26 profit after tax growing 26.7% in the quarter and return on equity of about 19%.

parts.name: B2B / sales finance (consumer durables financing)
parts.what: Lends to shoppers at the point of purchase for consumer discretionary goods; B2B disbursements were INR 16,026 crore in Q3 FY23, and management tracks it closely as a seasonal, demand-sensitive volume driver and a key source of new customers.

parts.name: B2C / consumer lending (including unsecured personal loans)
parts.what: Direct loans to individual customers, largely unsecured; management flagged customers with 3-plus unsecured loans as a risk area and deliberately pruned this exposure back to pre-COVID levels by March 2025.

parts.name: Mortgages / Bajaj Housing Finance Limited (BHFL)
parts.what: A separately managed housing finance subsidiary doing home and property loans; in Q3 FY23 it was the main reason overall AUM growth fell short, because of intense pricing pressure in mortgages.

parts.name: Gold loans
parts.what: Loans secured against gold, run through a dedicated branch network that crossed 1,000 branches by early 2025; the fastest-growing line, up 115% and 3.5% of total AUM in Q4 FY26, expected to exceed 5% of AUM by FY27.

parts.name: MSME lending
parts.what: Loans to micro, small and medium businesses; grew only 6% in FY26 (versus 22.5% for the company) because management cut exposure by about 30% after this book drove a meaningful share of credit costs, with a return to double-digit growth expected in FY27.

parts.name: Two-wheeler and three-wheeler financing (captive Bajaj Auto book)
parts.what: Financing of Bajaj Auto vehicles, discontinued after Bajaj Auto set up its own captive finance company; now under 1% of AUM but still 13% of gross NPAs in Q4 FY26, and being wound down to under INR 1,500 crore by September 2026.

parts.name: Deposits
parts.what: Fixed deposits taken from customers as a funding source rather than a lending product; the book stood at INR 68,533 crore in Q4 FY26, or 16% of consolidated borrowings, after being 21% of the balance sheet back in Q3 FY23.

parts.name: Co-branded credit cards
parts.what: Cards issued with RBL Bank and DBS where BFL sourced customers; new sourcing was stopped by mutual agreement in early 2025, but BFL continues to earn distribution fees and revenue share on the existing arrangement.

parts.name: Digital platform / Bajaj Finserv app and cross-sell
parts.what: An app and web platform used to sell and service products to the existing customer base; 31 million net app installs in Q3 FY23 rising to nearly 67 million customers by Q3 FY25, with a 'cross-sell franchise' of 61.56 million customers that management treats as a core growth engine.

parts.name: Partnerships (Bharti Airtel)
parts.what: A five-year strategic partnership announced in Q3 FY25 to distribute BFL products through the Airtel Thanks app, with two products live at the time and nine planned by March 2025.

parts.name: Microfinance (MFI)
parts.what: A small-ticket lending business mentioned only in passing; together with gold loans it accounted for half of the roughly 1,800 employees added in Q4 FY26, suggesting it is in a build-out phase.

parts.name: FinAI transformation (BFL 3.0)
parts.what: Not a lending product but the company-wide operating programme management spends the most airtime on — a 203-person AI unit expanding to about 363 by June 2027, 27 live voice and text bots, and 600-plus autonomous agents planned for FY27 to cut cost and manual effort across all business lines.

overview.what_it_does: Balaji Amines is an Indian chemical manufacturer that makes aliphatic amines, amine derivatives and specialty chemicals, selling them in bulk to other manufacturers — mainly pharmaceutical API makers, agrochemical companies, and buyers of solvents, water-treatment chemicals, refinery chemicals, paints, dyes and EV battery chemicals. It earns money by converting purchased raw materials into these chemicals at its own integrated plants and selling by the tonne, so profit depends on volumes sold and the gap between product prices and input/utility costs; management repeatedly stresses that much of what it makes replaces imports and is produced using in-house technology. Operations are run from multiple units in Maharashtra (Units I–IV around Solapur, plus a greenfield site at MIDC Chincholi), with a subsidiary, Balaji Specialty Chemicals, running a separate plant, and the company also owns a hotel. Scale is roughly INR 1,454 crores of consolidated revenue and INR 169 crores of profit in FY26, on about 27,000 tonnes of product sold per quarter, with the standalone company carrying zero debt.

parts.name: Amines
parts.what: The core bulk chemicals the company is named after — methylamines, ethylamines, n-butylamines, isopropylamines and similar — running about 7,700–8,900 tonnes a quarter, roughly a third of total volumes, and described by management as the business where it holds market leadership in India.

parts.name: Amines Derivatives
parts.what: Downstream products made from its own amines (for example morpholine, and planned items like N-Methyl Morpholine and DMF), selling about 8,400–9,700 tonnes a quarter and forming, together with amines, what management calls its stable operating base.

parts.name: Specialty Chemicals
parts.what: The largest block by volume at roughly 10,000–11,000 tonnes a quarter, a broad basket including acetonitrile, dimethyl carbonate (DMC), propylene glycol, NMP and dimethyl ether (DME), which management calls a key differentiator versus competitors.

parts.name: Electronic-grade / EV battery and other new high-value products
parts.what: A newer push within specialty chemicals — electronic-grade DMC, battery-grade NMP, pharma-grade propylene glycol and DME for aerosols and LPG blending — where plants are built but running well below capacity (DMC at about 20%) because Indian battery makers have not scaled up and some approvals are still pending, so earnings contribution is still expected rather than realised.

parts.name: Balaji Specialty Chemicals Limited (subsidiary)
parts.what: A separately run subsidiary plant making ethylenediamine-based and related products, historically a meaningful profit contributor but constrained by raw-material access, now undertaking an INR 750 crore phased expansion into DETA, TETA, PIP, AEEA, AEP, hydrogen cyanide, sodium cyanide and EDTA, with mega-project status from the Maharashtra government and commissioning spread across FY27.

parts.name: Hotel business
parts.what: A small non-chemical side operation running at 85–90% occupancy, to which management decided to add 40 rooms at a cost of about INR 30–35 crores — minor relative to the chemicals business but a steady revenue stream.

parts.name: Captive solar power
parts.what: A planned 20 MW solar plant with MIDC Solapur (first 8 MW phase targeted for December 2024) intended to supply the company's own manufacturing power needs rather than to be sold as a business.

overview.what_it_does: Balkrishna Industries (brand name "BKT") is an Indian company that makes rubber tyres, with its main business being large off-highway tyres (OHT) for farm tractors and agricultural equipment and for earth-moving, mining, industrial and construction machinery. Most of what it makes is exported and sold through distributors and dealers rather than to vehicle makers — replacement-market sales run about 70-73% of volumes, with OEMs about 25-28% — and roughly 44-49% of sales come from Europe, 16-19% from the Americas, 21-29% from India and the rest from other markets. It makes money by manufacturing tyres in India (plants at Waluj and Bhuj) and selling them abroad, so profits swing with rubber and crude-linked raw-material costs, sea-freight rates and the euro-rupee exchange rate (it hedges the euro, e.g. INR 85-91 in earlier years versus about INR 97 by Q3 FY26); quarterly standalone revenue was around INR 2,200-2,700 crores with EBITDA margins in the 19-25% range across the calls. Alongside tyres it runs a carbon black plant that supplies its own factories and sells to outside customers, and from FY26 it has started moving into on-highway tyres — truck-bus radials, two-wheelers and, planned, passenger-car radials.

parts.name: Off-Highway Tyre (OHT) business
parts.what: The core business — agricultural tyres (about 59-63% of the category mix) plus OTR, industrial and construction tyres (about 34-37%), sold worldwide mainly to the replacement market under the BKT brand; management describes it first on every call and it drove the highest-ever quarterly and annual volumes in FY26.

parts.name: Agricultural segment
parts.what: The largest product category within OHT, tyres for farm equipment, contributing 63% of sales in 9M FY23 and 59% in H1 FY25.

parts.name: OTR / industrial / construction segment
parts.what: Tyres for earthmoving, mining, industrial and construction machines, the second-biggest category at 34% in 9M FY23 and 37% in H1 FY25; the first phase of the FY25 tyre capex was directed at expanding this OTR range.

parts.name: Carbon black business
parts.what: An in-house plant making carbon black — a key tyre raw material — used captively and also sold to outside customers (third-party sales were about 9% of overall business in FY26), with capacity taken to 265,000 MTPA in December 2025 and heading to 360,000 MTPA, including higher-value 'advanced'/specialty grades approved for plastics, inks, paints, pressure pipes and power cables.

parts.name: On-Highway business
parts.what: A new and still small adjacency started in FY26 — truck-bus radial tyres launched February 2026, a re-launch of two-wheeler tyres for India, and passenger car radials (PCR) planned for FY27 — supported by a new distribution network and Ranveer Singh-fronted marketing, and management lists scaling it up as one of three company priorities.

parts.name: Captive power plant
parts.what: A power plant at the Bhuj site, expanded from 40 MW to 64 MW in February 2026, run alongside the carbon black operation for what management calls an 'energy circularity' model that supports cost and efficiency rather than being a separate revenue line.

overview.what_it_does: Balrampur Chini Mills is an Indian sugar company that buys sugarcane from farmers in Uttar Pradesh and crushes it at its own mills (units named Balrampur, Tulsipur, Gularia, Maizapur, Kumbhi) to make sugar, which it sells mainly in the domestic market at prices around Rs. 41-42 per kg, plus limited exports when the government permits them. It calls itself an 'integrated' model: the same cane also feeds distilleries that make ethanol sold into the government's petrol-blending programme, and bagasse (cane waste) feeds co-generation, so it tries to extract maximum value 'from each stick of cane.' Its economics are driven by how much cane it can crush (1,043 lakh quintals in season 2025-26, up 5.2%) and the sugar recovery rate (about 11.24%), against a state-set cane price that rose from Rs. 370 to Rs. 400 per quintal, so government policy on cane prices, ethanol prices, exports and blending targets shapes profits heavily. It is now adding a large new leg — a Rs. 3,080 crore Polylactic Acid (PLA) biodegradable-plastic plant — funded partly by a Rs. 450 crore preferential share issue and Rs. 200 crore of debentures.

parts.name: Sugar
parts.what: The core business — crushing sugarcane into sugar sold domestically (and exported when government allows); it is described as the segment that 'continues to perform well' and delivered 'resilient performance' in FY26 on higher crushing, higher sales volume and stable realisations.

parts.name: Distillery / Ethanol
parts.what: Converts sugarcane juice, B-heavy molasses and grain into ethanol sold under the government's blending programme; capacity was being taken to 1,050 KLPD (about 35 crore litres a year), and management calls it stable on volumes but under margin pressure because ethanol prices have not been revised for three years.

parts.name: Co-generation / power
parts.what: Burns bagasse, the leftover cane fibre, to generate power — management notes Balrampur was 'India's first sugar factory to enter into a co-generation project,' which turned a waste-disposal problem into a business that 'yielded rich dividends.'

parts.name: Cane development
parts.what: Not a revenue segment but a core activity: working with farmers on planting area (3.24 lakh hectares reported at one point), ratoon crop, irrigation, disease control and switching cane varieties (away from Co0238 toward higher-recovery types) — this is what determines how much cane and sugar the company actually gets.

parts.name: PLA (Polylactic Acid) project
parts.what: A new biodegradable-plastic plant at Kumbhi, the company's biggest bet at Rs. 3,080 crore (revised up from Rs. 2,850 crore) for roughly 80,000 tonnes a year, aimed at replacing fossil-based plastic in uses like gutka packaging, helped along by central and UP government non-plastic mandates; commissioning targeted for the third quarter of the year.

parts.name: Lactogypsum / gypsum board plant
parts.what: A Rs. 160 crore plant to turn lactogypsum, a by-product of PLA making (about 1.16-1.2 lakh tonnes per 80,000 tonnes of PLA), into roughly 63-76 lakh gypsum boards a year — annual revenue potential of around Rs. 150 crore with a five-year payback, started partly because gypsum is otherwise hard to dispose of.

parts.name: Investment in Auxilo (NBFC)
parts.what: A non-core financial stake in a lending company, last valued around Rs. 3,000-3,200 crore market cap at its most recent dilution; management says it is 'positively inclined' to eventually sell down the holding to reduce debt.

overview.what_it_does: Bandhan Bank is an Indian commercial bank, headquartered in Kolkata, that lends money to customers and takes deposits from the public. Its historic core is very small "microcredit" loans made to groups of low-income borrowers and small entrepreneurs — the segment management calls EEB (Emerging Entrepreneurs Business) — collected in person at group meetings by relationship officers, and it has been adding home loans, loans to NBFCs and small businesses, and ordinary retail loans (personal, gold, two-wheeler, auto) to diversify away from that base. It makes money mainly on the gap between the high rates it charges borrowers and what it pays depositors (margins of about 6.2% in Q1 FY27), plus fee income from things like card machines, payment gateways and corporate internet banking. It operates across India through a network of roughly 6,300 banking outlets serving over 3.35 crore customers, concentrated in the east and in rural/underserved areas — West Bengal alone was about 24% of loans, and the top five states (West Bengal, Maharashtra, Bihar, Gujarat, MP) about 60%.

parts.name: EEB (Emerging Entrepreneurs Business) / microcredit
parts.what: Small unsecured group loans to low-income entrepreneurs, collected at physical group meetings via tablets, with options like 18- and 36-month tenures and bi-weekly or monthly repayment; it was about 50% of gross advances as of March 2024 and is the bank's oldest and highest-yielding business, though also the one that caused most of its bad-loan problems and is now being deliberately grown cautiously.

parts.name: Housing finance
parts.what: Home loans, a secured business the bank has pushed hard as part of diversification — growing 27% year-on-year in the June 2022 quarter and making up about 24% of gross advances by March 2024.

parts.name: Commercial banking
parts.what: Lending mainly to NBFCs, small enterprise loans and SME/SMA borrowers; it grew 81% year-on-year in mid-2022 and 34% in FY24, reaching roughly 22% of gross advances by March 2024.

parts.name: Retail assets (other than housing)
parts.what: Personal loans, gold loans, two-wheeler and auto loans sold to individual customers, the smallest piece at about 4% of advances in March 2024 but growing fast (roughly 65% year-on-year on an adjusted basis that year) and pushed through branch cross-selling.

parts.name: Liabilities / deposits franchise
parts.what: Current and savings accounts (CASA) and term deposits from retail and bulk customers, which fund the lending book — deposits reached about INR 1.65 lakh crore by June 2026, with retail deposits plus CASA at 74% of the total and CASA alone at 29.4%, and management deliberately shrinking costly bulk deposits.

parts.name: Digital, merchant acquiring and payments
parts.what: Corporate internet banking, POS terminals that plug into customers' ERP systems, payment-gateway tie-ups (BillDesk, Cashfree, Razorpay) and an in-app mobile collection tool, described as a fee-and-service capability serving corporate, government, utility and education clients rather than a large reported loan segment.

parts.name: Stressed-asset resolution / ARC sales
parts.what: Not a product line but a recurring activity management highlights: recovering or selling off bad microfinance loans — for example in the December 2025 quarter it sold INR 3,707 crore of written-off loans at about 9% of value and INR 3,165 crore of NPAs at about 18%, which directly moved reported profits and NPA ratios.

overview.what_it_does: Bank of Baroda is a large Indian bank that takes deposits from the public and lends the money out at a higher interest rate — the gap between what it pays savers and what it earns from borrowers (its net interest margin, around 2.8–3.2%) is its main source of income. It lends to individuals (home, car, education, gold, mortgage and personal loans), to farmers, to small and mid-sized businesses, and to large companies, and it also runs a treasury that invests in bonds and trades. It operates mainly across India but has a meaningful overseas business too, taking international deposits and making international loans that were growing over 20% a year by 2026. By March 2026 its total business (deposits plus loans) had crossed Rs 30 lakh crore, with full-year net profit of about Rs 20,021 crore and a return on assets consistently above 1%.

parts.name: Retail
parts.what: Loans to individuals — home loans (historically about 70% of the retail book), auto, education, mortgage and personal loans — the fastest-growing lending segment, crossing Rs 3 lakh crore by March 2026 and growing 18% a year.

parts.name: Agriculture
parts.what: Farm lending, including a growing share of gold loans, which management highlights as improving the quality of this book; growing roughly 9–21% a year across the calls.

parts.name: MSME
parts.what: Loans to micro, small and medium businesses, run as its own vertical; growth picked up from around 10% in 2024 to over 20% by mid-2026.

parts.name: RAM (Retail, Agriculture, MSME combined)
parts.what: How management groups its three higher-yielding lending books and reports them as a bloc — described as the bank's core business model focus, at 61% of the loan book by March 2026.

parts.name: Corporate credit
parts.what: Big-ticket lending to large companies — historically the largest part of the balance sheet and the swing factor in overall growth, though the bank has at times deliberately slowed it to protect margins; grew 11–15% in the most recent quarters.

parts.name: International banking
parts.what: Overseas deposit-taking and lending, mostly corporate in nature, which management says has often carried better margins than domestic corporate lending; grew 23–24% a year in 2026 and is funded largely by overseas deposits rather than wholesale borrowing.

parts.name: Treasury
parts.what: Manages the bank's own investment portfolio and trading; its gains and mark-to-market losses swing operating profit from quarter to quarter, and RBI valuation rule changes have twice been cited for dips.

parts.name: Deposits / retail liability franchise
parts.what: The funding side of the bank — current and savings accounts (CASA), term deposits and bulk deposits; CASA is treated as the strategic prize because it is cheap money, running around 38–44% of deposits, while bulk deposits have been deliberately cut back to protect margins.

parts.name: Digital banking (bob World)
parts.what: The bank's digital platform, credited with driving very fast personal loan growth (nearly 150% in one early quarter) and run under an IT/platform-functions vertical.

parts.name: Stressed assets / recovery (SAMV)
parts.what: A dedicated vertical that collects on and recovers bad loans; the bank targeted Rs 10,000 crore of recoveries in FY25 and reports gross NPAs down from 3.5% to about 2% and credit costs under 0.5%.

overview.what_it_does: Bank of India is an Indian commercial bank that takes deposits from the public and lends the money out at higher interest rates — the gap between the two (net interest income) is its main source of earnings. It serves individuals, farmers, small and medium businesses (MSMEs) and large corporates, offering savings and current accounts, term deposits, home, education, vehicle and personal loans, farm credit, MSME working-capital loans and big-ticket corporate finance. Alongside interest, it earns fee and other 'non-interest' income from services such as payments, cards, cash management, and gains on its treasury/investment book. It is mainly a domestic Indian bank — roughly Rs.8.25 lakh crore of its Rs.9.58 lakh crore of deposits are domestic as of June 2026 — with overseas operations including Kenya and a presence at GIFT City IFSC in Gujarat; total 'global business' (deposits plus advances) was about Rs.17.55 lakh crore in June 2026, and net profit was Rs.10,527 crore for FY26.

parts.name: Deposits (CASA and term deposits)
parts.what: Collecting money from customers through low-cost current and savings accounts (CASA) plus fixed/retail term deposits, which funds all its lending; global deposits stood at Rs.9.58 lakh crore in June 2026 with CASA of Rs.3.02 lakh crore (a 36.68% CASA ratio, down from ~44% in 2022), and management repeatedly calls building this low-cost deposit franchise its top priority — including new Zonal Deposit Centres at every zonal office.

parts.name: RAM advances (Retail, Agriculture and MSME)
parts.what: Small-ticket lending to individuals, farmers and small businesses — home, education, vehicle and personal loans, farm credit, MUDRA and MSME working capital — which is the bank's declared growth engine, at Rs.3.93 lakh crore in June 2026, up ~20% year-on-year and making up 58.30% of all advances.

parts.name: Corporate advances
parts.what: Larger loans to companies (manufacturing, infrastructure, roads and similar), the remainder of the loan book outside RAM (roughly 40%); management says it continues to onboard new corporate clients but the emphasis has shifted toward RAM, and its new Strategic Business Branch in Mumbai targets pool buyouts, co-lending, TReDS and supply-chain financing.

parts.name: Treasury / investments
parts.what: Managing the bank's own portfolio of securities, which produces trading gains or mark-to-market losses that swing non-interest income — e.g. a Rs.295 crore MTM loss partly offset by Rs.147 crore of security sales in the June 2022 quarter, and a drop in treasury income that pulled down operating profit that year.

parts.name: Non-interest / fee income
parts.what: Fees and charges from everyday banking services, cards, payments and collections, plus recoveries from written-off loans; it came to Rs.9,874 crore in FY26 (up 10%) versus Rs.25,172 crore of net interest income, so it is a meaningful but secondary earnings stream.

parts.name: Digital banking and payments
parts.what: Online and app-based banking through the BOI Omni Neo app and an e-platform for straight-through loan and account opening, UPI payments, QR sound-boxes, virtual RuPay debit cards, digital savings accounts, Digital Banking Units and Bharat Connect biller services for corporates — presented as an efficiency and customer-acquisition channel rather than a separate profit line.

parts.name: International operations
parts.what: Overseas branches and units — the calls specifically mention a Kenya business with its own mobile app and M-PESA integration, and an investment with six other banks in CCIL-IFSC Ltd for foreign-currency settlement at GIFT City; the gap between 'global' and 'domestic' numbers implies roughly Rs.1.3 lakh crore of overseas deposits and Rs.1.2 lakh crore of overseas advances in June 2026.

parts.name: Subsidiaries and associates (RRBs, BOI Services Ltd)
parts.what: The bank sponsors three Regional Rural Banks (which have been given e-commerce-enabled debit cards) and owns BOI Services Ltd, which is being used to put dedicated field staff on the street to revamp cash management services and pull in deposits.

parts.name: Asset quality / recovery function
parts.what: A large ongoing effort to control and recover bad loans — restructured COVID-era books, slippage containment and recovery from written-off accounts (about Rs.40,000 crore of write-offs mentioned in 2024) — which has taken gross NPAs from 9.30% in June 2022 to 1.81% in June 2026 and net NPAs to 0.51%, directly driving the profit growth management highlights.

overview.what_it_does: Bata India is a footwear company that designs, sources, makes and sells shoes and slippers to everyday Indian consumers, from low-priced mass products up to premium ranges around Rs 2,000-3,000 and above. It sells under a family of brands the management names on the calls — Bata, Hush Puppies, Power, Floatz, Comfort and the licensed Nine West — plus a small but growing line of apparel and non-footwear accessories. Money comes from three routes: its own retail stores (both company-owned and franchise), wholesale distribution to independent multi-brand shoe shops across the country, and e-commerce; it also runs its own manufacturing plants, though it has been closing some to cut fixed costs and moving more sourcing closer to demand. It operates only in India, with a listed head office in Kolkata, a network that has grown from roughly 1,900 points of sale in 2022 to over 2,000 exclusive brand outlets plus about 20,000 multi-brand outlets across roughly 1,670 towns by 2026.

parts.name: Retail — COCO (company-owned, company-operated) stores
parts.what: Bata's own stores, which management describes as the core of the business but a network it has been rationalising rather than aggressively expanding — spend here goes into renovations (about 20-25 store facelifts a quarter) and the 'zero-based merchandising' project that had reached 550 stores by early 2026 with a plan to cover 75-80% of the network.

parts.name: Franchise stores / EBOs (exclusive brand outlets)
parts.what: Partner-run Bata stores, the company's main growth and penetration engine especially in tier-3 to tier-5 towns where management says it is often the first organised retailer; additions run roughly 40-50 a quarter and by mid-2026 the total EBO network crossed 2,000, with about half of new franchise stores opened by existing partners.

parts.name: Shop-in-shops (SIS)
parts.what: Bata counters inside other retailers' stores, counted alongside COCO and franchise in the point-of-sale total and grouped with franchise as the 'penetration and expansion' vector that delivered double-digit growth at higher profitability in FY26.

parts.name: Multi-brand outlet (MBO) distribution / wholesale
parts.what: Selling Bata product through independent shoe shops via distributors — roughly 20,000 outlets across about 1,670 towns; it was under pressure for several years as mass price points struggled, but management is now focusing on 'key retail outlets', the top ~10% of outlets that contribute 25-30% of the channel's turnover.

parts.name: E-commerce and omni-channel
parts.what: Described as the fastest-growing channel, spanning online marketplaces, the company's own Bata.com and app, and omni-channel fulfilment where 700-plus physical stores ship online orders using existing store inventory; the newly launched Bata app already carried about 14% of direct-to-consumer sales within six months.

parts.name: Sneakers / Sneaker Studios
parts.what: A dedicated sneaker push, sold through in-store 'Sneaker Studio' sections that grew from about 125 in 2022 to roughly 740 stores by 2024; sneakers consistently grew faster than the overall business.

parts.name: Power (athleisure / sports brand)
parts.what: The mass-to-mid sports and athleisure brand priced around Rs 2,000-3,000, growing in double digits, with its own compact standalone 'Power EBO' stores of about 1,000 sq ft being trialled and a Power apparel line in about 70 stores.

parts.name: Hush Puppies and other premium brands
parts.what: The premium end — Hush Puppies (called the number one brand in its space, strong in men's dress and premium ladies' fashion), plus Comfort and the licensed Nine West women's brand rolled out in about 60 stores; the premium portfolio consistently grows faster than the company average.

parts.name: Floatz
parts.what: A newer casual/slipper brand management says it runs 'like a start-up', investing in moulds, stores and technology; it contributes upwards of about 4.5% of retail sales and kept setting record quarterly sales.

parts.name: In-house manufacturing and supply chain
parts.what: Bata's own factories plus sourcing and distribution centres; capacity utilisation and inventory are managed tightly — inventory was cut 28% over two years while product availability rose about 1,000 basis points — and the company closed a manufacturing facility in FY26 (an exceptional charge) to lower structural employee cost by roughly 10%.

parts.name: Corner stores channel
parts.what: A small-format store channel that had been paused and rationalised and, as of early 2026, was showing both growth and what management called extremely strong margins.

overview.what_it_does: Bayer CropScience Limited is the India-listed arm of the global Bayer CropScience business, selling farm inputs — crop protection chemicals (insecticides, herbicides, fungicides) and seeds, especially hybrid corn seed — to Indian farmers, the large majority of them smallholders (management says it reaches about 20 million of the 50 million smallholders Bayer touches worldwide). It makes money by selling these products through a farm-input distribution channel each cropping season, so revenue swings with the monsoon, sowing acreage and how much stock the channel can 'liquidate'; margins depend on input/raw-material costs (much of its production base is in Europe, and Chinese agrochemical supply and prices set the price ceiling in the market). Named brands include Dekalb, Roundup, Nativo, Laudis and Council Activ. It operates in India (registered office in Thane, Maharashtra; present in the country over 125 years, merged with Monsanto India in 2019), is among Bayer CropScience's top 5 countries globally, and has a small export component; it pays out most of its cash as dividends (cumulatively over 80% of cash flow, Rs 90 per share at the last half year).

parts.name: Crop Protection (CP) portfolio
parts.what: Agrochemicals — insecticides, herbicides and fungicides sold to farmers to protect crops; management calls it the 'dominant portfolio' by revenue, but the slower grower at just under 6% annual growth over five years, and the part hardest hit by high input prices in FY2024-25 and by the washed-out second quarter of FY2025-26.

parts.name: Corn seeds portfolio
parts.what: Hybrid corn (maize) seed, the company's clear growth engine — nearly doubled over five years at roughly 15-16% annual growth, grew double-digit in the first half of FY2025-26 on both volume and price, and is riding corn becoming India's third field crop on ethanol and animal-feed/silage demand.

parts.name: Others (exports, Roundup, traded seeds)
parts.what: A residual bucket management describes as exports, the Roundup herbicide line and seeds it buys in and resells; Roundup pricing was called out as a drag on revenue in FY2023-24, but no size is given for the bucket.

parts.name: Transformation / partnerships (not a revenue line)
parts.what: Management's label for its ecosystem-building work — digitisation of farming, working with farmer producer organisations (FPOs), mechanisation, agronomy advice, financing and market linkage — framed as investment in future growth drivers rather than a segment that reports sales today.

parts.name: Environmental Science (divested)
parts.what: A business the company sold, generating one-off exceptional income in FY2022-23; an earlier seeds divestment to Crystal did the same in FY2021-22 — both are gone from the ongoing business.

overview.what_it_does: Black Box is a global systems integrator for digital and IT infrastructure: it consults, designs, installs, manages and secures the networks, data centers, workplace technology and communications systems that large organizations run on, and it also sells its own branded IT hardware. Its customers are big enterprises and institutions — over 120 Fortune 500 names, including four of the top six hyperscalers, four of the top five US banks, major hospital systems, retailers, airports, manufacturers and US public-sector bodies — with the top 10 customers historically around 40% of revenue. It earns money mainly from integration projects (booked as an order backlog, about $800 million entering FY27, executed into revenue over time) plus recurring managed and support services, and from margin on the products it sells through resellers and integration partners. It operates in 35 countries across six continents from about 75 delivery centers with roughly 4,000+ staff, but the revenue is heavily North America-weighted (about 74%, with Europe ~10%, India ~7%, APAC ~5% as of FY22), delivered under a "think global, act local" model supported by a low-cost Center of Excellence/GCC in India; FY26 revenue was over INR 6,000 crore with an ambition to reach $2 billion by fiscal 2029-30, including via acquisitions such as the Brazilian integrator 2S.

parts.name: Global Solution Integration (GSI)
parts.what: The core services business — consulting, designing, deploying, managing and securing customers' technology infrastructure using best-of-breed partner equipment — described as about 80% of the company's business and the engine of its order book and backlog.

parts.name: Technology Product Solutions (TPS)
parts.what: Sells Black Box's own-brand and white-label IT products — signal switching, KVM, visualization, IoT, networking, infrastructure and connectivity gear — plus warranty and tech support, sold through integration partners and value-added resellers, and described as about 20% of the business.

parts.name: Data center solutions
parts.what: Builds and fits out data centers for hyperscalers, multi-tenant operators and large enterprises; management calls it the key growth driver, the main target of the INR 410 crore capital raise, and the source of the biggest recent order wins (though 2026 execution slipped on shortages of fiber, cables, GPUs, racks and power gear).

parts.name: Connectivity and network infrastructure
parts.what: Enterprise and campus networking, in-building connectivity, wireless and mobility including 5G/LTE, and edge networks — a long-standing core capability that management is expanding to carry rising data traffic for enterprises and data center operators.

parts.name: Modern/digital workplace and customer experience (CX)
parts.what: Collaboration, unified communications, connected buildings and contact-center/customer-experience systems — grouped with networking and managed services in deal-win disclosures (for example over $13 million of such wins in one quarter).

parts.name: Cybersecurity
parts.what: Securing customer IT and communication infrastructure; consistently named as one of the four solution pillars ("Connect, Network, Modernize, Secure") and an area of continued investment rather than a separately sized segment.

parts.name: Managed and professional services
parts.what: Ongoing support, on-demand and managed services for the systems it installs across roughly 5,000 active client sites, providing the recurring, mission-critical layer bundled with project work.

parts.name: 2S Inovações Tecnológicas (Brazil, announced Feb 2026)
parts.what: A 30-year-old Brazilian IT infrastructure and cybersecurity integrator and Cisco partner with about 650 customers, being acquired to build scale in Latin America and expected to add roughly INR 500 crore of revenue in FY27.

overview.what_it_does: The Bombay Burmah Trading Corporation (BBTC) is a very old Indian company (its 158th annual meeting was held in 2023) that runs a handful of small, unrelated operating businesses and also sits on large shareholdings in other companies. Its own operations are tea plantations in South India and Tanzania, a coffee plantation business (sold off during FY23), a factory business making auto electrical components, and a division selling dental products such as alloys to dental colleges and clinics. Revenue from these operations was about Rs.335 crores in FY2022-23 (Rs.374 crores the prior year), while on a consolidated basis sales were Rs.16,303 crores, up 14% — the difference coming almost entirely from its controlling stake in the biscuit maker Britannia, which is consolidated into its accounts and also pays it dividends (Rs.70 per share mentioned in FY23). It also holds stakes in other Wadia group companies, and its FY23 consolidated result was a loss of Rs.533 crores because it had to write off Rs.1,866 crores of exposure to associate airline Go Airlines (GoAir), which went into insolvency in May 2023.

parts.name: Tea (plantations)
parts.what: Grows and sells tea from estates in South India (Mudis is named) and in Tanzania; production was 37.38 lakh kilos in FY23 versus 41.72 lakh kilos the year before, with output swinging on weather, and it is one of the two oldest core operating businesses.

parts.name: Coffee (plantations)
parts.what: Grew and processed coffee (639 metric tonnes in FY23 plus 135 tonnes of bought coffee, sold at about Rs.280 a kilo), but management said returns were very low relative to the value of the land, and the business was divested for Rs.291 crores to pay down the company's secured debt.

parts.name: Auto electric components (Electro Mags)
parts.what: Makes and sells electrical components to the Indian and export auto-parts market, with turnover of Rs.151.7 crores in FY23 against Rs.133 crores in FY22 — the largest of the company's own operating divisions and the one management points to for growth.

parts.name: Healthcare / dental products
parts.what: Sells dental products, including alloys, to dental colleges and clinics; turnover rose to Rs.29.17 crores in FY23 from Rs.19.41 crores as COVID restrictions lifted, and better pricing made it notably more profitable — small in size but the fastest-growing division.

parts.name: Investments in group companies (Britannia, GoAir, National Peroxide)
parts.what: Holds shares in other companies — most importantly Britannia, whose consolidation and dividends dwarf everything else on the group's accounts; associate GoAir caused a Rs.1,866 crore consolidated impairment in FY23 after filing for insolvency, and National Peroxide became an associate that year.

parts.name: Land and property
parts.what: Owns land, including plantation estates, that it occasionally sells to raise cash — an equity land sale contributed Rs.80.77 crores of FY22 revenue — and shareholders repeatedly asked about the size and value of this land bank.

overview.what_it_does: Mrs. Bectors Food Specialities is an Indian packaged-food maker that bakes and sells two things: biscuits and cookies (mostly under the 'Cremica' brand) and bakery items like breads, buns, cookies and frozen/ready-to-eat desserts (mostly under the 'English Oven' brand, plus a clean-label 'NaturBaked' range). It earns money by manufacturing these in its own plants — biscuit plants at Rajpura and Indore, bakery plants at Kolkata, Khopoli/Mumbai, Bhiwadi and Noida — and selling them to Indian consumers through a distributor and salesman network across general trade, modern trade and quick commerce (Blinkit), to institutional buyers such as QSR chains, and to customers in more than 70 countries as exports. Revenue is driven by volume plus price/'premiumization', with input costs (wheat, palm oil, crude-linked packaging) and pricing power being the main swing factors on margin. The company grew from INR988 crores of revenue in FY22 to INR2,044 crores in FY26 (about 20% a year), earning an EBITDA margin of roughly 12-13% and a net profit of INR141 crores in FY26.

parts.name: Biscuits
parts.what: Makes and sells biscuits, crackers and cookies (Cremica brand, including Danish Butter Cookie tins and Diwali gifting packs) for the Indian market and for export; it is the larger of the two verticals — INR325 crores of the INR533 crores quarterly revenue in Q3 FY26 — and grew at about 20% a year over FY22-FY26.

parts.name: Bakery
parts.what: Makes and sells breads, buns, cakes, bakery cookies and frozen/ready-to-eat desserts, led by the English Oven brand; it is the smaller but faster-growing vertical — INR198 crores in Q3 FY26 and 14% growth in FY26 — and management reports it in two pieces, retail bakery and institutional.

parts.name: Retail Bakery (within Bakery)
parts.what: The branded, shop-shelf side of bakery sold to households under English Oven and NaturBaked, including health-led launches like Zero Maida and protein bread and premium items like Cheesecake Jars; management calls English Oven the key driver of bakery performance.

parts.name: Institutional Bakery (within Bakery)
parts.what: Supplies buns and bakery products in bulk to business customers, notably quick-service restaurant partnerships, which management cites as a source of sustained momentum for the bakery vertical.

parts.name: Exports / International business
parts.what: Sells biscuits and other products to more than 70 countries (Cremica alone in over 65), described as a strong performer that was hurt by 50% punitive US tariffs in FY26 and is expected to recover as tariffs drop to 18% under the India-US trade agreement.

parts.name: Sales, distribution and technology build-out
parts.what: Not a revenue segment but a repeatedly discussed engine of growth: adding hundreds of area distributor salesmen, doubling the North India distribution network while expanding into West, South and now East India, and rolling out salesforce (SFA) and distributor (DMS) management systems plus handheld billing devices.

parts.name: Capacity expansion / capex
parts.what: Ongoing plant building — new biscuit lines at Rajpura, a greenfield biscuit plant in Indore and greenfield bakery plants at Khopoli (Mumbai) and Kolkata — running at roughly INR350 crores in FY25, which management said could eventually support INR2,800-2,900 crores of sales at full utilisation, at an asset turn of about 2-2.5x for Khopoli after roughly three years.

parts.name: Project IMPACT
parts.what: A company-wide cost-structure and efficiency programme started in FY24 that management repeatedly points to as the main lever, alongside calibrated price increases, for protecting margins against raw material, packaging, fuel and minimum-wage inflation.

overview.what_it_does: Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) is an Indian government-owned company under the Ministry of Defence that designs, builds and supplies electronic systems used by the armed forces — radars, missile-system electronics, electronic warfare systems, military communication networks, naval fire-control and command-and-control systems, and land-navigation equipment. Almost all of its customers are Indian government buyers: the Army, Navy and Air Force via the Ministry of Defence, plus sister defence bodies such as DRDO (it calls itself DRDO's largest development-cum-production partner on Project Kusha) and Bharat Dynamics (Akash Prime), Indian shipbuilders that nominate BEL kit onto new warships, and a smaller stream of civilian government work such as an IT project for the Central Board of Indirect Taxes. It makes money by winning large, multi-year contracts, holding them as an order book (about INR 72,258 crores as on 1 July 2026) and converting that backlog into revenue over several years — FY26 revenue was INR 27,480 crores with profit after tax of INR 6,048 crores and EBITDA around 30%, and roughly 58-62% of sales goes on bought-in materials, including imported semiconductors. It operates entirely from India through some 29 Strategic Business Units and plants including Bangalore (registered office), Chennai, Ghaziabad, Palasamudram and Hyderabad-area facilities, with capability centres for research, software, unmanned systems and cyber security.

parts.name: Missile and weapon systems (LRSAM, Akash, QRSAM, Project Kusha)
parts.what: Supplies the electronics and subsystems for surface-to-air and other missile programmes — LRSAM alone contributed about INR 842 crores of execution in a single quarter, an Akash Prime order from BDL was flagged at around INR 4,000 crores, and management expects a QRSAM order plus a Kusha programme it sizes at INR 40,000-plus crores over time, making this the company's biggest single growth driver.

parts.name: Radars
parts.what: Builds ground, air-force and test-range radars such as Rudra (~INR 3,000 crores), Weapon Locating Radars (12 more approved, ~INR 1,000 crores) and an MPR radar for the ITR Chandipur test range; repeatedly named among the largest expected order categories each year.

parts.name: Electronic warfare (EW) systems
parts.what: Makes jamming and signal-intercept systems for land, air and naval use — the Himshakti land-based EW system (~INR 3,200 crores), a Mi-17 helicopter EW mid-life upgrade (~INR 1,500 crores) and Shakti naval EW deliveries (~INR 127 crores in one quarter); described as one of the recurring large-order lines.

parts.name: Communication and network systems
parts.what: Supplies military communication equipment and networks including AFNET for the Air Force, the CSS programme and shipborne communication sets for P-15B destroyers; management treats these as steady 'regular' orders that come in every year alongside the big projects.

parts.name: Command, control and network-centric systems (IACCS, CMS)
parts.what: Delivers large integration projects that tie sensors and weapons together, such as the Air Force's IACCS — a multi-year project still contributing about INR 132 crores of revenue in one quarter years after starting — and naval Combat Management Systems.

parts.name: Naval systems and shipborne equipment
parts.what: Acts as a 'buyer nominated' equipment supplier on new ship programmes (NGMV, NGOPV, MPV, CTS), each averaging roughly INR 2,500 crores of BEL content, plus standalone fire-control systems like Lynx-U2 (bid value around INR 2,500 crores, INR 95 crores executed in one quarter).

parts.name: Land systems and armoured-vehicle electronics
parts.what: Upgrades and supplies electronics for army vehicles — BMP-2 upgrade orders, T-90 stabiliser spares and a tank upgrade programme management pegged at about INR 2,000 crores.

parts.name: Advanced Land Navigation System (ALNS)
parts.what: A wholly in-house navigation product made at the Chennai unit, already delivered in Mark-I to the armed forces, with a Mark-II adding support for India's own NavIC/IRNSS satellite signals; order size not yet disclosed.

parts.name: Optronics and other standard defence products
parts.what: Smaller-ticket sighting and optical devices sold alongside communication gear; described as part of the routine, smaller-size order flow rather than the headline programmes.

parts.name: New-age technologies (drone electronics, AI, quantum, cyber security)
parts.what: An emerging area built with DRDO, start-ups, academia and in-house teams covering drone electronics, quantum key distribution and quantum-safe communication, backed by over INR 100 crores of computing capex in two years and another INR 100-200 crores in approval; still pre-revenue with proof-of-concepts given to defence users, but management expects higher margins from it.

parts.name: Services and annual maintenance contracts (AMC)
parts.what: Ongoing maintenance and support on installed systems, such as the Akash AMC, which management counts as part of the dependable base order flow every year.

parts.name: Civil / non-defence business
parts.what: Non-military government projects such as CBIT for the Central Board of Indirect Taxes (about INR 300 crores executed in one quarter); management guides to a minimum of around INR 500 crores of civil orders a year, i.e. a small add-on to the defence base.

parts.name: Component and third-party supply
parts.what: Occasional build-to-print work for outside customers, for example TR Modules supplied to Thales, mentioned as part of a quarter's order intake.

overview.what_it_does: Belrise Industries (formerly Badve Engineering, founded 1996, listed in May 2025) is an Indian auto-parts maker that builds the metal and plastic structural pieces vehicles are made of — chassis frames, body-in-white parts, exhaust systems, suspensions, steering columns and moulded plastic components — and sells them directly to vehicle manufacturers (OEMs) rather than to consumers. Its core skill is precision sheet-metal pressing, fabrication, robotic welding, coating and plastic moulding, and it earns money on a per-part basis under long-term OEM programs, often as the single-source supplier, with steel and plastic cost swings passed back to customers with a lag under a back-to-back pricing model. It serves 2-wheelers (its stronghold, ~24% share of Indian 2-wheeler metal components), plus 3-wheelers, cars, commercial vehicles and agri-vehicles, across roughly 22 plants in India (Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Uttarakhand and more) plus France, with quarterly revenue around INR 23–25.5 billion and PAT around INR 1.3 billion. Management's stated push is to move from being a parts vendor to a 'Tier-0.5' supplier delivering whole systems and sub-assemblies, raising rupee content per vehicle, while diversifying into solar structures and aerospace/defence.

parts.name: Two-wheeler metal components / chassis systems
parts.what: The historic core: pressed and fabricated metal chassis and frames for motorcycles and scooters, where Belrise is the largest Indian player at ~24% market share (roughly 1 in 4 chassis on Indian roads or exported from India), with content per 2-wheeler quoted at ~INR 12,500 in FY25 and said to have grown 65–70% during FY26.

parts.name: Four-wheeler and commercial vehicle components (BIW, cross car beams, long members)
parts.what: Body-in-white sheet-metal parts, cross car beams and high-tensile structural 'long members' for cars, SUVs and medium/heavy trucks — only ~12% of manufacturing revenue in FY25, but the declared growth priority, and management says 4-wheeler revenue grew 37% and CV 35% in FY26 with content per vehicle up 40–45% helped by the H-One addition.

parts.name: Polymer / plastic-moulded components
parts.what: Injection-moulded plastic parts, painting, aesthetic finishing and fairing assemblies for 2-wheelers, cars and even consumer-durables OEMs; Belrise alone holds ~10% share of Indian 2-wheeler plastics, rising to ~25% once promoter entities Badve Autocomps (FY25 revenue ~INR 14bn) and Eximius Infra Tech (~INR 7bn) merge in.

parts.name: Proprietary / premium products
parts.what: Self-designed higher-value items — suspensions, steering columns, braking systems, high-tensile parts, air tanks, filtration systems and premium exhausts — which management calls a key growth driver and where it says it added four new marquee customers each in suspensions, steering columns and high-tensile, and two in braking, during FY26.

parts.name: Aerospace and defence (Belrise Aerospace & Defence)
parts.what: A new, strategically emphasised arm built by acquiring SDM in France (Q3 FY26) and Chester Hall in the UK (Q4 FY26), now supplying two of the world's largest aircraft OEMs and their engine suppliers, plus a partnership with Israel's Plasan Sasa to bring the ATEMM platform to India; still loss-making (INR 94.7mn one-time operational loss in Q4 FY26) with SDM expected to turn EBITDA-positive in 2027.

parts.name: Non-auto engineering / renewable structures
parts.what: Fabricated solar mounting structures made with the same fabrication and surface-treatment lines, with first supplies begun in Q2 FY26 to a large global solar tracker maker for North America and talks on for India and Europe; described as small but fast-converting because of its short execution cycle.

parts.name: EV-related components
parts.what: Not a separate reported segment but repeatedly highlighted: over 73% of FY25 manufacturing revenue came from powertrain-agnostic products that fit both petrol and electric vehicles, plus specific EV wins — a single-source chassis and BIW package for a 2-wheeler EV platform out of Chennai (~INR 1,500mn at peak), a 3-wheeler EV suspension order, and copper bus bars for battery systems coming in via the Eximius merger.

parts.name: Non-manufacturing revenue
parts.what: In every quarter management quotes total revenue separately from a smaller 'manufacturing revenue' figure (e.g. INR 25,528mn total vs INR 21,763mn manufacturing in Q4 FY26), so roughly INR 4–5bn a quarter sits outside manufacturing and carries much thinner margins, but the excerpts never say what this activity is.

overview.what_it_does: BEML Limited is an Indian government-controlled engineering company (incorporated in 1964, with the Ministry of Defence holding about 54% of the shares) that designs, builds and services heavy machinery — mining and earthmoving equipment, rail coaches and metro trains, and military vehicles. Its customers are almost entirely large institutional buyers: Coal India and its subsidiaries for mining equipment, Indian Railways and city metro corporations (Delhi, Mumbai, Bangalore, Chennai, Kolkata, Jaipur) for rolling stock, and the Indian Army and Ministry of Defence for defence platforms. It makes money mainly by winning tenders and contracts to build and deliver equipment, plus a growing stream from spare parts, overhauling and annual maintenance contracts (management says about 20% of revenue is service revenue, which carries higher margins). It manufactures from complexes at Bengaluru, Kolar Gold Fields, Mysore and Palakkad (with a new rolling-stock plant at Bhopal), sells across India through regional and district offices, and exports to 73 countries — Africa is its biggest export market, followed by the Middle East — with an all-time-high export order booking of $107 million in FY26.

parts.name: Mining & Construction (M&C)
parts.what: Builds excavators, dump trucks, rope shovels, motor graders and other earthmoving equipment sold mostly to Coal India — it was 41% of FY26 revenue and the historic core of the company, but only 5-7% of the order book because these are quick-turnaround products, and management expects only 3-5% annual growth as Coal India shifts to contractor (MDO) mining.

parts.name: Rail & Metro (R&M)
parts.what: Makes metro cars, EMU and LHB rail coaches, the Vande Bharat sleeper train and track machines for Indian Railways and metro authorities — it is the biggest part of the order book (65-68%, of about Rs 16,000 crore) but only 24% of FY26 revenue because deliveries on orders won in 2022-24 are just starting, so management expects a large revenue jump as Bangalore, Chennai and Mumbai metro projects run in parallel.

parts.name: Defence & Aerospace (D&A)
parts.what: Supplies high-mobility trucks that carry missile, radar and command systems for the Indian Army (over 9,000 delivered since 1986), armoured recovery vehicles, BMP transmissions and aggregates, and newer items like mine-laying equipment and a light armoured vehicle — 35% of FY26 revenue, roughly 25-30% of the order book, and the fastest-growing vertical (revenue up from about Rs 1,000 crore to Rs 1,500 crore, with management guiding to 70-80% growth in FY26).

parts.name: Strategic Systems (new SBU)
parts.what: A newly created business unit reflecting BEML's shift from supplying just the truck to supplying complete defence systems — minefield marking equipment, self-propelled mine barriers and command post vehicles — several of which enter bulk production from FY27.

parts.name: Spares, service, overhaul and AMCs
parts.what: Sells replacement parts and maintenance on its large installed fleet (33,100 mining machines, 18,000 rail coaches, 9,000 defence vehicles delivered to date), described by management as about 20% of revenue with high margin and high growth, now being expanded through a hub-and-spoke warehouse model.

parts.name: Exports
