parts.what: Sells equipment overseas to 73 countries — mining equipment to West Asia, rolling stock to Africa, and business developing in CIS, SAARC and Asia-Pacific — with a record $107 million of export orders in FY26 and a pipeline including Tel Aviv Metro (~$250 million) and Dublin Metrolink (~$90 million).

parts.name: New diversification: maritime cranes and tunnel boring machines
parts.what: Two businesses BEML is entering from scratch using its existing fabrication and hydraulics skills — port and shipbuilding cranes, which management believes could eventually be worth Rs 4,000-5,000 crore of annual revenue, and 6.5-metre tunnel boring machines for metro projects, against an India requirement management pegs at about $5 billion over ten years; neither contributes meaningful revenue yet.

overview.what_it_does: Berger Paints India is an India-based paint and coatings maker that sells decorative paints for homes and buildings (emulsions, exterior and interior premium products, enamels, putty, distemper, primers, textures and wood coatings) plus waterproofing and construction chemicals, and industrial coatings for infrastructure, factories and vehicles. It makes money by manufacturing and selling these products through a very large dealer and retail network — management talks about adding roughly 2,000-2,200 retail touch points a quarter, installing 2,000-2,500 tinting 'colour bank' machines a quarter, and running more than 1,800 branded stores across the country — with growth driven by volume, periodic product price changes, and a shift in mix toward premium, higher-margin products. Management describes itself as the number two player in Indian decorative paints with a market share above 20%, running gross margins around 40-41% and an EBITDA margin guided to 15-17%. Beyond India it operates through overseas subsidiaries in Poland (Bolix) and Nepal (BJN), plus Indian subsidiaries and joint ventures in specialty, construction-chemical and automotive coatings.

parts.name: Decorative business
parts.what: The core business: paints for walls and homes sold to retail consumers and painters through dealers, running high single-digit volume growth in most quarters, with premium and luxury products growing double digits while mass products like putty, distemper, primer and enamel are flat or declining.

parts.name: Construction chemicals and waterproofing
parts.what: A fast-growing add-on range — waterproofing coatings, tile adhesives, admixtures, roof and damp-proofing products such as Roof Cool & Seal and DAMShield — which management repeatedly calls a strong double-digit grower and says now covers about 80-85% of the major products in the category.

parts.name: Wood coatings
parts.what: Paints and finishes for wood, consistently described as having robust performance and strong double-digit volume growth, though it is a smaller line than decorative paints.

parts.name: Protective and infrastructure coatings
parts.what: Industrial coatings sold to infrastructure and construction projects, where management says Berger holds a leadership position; it grew strongly when government infrastructure spending was high (FY25) but had gone muted by the December 2025 quarter.

parts.name: Automotive, general industrial and powder coatings
parts.what: Coatings sold to vehicle makers, appliance makers and other factories; growth was flat or muted through FY25 on weak two-wheeler and commercial-vehicle demand, and had turned steady by Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Bolix (Poland subsidiary)
parts.what: An overseas subsidiary in Poland doing project-linked exterior/insulation-type work, which delivered solid top-line growth throughout but saw profits dented by one-off project costs in FY25 before showing strong sales and operating profit growth in FY26.

parts.name: BJN Nepal (subsidiary)
parts.what: The Nepal paints subsidiary, which shrank during a local credit crunch in FY25, rebounded sharply afterwards and even paid a dividend up to the parent, then turned muted again in FY26 amid political disruption.

parts.name: STP Limited (subsidiary)
parts.what: A subsidiary in construction chemicals and admixtures whose results have been choppy — hurt by raw material costs and weak admixture sales in FY25, and by a temporary plant shutdown at Jamshedpur that normalised from January 2026.

parts.name: SBL Speciality Coatings (subsidiary)
parts.what: A smaller specialty coatings arm with mostly flat to modest growth, hit in FY26 by weak industrial demand, tariffs and start-up costs from a new factory near Chandigarh.

parts.name: Berger Becker Coatings (joint venture)
parts.what: A coatings joint venture that management consistently reports as delivering healthy or robust growth in both sales and profitability.

parts.name: Berger Nippon Paint Automotive Coatings (joint venture)
parts.what: A joint venture supplying coatings to the automotive industry, which moved from small top-line growth with strong profit gains in FY25 to strong double-digit revenue and profit growth in FY26 as auto demand improved.

overview.what_it_does: Bharat Forge is an India-based engineering manufacturer that forges, casts and machines metal parts — steel and aluminium — and increasingly sells finished systems rather than just components. Its parts go into commercial trucks (especially US Class 8 and Indian CVs), passenger cars, and a range of industrial end-markets such as oil and gas, aerospace, construction and mining equipment, renewable energy and hydraulics, sold mostly to large global OEMs and Tier-1 customers; alongside this it has built a defence business selling artillery guns, armoured vehicles, small arms, naval solutions and unmanned systems, largely on government orders. It makes money by winning long-term component programmes and order books and then supplying at volume, with the high-margin Indian operations (FY26 standalone revenue about INR 8,396 crores at roughly 27.5% EBITDA margin) doing far better than the thin-margin overseas plants. Operations span India (Pune/Mundhwa and other Indian units), Europe (a German steel forging business, CDP Bharat Forge, now being restructured) and the United States (an aluminium forging plant), with FY26 consolidated revenue of about INR 16,812 crores and EBITDA of INR 2,921 crores.

parts.name: Standalone / India forging and components business (Components Division)
parts.what: The core Indian forging and machining operation making automotive and industrial parts for domestic customers and for export; it is the profit engine of the group, roughly INR 8,396 crores of revenue in FY26 at about 27.5% EBITDA margin versus low-single-digit margins overseas.

parts.name: Automotive (commercial vehicle and passenger vehicle components)
parts.what: Parts for heavy trucks — notably North American Class 7/8 — and for passenger cars, including a record quarter of nearly INR 200 crores of car-component exports in FY23; it is the most cyclical piece, with North American truck revenue down 51% year-on-year in Q3 FY26 before the market bottomed out.

parts.name: Industrial / non-automotive exports (oil and gas, construction, mining, renewables)
parts.what: Non-auto forged and machined products sold to industrial customers worldwide; management repeatedly points to it as the diversifier that offsets auto weakness, and it grew 11% in Q3 FY26 while auto fell 13%.

parts.name: Aerospace
parts.what: Components for jet engine structures and landing systems supplied to global aircraft OEMs under long-term programmes; it went from 2% to over 10% of industrial export revenue between FY22 and FY23 and by Q4 FY26 was about 26% of non-auto exports, the second-largest contributor, with strong growth expected as new capacity comes online.

parts.name: Defence
parts.what: Artillery (including the ATAGS gun co-developed with DRDO), military vehicles, CQB carbines and small arms, naval solutions, drones and unmanned sea and air platforms, plus MRO and consumables; the order book was close to INR 11,000 crores as of FY26 with INR 2,816 crores of new defence orders won that year and management guiding to 30-40%+ growth in FY27.

parts.name: JSA (JS Auto) — castings business
parts.what: An Indian castings company acquired in mid-2022 for an enterprise value of INR 490 crores that supplies construction, mining, renewable-energy and hydraulics customers; it crossed the INR 1,000 crore sales mark, grew revenue 22% and EBITDA 39% in Q3 FY26, and Premji Invest took a 23% stake at a INR 1,300 crore valuation — three-and-a-half to four times the purchase price.

parts.name: K Drive
parts.what: A recently acquired Indian business whose top line has been muted but whose EBITDA margin improved from 3% to about 5% in Q3 FY26; it won roughly INR 500 crores of new OEM business in FY26 that starts flowing from the following year.

parts.name: European operations (CDP Bharat Forge — German steel forging)
parts.what: The European steel forging plants serving mostly European auto and industrial customers; they run at low utilisation (60-65%) and thin margins (FY26 revenue INR 3,865 crores at 4% EBITDA) and are now being formally restructured, a process expected to finish by end of the next calendar year.

parts.name: US aluminium forging operations
parts.what: A newer American plant making specialty aluminium chassis components for EV, hybrid and high-end passenger car, pickup and SUV programmes; it started up in 2022 with losses of over USD 1 million a month, and by FY26 had turned to INR 1,534 crores of revenue and INR 54 crores of EBITDA (3.5% margin), though US aluminium tariffs are hurting demand and profitability.

parts.name: E-mobility (including Tork Motors)
parts.what: Electric-vehicle components, subsystems and powertrains plus a stake of over INR 150 crores in electric two-wheeler maker Tork Motors; management impaired the Tork investment in FY25 after funding fell through and wrote off further e-mobility investments in FY26 as global EV adoption took a different path.

parts.name: Fortuna Engineering (30% stake, machining)
parts.what: A Nashik-based machining company in which Bharat Forge bought a 30% stake in May 2026; it machines connecting rods and other high-value parts, letting Bharat Forge feed its own forgings into their machining lines.

overview.what_it_does: Bharti Airtel is an Indian telecom operator that sells mobile phone service, home broadband and TV, and communications services to businesses, in India (including through its listed subsidiary Bharti Hexacom) and across Africa. It makes money mainly from monthly/prepaid subscription fees from hundreds of millions of retail customers — management tracks average revenue per user (ARPU), which rose from Rs.183 in mid-2022 to Rs.259 by late 2025 — plus contracts with enterprises and government bodies, and fees from newer digital businesses like payments, lending, data centres and cloud. It runs the underlying network itself, spending heavily on spectrum licences, mobile towers/5G sites and fibre, which makes it capital-intensive but high-margin (FY2026 EBITDAaL margin ~51%). FY2026 consolidated revenue was about Rs.2,11,000 crores, split roughly India mobile 52%, Africa 29%, India non-mobile 13% and Indus (passive tower infrastructure) 6%.

parts.name: Mobility (India mobile)
parts.what: Prepaid and postpaid mobile voice and data, now including 5G (181 million 5G customers and ~74% population coverage by Q3 FY2026) plus international roaming; the single largest business at about 52% of group revenue, with growth coming from feature-phone-to-smartphone and prepaid-to-postpaid upgrades and periodic tariff increases.

parts.name: Homes / broadband
parts.what: Fixed home internet delivered both by fibre-to-the-home and fixed wireless access (FWA), available in 1,300+ cities; a consistent growth engine — 13 million connected homes and a record 1.2 million net adds in the December 2025 quarter, with FWA alone over 3 million customers.

parts.name: Digital TV (DTH) and IPTV
parts.what: Satellite pay-TV plus a fast-growing IPTV service bundled with broadband under the 'Airtel Black' converged plans; the DTH industry has been shrinking under regulation and free content, so management is now prioritising profitable growth here while IPTV carries the growth.

parts.name: Airtel Business (B2B)
parts.what: Connectivity and IT services sold to companies and government — leased lines, SD-WAN and secure networking (e.g. a multi-year deal as the Central Board of Direct Taxes' connectivity partner), plus CPaaS messaging, IoT connections, cyber security and cloud; described by management as 'a jewel in the portfolio' and India's #1 B2B player, though revenue growth has been lumpy and the global/wholesale piece was muted through 2024.

parts.name: Airtel Payments Bank
parts.what: A digital bank/fintech for everyday payments and deposits, called the only profitable fintech player in India; grew from 44.4 million monthly transacting users and a Rs.1,100 crore revenue run-rate in 2022 to about 120 million users, a ~Rs.3,400 crore run-rate and Rs.4,600 crore of deposits by Q4 FY2026.

parts.name: Airtel Finance / Airtel Money (lending)
parts.what: Consumer lending built on Airtel's customer data and app, run for three years as a loan service provider (partnering with lenders) at a monthly disbursement run-rate over Rs.550 crores; subsidiary Airtel Money Limited received RBI approval as a non-deposit-taking NBFC and is moving to commercial launch — one of three named 'new growth bets'.

parts.name: Nxtra (data centres)
parts.what: The group's data-centre arm, targeting 1 gigawatt of capacity over the next few years and raising $1 billion from outside investors alongside Airtel; also the flagship for the company's renewable-energy and ESG claims.

parts.name: Airtel Cloud
parts.what: A 'telco-grade sovereign cloud' offering launched as the third new growth bet — early stage, with 24 customer deals signed by end-FY2026 and more in the pipeline.

parts.name: Africa operations (Airtel Africa)
parts.what: Mobile, data and Airtel Money services across African markets, about 29% of group revenue and growing faster than India in constant currency; the board approved a share swap to buy an additional 16.3% stake, with the growth case resting on low tele-density (~45%), ~52% smartphone penetration and a young population.

parts.name: Indus Towers / passive infrastructure
parts.what: The shared mobile-tower (passive infrastructure) business, reported separately and roughly 6% of group revenue; management usually quotes India numbers 'excluding passive infra' so the underlying service business is comparable.

overview.what_it_does: Bharti Hexacom is an Indian telecom operator listed on the NSE and BSE (symbol BHARTIHEXA, IPO completed shortly before the May 2024 call) that runs under the Airtel brand and reports alongside Bharti Airtel on the same joint quarterly earnings calls, with offices in Gurugram and New Delhi. Per those calls it sells connectivity services to Indian consumers and businesses: prepaid and postpaid mobile plans (including 5G), home broadband over fiber and fixed-wireless access, television service via DTH and now IPTV, and enterprise/B2B connectivity sold as 'Airtel Business'. It makes money mainly from recurring monthly subscriptions and usage — management tracks it as ARPU (average revenue per user, quoted as Rs.209 in Q4 FY2024 rising to Rs.259 by Q3 FY2026) multiplied by a customer base that grows through net adds, plus enterprise contracts — and profitability is discussed as EBITDA/EBITDAaL margin against heavy network capex on towers, 5G sites and fiber. Note that the calls are shared Airtel-plus-Hexacom events and nearly all figures quoted are Airtel's India or consolidated numbers; the transcripts never break out Hexacom's own revenue, geography or customer count separately.

parts.name: Mobility / mobile business
parts.what: Prepaid and postpaid mobile voice and data, including a 5G network that management says reached 181 million 5G customers and about 74% population coverage by Q3 FY2026; described on the calls as the largest piece, with India mobile at 56% of Airtel's consolidated revenue in FY2025 and 52% in FY2026.

parts.name: Homes / broadband
parts.what: Fixed home internet delivered both by fiber to the home (FTTH) and fixed wireless access (FWA), with over 13 million connected homes and over 3 million FWA customers by Q3 FY2026 — a fast-growing segment management repeatedly calls a strategic priority where it 'needs to raise its game'.

parts.name: Digital TV (DTH and IPTV)
parts.what: Pay-television service, historically satellite DTH — an industry facing 'macro headwinds' where the company has stopped subsidising set-top boxes — now increasingly IPTV delivered over its own broadband, adding roughly 73,000–76,000 customers a quarter and used to bundle TV with internet ('convergence').

parts.name: Airtel Business (B2B / enterprise)
parts.what: Connectivity and network services sold to companies, including global capacity from subsea cables landed in FY2025; revenue of about Rs.5,316 crore in Q4 FY2025 and Rs.5,350 crore in Q3 FY2026, and deliberately shrunk for a period as management exited 'commoditized low margin' work.

parts.name: Digital businesses / new growth bets
parts.what: A smaller portfolio of newer services — Airtel Cloud (a 'telco-grade sovereign cloud' with 24 deals signed in FY2026), cybersecurity, IoT and CPaaS — described by management as early-stage but receiving additional investment.

parts.name: Financial services (Airtel Payments Bank, Airtel Money)
parts.what: Digital payments and lending: the Payments Bank had about 120 million monthly transacting users, roughly Rs.3,400 crore annualised revenue and over Rs.4,600 crore of deposits by Q4 FY2026, and subsidiary Airtel Money received RBI approval to operate as a non-deposit-taking NBFC, with loan disbursements running over Rs.550 crore a month.

parts.name: Data centres (Nxtra)
parts.what: A data-centre business targeting 1 gigawatt of capacity over the next few years, which raised $1 billion from outside investors alongside Airtel in FY2026; still small relative to connectivity but named one of three priority 'adjacencies'.

parts.name: Passive infrastructure (Indus Towers) and Airtel Africa
parts.what: Group-level items that appear in the consolidated numbers discussed on these calls — the tower business Indus at about 6-7% of revenue and African mobile operations at 24-29% — though the calls give no indication these belong to Hexacom itself rather than to Bharti Airtel.

overview.what_it_does: BHEL is an Indian engineering and manufacturing company that designs, builds, supplies and installs the heavy equipment used to generate and move electricity — boilers, turbines and generators for coal-fired thermal plants, hydro and nuclear equipment, and pollution-control kit like flue gas desulphurisation (FGD) systems — mostly for large government-owned power utilities such as NTPC and NPCIL, state power companies, and private groups like Adani. It earns money by winning large, multi-year tenders (either full EPC turnkey projects or narrower BTG/equipment packages), booking revenue as project milestones are met, and it supplements this with a higher-margin, short-cycle spares and services business (around Rs 3,500-3,800 crores of orders a year). Alongside power, it runs an 'Industry' business selling railway propulsion systems and locomotives, Vande Bharat train sets, naval guns and defence equipment, transmission gear (transformers, substations, HVDC), industrial motors, compressors and captive power plants. It operates mainly across India with some exports — projects in Bangladesh, Mauritius and gas turbine parts to UAE — and carried an order book of about Rs 1,31,600 crores as of 1 April 2024 against annual revenue of roughly Rs 24,000 crores.

parts.name: Power Sector
parts.what: Supplies and erects thermal (coal), hydro and nuclear power plant equipment, including full EPC projects, BTG packages, FGD emission-control systems and renovation & modernisation (R&M) work; it is the larger half of the company — Rs 92,559 crores of the Rs 1,31,600 crore order book at April 2024, and Rs 52,000 crores (9.6 GW) of new thermal orders in FY24 alone.

parts.name: Thermal (coal) power equipment
parts.what: The company's self-described core business and where it claims market leadership with essentially one domestic competitor, covering 660 MW and 800 MW supercritical units at sites like Talcher, Talabira, Yamuna Nagar, Singrauli, Lara, Mahan and Raigarh; management sees roughly 10-12 GW of ordering a year for the next several years.

parts.name: Hydro
parts.what: Supplies turbines, generators and the electro-mechanical package for hydro projects — about 1 GW of orders in FY23 including the 850 MW Ratle project, plus the 2.8 GW Dibang package (over Rs 2,600 crores), described as the country's largest.

parts.name: Nuclear
parts.what: Supplies equipment to NPCIL for atomic power projects (Kakrapar Unit 3 capacity addition); management calls it cyclical with no major package ordered in FY23, but flags it alongside hydro as a major long-term area.

parts.name: Industry Sector (Industrial Systems & Products)
parts.what: The non-power half — transportation, defence, transmission and industrial products — which booked its highest-ever order inflow of about Rs 22,000 crores in FY24 (Rs 9,537 crores in FY23, the highest in 13 years) and currently runs at roughly 30-35% of order intake, with management targeting a 50:50 split with power over the long term.

parts.name: Transportation / Railways
parts.what: Makes electric locomotives, traction motors, transformers and IGBT-based three-phase propulsion and control systems for Indian Railways and metros; its largest-ever single order is 80 Vande Bharat train sets worth about Rs 23,500 crores (won with Titagarh Wagons, BHEL doing electrics, control systems and bogies), executed over 6+ years with a 35-year maintenance tail where much of the profit is expected.

parts.name: Defence
parts.what: Supplies Super Rapid Gun Mounts (the main gun on Indian warships — 38 guns ordered in 18 months versus 44 in the prior 30 years), plus bids on air defence guns, marine gas turbines, confidential strategic naval equipment and compact heat exchangers for the LCA Tejas; management calls it a major growth area, often partnered with European OEMs.

parts.name: Transmission
parts.what: Sells extra-high-voltage substations (400 kV and 765 kV), power transformers, GIS/AIS equipment and, increasingly, HVDC systems with an international partner; management calls HVDC the high-value, steady-margin piece and names it one of three priority industry areas.

parts.name: Spares and Services
parts.what: Sells replacement parts and servicing on the installed base of plants — highest-ever bookings of over Rs 3,800 crores in FY23 and about Rs 3,500 crores in FY24, with 25%+ revenue growth; management describes these as short-duration, high-margin orders expected to lift profitability.

parts.name: Industrial products and captive power
parts.what: Supplies industrial motors, compressors (including centrifugal compressors for refineries), CFBC boilers, steam turbine-generator packages and captive power plants to steel, cement and refinery customers — seven STG packages totalling 383 MW were booked in FY23.

parts.name: New growth / diversification areas
parts.what: A cluster of newer bets: coal gasification using BHEL's in-house PFBG technology suited to high-ash Indian coal (a JV and 2,000 TPD coal-to-ammonium-nitrate plant with Coal India), flexible operations retrofits for existing coal plants, solar EPC (100 MW Raghanesda, 8 MW Mauritius), battery energy storage, hydrogen, railway signalling and Industry 4.0 remote monitoring — all small today but positioned as the path to a bigger non-thermal business.

parts.name: Exports / International
parts.what: A small slice of orders — the remainder after power and industry in FY23 — covering overseas projects such as the 660 MW Maitree plant in Bangladesh, a Mauritius solar project, and gas turbine rotors and parts sold to UAE.

overview.what_it_does: Bikaji Foods International is an Indian packaged-food maker that sells traditional Indian salty snacks and sweets under its own "Bikaji" brand, a family business rooted in Bikaner, Rajasthan and descended from the original Haldiram's lineage. It makes and sells bhujia and other namkeen, papad, packaged sweets, western-style snacks like chips and extruded snacks, and frozen foods, sold to ordinary consumers through kirana shops, modern trade and increasingly e-commerce/quick-commerce. Money comes from manufacturing these products in its own plants (Bikaner, Guwahati, Muzaffarpur, Tumkur, Kanpur and contract units) and pushing them through a distributor network — roughly 3.5 lakh outlets reached directly and about 1.4 million outlets in total — supported by heavy TV, digital and celebrity advertising. FY26 revenue was about INR 2,994 crores; its core markets are Rajasthan, Bihar and Assam (historically ~70% of sales), with Uttar Pradesh, Delhi/NCR, Punjab, Haryana, Gujarat, Karnataka and Telangana as focus states, plus exports to 25+ countries that crossed INR 100 crores for the first time in FY26.

parts.name: Ethnic Snacks (namkeen / bhujia)
parts.what: The core business — Bikaneri bhujia and other traditional Indian savoury snacks, where management says Bikaji is the largest bhujia manufacturer in India; it is by far the biggest segment at roughly 65-70% of sales and grew in the low-to-mid teens in recent quarters.

parts.name: Packaged Sweets
parts.what: Branded Indian mithai such as kaju katli and ladoo, roughly 13% of sales, heavily tied to the Diwali festive quarter and to gifting, so its growth swings between Q2 and Q3 depending on when Diwali falls; the company is adding sweets capacity.

parts.name: Western Snacks
parts.what: Chips, extruded snacks and similar non-traditional snack formats, about 9% of sales and one of the faster-growing lines at 20%+ growth in recent quarters.

parts.name: Papad
parts.what: Handmade papad, where management calls itself the second-largest maker in India after Lijjat, employing over 5,000 women monthly; small at about 5% of sales but growing at high-teens to mid-20s rates.

parts.name: Others (incl. frozen food)
parts.what: Frozen and miscellaneous items at roughly 2.5-2.6% of sales; frozen capability (built partly through Ariba Foods) is described as especially important for the export markets.

parts.name: Exports
parts.what: Sales to 25+ countries, only ~2.6% of revenue back in FY23 but growing at strong double digits and crossing INR 100 crores for the first time in FY26, with management expecting similar growth for the next 2-3 years.

parts.name: Hazelnut Factory (investment)
parts.what: A separately branded business the company invested about INR 131 crores into for a stake rising to roughly 48%; it crossed INR 100 crores of revenue in FY26 and is targeted to grow 50-60% a year.

parts.name: Bikaji Bakes (JV)
parts.what: A newly formed bakery joint venture, 70% Bikaji and 30% Middle East bakery veteran T. K. Khaleel, described as a small, futuristic bet management thinks could become a INR 100 crore business.

parts.name: Family packs vs impulse packs
parts.what: Not a product category but how management splits sales by pack size — large family packs are about 60%+ of the business and the growth priority (grew 20% in Q4 FY26), while smaller impulse packs lag.

parts.name: E-commerce / Quick-commerce
parts.what: Online and quick-delivery channel sales, which reached about 3% of overall business in FY26 after roughly doubling, with a similar doubling targeted again.

overview.what_it_does: Biocon is an India-based biopharmaceutical company, headquartered in Bangalore and listed on the BSE and NSE, that makes affordable versions of expensive medicines and sells them worldwide. It earns money three ways: selling biosimilars (lower-cost copies of complex biologic drugs such as insulins, ustekinumab, denosumab, bevacizumab, trastuzumab and aflibercept) to markets including the US, Europe, Canada and emerging markets; selling generic drugs, both bulk active ingredients (APIs like statins and immunosuppressants) and finished formulations (including GLP-1 peptides such as liraglutide and semaglutide); and providing contract research and manufacturing services to other drug companies through its listed subsidiary Syngene. It manufactures at its own plants in Bangalore and Visakhapatnam, which are inspected by regulators such as the US FDA, UK MHRA and Brazil's ANVISA, and sells either directly in key countries or through local partners elsewhere. Group operating revenue was around INR 4,173 crores in the quarter ending December 2025 (up 9% year-on-year), and in 2025-26 it merged its biosimilars arm, Biocon Biologics, into the parent to run as a single listed biopharma company.

parts.name: Biosimilars (Biocon Biologics)
parts.what: Develops, manufactures and sells lower-cost copies of biologic drugs — insulins, and oncology, immunology, bone-health and eye-care biologics — across the US, Europe, Canada and emerging markets; it is by far the largest part of the group, at INR 2,756 crores of revenue in the January-March 2026 quarter and the main driver of group growth and margin improvement.

parts.name: Generics
parts.what: Makes and sells bulk active pharmaceutical ingredients (statins, immunosuppressants) and finished generic pills and injectables, increasingly focused on GLP-1 peptides like liraglutide and semaglutide for diabetes and obesity; it is the second-largest segment (about INR 659 crores of revenue in the June 2024 quarter) and swings between price-erosion pressure and strong growth from new launches.

parts.name: Research Services / CRDMO (Syngene International)
parts.what: A separately listed subsidiary that does contract research, development and manufacturing for other pharmaceutical companies; it is the smallest of the three segments and has recently been the weak spot, declining 3% year-on-year in the December 2025 quarter and growing only 2% in the March 2026 quarter.

overview.what_it_does: Birla Corporation is a more than 100-year-old Indian company, part of the MP Birla Group, whose main business today is making and selling cement — management describes it as roughly a 20 million tonne capacity company, going to 27.5 million tonnes once its Maihar Line-II and linked grinding units come up around FY29. It makes money by mining limestone and manufacturing cement at integrated plants and grinding units, then selling it mostly through dealers to individual house-builders (the 'trade' segment, 77% of volumes in FY26) rather than to bulk industrial buyers ('non-trade'), with a deliberate tilt toward higher-margin blended cement (88% of volumes in FY26) over plain OPC, sold under brands positioned at premium (Perfect Plus), mid (Samrat Advanced) and popular price points. Its plants and markets are concentrated in Central India (Maihar in MP, Kundanganj in eastern UP), the North (Chanderia in Rajasthan, its single biggest unit) and Maharashtra/Vidarbha (Mukutban), with only a very small presence in the East. Profitability swings with regional cement prices, freight (average lead distance 337 km in FY26), fuel costs (pet coke, diesel) and state incentive accruals; FY26 volumes grew about 4% with EBITDA near INR 800 a tonne, and net debt was about INR 2,300 crore as of June 2026.

parts.name: Cement
parts.what: The overwhelming bulk of the business and essentially all of what management discusses on these calls — manufacturing and branded selling of cement across Central India, the North and Maharashtra, with capacity of about 20 million tonnes rising to a planned 27.5 million tonnes by FY29.

parts.name: Jute
parts.what: The company's original business — management says it runs the first Indian jute mill, still operating, and is one of the largest players in the jute sector, but the MD explicitly says it is 'not the real focus' for investors, implying it is small relative to cement.

parts.name: Mukutban (Maharashtra/Vidarbha operations)
parts.what: A newer plant in a market where the company had no prior presence, ramped from cash-negative to a profit and growth engine — volumes rose to 27.7 lakh tonnes in FY26 at capacity utilisation in the high 60s, though it sells at lower net realisations than the older markets.

parts.name: RCCPL Private Limited (the acquired Reliance cement business)
parts.what: The cement business bought from Reliance in 2016 — the Maihar integrated plant and Kundanganj grinding unit — which roughly doubled capacity, was rebranded into Perfect Plus, and is run as a subsidiary with its own CFO; management treats its successful integration and premium repositioning as the company's proof point.

parts.name: Trade vs non-trade / blended vs OPC mix
parts.what: Not separate legal segments but the split management manages the business by — it deliberately concentrates on dealer (trade) sales of blended, value-added, premium-branded cement and has de-focused OPC and industrial sales, which helped in FY25–FY26 but hurt in Q1 FY27 when price increases came through in non-trade and OPC instead.

parts.name: Wider MP Birla Group activities
parts.what: Mentioned as context rather than as part of the listed company's earnings — other group companies in cables and guar gum, plus social-sector institutions such as Bombay Hospital, Belle Vue Clinic, South Point School and the Birla Planetarium.

overview.what_it_does: BlackBuck (legally Zinka Logistics Solutions Ltd, renamed BlackBuck Limited) runs India's largest digital platform for truck owners — mostly small operators who own fewer than five trucks in a highly fragmented, largely unorganised trucking market. Through its mobile app, backed by an offline network of more than 10,000 touchpoints (salespeople, technicians, channel partners such as garages and lubricant shops, and call centres), it sells truckers a bundle of services: toll and fuel payments, GPS and mandate-driven vehicle tracking devices, fuel sensors, digital fleet documents, help finding loads, and loans. It earns money from subscription fees collected upfront from customers, from commissions/spreads on the payments flowing through the platform (about ₹6,800 crore of payment GTV in a single quarter), from selling telematics hardware and services, and from lending. It operates only in India, served about 8.2–8.5 lakh monthly transacting truck operators (roughly a quarter to 30% of the country's ~3.5 million truck operators) and reported FY26 total income of about ₹715 crore, up 55%, with ₹190 crore EBITDA and ₹160 crore PAT — its first full year of profit.

parts.name: Core businesses
parts.what: The established, cash-generating half of the company — payments/tolling plus telematics — which grew about 30–34% in FY26 and funds the investment in the newer lines.

parts.name: Payments (tolling and fuel payments)
parts.what: Lets truckers pay tolls and buy fuel digitally through the app; management calls it a core revenue lever, with toll GTV up 27% in FY26 versus industry growth of about 16%, so its market share keeps rising.

parts.name: Telematics
parts.what: Sells and services vehicle-tracking hardware — basic GPS, regulator-mandated AIS tracking devices, and fuel sensors — described as the second core vertical, with record incremental sales in Q3 FY26 and AIS unit sales doubling in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Growth (newer) businesses
parts.what: The loss-making, heavily invested expansion bucket made up of Superloads and vehicle finance; small in absolute terms but growing roughly 271% year-on-year in Q3 FY26 and about 300% in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Superloads
parts.what: A load-matching business connecting cargo with truckers, still in what management calls the playbook-building phase — expanded from four cities to nine and then to ten new cities on top of the original Bangalore and Hyderabad hubs, with the newer cities scaling faster than the first ones.

parts.name: Vehicle finance
parts.what: Lends to truck operators to buy vehicles; the older of the two growth businesses, with disbursals up 30% and then a further 25% in consecutive quarters, and management expects it to stop consuming cash and start generating it by the end of FY27.

parts.name: The BlackBuck app (platform) and distribution
parts.what: Not a revenue line but the two assets management calls the crown jewel and the moat — truckers spend about 45 minutes a day in the app, and the 10,000-plus offline touchpoints mean each new offering can be launched at close to zero incremental cost; both were largely built out before FY24.

overview.what_it_does: BLS International is an Indian-listed outsourcing company that runs the paperwork side of government services. Its main business is visa and consular work: foreign governments hire it to set up and run visa application centres, where it collects applications, documents and biometrics from travellers on the government's behalf, plus related services like passport, attestation and apostille work; it earns a service fee on each application (net revenue per application was about INR3,302 in FY26, on 44.1 lakh applications), so revenue rises with travel volumes, new contract wins and higher service charges. Its second business, called Digital Services, works mainly inside India: acting as a 'business correspondent' for banks (opening accounts and handling deposits, transfers and passbook updates in mostly rural areas through a network of local agents), distributing loans, and running citizen-service and e-governance projects such as Aadhaar enrolment centres for state governments and UIDAI. It operates in 80+ countries for more than 40 client governments, on an asset-light model of ~155,000 touch points and ~45,800 channel partners. In FY26 it reported revenue of INR2,998 crores and profit after tax of INR724 crores, with visa and consular contributing INR1,840 crores of revenue and digital INR1,158 crores.

parts.name: Visa & Consular Services
parts.what: Sets up and operates visa application centres and related consular services (attestation, apostille) for client governments worldwide, charging a fee per application; it is the profit engine — INR1,840 crores of FY26 revenue at a 40% EBITDA margin, versus roughly 80-85% of total revenue back in FY23, and it grew via the INR720 crore acquisition of Turkey-based iDATA and wins like a 5-year Slovak Republic contract covering 80+ countries and Indian visa centres in China for India's Ministry of External Affairs.

parts.name: Digital Services (reported segment, run partly through listed subsidiary BLS E-Services)
parts.what: The umbrella for the India-facing businesses — banking correspondent work, loan distribution and citizen/e-governance services — which more than doubled to INR1,158 crores of revenue in FY26 (EBITDA INR81 crores) and is now the faster-growing but much lower-margin half of the company.

parts.name: Business Correspondent (BC) banking business
parts.what: Acts as the outsourced last-mile arm for banks — opening accounts and processing deposits, transfers and passbook updates through local agents (CSPs) in areas banks don't cover — built on the 2022 purchase of an 88.71% stake in Zero Mass Private Limited (SBI's largest BC) for an enterprise value of INR135 crores; it handled gross transaction value of over INR1.1 lakh crores in FY26 and has crossed INR10,000 crores of aggregate balances in accounts it opened.

parts.name: Loan distribution (Aadifidelis)
parts.what: A loan lead-generation and distribution business added by buying a 55% controlling stake in Aadifidelis Loan Solutions, with 8,600+ channel partners; it generated loan leads worth more than INR36,800 crores in FY26 and is cross-sold alongside the banking correspondent network.

parts.name: Citizen / e-governance services
parts.what: Runs government-facing service counters and registration projects under contract — early examples were nine registration projects for the West Bengal government and 4,000 offices for Karnataka, and more recently a INR100 crore Aadhaar Permanent Enrolment Centre project for Bihar plus a roughly INR2,000 crore UIDAI mandate to upgrade Seva Kendras; it was described in FY23 as part of the 15-20% of revenue outside visa, and is now folded into the Digital segment.

overview.what_it_does: Blue Dart Express is an Indian courier and express delivery company: it picks up parcels, documents and freight from businesses and delivers them across India on a time-definite basis, using its own combined air and ground network. Its customers are mostly businesses — large corporates, SMEs and e-commerce sellers shipping to consumers — with demand spread across metros and increasingly Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns. It makes money by charging per shipment or per kilo (air shipments fetch a higher realisation per kilo than ground, though margins are broadly comparable), and it pushes through an annual general price increase, typically effective 1st January, to offset inflation; fuel is a major cost, since jet fuel (ATF) and diesel prices flow straight into its cost base. In FY2026 it reported revenue of about INR 6,141 crore and profit after tax of about INR 240 crore, moving roughly 1.44 million tonnes and about 404 million shipments in the year.

parts.name: Air Express (including documents and time-definite air products)
parts.what: Overnight/time-critical delivery of documents and lighter, urgent packages flown on the company's own aircraft; air is the larger half of the business at roughly 60% of revenue in FY2026, but management describes these traditional products as growing more slowly than the rest.

parts.name: Ground / Surface Express (B2B)
parts.what: Business-to-business shipments moved by road rather than air, typically heavier consignments at a lower price per kilo; management puts it at around 28.6% of revenue in the December 2025 quarter and says it normally runs near 30%, and calls ground a key growth driver.

parts.name: E-commerce (B2C) — split into e-com air and e-com light surface
parts.what: Delivery of online-shopping parcels to consumers, either flown or moved as light packages on the ground network; it is roughly 30-31% of revenue and the main driver of both shipment and tonnage growth, with the light-surface piece growing much faster than the air piece.

parts.name: International
parts.what: Cross-border shipments, mentioned only as one of the smaller 'other products' that continues to grow but at a slower rate than e-commerce and surface.

parts.name: Own air fleet (aviation capacity)
parts.what: The company runs its own dedicated freighter aircraft — six Boeing 757-200s giving about 500 tonnes of capacity per night as of 2022, with two 737-800s being added to lift capacity 15-20% — which is what allows the overnight air product and also exposes earnings directly to jet fuel prices.

parts.name: Hubs and ground infrastructure
parts.what: Sorting and linehaul facilities that tie the network together, including a new 'green integrated hub' at Pataudi, Haryana serving North India and a consolidated ground hub at Gurgaon that handles both B2B surface and e-com light surface volumes; capex is described as mostly replacement and renewal with some expansion.

overview.what_it_does: Blue Jet Healthcare is an India-based contract development and manufacturing company (CDMO) that makes the chemical building blocks — "intermediates" and active ingredients — that other companies use to make finished medical products, rather than selling anything to patients itself. Its customers are large global innovator companies: the four dominant makers of contrast media (the injectable dyes used in X-ray/CT and MRI scans), big pharma and smaller biotech firms, and the "who's who" of the beverage, oral-care and pharma industries who buy its artificial sweetener. It earns money by manufacturing to order under long-term supply contracts and customer lock-ins, mostly for export, with revenue of INR 947 crores in FY26 and gross margins in the low-50% range. It operates from Navi Mumbai with plants at Shahad (Unit 1), Ambernath (Unit 2, US FDA approved) and Mahad (Unit 3), a new ~100-acre greenfield site coming up at Vizag (~INR 1,000 crores over about three years) and R&D centres including a planned one in Hyderabad.

parts.name: Contrast media intermediates
parts.what: Supplies advanced building blocks for the iodinated dyes used in X-ray/CT scans (plus newer gadolinium-based ones for MRI) to the four global players who control ~75% of that market; it is the largest and currently best-performing segment at INR 495 crores in FY26, up 23% year-on-year, with 3-4 new product launches expected in FY27.

parts.name: Pharma intermediates and APIs (PI/API, the CDMO/CRAMS business)
parts.what: Develops and manufactures intermediates and active ingredients for innovator drug companies from lab bench to commercial bulk scale, focused on chronic therapies — its big earner has been an intermediate for a cardiovascular drug, and the segment swung from a growth driver to INR 298 crores in FY26 (down 35%) because the customer was working off excess inventory, with ~20 active RFPs including GLP-1 and peptide-linked programs in the pipeline.

parts.name: High-intensity sweeteners (HIS)
parts.what: A legacy business of more than three decades making saccharin — the cheapest, zero-calorie sugar substitute — in a US FDA-approved plant with about 3,500-4,000 tonnes of capacity, roughly 10% of world capacity; historically about 20% of the top line, it contributed INR 131 crores in FY26 (down 2%, with pricing pressure), and a new sweetener product is being readied for trial batches in FY27.

overview.what_it_does: Blue Star Limited is an Indian air-conditioning and refrigeration company that both makes cooling products and installs cooling and electrical systems inside buildings. On the consumer side it sells room air conditioners, water coolers/purifiers and commercial refrigeration products (like deep freezers) through a dealer network; on the business side it sells commercial air-conditioning equipment — ducted systems, VRF systems, scroll and screw chillers — and takes on contracted electro-mechanical projects for offices, factories, data centres, hospitals, malls, metro rail, railways, water and power infrastructure. Money comes partly from selling equipment it manufactures at plants such as Wada and Sri City, and partly from executing project orders booked into a carried-forward order book (Rs 6,923 cr as of March 31, 2026). It is primarily an India business but also exports and operates internationally — the GCC/Middle East, Qatar projects, a Malaysia joint venture, newer markets like Nigeria, Bangladesh and Nepal, and recent entries into the U.S. and Europe. FY26 consolidated revenue was Rs 12,402 cr with net profit of Rs 527.3 cr.

parts.name: Segment I: Electro-Mechanical Projects & Commercial Air Conditioning Systems
parts.what: The business-to-business half of the company, roughly Rs 6,763 cr of revenue in FY26 (about 55% of the total) at ~7.4% segment margin, combining contracted building/infrastructure projects with sales of commercial cooling equipment.

parts.name: Electro-Mechanical Projects business
parts.what: Wins and executes contracts to install air-conditioning, electrical and related systems in commercial buildings, factories, data centres, hospitals, malls, metro rail, railway electrification, water and power projects; it holds the bulk of the order book (Rs 4,664.5 cr as of March 31, 2026) and management calls infrastructure work less profitable than buildings/factories/data centres.

parts.name: Commercial Air-Conditioning Systems
parts.what: Sells and services larger cooling equipment — conventional and inverter ducted systems, VRF systems, scroll and screw chillers — to customers such as retail, manufacturing, healthcare, education, government and entertainment; management claims No. 1 share in ducted systems and scroll chillers and No. 2 in VRF and screw chillers.

parts.name: International Business
parts.what: Exports and overseas operations reported inside Segment I, covering the Middle East/GCC (including a projects business in Qatar), a Malaysia joint venture, Nigeria, Bangladesh and Nepal, plus a newer push into the U.S. and Europe whose outlook management says depends heavily on the India–U.S. trade deal and tariffs.

parts.name: Segment II: Unitary Products
parts.what: The consumer- and shop-facing products half, Rs 5,332.4 cr of revenue in FY26 (about 43% of the total) at ~8.2% segment margin, sold through dealers and highly dependent on how hot the summer is.

parts.name: Room Air Conditioners (within Unitary Products)
parts.what: The single biggest swing factor in the company's results — household and small-office ACs sold through an expanding dealer network, where regulatory energy-label changes, GST changes and summer weather visibly drive quarterly sales up or down.

parts.name: Commercial Refrigeration / Cooling and Purification Products
parts.what: Products like deep freezers, storage water coolers and other refrigeration and purification lines sold to shops and institutions (and exported to the Middle East); in FY26 most of these lines shrank apart from storage water coolers.

parts.name: Segment III: Professional Electronics and Industrial Systems
parts.what: A small niche arm — about Rs 75 cr of revenue in the December 2025 quarter, under 3% of company revenue — that distributes and supports Med-Tech Solutions (slowed by unresolved regulation), Industrial Solutions (growing on automotive and steel demand) and Data Security Solutions.

overview.what_it_does: BlueStone Jewellery and Lifestyle Limited is an Indian jewellery brand that designs, manufactures and sells its own gold and diamond (studded) jewellery — rings, earrings, pendants and similar pieces — directly to retail consumers rather than through a marketplace or other people's designs. It started in 2011 as an online-only, direct-to-consumer brand on bluestone.com and now runs an 'omnichannel' model where customers discover and research online (management says more than 80% of sales originate online) and usually complete the purchase in a physical store; it operated 340 stores across 134 cities at March 2026 and 352 stores by the June 2026 quarter. It makes money on the retail sale price of each piece, with margins coming from design-led, higher-value studded jewellery and from in-house ('vertically integrated') manufacturing, rather than from low-margin commodity items like coins and chains, which it deliberately does not push. It operates only in India, spanning metros and smaller Tier-2 cities, and reported standalone revenue of Rs. 2,441 crore for FY26 and Rs. 733 crore in Q1 FY27 (up 49% year-on-year), with its first reported quarterly net profit (Rs. 71.5 crore) in Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Online / D2C channel (bluestone.com)
parts.what: The original business — the company's own website and app where customers browse its own designs (shown via 3D renders rather than photographs); management says over 80% of all sales now originate online even when the final purchase happens in a store.

parts.name: Physical retail store network (own + franchisee stores)
parts.what: Company-operated and franchisee stores where customers see and try the pieces and complete the purchase — 323 stores in 130 cities at December 2025, 340 in 134 cities at March 2026 and 352 by the Q1 FY27 call, with 65 stores added during FY26; all sales including franchisee stores are booked at retail (consumer) value.

parts.name: Omnichannel model
parts.what: Management's term for treating online and stores as one continuous customer journey rather than separate channels; they call it the key driver of performance and say online-built intent makes their stores convert better than a purely physical retailer's.

parts.name: In-house design and manufacturing (vertical integration)
parts.what: The company brought jewellery manufacturing in-house by 2013-14 to enable just-in-time production (cut turnaround from 3-4 weeks to 3-5 days) and still uses it to control design, costs and margins — it credits this for quickly re-creating affordable entry-level price points after gold prices spiked.

parts.name: Studded (diamond) versus plain gold jewellery
parts.what: Studded pieces are the higher-margin core of the product mix — 61% of revenue in Q3 FY26 — and the company deliberately avoids commodity, investment-led items such as gold coins and chains, which it describes as price-led and lower margin.

parts.name: In-house technology stack
parts.what: The company says it is the only jewellery company to have built its entire technology stack internally and asks investors to view it as a consumer internet company that chose jewellery as its category; it uses internet-style metrics such as cohorts, repeat share and customer lifetime to run the business.

parts.name: Repeat customer business
parts.what: Sales to existing customers, which management highlights as a growing and cost-efficient revenue source — 57.8% of revenue in Q3 FY26 rising to about 60% by Q1 FY27 — and which helps keep advertising spend low (5.7% of sales in Q3 FY26).

parts.name: Old gold exchange programme
parts.what: A scheme letting customers trade in old gold against new purchases, which management describes as the most competitive such offer in the market and a support to demand; no separate size is given.

parts.name: Men's and kids' jewellery store format
parts.what: A new, small initiative described as an industry first — an exclusive store selling only men's and kids' jewellery — intended to widen the range beyond the traditional women's focus; presented as an early experiment rather than a material revenue line.

overview.what_it_does: Borosil Renewables makes solar tempered glass — the thick protective glass sheet that goes on the front of a solar panel — and sells it in bulk to companies that assemble solar modules. It runs glass furnaces at its plant in Jhagadia, Bharuch district, Gujarat, and earns money on the volume of glass melted and sold, priced per millimetre of thickness per square metre (about INR 160.3/mm in the June 2026 quarter, up from about INR 105–141 in earlier years), so profits swing with selling prices, fuel and soda ash costs, and how full the furnaces run. Most sales are to Indian module makers, with a small export slice (7.4% of FY26 sales, down to 2.8% in Q1 FY27 as export markets stayed weak). Its fortunes are tied closely to Indian government policy — import duties, anti-dumping and countervailing duties on Chinese, Vietnamese and Malaysian glass, and the ALMM local-content rules — because roughly 70% of India's solar glass is still imported; standalone FY26 sales were INR 1,534.83 crores with EBITDA of INR 491.68 crores (32% of sales).

parts.name: Solar tempered glass (India / standalone operations)
parts.what: The core and now essentially the only revenue-generating business — glass furnaces at Jhagadia, Gujarat producing tempered glass for solar modules; it accounts for effectively all of the company's INR 1,534.83 crores FY26 sales, and a 600 tonnes-per-day expansion at the same site is due to commission in Q4 FY27, which management says will lift sales by about 60%.

parts.name: Overseas subsidiaries (Interfloat / GMB, Germany)
parts.what: A European solar glass manufacturing arm acquired around 2022 that was hit by cheap Chinese module imports killing off German module makers; it swung between roughly INR 55–130 crores of quarterly revenue with negative EBITDA in FY25, then GMB filed for insolvency and the company wrote off its INR 325.91 crores exposure in FY26 — by Q1 FY27 the overseas subsidiaries generated no revenue at all.

parts.name: Captive renewable power
parts.what: Solar-plus-wind hybrid power plants set up to supply the glass plant's own electricity — a 10 MW project via an SPV (BRL holding 31.2%) targeted for December 2022 and a further 16.5 MW hybrid plant commissioned in March 2026 — which by Q1 FY27 covered 93% of the company's power needs and cuts energy cost rather than earning outside revenue.

parts.name: Rooftop solutions division
parts.what: A new, small trading-style business announced in the May 2026 call to sell rooftop solar products sourced from outside suppliers under the Borosil brand and distribution network, aimed at the PM Surya Ghar Yojana and commercial/industrial rooftop market, with no capex planned initially and no revenue reported yet.

overview.what_it_does: Bosch Limited is an India-listed company (Bangalore head office, majority-owned by Robert Bosch entities in the Netherlands and the US) that mainly makes and sells automotive parts — fuel injection and engine management systems, pumps, nozzle holders, electronic throttle bodies, fuel injectors and exhaust gas sensors — to vehicle manufacturers in India across cars, heavy and light commercial vehicles, tractors, two- and three-wheelers, plus some exports. Beyond parts for new vehicles, it earns from selling spares into the vehicle repair/aftermarket, from power tools sold to consumers and trade, from building/security systems, and from R&D engineering services billed to OEMs and to Bosch Germany, with smaller income from leasing space at its Spark.NXT campus. Revenue is essentially product sales, so results track Indian automotive production volumes and regulatory changes such as new emission norms; FY '25-'26 revenue was about INR 200,347 million with EBITDA of about INR 26,503 million and profit after tax of INR 27,702 million. Management has been reshaping the portfolio — selling the Project House Mobility Solutions, OE/OES Diagnostics and most Building Technologies businesses, and in April 2026 agreeing to buy group company Bosch Chassis Systems India (braking and safety systems) for cash as a 100% subsidiary.

parts.name: Mobility business
parts.what: The umbrella automotive segment covering everything sold into vehicles and vehicle servicing; it is by far the dominant part of the company and grew 16.9% in FY '25-'26.

parts.name: Power Solutions
parts.what: The largest division, making powertrain/propulsion parts — diesel and gasoline injection, engine management systems, common rail for gensets, throttle bodies, EGT components — and it crossed INR 130 billion of net sales in calendar 2025, growing 17.6% in FY '26.

parts.name: Mobility Aftermarket
parts.what: Sells replacement parts and consumables — diesel systems, rotating machines, lubricants — into the vehicle repair market; a steady mid-single-digit grower (3.7% in FY '26, 8.4% in H1 FY '25).

parts.name: Two-Wheeler and PowerSports
parts.what: Supplies fuel injectors, exhaust gas sensors and engine management systems (including the world's first CNG bike EMS) to motorcycle makers; the fastest-growing part recently, up 69.1% in FY '26 on the OBD2 norms rollout.

parts.name: Consumer Goods
parts.what: The non-automotive power tools business — grinders, drills, cutters, spares and accessories sold through traditional trade and e-commerce — a modest but consistent grower (6.4% in FY '26).

parts.name: Building Technologies
parts.what: Installed video surveillance and communication systems for customers and grew about 20% in FY '25, but its Video Solutions, Access and Intrusion and Communication Systems lines were sold during FY '25-'26, giving a large one-off profit.

parts.name: Income from services (R&D services)
parts.what: Engineering and R&D work billed to vehicle OEMs and to Bosch Germany, recognised only when the customer's start-of-production dates are hit, so it is lumpy quarter to quarter (INR 1,701 million recognised in Q3 FY '23).

parts.name: Other operating income
parts.what: Small side income from lease rentals — notably leasing out the Spark.NXT smart campus — plus export incentives and miscellaneous recoveries.

parts.name: Bosch Chassis Systems India (being acquired)
parts.what: A group company described as India's market leader in braking and safety systems — ABS, ESP, airbag controllers, sensors and conventional actuation — with a main plant at Chakan and about 2,000 people, bought all-cash to become a 100% subsidiary and expected to lift both revenue and margins.

overview.what_it_does: BPCL is an Indian state-run (PSU) oil company that buys crude oil from around the world, refines it at its own refineries (Mumbai, Kochi and Bina), and sells the resulting fuels — petrol (MS), diesel (HSD), jet fuel (ATF), cooking gas (LPG) and CNG — mainly to Indian motorists, households, airlines and industrial/commercial customers. It makes money two ways: a refining margin (the gap between what crude costs and what the products fetch, quoted as GRM per barrel, e.g. $11.74/bbl for FY26) and a marketing margin on the roughly 54 MMT of product it sold domestically in FY26 through a network of over 25,000 petrol pumps ('retail outlets'). Its economics swing with crude prices, the rupee, and government-influenced pump prices — notably on domestic LPG, where it has been selling below cost and carrying a large 'negative buffer' (about Rs 12,300 crore) pending government compensation. It operates almost entirely in India, with quarterly revenue in the range of Rs 1.2 lakh crore, plus a small overseas oil-and-gas exploration interest in Mozambique and Brazil.

parts.name: Refining
parts.what: Three refineries process crude into fuels, running at 114–118% of nameplate capacity (41.15 MMT throughput in FY26, its highest ever) with a high distillate yield of about 84.5%, and management stresses flexible crude sourcing — Russian crude was 31% of the mix in Q4 FY26, alongside Brazil, US and West Africa grades.

parts.name: Marketing (retail fuels)
parts.what: The petrol-pump business is the volume engine — 25,323 outlets at end-FY26, about 30% retail market share in both petrol and diesel, and the highest sales per outlet among PSU peers (143–153 kilolitres per month), with roughly 1,000–1,700 new outlets added a year.

parts.name: LPG (cooking gas)
parts.what: Bottled domestic cooking gas sold to households at government-set prices below cost, which has been a major drag — losses of about Rs 2,100 crore in a single quarter in FY25 and a cumulative unrecovered 'negative buffer' of roughly Rs 12,300 crore, partly offset by government compensation received from November 2025.

parts.name: Gas business (CGD / CNG, PNG, LNG)
parts.what: Piped and compressed natural gas sold in 25 licensed geographical areas won in bidding, with 2,650 CNG stations and FY26 gas sales of 2.29 MMT growing 26.5% year-on-year; management flagged a roughly Rs 48,000 crore investment commitment over the life of these licences.

parts.name: Petrochemicals
parts.what: Plastics and chemical feedstock made from refinery streams — currently the PDPP unit at Kochi (about 80% utilisation, contributing around $0.79/bbl to margin in H1 FY25) — being scaled up substantially through the Rs 49,000 crore Bina petrochemical-plus-refinery-expansion project and a polypropylene unit at Kochi.

parts.name: Pipelines and supply infrastructure
parts.what: Pipelines, depots, LPG bottling plants and aviation fuelling stations that move and store product — described as a distinct business alongside refining and marketing, with the 425-km Krishnapatnam–Hyderabad multiproduct pipeline commissioned in FY26.

parts.name: Non-fuel retail
parts.what: Shops and services at petrol pumps — In & Out convenience stores, BeCafé cafés, Apna Ghar truckers' facilities and highway wayside amenities — a small but expanding add-on to the fuel network (from ~300 stores in 2023, with a target of 1,000 rural stores).

parts.name: EV charging and future fuels
parts.what: Electric-vehicle charging points at outlets (6,823–7,402 stations), plus battery swapping and the first LNG fuelling stations, positioned as turning pumps into 'energy stations' rather than as a meaningful earnings contributor today.

parts.name: Renewables, green hydrogen and biofuels
parts.what: Wind and solar projects (100 MW of wind awarded, 46 MW installed as of 2023), a green-hydrogen joint venture with Sembcorp called NeuEn Green Energy, compressed-biogas plants and ethanol plants — all tied to a net-zero-by-2040 Scope 1 and 2 pledge and to ethanol blending, which reached 19.6% of petrol in Q1 FY26.

parts.name: Upstream (oil and gas exploration)
parts.what: Minority overseas exploration and production interests — a Mozambique LNG block, 42% complete with first cargo expected mid-2028, and the BM-SEAL-11 block in Brazil — a long-dated side business rather than a current earnings source.

overview.what_it_does: Brigade Enterprises is an Indian property developer that builds and sells homes, and also owns and rents out commercial property. Its main business is developing residential projects — apartments, plotted developments and mixed-use townships — which it pre-sells to buyers (mostly end-users, plus about 10% NRI buyers) and collects cash from as construction progresses; in FY26 it sold INR 7,424 crores of homes at an average realization of INR 12,107 per square foot. Alongside that, it keeps ownership of office buildings and shopping malls that it leases to corporate tenants and retailers for recurring rent, and it owns and operates hotels. It operates almost entirely in south India — Bengaluru is the core market, with Chennai, Hyderabad, Mysore and Kochi, plus an office project at GIFT City, Gandhinagar; FY26 consolidated revenue was INR 5,909 crores with a 28% EBITDA margin and PAT of INR 725 crores.

parts.name: Real Estate (residential)
parts.what: Buys land, builds and sells apartments, plotted developments and mixed-use townships under the Brigade brand — the largest segment and the main driver of performance, with FY26 turnover of INR 4,002 crores (EBITDA INR 525 crores) and about 85% of pre-sales above the INR 1 crore ticket size.

parts.name: Leasing (commercial office)
parts.what: Develops and holds Grade A office buildings (e.g. Brigade Tech Gardens in Bengaluru, Brigade International Financial Centre at GIFT City) and rents them to global capability centres, IT/ITES, BFSI and flex operators — portfolio occupancy around 93%, rental collections at 99%, with roughly 10 million square feet more to launch over FY27–FY28.

parts.name: Leasing (retail malls)
parts.what: Owns and runs three Orion shopping malls, earning rent from retail, F&B, cinema and family-entertainment-centre tenants; reported inside the leasing segment, which together with offices generated FY26 turnover of INR 1,303 crores and EBITDA of INR 906 crores — the most profitable segment by margin.

parts.name: Hospitality
parts.what: Owns hotels operated under brands such as Sheraton Grand, Grand Mercure and Four Points, earning room, restaurant and banquet/MICE revenue; FY26 turnover was INR 604 crores with EBITDA of INR 207 crores and occupancy around 78%, and the separately named Brigade Hotel Ventures Limited is building out 1,700 keys across 9 hotels.

parts.name: Industrial Parks & Logistics
parts.what: A smaller, newer effort with its own COO, tied to land such as the 75 acres added near the Bengaluru aerospace park for possible industrial, logistics, office and residential use; the calls give it no separate revenue or profit figures.

overview.what_it_does: Britannia Industries is an Indian packaged-foods (FMCG) company whose core business is making and selling biscuits and cookies under brands like Good Day, NutriChoice, 50-50, JimJam, Little Hearts, Marie and Pure Magic, alongside other bakery and dairy items. It makes money by manufacturing these products in its own plants (in India, plus facilities in Oman and Dubai and an export-oriented unit at Mundra) and selling them in small packs — roughly 60-65% of biscuit sales sit at the INR 5 and INR 10 price points — through a very wide distribution network to ordinary retail shoppers across India, with an international/export business on top. Profit depends heavily on the gap between selling prices and input costs such as wheat flour, palm oil, sugar, cocoa, milk, packaging laminates and industrial fuel, which management manages through price increases and a running cost-efficiency programme worth roughly 2-3% of revenue. For FY 2025-26 the company reported revenue of about INR 18,858 crore with profit after tax at about 13.4% of revenue.

parts.name: Biscuits (base/core business)
parts.what: The main money-maker — mass-market and premium biscuits, cookies and crackers (Good Day, Good Day Crafted, NutriChoice, 50-50, JimJam, Little Hearts, Marie, Pure Magic, Biscafe, Golmaal), described by management as the business it has led and gained market share in for 36-plus consecutive quarters.

parts.name: Bakery adjacencies
parts.what: Cake, rusk (Toastea), croissant and wafers — the fast-growing 'adjacency' businesses management calls out separately; in the Dec-2025 quarter all four were growing in double digits and growing about 3x faster than biscuits in e-commerce.

parts.name: Dairy
parts.what: Cheese (including Cheese Triangles under the Laughing Cow brand), milk drinks (Winkin' Cow, which is seasonal with pipeline building from February), and Sattvam Cow Ghee — cheese was described as growing only marginally while ghee was growing much faster.

parts.name: International business
parts.what: Exports and overseas sales where a significant portion of manufacturing for those markets is done in Oman and Dubai, plus the Mundra export-oriented unit serving North America; revenue and profitability here were hit in Q4 FY26 by the West Asia conflict, shipping disruption and higher freight.

parts.name: General trade / rural distribution
parts.what: The traditional shop-by-shop network that management calls the most profitable part of the business — direct reach of about 28.2 lakh outlets and around 30,000 rural distributors, with rural growth running ahead of urban in recent periods.

parts.name: Organized / modern trade
parts.what: Supermarket and chain-store channel that rose from roughly 20-21% saliency in FY23 and is where premium products like Good Day Crafted and modern-trade-only launches get pushed.

parts.name: E-commerce and quick commerce
parts.what: Smallest but fastest-growing channel — about 2.5% of revenue in FY23, 4% in FY24-25 and 6% of domestic sales in FY25-26 (management argues it is effectively 12%+ excluding low-price-point biscuits), with roughly 70% of it now coming from quick commerce; deliberately B2C-only to avoid disrupting its own distributors.

overview.what_it_does: BSE Limited runs India's stock exchange business out of Mumbai (Dalal Street) — a 150-year-old marketplace where companies list their shares and bonds to raise money, and where investors and brokers buy and sell those securities. Its customers are listed companies and issuers (main board, SME and startup platforms), trading members/brokers and their retail and institutional clients, mutual fund distributors, and data and index users; over 25 crore investor accounts were registered on BSE as of FY26. It earns money mainly from transaction charges on trades it matches and settles (equity cash, equity derivatives, mutual fund orders and clearing-house fees — Rs. 3,795 crores of FY26's Rs. 5,148 crores total revenue), plus listing fees and book-building fees from issuers, data dissemination, co-location and index fees, and interest/treasury income on its own funds and on clearing-and-settlement money it holds. It operates in India under SEBI regulation, with an additional international arm at GIFT City, Gandhinagar, and reported FY26 net profit of Rs. 2,497 crores on 59% revenue growth.

parts.name: Listing / primary market (main board, SME and Startup platforms)
parts.what: Companies list shares, bonds, commercial paper, municipal bonds, REITs and InvITs on BSE's platforms and pay listing and book-building fees; management calls it a core franchise — Rs. 26.9 lakh crores raised across BSE fundraising platforms in FY26, 255 new listings ranked first globally for IPO listings, and the SME platform alone hit its 700th listing in Feb 2026 (Rs. 14,735 crores raised, ~Rs. 1.8 lakh crores market value).

parts.name: Trading — equity cash segment
parts.what: The traditional share-trading market where BSE charges transaction fees on turnover; average daily turnover rose from about Rs. 4,057 crores in Q1 FY23 to a record Rs. 7,950 crores for FY26, though management describes cash volumes as being at 'long-term normalized levels'.

parts.name: Trading — equity derivatives (Sensex, Bankex index options/futures and single stock derivatives)
parts.what: Futures and options on BSE's own indices (plus single stock derivatives launched July 2024) are the biggest growth engine and the main reason transaction charges jumped 87% in FY26 — average daily premium turnover reached a record Rs. 19,523 crores in FY26 versus Rs. 8,978 crores in FY25, and management flags SEBI's changing derivatives rules and charge structures as the key swing factor.

parts.name: Currency derivatives
parts.what: A smaller trading segment in foreign-exchange contracts, with average daily turnover of about Rs. 24,567 crores in Q1 FY23.

parts.name: Clearing and settlement (ICCL, the clearing corporation)
parts.what: The back-end arm that guarantees and settles trades, earning clearing fees (Rs. 33.8 crores in Q1 FY25) plus treasury income on the cash it holds from members (Rs. 62 crores in Q1 FY25); it also funds a Core Settlement Guarantee Fund — 5% of transaction-linked revenue is set aside monthly, taking the fund to Rs. 1,202 crores by Jan 2026.

parts.name: BSE StAR MF (mutual fund distribution platform)
parts.what: India's largest mutual fund order-routing platform, used by distributors to place investor buy/sell orders, charging per transaction — it processed 14.1 crore transactions in Q1 FY25 (up 72%) for Rs. 48 crores of quarterly revenue, and its fees are counted inside BSE's transaction charges.

parts.name: Data, co-location and index services (including Asia Index / BSE Index Services)
parts.what: Selling market data feeds, renting server space next to the exchange's systems, and licensing indices such as Sensex — grouped as 'other operating income' at Rs. 349 crores in FY26, up 59%; BSE bought out S&P Dow Jones Indices' stake in Asia Index to own the index business fully.

parts.name: Investment / treasury income on own funds
parts.what: Interest and returns on BSE's own cash and investments, a meaningful but secondary earnings source — Rs. 84 crores in Q3 FY26, up 47% year on year.

parts.name: India INX and India International Clearing Corporation (GIFT City, Gandhinagar)
parts.what: BSE's majority-owned international exchange and clearing house at India's offshore financial centre, quoted at about USD 9.9 billion average daily turnover and 92.2% market share in Q1 FY23, with BSE holding roughly 62% and 59% stakes respectively.

parts.name: BSE Technology (wholly owned subsidiary)
parts.what: Builds and supplies trading technology — it is the technology provider for the International Bullion Exchange at GIFT City and for BSE's Electronic Gold Receipt segment, and received SEBI in-principle approval to run a KYC Registration Agency (KRA) and a TReDS receivables-financing platform with no extra capital needed from BSE.

parts.name: Electronic Gold Receipts (EGR)
parts.what: A then-planned segment for trading spot gold in India, awaiting final SEBI approval as of Aug 2022 and intended to use BSE Technology's bullion-exchange systems.

parts.name: BSE Ebix Insurance Broking (40% stake via BSE Investments)
parts.what: An insurance distribution venture integrated with 23 insurance companies, small in scale — Rs. 8.1 crores of premium collected in the June 2022 quarter, though growing fast.

parts.name: BSE E-Agricultural Markets Limited
parts.what: A spot trading platform for physical commodities (agri and steel) working with government buyers — very small, with 926 enrolled members and Rs. 17 crores of trades in the June 2022 quarter.

parts.name: Hindustan Power Exchange (22.61% stake via BSE Investments)
parts.what: An associate power-trading exchange that began operating in July 2022 across day-ahead, real-time and green day-ahead segments, reaching over 20% share of the contingency market early on.

parts.name: Investor protection, education and awareness
parts.what: A cost/regulatory function rather than a revenue line — funded through BSE's Investor Protection Fund, it ran 16,663 investor awareness programmes covering over 8.5 lakh investors in FY26.

overview.what_it_does: Birlasoft is an India-based IT services company that gets paid by large companies to build, modernise and run their business software and technology systems — things like SAP/ERP implementations, digital and data projects, cloud migration, IT infrastructure support and, more recently, AI and 'agentic AI' solutions built on its own Cogito platform. It earns money project-by-project and through multi-year managed-service contracts, which it reports as new deal wins or total contract value (TCV) — roughly $160-210 million of TCV signed per quarter recently — that then convert into billed revenue as teams of engineers work on them. Revenue is about $150 million a quarter (FY26 full-year revenue of Rs. 53,100 million, roughly flat to slightly down), earned mostly in US dollars from clients in the Americas, with smaller businesses in Europe and the Rest of the World, while most of the delivery work is done offshore in India by a workforce of over 12,000 people. Profitability depends on utilisation of staff, offshore versus onshore mix, and fixed-price versus time-based contracts — EBITDA margin was 16.3% for FY26 versus 13% the year before.

parts.name: ERP
parts.what: Implements and upgrades enterprise resource planning software, especially SAP (including cloud-based 'RISE with SAP'), and management calls it a large, historically important service line whose project slowdowns have repeatedly dragged the whole company's revenue down; a 25-year SAP veteran was hired in FY26 specifically to return it to growth.

parts.name: Digital & Data
parts.what: Covers digital transformation, data modernisation and AI/GenAI work — the faster-growing, higher-value part of the business that management describes as making Birlasoft an 'enterprise digital company' and that now anchors most of its marquee deal wins.

parts.name: Infra
parts.what: IT infrastructure and support services — described as a newer, smaller service line that management is deliberately building, and which delivered strong sequential growth from fresh engagements.

parts.name: Manufacturing (vertical)
parts.what: Serving manufacturing clients is one of the company's biggest end-markets and the source of most of its ERP revenue, so its ups and downs swing overall results; management notes exposure is 'higher to manufacturing-led customers'.

parts.name: BFSI (banking, financial services and insurance) (vertical)
parts.what: Work for banks, payments/card companies and insurers, including AI and GenAI deployments such as scaling GenAI services in the North American property & casualty insurance market; described as one of the steadier verticals and a repeated growth driver.

parts.name: Life Sciences & Services (vertical)
parts.what: Serves pharmaceutical, medtech and related clients — including a multi-year AI and data modernisation programme for a Fortune 500 MedTech customer — and is grouped by management with Manufacturing as a 'manufacturing-led' exposure.

parts.name: Energy & Utilities (vertical)
