parts.what: A smaller vertical serving energy and utility clients, which management repeatedly cites alongside BFSI as one of the steadier, growing parts of the portfolio.

parts.name: Geographies
parts.what: The Americas is by far the main market and where the largest accounts and sales investment sit, with Europe and a smaller 'Rest of the World' business that grew strongly off a low base.

parts.name: Large-account mining
parts.what: Not a segment but a stated revenue engine: the top 5, 10 and 20 clients contributed about 36%, 53% and 65% of revenue respectively, from an active client base of roughly 300 accounts, so growth depends heavily on expanding within existing large customers.

overview.what_it_does: Campus Activewear is an Indian branded footwear company — it designs, makes and sells sports and athleisure shoes (sneakers, running/closed shoes and lower-priced open footwear like sandals) for men, women and kids, positioned as premium-looking, design-led product at affordable prices. It makes money by selling pairs of shoes: FY26 revenue was about INR 1,774 crore on roughly 26 million pairs at an average selling price of INR 683, with gross margin ~53%, EBITDA margin ~17.5% and PAT of INR 150 crore. It sells almost entirely in India, through a wide network of distributors and around 23,000-29,000 retail touchpoints, its own ~300 exclusive brand outlets, large-format store chains, and online (Flipkart, Amazon, Myntra, Snapdeal and its own brand.com). Manufacturing is largely in-house — all assembly is done internally, over 90% of raw materials are sourced locally, and it runs shoe-upper plants at Paonta Sahib and Pant Nagar; in January 2026 it extended the brand into athleisure apparel.

parts.name: Trade Distribution
parts.what: Sells to distributors and super stockists who supply tens of thousands of multi-brand retail shops across India (23,100+ retailers in FY25, ~29,000 touchpoints by FY26); management calls this its volume-growth channel and it is the largest route to market, growing ~10.5% in FY26.

parts.name: D2C Online (marketplaces and brand.com)
parts.what: Sells directly to shoppers on e-commerce platforms — Flipkart is the biggest partner, plus Amazon, Snapdeal, Myntra and the company's own website — and was the fastest-growing channel in FY26 at ~19% in Q4, helped by performance marketing.

parts.name: D2C Offline / Exclusive Brand Outlets (EBOs)
parts.what: Company-owned and franchise Campus stores (about 275 in FY25, steady at 300 by FY26) that, along with brand.com, are used to push higher-priced, premium product rather than pure volume.

parts.name: B2B online / O2O
parts.what: Bulk online business the company deliberately shrank; it fell more than 40% at one point and was a drag on the online numbers through FY25 before the base effect washed out.

parts.name: Large Format Stores (LFS)
parts.what: Sales into big retail chain accounts, added selectively (one new account in Q1 FY25) as an extra way to widen consumer reach.

parts.name: Closed footwear (including Sneakers)
parts.what: The core, higher-priced part of the range that the company says it dominates; sneakers are the newest and most premium piece — entered roughly 1-1.5 years before FY26, doubling volume nearly every quarter, at an ASP of about INR 900-910.

parts.name: Open footwear
parts.what: Sandals and similar summer product at lower prices — a smaller portfolio (around 18-22% of sales in the June quarter) that spikes in hot months and pulls the average selling price down.

parts.name: Women's and kids' category
parts.what: A deliberate expansion beyond the men's-dominated base, supported by the 'You Go, Girl' campaign with actor Kriti Sanon; the mix moved from 16% of revenue in FY22 to about 21-22% by FY26.

parts.name: In-house manufacturing (uppers and assembly)
parts.what: Owned plants — Paonta Sahib now stabilised and Pant Nagar started in January 2026, together making about 2 lakh uppers a month with plans to double by end-FY27 — which management credits for an 80-100 day time-to-market and ~250 new SKUs launched in FY26.

parts.name: Athleisure apparel
parts.what: A new clothing line launched in January 2026 to sell more to existing customers and lift store productivity; described as an early-stage extension of the brand rather than a material revenue contributor yet.

overview.what_it_does: CAMS (Computer Age Management Services) is the back-office and technology plumbing behind India's mutual fund industry: it acts as a registrar and transfer agent (RTA), meaning it processes investor transactions, keeps the records of who owns which fund units, handles new purchases, SIPs, redemptions and new fund offers, and runs the investor-facing apps and platforms that sit on top of that. Its customers are asset management companies (fund houses) — it serves 4 of the top 5 AMCs by equity assets — and it earns money mainly as a fee on the assets under management it services, so revenue moves with fund AUM (over INR55 lakh crore serviced, roughly 68% of industry AUM, and about 67% of industry equity assets), plus per-transaction and platform fees. Around this core it has built a set of adjacent 'non-MF' businesses — KYC registration, payments, alternative-fund servicing, insurance repository, account aggregation, pension records — which management is deliberately scaling and which now contribute roughly 15% of total revenue. It operates in India (including GIFT City funds), with the mutual fund business still the bulk of revenue and margins in the mid-40s percent EBITDA.

parts.name: Mutual Fund (MF) services / core RTA business
parts.what: Keeps the official records and processes every buy, sell, SIP and new-fund-offer for the fund houses it serves — by far the biggest part of the company (around 85% of revenue), servicing INR55 lakh crore of AUM at ~68% industry share and processing over 107 crore financial transactions a year, and it is being rebuilt from scratch on a new Google Cloud platform.

parts.name: CAMS KRA
parts.what: A KYC registration agency that stores and verifies investor identity records so investors don't have to re-do KYC with every provider — originally serving mutual funds, now also brokerages and depository participants; it grew over 100% in one quarter in FY25 and became the second-largest KRA after taking over NSE's KRA business.

parts.name: CAMSPay
parts.what: The payments arm that collects money from investors for financial firms — notably UPI AutoPay for SIP mandates, where CAMS says it was first to market and is now a top BFSI player — and it has added a payment gateway and a payment aggregator licence; growth of 23%–59% year-on-year in recent quarters.

parts.name: Alternatives (AIF / PMS services, incl. CAMS WealthServ)
parts.what: Does the same record-keeping and fund-administration work for alternative investment funds and portfolio management services, plus a digital client-onboarding platform (WealthServ); it services over INR3 lakh crore of AUM, about 50% of the outsourced market, growing 16%–25% a year with roughly 250 onboarding mandates signed.

parts.name: CAMSRep (insurance repository) and Bima Central
parts.what: Holds insurance policies in electronic form for policyholders and gives them an app (Bima Central) to manage their portfolio, plus tools that helped insurers trace and settle unclaimed benefits; it has crossed 1 crore electronic insurance accounts and ~1.3 crore policies at about 40% market share, but management repeatedly says the revenue is still small and 'scratching the surface'.

parts.name: Account Aggregator (CAMS Finserv)
parts.what: A consent-based service that lets a consumer share their financial data with lenders or advisers, sold alongside an analytics product called Amaze for personal finance and lending use cases; market share climbed from 2%–3% to the low-to-mid teens, but revenue was still only about INR1–2 crore a quarter as of FY25.

parts.name: NPS CRA (pension record-keeping)
parts.what: A central record-keeping agency licensed by the pension regulator for the National Pension System, launched in 2022 as the first cloud-based CRA; it quickly reached over 10% share and the number-two position in direct-to-consumer eNPS sales, with corporate and distributor channels in pilot at the time.

parts.name: MFCentral and myCAMS (investor-facing digital platforms)
parts.what: Free investor-facing platforms — MFCentral, built jointly with the other RTA, lets investors see and transact across all their mutual fund holdings in one place, and myCAMS is described as the largest mutual fund app in the country with over 5.25 million users; they serve mainly as ecosystem hooks and as a source of APIs sold to fintechs and advisers rather than large direct revenue.

parts.name: Digital / platform stack for capital markets
parts.what: A bundle of supporting services sold across the ecosystem — eKYC, e-signing, digital onboarding, anti-money-laundering checks, validation, reconciliation products and loan-against-mutual-funds enablement for banks and NBFCs — which management frames as making CAMS a 'full stack' platform for capital markets rather than as a separately sized revenue line.

overview.what_it_does: Canara Bank is an Indian government-linked (public sector) bank headquartered at 112 J C Road, Bengaluru, listed on the BSE and NSE under the code CANBK, and run by a Managing Director & CEO plus several Executive Directors. It takes deposits from the public (about Rs. 16.1 lakh crore as of June 2026) and lends that money out as loans (about Rs. 12.9 lakh crore), giving a total 'global business' of roughly Rs. 29 lakh crore; borrowers range from individual home, vehicle and gold-loan customers to farmers, small businesses and large corporates. It earns mainly from the spread between interest charged on loans and interest paid on deposits — net interest income crossed Rs. 10,215 crore in a single quarter — topped up by 'non-interest' income such as fees and commissions, treasury (bond and investment) gains, PSLC commission, and cash recovered from loans it had earlier written off (roughly Rs. 6,500 crore a year). Business is sourced through its own countrywide branch network ('brick and mortar outlets'), it also participates in government credit schemes routed through the Jan Samarth portal, and it holds stakes in subsidiaries including Canara HSBC and Canara Robeco, whose stock-market listings produced a one-time Rs. 1,930 crore gain.

parts.name: RAM credit (Retail, Agriculture and MSME)
parts.what: The bank's priority engine of small-ticket lending to individuals, farmers and small businesses — management has deliberately pushed it from about 55% to roughly 57-58% of the total loan book, and it stood at Rs. 7.65 lakh crore growing over 21% a year in the June 2026 quarter.

parts.name: Retail credit
parts.what: Loans to individual customers — the fastest-growing piece at Rs. 3.20 lakh crore and 35.9% growth, driven by home loans, vehicle loans and a non-agricultural gold loan product introduced for city customers at a higher rate and lower loan-to-value.

parts.name: Housing loan
parts.what: Home loans, the biggest single retail product at Rs. 1.29 lakh crore growing about 17-18%; management says it is one of the few banks steadily gaining market share here and does not buy loan portfolios from others.

parts.name: Vehicle loan
parts.what: Car and vehicle finance at Rs. 27,315 crore growing about 26% — a book management notes the bank historically never grew in double digits until recently.

parts.name: Gold loan
parts.what: Loans against gold, which crossed Rs. 1 lakh crore back in 2022; split between an agriculture version yielding about 8.75% and a retail city version yielding over 9%, after the bank stopped agri gold lending in metro cities to be more conservative.

parts.name: MSME credit
parts.what: Working capital and term loans to micro, small and medium enterprises, at Rs. 1.69 lakh crore growing about 15%; it is also where management admits most of the loan stress sits (Rs. 1,333 crore of one quarter's Rs. 2,771 crore of new bad loans).

parts.name: Agriculture
parts.what: Farm and allied lending including agri gold loans and term loans, part of RAM; growth here was deliberately slowed when the bank pulled back from metro agri gold lending.

parts.name: Corporate credit
parts.what: Large-company and project lending — roughly 44-45% of the book, spread across road infrastructure (Rs. 50,000 crore of HAM projects underwritten in 2022), AAA/AA-rated NBFCs, iron and steel, real estate for housing, engineering, construction and chemicals; the bank says it is deliberately choosy, with about 78% of rated exposure at A or above, and has at times shed low-yielding corporate loans.

parts.name: Treasury / investments
parts.what: The bank's bond and equity investment book, which produces lumpy gains or losses — over Rs. 1,000 crore of treasury income in one quarter, but Rs. 800 crore of mark-to-market losses in another when bond yields rose and markets fell.

parts.name: Fee-based and other income
parts.what: Commissions and charges on banking services, including PSLC commission, running around Rs. 1,900 crore in a quarter and growing in the mid-teens.

parts.name: Recovery from written-off accounts (TWO recovery)
parts.what: Cash collected on loans already fully written off, a steady profit contributor of roughly Rs. 1,500-1,600 crore per quarter and about Rs. 6,500-6,800 crore per year.

parts.name: Subsidiaries (Canara HSBC, Canara Robeco)
parts.what: Associated financial-services companies in which the bank holds stakes; their stock-market listings delivered a one-off Rs. 1,930 crore gain in the March 2026 quarter.

parts.name: Government-scheme lending (ECLGS 5.0)
parts.what: Credit extended under a government emergency guarantee scheme — the bank identified about Rs. 90,000 crore of eligible accounts and roughly Rs. 18,000 crore of potential extra lending, of which over Rs. 11,000 crore was sanctioned and Rs. 10,000 crore disbursed by July 2026.

overview.what_it_does: Can Fin Homes is an Indian housing finance company, sponsored by Canara Bank and headquartered in Bengaluru, that lends money to individuals to buy or build homes, plus some non-housing loans against property-type lending. It borrows wholesale (bank term loans, commercial paper, non-convertible debentures and refinance from the National Housing Bank) and lends that money out at a higher rate — in the latest quarter earning about 9.81% on its loan book against a 6.98% cost of borrowing, for a spread of roughly 2.8%; almost all its profit comes from this interest margin. Customers are ordinary retail borrowers split between salaried people and self-employed/non-professionals (SENP), and the loans are secured on the property. It runs a branch network across India (about 200 branches in 2022, organised into 6 zones), with Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh repeatedly called out; the loan book grew from about INR 22,000 crores in 2022 to over INR 40,000 crores by FY26, with FY26 disbursements of INR 10,531 crores.

parts.name: Housing loans
parts.what: The core product — loans to individuals to buy or construct a home, which management treats as the main engine of the book; housing disbursements grew 28% year-on-year in Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Non-housing loans (NHL)
parts.what: The smaller secondary lending line management reports alongside housing, growing slightly faster (32% in Q1 FY27), used to lift overall yield.

parts.name: Salaried segment
parts.what: Borrowers with regular jobs — the larger and traditionally safer half of new lending, growing 21% year-on-year in Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Self-employed / non-professional (SENP) segment
parts.what: Borrowers with business or irregular income, the faster-growing half of disbursements (up 44% in Q1 FY27) and the part management is deliberately expanding.

parts.name: Borrowing / treasury (liability side)
parts.what: Raising funds through bank term loans linked to T-bill or repo, commercial paper, NCDs and NHB refinance under the Affordable Housing Fund — management describes managing this cost as the main lever on the ~2.75–2.85% spread it guides to.

parts.name: Branch and zonal network
parts.what: Around 200 branches (in 2022) grouped into 6 zones that source loans, with branches opened after March 2023 and a dedicated sales team named as contributors to recent growth.

parts.name: Recovery / collections
parts.what: Chasing overdue loans, including selling seized property under SARFAESI; the calls describe this as small in scale — gross NPAs of 0.85% and credit cost of about 10–15 basis points.

overview.what_it_does: Canara HSBC Life Insurance is an Indian life insurance company (IRDAI Regn No. 136), listed in FY26 on the NSE and BSE under the symbol CANHLIFE, that sells long-term life insurance policies to retail customers across India — including Tier-2, Tier-3 and Tier-4 towns — as well as group cover tied to bank loans. Its products span unit-linked savings plans (ULIPs) that invest customers' money in equity and debt funds, traditional par and non-par savings plans, annuity/retirement plans, and pure protection (term) cover, with small add-on 'riders' attached to boost protection. It earns money by collecting first-year and renewal premiums, charging fees such as fund management charges on unit-linked assets, and investing the resulting pool — assets under management were roughly Rs. 44,000 crores as of September 2025 — with profitability tracked as value of new business (Rs. 627 crores in FY26 at a 22.4% margin), profit after tax (Rs. 127 crores in FY26) and embedded value (Rs. 7,233 crores). It sells almost entirely through banks — mainly Canara Bank branches plus a partnership with HSBC — and ranked 9th among Indian private life insurers in FY26 with about a 2.6% share of the private market.

parts.name: Linked business (ULIP)
parts.what: Unit-linked savings plans where the customer's premium is invested in market funds for wealth creation; the calls say it is roughly half the business (about 50-51% of the FY26 mix) and grew 23% year-on-year over the first nine months of FY26, though a fall in equity markets hurt embedded value through lower future fund management charges.

parts.name: Traditional / non-linked business (par and non-par)
parts.what: Guaranteed-style savings policies that do not move with markets; management says the mix shifted sharply toward these in Q4 FY26 (81% of that quarter's sales versus 39% up to December 2025), with par and non-par together growing 15% year-on-year in FY26 and making up 28% of total APE.

parts.name: Annuity (retirement) business
parts.what: Retirement products, with a stated focus on deferred annuity, that pay customers a regular income later in life; annuity APE grew 24% year-on-year in FY26 and is about 14-16% of the overall business, described as profitable and giving long-term earnings visibility.

parts.name: Individual / retail protection
parts.what: Pure life cover sold to individual customers, growing from a small base but tripling quarter-on-quarter in Q3 FY26 as the GST exemption on life premiums made it cheaper; it is a key driver of margin improvement.

parts.name: Group credit life
parts.what: Cover sold alongside loans that repays the borrower's outstanding loan if they die — a fast-growing, profitable segment, up over 40% year-on-year in H1 FY26, about 50% in Q3 FY26 and 40% in Q4 FY26; total protection (individual plus credit life) rose to 7% of FY26 business from 4% in FY25.

parts.name: Riders attached to ULIPs
parts.what: Small add-on protection covers bolted onto unit-linked policies, attached to about 70% of eligible policies but only around 5% of unit-linked premium — small in money terms, but management repeatedly credits them with lifting ULIP margins.

parts.name: Bancassurance distribution (Canara Bank and HSBC)
parts.what: The main sales engine: policies sold through Canara Bank branches, with deeper penetration into Tier-3 and Tier-4 markets using customer data analytics, plus an HSBC partnership that brings a niche, better-persistency customer segment.

parts.name: Agency channel
parts.what: A newly launched own-sales-force channel started 1 October 2025, with about 500 distributors onboarded and Rs. 14 crores of APE collected in under six months; management targets roughly 5% of business from it over three years.

parts.name: Alternate channels
parts.what: Distribution outside the two parent banks and agency, which grew 29% year-on-year and contributes about 9% of weighted premium income, with a stated goal of reaching 15% over the next three years.

overview.what_it_does: Capillary sells cloud software that large companies use to run their customer loyalty programmes — the points, tiers, rewards and 'earn and burn' schemes behind things like IndiGo's BluChip, Taj InnerCircle and Tata Neu. Its customers are big enterprises and multinationals (about 115 customers covering roughly 400-410 brands, including 20 Fortune 500 names and two of the Fortune 10), spanning retail, hotels, airlines, healthcare, banks and telcos. It makes money from long-term subscription contracts of three to seven years, billed annually and priced on how many loyalty members or loyalty transactions run through the platform, so revenue grows automatically as customers use it more (plus contracted inflation increases and overage charges); management describes it as 'bank-ledger-like' pricing on a system of record. It operates globally from about 16 offices with roughly 700 staff, serving customers in about 49 countries, and reported revenue of about INR 543 crores for the first nine months of FY26 (~22-23% growth) with adjusted EBITDA margins in the 13-15% range; growth comes from existing customers spending more (110-111% net retention), new client wins, and buying up rival loyalty platforms cheaply (0.5x-1.5x revenue) and migrating those customers onto its own system.

parts.name: Loyalty stack (core loyalty platform)
parts.what: The main product and 'bread and butter' — the system of record that tracks every member, point and reward transaction for a brand's loyalty programme, priced per member or per transaction; management says it is roughly 90% of revenues.

parts.name: Customer Data Platform (CDP)
parts.what: The underlying base layer that plugs into every customer touchpoint (point-of-sale, e-commerce, mobile apps, kiosks, NPS surveys) to pull all customer data into one place; management says they don't monetise it much on its own — it exists to support the loyalty product.

parts.name: Engage (Engage+)
parts.what: Marketing automation for running campaigns and promotions off the loyalty data, sold as an add-on to loyalty customers; about 5%-7% of revenues and described as the company's 'wedge' into marketing automation.

parts.name: Insights (Insights+)
parts.what: Dashboards and reporting on loyalty performance, another add-on to the core platform; management expects the AI product to eventually replace this piece.

parts.name: Rewards
parts.what: Powers third-party rewards catalogues for clients, especially banks and telcos, and is also treated as a system of record; around 5%-7% of revenues.

parts.name: aiRA (AI-powered Research Assistant)
parts.what: An AI layer running across all the products that lets marketers ask questions in plain English, get analytics, run campaigns and generate creatives instead of hiring an agency — priced per question or analysis; it is a few million dollars of revenue so far, with about a quarter of customers piloting or already paying, and management calls it their fastest-adopted product.

parts.name: M&A / acquired platforms
parts.what: Not a product but a stated third engine of growth: Capillary buys competing loyalty platforms cheaply (four done including Brierley, Kognitiv in May 2025, and SessionM bought from Mastercard for $35 million and closed 1 May 2026) and migrates those customers onto its own stack, lifting gross margins from about 30% to 65%-70%; this business runs at 94%-96% net retention while migration discounts wash through, and is expected to take total ARR past $115 million over 12-18 months.

overview.what_it_does: Caplin Point Laboratories is an India-based generic drug maker that manufactures affordable medicines — mainly sterile injectables, ophthalmics, tablets/capsules and soft-gelatin capsules — and sells them under its own labels through its own subsidiaries and warehouses in Latin America, and as approved generics in the US and other regulated markets. Its original and still-largest engine is Latin America (Central America since 2002, plus Mexico, Chile, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil), where it supplies thousands of small independent pharmacies in the 'private market' and also wins large government institutional tenders; management says it holds about 41% of shelf space in independent Central American pharmacies and keeps roughly six months of stock sitting close to the customer, which is how it earns its cash. The second engine is Caplin Steriles, a US FDA-approved injectables plant that sells in the US both through partners and, since about 2025, through its own front-end label (Caplin Steriles USA), plus contract manufacturing (CMO) for other firms — US-side revenue splits roughly 75% product sales and 25% milestone and profit-share payments. The group has grown revenue from about INR 1,085 crore five years ago to about INR 2,300 crore in FY26, holds INR 2,726 crore of liquid assets and INR 1,471 crore of free cash, and is spending heavily on new factories (17 injectable lines planned over two to three years), its own APIs, and product registrations.

parts.name: Latin America / LatAm (branded and unbranded generics, private market + tenders)
parts.what: Sells finished generic medicines through Caplin's own subsidiaries, warehouses and distribution in Central America (Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Dominican Republic), Mexico, Chile, Peru, Costa Rica, Ecuador and Colombia, split between everyday private-market sales to independent pharmacies and lumpy government tenders (e.g. USD 6.2m in El Salvador, USD 14.5m in Ecuador); management repeatedly calls this the mainstay that generates the group's cash flow and profits, with Mexico now its biggest LatAm market and Chile the newest (135 registrations, ~USD 10m of supply booked over 18 months).

parts.name: Caplin Steriles Limited (regulated-market injectables and ophthalmics)
parts.what: The US FDA-approved sterile plant that develops, files and manufactures injectables, ophthalmics and pre-filled syringes for the US, Canada, Mexico, South Africa, Australia, China and Europe — it went from roughly break-even in FY23 to being the company's main growth story, with about 65 ANDAs approved or near-approval under Caplin's name and consistent high growth expected.

parts.name: Caplin Steriles USA / own US front end
parts.what: Caplin's own US sales label, launched around 2025, which sells its approved products directly to US wholesalers rather than only through partners; it reached nearly USD 10 million of revenue since inception and management calls the decision to go direct a good one in hindsight.

parts.name: US partnering, licensing and CMO work
parts.what: A 'hybrid' model where Caplin files its own products and licenses them to partners, and also contract-manufactures for other companies — this is what produces the milestone and profit-share income that makes up roughly 25% of US revenue.

parts.name: Acquired ANDAs / source-and-outsource distribution
parts.what: Using its cash pile to buy ready-made US product approvals (about 14 ANDAs bought recently, four of them oncology) and to source products from other CMOs in India and China for resale to US wholesalers, so its US label has more to sell than it can make itself.

parts.name: API business (Vizag plant and R&D centres)
parts.what: A bought-and-refurbished active-ingredient plant in Vizag plus two API R&D centres, meant mainly for backward integration — making the key raw materials for Caplin's own products and filing its own DMFs; three critical APIs were scaled up by early 2026 with the first DMF filing expected by end of that year.

parts.name: Caplin One Labs (oncology injectables, oral solids, onco API)
parts.what: A set of new factories under construction covering oncology injectables, oral solid dosage and oncology APIs; the onco injectable plant began exhibit batches in early 2026 with about 12 organic products in development, and completing these units also brings an ~8% tax benefit.

parts.name: Soft gelatin capsules (Pondicherry)
parts.what: An older formulations division whose capacity was doubled from about 2 crore to 4 crore capsules a month in FY23 because of strong demand and market shortage.

parts.name: Amaris Clinical (CRO wing)
parts.what: The in-house clinical research arm that runs bio-equivalence and clinical studies for Caplin's filings; it holds a US FDA EIR and an approval from Chile, and supports work such as the 40-plus bio-studies being run for Chilean products.

parts.name: New sterile capabilities under build-out (BFS, PFS/cartridges, ophthalmic ointments, hormones, inhalers)
parts.what: Ongoing investment to cover 'pretty much the complete gamut' of sterile forms — a blow-fill-seal line ordered from Rommelag with 14 products in development, a pre-filled-syringe and cartridge line, ophthalmic ointments, plus R&D into hormone injections and inhalers, with first approvals expected FY27-FY28.

parts.name: Digitalisation and Video/Visual SOP
parts.what: Not a revenue line but a capability management stresses heavily — patent-filed video-based standard operating procedures, automation and in-house software logbooks/BMR-BPR, used to keep regulatory compliance clean (EU GMP and Saudi FDA audits passed with no critical observations) and pitched as a bargaining chip to win product-sourcing tie-ups with Chinese and Mexican firms.

overview.what_it_does: Carborundum Universal (CUMI) is an India-based industrial manufacturer that makes grinding and cutting products, industrial ceramics, and the raw abrasive minerals that go into them, selling mainly to other manufacturers rather than to consumers. It earns money by selling physical volumes at a price per unit, so its profits swing with input costs, selling-price realisation and currency moves; management discusses results as three reported segments — Abrasives, Electrominerals and Ceramics — at both standalone (India) and consolidated (group) level. Its end customers are in steel, cement, power, glass, carbon black, solid oxide fuel cells, autos, construction and agriculture. Beyond India it operates through subsidiaries in Russia (Volzhsky Abrasives), Germany (Rhodius, Awuko), South Africa (Foskor Zirconia), plus America and Australia; FY26 consolidated sales were about INR 5,149 crores against standalone INR 3,024 crores, so roughly 40% of group revenue comes from outside the Indian parent.

parts.name: Abrasives
parts.what: Grinding wheels, cutting discs and coated abrasives sold into retail, industrial and precision end-uses; the largest segment at about INR 2,271 crores consolidated in FY26 (INR 1,270 crores standalone), but the lowest-margin one — consolidated PBIT margin was around 10% in Q1 FY25 versus about 17.6% standalone, because the overseas abrasive subsidiaries drag it down.

parts.name: Electrominerals
parts.what: Makes the raw minerals — silicon carbide, aluminas and zirconia — that feed abrasives and refractories, sold both internally and to outside customers including a growing export book; about INR 1,632 crores consolidated and INR 906 crores standalone in FY26, and historically the segment most exposed to the Russian operation.

parts.name: Ceramics
parts.what: Industrial and engineered ceramic products (including wear-resistant and specialty applications, with subsidiaries in Australia and America); smallest of the three by revenue at about INR 1,268 crores consolidated and INR 1,000 crores standalone in FY26, but consistently the highest-margin segment — standalone PBIT margins in the mid-20s percent.

parts.name: Volzhsky Abrasives (VAW), Russia
parts.what: Russian subsidiary producing silicon carbide, refractories and abrasives with a large export share (43% of volume in Q1 FY25); a major profit contributor historically, but sanctions imposed in January 2025 cut it out of the consolidated FY26 numbers and cost roughly INR 87 crores of consolidated profit before tax.

parts.name: Rhodius (Germany)
parts.what: Acquired European abrasives maker selling cutting/grinding products into Europe and the Americas, around EUR 60 million of annual sales in FY26; loss-making that year (expected full-year loss of about EUR 4.5 million) after a disruptive warehouse shift and a purchase-price-allocation write-off.

parts.name: AWUKO (Germany)
parts.what: Small coated-abrasives subsidiary running roughly EUR 3 million of sales a quarter that never turned profitable; CUMI decided in FY26 to wind it up voluntarily, booking an exceptional charge of about INR 119 crores.

parts.name: Sterling Abrasives (India)
parts.what: Domestic abrasives subsidiary whose sales are tied to the agricultural market plus exports; small relative to the group and cited mainly as a swing factor when Indian agro demand slows.

parts.name: Foskor Zirconia (South Africa)
parts.what: 51%-held zirconia minerals operation that has not made sustainable profits since 2013; high South African electricity costs and global competition made it unviable, and the board decided in FY26 to stop operations, with a INR 16 crore asset write-down.

parts.name: SEDCO (power generation)
parts.what: A power-generating subsidiary mentioned in FY23 as a drag on consolidated profits when gas prices spiked; a side operation rather than a core product line.

overview.what_it_does: CarTrade Tech runs India's largest online marketplaces for vehicles — the websites and apps CarWale, BikeWale, CarTrade and OLX — where ordinary consumers research and buy new and used cars, two-wheelers and (on OLX) other used goods. It makes money mainly from car manufacturers (OEMs) and car dealers who pay to advertise and get customer leads on its sites, from fees on vehicles sold through its auction platform, and from classified listing and newer paid seller/buyer products on OLX such as Elite Buyer and Verification. Alongside the websites it runs a physical network — over 350 locations including Shriram Automall auction yards and abSure used-car outlets — where banks, financiers, fleet owners and individuals sell used vehicles by auction, at a run rate of about 1.9 million vehicles auctioned a year. The business is entirely India-based, debt free, with roughly INR1,244 crores of cash, about 85 million monthly users (95% of whom arrive without paid marketing), FY26 revenue growing 22% and profit after tax of about INR243 crores.

parts.name: Consumer Group (CarWale, BikeWale, CarTrade, abSure)
parts.what: The auto classifieds and media business where people research and shop for new and used cars and bikes, earning advertising and lead fees from manufacturers and dealers; it is the largest of the three businesses, growing revenue about 30% in FY26 at a 43% EBITDA margin, and includes the abSure used-car retail outlets.

parts.name: Remarketing (Shriram Automall)
parts.what: The used-vehicle auction business, run through physical auto malls plus online bidding, selling repossessed vehicles for financiers and increasingly retail/other seller supply — roughly 1.9 million vehicles auctioned a year, with FY26 revenue up 22% and margins crossing 28-30% after a flat patch in FY24.

parts.name: OLX India (Sobek Auto)
parts.what: The general online classifieds platform acquired in August 2023 where users buy and sell used items — about half automotive and half non-automotive — running at roughly INR61.7 crores of revenue a quarter with a 37% EBITDA margin, and now being monetised further through Elite Buyer, Verification and AI matchmaking/pricing tools.

overview.what_it_does: Castrol India Limited makes and sells lubricants — engine oils, greases and related fluids — under the Castrol brand in India, and is part of the global Castrol/BP group. Most of its money comes from selling branded oil to ordinary vehicle owners through an aftermarket retail network: as of 1Q 2026 more than 150,000 outlets nationwide, including 40,000 rural outlets, 34,000 independent bike workshops, 13,000 multi-brand car workshops and 800 Castrol Auto Service points, alongside sales to industrial customers and tie-ups with vehicle makers (OEMs). It buys base oil (a crude-derived feedstock) and additives from outside suppliers, blends them at plants such as Patalganga, Silvassa and Paharpur, and earns a margin on top — so profits swing with crude prices, the rupee and how quickly it can push through price increases. It reports on a January–December calendar year; FY2025 revenue was INR 5,722 crores with profit after tax of INR 950 crores, and it pays regular dividends (INR 8.75 per share for FY2025).

parts.name: Core automotive lubricants – personal mobility (cars and bikes)
parts.what: Engine oils for passenger cars and motorcycles sold through the retail aftermarket under brands like MAGNATEC, EDGE and POWER1; management calls this the core business, says its share of the automotive aftermarket retail market runs around 21–22%, and expects low car and bike ownership in India to keep this demand growing for years.

parts.name: Commercial vehicle and agriculture lubricants
parts.what: Heavy-duty oils for trucks and farm vehicles, sold under the CRB range (CRB Plus CI-4, CRB TURBOMAX+ CK4), supported by trucker-focused campaigns and programmes; described as an important, long-standing part of the business rather than a new entry.

parts.name: Industrial business
parts.what: Lubricants and fluids for factories and manufacturing customers, with products such as Hysol, Alusol and the Spheerol range increasingly made and tailored in India; management highlights it as a scale-up area that has delivered double-digit growth for multiple consecutive quarters and expects government manufacturing push to support it.

parts.name: Castrol Auto Care
parts.what: A newer non-oil range of car and bike care products (for example the Shiner Sponge), sold through e-commerce, modern trade and roughly 67,000 physical retail outlets as of end-2025, up from about 45,000 outlets in mid-2024.

parts.name: Services network (Castrol Auto Service, Express Oil Change, bike points, Rural Service Express)
parts.what: Branded workshop and quick oil-change formats that pull consumers toward Castrol products — grown from 163 auto service workshops in 2022 to 800 by March 2026, plus 30,000-plus bike workshops, over 500–700 Rural Service Express units for bikes, and Express Oil Change outlets sited at Jio-BP fuel stations.

parts.name: Rural distribution
parts.what: A deliberate push into small-town and village markets — over 40,000 rural outlets, targeting villages under 20,000 population — which management repeatedly names as a double-digit growth driver behind recent volume gains.

parts.name: EV fluids (Castrol ON)
parts.what: A range of e-coolants, e-transmission fluids and e-greases for electric vehicles, currently sold mainly to vehicle makers rather than the aftermarket because the EV vehicle population is still small; supported by BP's ~GBP 50 crore-equivalent (INR 500 crores) global battery R&D centre at Castrol's UK headquarters and an India Technology Centre at Patalganga.

parts.name: Data centre immersion cooling fluids
parts.what: A global Castrol initiative to sell thermal-management fluids that cool data centre equipment; management explicitly says it is very early, still at testing and proof-of-concept stage with partners, and too soon to talk about revenue.

parts.name: OEM partnerships and sustainability-linked products
parts.what: Collaborations with vehicle makers (Triumph Motorcycles for POWER1, an MOU with VinFast Auto India for EV after-sales at Castrol service centres) and re-refined base oil work, including India's first RRBO-based engine oil for BS-VI engines and an MOU with Hindustan Petroleum to explore a re-refined base oil ecosystem.

overview.what_it_does: AvenuesAI (formerly Infibeam Avenues, listed as CCAVENUE) runs CCAvenue, a payment gateway that lets businesses accept digital payments — credit and debit cards, net banking, prepaid instruments, NEFT/RTGS, UPI — online and, increasingly, at physical stores; alongside this it sells software platforms to governments and enterprises, the biggest being the technology behind India's Government e-Marketplace (GeM). It sells mainly to merchants and banks, from very large enterprises in utilities, telecom, travel and hospitality down to SMEs and cooperative banks, adding roughly 2,550 new merchants a day in Q1 FY25 (230,022 in the quarter). It earns money by keeping a thin slice of every rupee processed: gross revenue is huge because it includes money passed through to banks and networks, while the 'net revenue' it actually keeps is a take rate of a few basis points — 6.9 bps in Q1 FY23 rising to 11.2 bps in Q1 FY25 — so Q1 FY25 gross revenue of INR753 crores translated into net revenue of INR119 crores, EBITDA of INR70 crores and profit of INR50 crores. It is primarily an India business (total transaction processing volume of INR87,218 crores in Q1 FY23 alone), with a growing international arm in the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Oman plus a GIFT City base for cross-border and dollar settlement, targeted to reach 12–15% of net revenue.

parts.name: CCAvenue (India payments / payment gateway)
parts.what: The core business and, in management's words, 'the economic engine' — it processes card, net-banking and other digital payments for merchants and holds an RBI payment aggregator licence, an in-principle licence to issue prepaid wallets and RBI authorisation for offline (POS) payment aggregation; it drives essentially all of the transaction volume and take-rate income.

parts.name: Platform business (including GeM)
parts.what: Software platforms sold to government and enterprises, most notably the Government e-Marketplace, whose volumes are counted inside reported transaction processing volume and which had crossed INR50,000 crores by 1 August 2022 at double the prior year's pace; it is reported together with the India payments business as the 'standalone' core.

parts.name: International payments
parts.what: Merchant acquiring and payment infrastructure work in the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Oman (where it works with several leading banks as a technology partner), plus IFSCA approval at GIFT City for cross-border payments, escrow and international acquiring — currently a single-digit share of net revenue that management wants to lift to 12–15%, with the US named as the next focus.

parts.name: Rediff / RediffOne / RediffPay (consumer and business platform)
parts.what: A majority stake in Rediff.com, bought in 2024, bringing cloud e-mail, content and commerce services with over 55 million monthly visitors; management is turning it into a consumer engagement and payments front-end (RediffPay, UPI) and an 'AI-native back office' for SMEs and enterprises (RediffOne), described as a customer-acquisition and lock-in layer rather than a major revenue line today.

parts.name: Phronetic AI (AI vertical)
parts.what: The in-house artificial-intelligence arm — set up partly as a new subsidiary for AI-based fraud detection and prevention and holder of a US patent filing — which management calls 'the invisible orchestrator', automating transaction routing, risk, reconciliation and compliance across the group; it is framed as a margin and efficiency driver rather than a separately sized revenue business.

parts.name: Embedded finance and lending
parts.what: A stated priority for FY27 rather than a running business: instead of lending off its own balance sheet, the company plans to distribute and underwrite merchant, checkout and consumer credit using its payments data, via a proposed investment in Online PSB Loans and a stake in NBFC Ratnaafin.

parts.name: Infibeam Digital Entertainment
parts.what: A subsidiary in digital media technology and live events, taken to 100% ownership in 2024; mentioned only in passing and clearly small relative to payments.

overview.what_it_does: CCL Products (India) Limited buys green (raw) coffee beans and processes them into instant/soluble coffee — spray-dried and freeze-dried — which it sells mostly business-to-business to overseas customers in bulk or as private-label packs that those customers sell under their own brand names. It also sells its own retail brand, Continental Coffee, in India, plus the UK retail brand Percol it acquired in July 2023. Management describes it as a cost-plus model where profit is earned as a roughly fixed EBITDA per kilo (about INR 130-140/kg recently), so earnings track volume growth rather than the sales figure, which moves up and down with green coffee prices; volume growth has run roughly 14-20% a year with FY26 group revenue of about INR 4,466 crore and net profit of about INR 388 crore. It manufactures in India (registered at Duggirala, Guntur district, Andhra Pradesh, plus units referred to as NCL and F&B) and in Vietnam, and is described as naturally hedged because it imports much of its coffee and exports the finished product.

parts.name: Exports / international B2B (bulk and private label)
parts.what: Sells instant coffee in bulk and in private-label packs to overseas customers across North America, Europe, East Asia/China and other geographies; this is the bulk of the business — management said the domestic market used only about 10% of capacity in FY23, and in FY26 India was roughly INR 650 crore of about INR 4,466 crore group revenue.

parts.name: Domestic branded business (Continental Coffee)
parts.what: CCL's own consumer coffee brand sold in India, now the number 3 player nationally (number 2 in some regions and platforms), at about INR 440 crore of branded sales in FY26 (up from roughly INR 210 crore in FY24) and INR 125 crore in Q1 FY27, growing fast off a small base and requiring ongoing brand investment.

parts.name: Domestic bulk and private label
parts.what: Unbranded and own-label instant coffee sold to other Indian buyers, making up the remainder of the roughly INR 650 crore India gross turnover in FY26 (about INR 180 crore gross in Q1 FY27 with INR 125 crore of that branded).

parts.name: Percol (UK retail brand)
parts.what: A retail coffee brand acquired in July 2023, relaunched in 2024 with new packaging, design and formulation, with supply shifted from a third party to CCL's own plants so the company can invest behind and grow it.

parts.name: Product mix: spray-dried vs freeze-dried
parts.what: Two manufacturing routes with different economics — freeze-dried historically earned a higher EBITDA per kilo than spray-dried — with freeze-dried capacity added in Vietnam (commercial operations targeted for late 2024) and freeze-dried utilisation improving fast enough by FY26 that management is weighing more capacity or a strategic tie-up.

parts.name: Manufacturing capacity and expansion
parts.what: Capacity was about 38,500 tonnes in FY22 with plans taking it past 70,000 tonnes, built out through Indian units and the Vietnam plant; as of May 2026 management says existing capacity is sufficient for the next two years of planned growth.

overview.what_it_does: CDSL is an Indian 'depository' — a market infrastructure institution that holds shares and other securities in electronic (demat) form on behalf of investors, so that buying, selling and transferring them happens as book entries instead of paper. Its customers are three groups: the depository participants (brokers and banks, over 20,700 service locations covering ~98% of India's pin codes) who open demat accounts for investors, the investors themselves (17.27 crore accounts as of Dec 2025, 18.01 crore by March 2026, an ~80%+ share of the industry), and the issuer companies whose securities sit in the system (about 18,798 active companies in mid-2022). It earns fees from these parties — annual charges billed to issuer companies based on their folio counts (billed largely in the first quarter), account and transaction-related charges from depository participants, and per-record fees in its KYC business, where roughly 80% of income comes from 'fetches' (other financial firms pulling an existing KYC record). It operates in India, regulated by SEBI, with a new unit being set up at GIFT City IFSC; FY2025-26 standalone income was INR1,096 crores with net profit of INR468 crores.

parts.name: Depository (standalone CDSL)
parts.what: The core business — holding securities in demat accounts for investors, settling transfers, and servicing issuer companies; it is by far the largest part, with standalone FY26 income of INR1,096 crores and net profit of INR468 crores versus a much smaller subsidiary contribution, and management repeatedly compares it to an infrastructure company that must keep adding technology capacity ahead of volume surges.

parts.name: CDSL Ventures Limited (CVL) — KYC Registration Agency
parts.what: Wholly owned subsidiary that creates and stores investor KYC (identity verification) records and lets other financial firms 'fetch' them, described as the first and largest KYC registration agency; income is cyclical with market activity — it grew 65% to INR169 crores of operational revenue in FY24 but fell to INR132 crores in the first nine months of FY26, and management was questioned about pricing risk from the government's CKYC 2.0.

parts.name: Registrar & Transfer Agency (RTA) and GST filing services (within CVL)
parts.what: Smaller add-on services run out of the subsidiary — acting as record-keeper for companies (870 companies by June 2022, 30 added that quarter) and processing GST filings (55.48 lakh in Q1 FY23, up 14%).

parts.name: Centrico Insurance Repository Limited
parts.what: Subsidiary that applies the same dematerialisation idea to insurance policies, holding them in electronic form; management called it 'work in progress' with a dedicated team in 2024 and it now has its own MD & CEO on the earnings calls, but no revenue figures are given, suggesting it is still small.

parts.name: Countrywide Commodity Repository Limited
parts.what: Subsidiary extending electronic record-keeping to commodities; it is named on the calls with its own MD & CEO present, but the excerpts give no size or revenue detail.

parts.name: CDSL IFSC (GIFT City)
parts.what: A new unit at GIFT City for which CDSL Ventures received SEBI's no-objection, to be registered with IFSCA as the first KYC registration agency there, aimed at serving international issuers and investors — described as a step for future growth rather than a current earner.

parts.name: Investor education / CDSL IPF
parts.what: Not a revenue line but a stated priority — free multilingual services (electronic account statements in 23 languages), a 100-million-view YouTube channel, comic books with Amar Chitra Katha in 12 languages, and the annual Reimagine Symposium, all aimed at bringing more first-time investors into the market that CDSL ultimately gets paid to service.

overview.what_it_does: CEAT Limited is an Indian tyre manufacturer that makes and sells tyres for two- and three-wheelers, passenger cars and SUVs, trucks and buses (both bias and radial), farm/agricultural vehicles, and off-highway equipment. It sells through three routes: the replacement market (aftermarket buyers replacing worn tyres via its distribution network, including rural dealers and a small direct-to-consumer online channel), OEMs (vehicle makers such as Maruti Suzuki, Mahindra, Renault-Nissan and Daimler who fit CEAT tyres on new vehicles), and international markets (Europe, the U.S., Middle East, Brazil, Vietnam, Peru and others). It earns money on the spread between tyre selling prices and raw material costs — mainly natural rubber and crude-linked inputs — so profit swings with commodity prices and how fast it can push through price increases, with roughly 20% of standalone revenue from international sales and about 23% including CAMSO. Manufacturing is centred in India (Halol, Chennai, Ambernath, Nagpur) plus off-highway operations in Sri Lanka, with quarterly standalone revenue around INR4,163 crore and EBITDA margins that have run between roughly 9% and 15%.

parts.name: Replacement (aftermarket)
parts.what: Selling tyres to existing vehicle owners through dealers and distributors — described as a core growth engine that grew in the mid-teens in recent quarters, with a distribution advantage in rural India where growth ran 40%-50% faster than urban.

parts.name: OEM
parts.what: Supplying tyres fitted onto new vehicles at the factory, spanning two-wheelers, passenger cars, trucks/buses and farm vehicles; management says CEAT holds close to 50% share of business in two-wheeler OEMs and around 25%-29% share on electric-vehicle launches.

parts.name: International Business (exports)
parts.what: Exporting tyres to Europe, the U.S., Middle East, Latin America and other markets, which management calls a core focus area and margin-accretive; it has risen to about 20% of standalone revenue (23% with CAMSO) and grew around 30% in the latest quarter, supported by new branches in Germany, the U.K., France and Poland.

parts.name: Two-wheeler and three-wheeler tyres
parts.what: Motorcycle and scooter tyres, one of the strongest-growing categories (replacement volumes up in the mid-20s in one quarter), with a premium sub-segment of radials and tyres for 250cc-plus bikes.

parts.name: Passenger car and SUV (PC/UV) tyres
parts.what: Car and SUV tyres where management pushes 'premiumisation' via 17-inch-plus rim sizes; premium 17-inch-plus replacement volumes reportedly doubled in one quarter and the company targets market leadership in the category.

parts.name: Truck and bus tyres (TBR and bias)
parts.what: Commercial vehicle tyres, split between newer truck-bus radials (TBR) and older bias tyres; a large commercial category that grew in low teens in replacement and has recently begun launching top-of-the-line premium products offering lower total cost of ownership.

parts.name: Farm / agricultural tyres
parts.what: Tyres for tractors and farm equipment, tied to rural incomes and harvests, with capacity expansion at the Ambernath agri-radial plant and OEM approvals from names like AGCO Massey Ferguson and John Deere Brazil.

parts.name: Off-highway tyres (OHT) / specialty
parts.what: Tyres for construction, mining and other off-road machinery, sold heavily into European and U.S. aftermarkets; the company launched 130-plus new OHT SKUs in one year and treats it as a high-realisation specialty business.

parts.name: CAMSO
parts.what: An acquired premium off-highway tyre and rubber-track brand (operations in Sri Lanka) closed around May 2025, described as running roughly USD10 million of quarterly topline at customer prices; it is still in a multi-quarter transition where CEAT sells through Michelin and buys semi-finished goods from Michelin, with full value-chain control expected by FY28.

parts.name: CEAT Sri Lanka OHT
parts.what: An overseas manufacturing entity making off-highway tyres and tracks in Sri Lanka; it carries about USD80 million of debt, and Sri Lankan rupee depreciation cost roughly INR48 crore in one quarter, which is why consolidated profit lagged standalone profit.

parts.name: Digital / D2C and AI
parts.what: Online and direct-to-consumer selling plus internal digitisation — D2C was about 6% of passenger replacement sales in FY23 (peaking 8%-9%), and the company runs WEF 'Lighthouse'-recognised smart factories at Chennai and Halol alongside an enterprise data lake and agentic-AI programmes.

overview.what_it_does: Cello World is an Indian consumer-goods company that makes and sells everyday household items — insulated steel water bottles and flasks, dinnerware, glassware and opalware, plastic storage and cleaning products, small electric kitchenware, pens and stationery, and plastic moulded furniture — under its own brands, mainly Cello and Unomax. It sells to ordinary Indian households (management calls the middle class its largest customer segment) through shops, with general trade the backbone at roughly 75% of sales, plus online/quick-commerce (grown to about 15-17%), exports (~8-9%) and modern retail. It earns money by manufacturing most of what it sells — about 80% of revenue comes from its own 13-plus plants in Daman, Baddi, Haridwar, Kolkata, Chennai and a newer Rajasthan site — and selling at high gross margins of roughly 50%, giving an EBITDA margin in the low-to-mid 20s. It is almost entirely India-focused, with a modest export business (largest in pens); FY26 revenue was about INR 2,324 crores with PAT of INR 331 crores.

parts.name: Consumerware
parts.what: The core and largest business at roughly 66-70% of revenue, covering insulated steel bottles/flasks ("hydration"), opalware and glassware, storage, houseware, cleanware and electric kitchenware, at about 50% gross margin; management says growth here drives the whole company, and a Q3 FY26 stock-out in insulated steel dented sales and margins.

parts.name: Writing Instruments
parts.what: Ball and gel pens plus stationery, sold under Unomax and, from Q4 FY26, the Cello brand as well; about 14-20% of revenue, the highest-margin vertical at 55-57% gross margin, with a meaningful export component, and management targets INR 500 crores-plus in FY27 and INR 1,000 crores in a couple of years.

parts.name: Moulded Furniture and Allied Products
parts.what: Plastic chairs and furniture, roughly 14-17% of revenue and the lowest-margin part at about 40% gross margin, facing heavy unorganized competition, so management is pushing value-added products; Wimplast Limited was merged into Cello World in FY26 to combine it with consumerware.

parts.name: Glassware plant (Rajasthan)
parts.what: A greenfield soda-lime glass unit costing about INR 200 crores that began commercial production in February 2025 to make tumblers, storage containers and drinkware; it is running at only ~60% utilisation and is merely at breakeven because of cheap Chinese imports, and management calls it a long-term strategic bet rather than a near-term profit source (peak potential ~INR 250 crores of revenue).

parts.name: Insulated steel bottle plant (Rajasthan)
parts.what: A newly commissioned, fully integrated plant for insulated steel bottles, being brought up line by line through FY27; management blames its slow ramp plus the resulting stock-outs for weak consumerware sales and softer margins in FY26, and expects the steel business to normalise over the following couple of quarters.

overview.what_it_does: Cemindia Projects Limited (NSE code CEMPRO, formerly ITD Cementation India Limited) is an Indian heavy civil-engineering and construction contractor that builds large infrastructure to order for others — it does not own or operate the assets it builds. Its customers are mainly government bodies and state agencies (metro rail corporations, the Navy, state governments, port authorities like Vadhvan and JNPT) plus large private and group clients such as Adani, JSW and Petronet. It makes money by winning tenders and executing contracts — some fixed-price, some 'star price' where key input costs are passed through — recognising revenue as work progresses and earning a thin contractor's margin, roughly 10-12% EBITDA and 5-6% net profit, on FY26 revenue of about INR 10,061 crores. It works across India (Chennai, Bangalore, Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi and Pune metros, Ganga Expressway in UP, ports in Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Odisha, a Bihar road) and has been pushing into overseas markets — Colombo, Bangladesh and Abu Dhabi. As of April 2026 it was sitting on an order book of about INR 29,000 crores, roughly three years of revenue.

parts.name: MRTS / Metro (underground and elevated)
parts.what: Builds metro rail civil works — tunnels bored with TBMs, underground stations, and elevated viaducts — across Chennai, Bangalore, Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi and Pune; described repeatedly as the company's core technical strength and a steady source of large orders, with several signature metro jobs completed in FY26.

parts.name: Marine / Maritime structures
parts.what: Constructs ports, jetties and breakwaters — Udangudi (a breakwater 9 km out to sea, called a first in Asia), Vizhinjam deep-sea port, Sea Bird, JNPT/BMCT, Navy's Project Varsha and the awaited Vadhvan Port; a major segment (around INR 6,400 crores of order-book exposure in 2024) though management calls marine 'a limited market'.

parts.name: Roads and highways
parts.what: Executes greenfield road and elevated-corridor projects, notably the Ganga Expressway in UP (won for about INR 4,850 crores, contributing over INR 600 crores of revenue in a single quarter at peak) and a newer road-cum-bridge job in Bihar; management notes road margins are structurally lower than its other work.

parts.name: Buildings and general civil works
parts.what: Puts up institutional and commercial buildings — Sikkim University, a Guwahati riverside development, the new High Court/Circuit Bench building handed to the Government of West Bengal — a smaller, supporting line rather than a headline driver.

parts.name: Industrial and group projects (including data centres)
parts.what: Newer work for industrial and private-group clients, such as the Petronet job at Dahej and prospective data-centre construction for Adani group entities; small today but flagged on recent calls as a growing order source since the promoter change.

parts.name: Overseas / international
parts.what: Contracts outside India — West Container Terminal in Colombo, a project in Bangladesh (worth about INR 1,500 crores, delayed by political unrest), and Ruwais in Abu Dhabi; presence was 'nil' two years before 2024 and management repeatedly calls it the key focus area because overseas contract terms are more equitable.

overview.what_it_does: Central Bank of India is an Indian public-sector bank, over 114 years old, that takes deposits from the public and lends that money out — its total business (deposits plus loans) stood at about INR 8.33 lakh crore as of June 2026, split between INR 4.79 lakh crore of deposits and INR 3.54 lakh crore of loans. It sells everyday banking to households, farmers, small businesses and large companies through a pan-India branch network of 4,605 branches (65% of them in rural and semi-urban areas), 3,820 ATMs, 13,890 business-correspondent outlets and 22,346 total touch points, plus a new IFSC banking unit at GIFT City for overseas business and 159 NRI desks. It earns mainly from net interest income — interest on loans (yield ~8.8%) and on its investment book, minus what it pays depositors (cost of deposits ~4.6%) — which was INR 14,171 crore for FY26, helped by a very high share of cheap current and savings deposits (CASA around 47% of deposits, one of the best in the industry). A smaller slice of income comes from fees, treasury/investment gains, forex and bank guarantees, and from recovering money on loans it had already written off (e.g. INR 1,062 crore in one quarter). The bank also meets government-mandated priority-sector lending targets (58% of lending versus a 40% requirement) and holds joint ventures in home finance and financial services, with approved stakes of 25.18% in Future Generali's life insurance and 24.91% in its non-life insurance arms.

parts.name: Deposits / CASA
parts.what: The funding side of the bank — current and savings accounts plus term deposits from retail and government customers; deposits were INR 4.79 lakh crore in June 2026, with CASA at 46.61% (savings alone crossed INR 2 lakh crore) which management repeatedly calls the bank's single biggest strength, and it markets specific deposit products such as Cent Queen (INR 1,457 crore mobilised) and Salary Cent Prestige (INR 787 crore).

parts.name: RAM (Retail, Agriculture and MSME)
parts.what: Management's core 'growth engine', making up roughly 68% of the loan book against a guided 65:35 RAM-to-corporate mix, and growing about 21% a year.

parts.name: Retail
parts.what: Home, auto, education and personal loans to individuals — about INR 1.05 lakh crore in June 2026 and roughly 30% of total advances, with housing loans alone making up around 63% of retail; management says retail needs constant monitoring and follow-up, so it uses call centres, bots and 'feet on street'.

parts.name: Agriculture
parts.what: Farm and allied lending, INR 64,274 crore in June 2026, which also helps the bank clear its mandated targets for agriculture and for small and marginal farmers (11% versus a 9.5% norm).

parts.name: MSME
parts.what: Loans to micro, small and medium enterprises, INR 71,308 crore in June 2026 and growing ~18%; lending to micro enterprises alone is over 15% versus a 7.5% regulatory threshold.

parts.name: Corporate
parts.what: Large-company and project lending, INR 1,12,770 crore in June 2026 after 46.5% growth off a low base (the bank had deliberately shrunk this book earlier), concentrated in renewable energy, data centres, HAM road projects and commercial real estate, with new corporate and mid-corporate branches being opened.

parts.name: Gold loan and SHG verticals
parts.what: Two newly carved-out dedicated divisions reporting to an Executive Director — the gold loan book is about INR 36,000 crore with management saying there is still a lot of untapped scope, especially in South India — flagged as future credit growth engines.

parts.name: Treasury / investment book
parts.what: The bank's portfolio of investments (largely securities), which earns interest income of around INR 2,547 crore a quarter at a ~6.9% yield plus trading gains that swing a lot — treasury income fell from over INR 300 crore in one quarter to INR 9 crore the next on mark-to-market.

parts.name: Non-interest income (fees, recovery in written-off accounts, forex, guarantees)
parts.what: Fee-based earnings plus cash recovered from loans already written off — INR 1,647 crore in one quarter, of which INR 620 crore was write-off recovery — and the bank has set up a centralised bank-guarantee cell and a centralised forex cell to push this line higher.

parts.name: Co-lending
parts.what: Loans originated jointly with partners, described as a newer stream that scaled from INR 355 crore outstanding in Sept 2021 to INR 3,362 crore a year later and called 'very robust' in later calls.

parts.name: Joint ventures and insurance stakes
parts.what: Two existing JVs in home finance and financial services, to which the bank added approved acquisitions of 25.18% of Future Generali's life insurance arm and 24.91% of its non-life arm.

parts.name: Branch network and overseas/GIFT City unit
parts.what: The distribution engine — 4,605 branches with 65% in rural and semi-urban India, business correspondents, customer acquisition centres at 35 places and government business centres at 9, plus one new GIFT City IFSC banking unit opened June 2026 that management intends to use as its platform for overseas business.

overview.what_it_does: Century Plyboards (India) Limited is an Indian building-materials and interior-products manufacturer that makes and sells branded wood panels — plywood, decorative laminates, MDF (medium-density fibreboard) and particleboard — used in home and office interiors, furniture and fit-outs. It earns money by manufacturing these boards in its own plants and selling them through a dealer/distribution network to the trade (dealers, retailers and carpenters), supported by heavy brand-building spend such as IPL advertising, with brands including Century and the value brand 'Sainik'; a laminate line at Andhra is also aimed at exports. Operations are almost entirely in India, with plants at Hoshiarpur (Punjab), Andhra Pradesh (Badvel), Chennai, Kandla, Guwahati and Joka, plus a large new INR 1,100 crore project announced for Uttar Pradesh; overseas arms such as a Singapore subsidiary were sold off in April 2024. Consolidated revenue reached a record INR 1,492 crores in the March 2026 quarter (FY26 revenue up 19.2%, EBITDA INR 702 crores, PAT INR 268 crores), and management has stated a long-term ambition of INR 12,000 crores of revenue by FY31.

parts.name: Plywood
parts.what: The core and biggest business — making and selling branded plywood (including premium and the mass-market 'Sainik' range) — at INR 710 crores of revenue in the Dec-2025 quarter it is roughly half of company sales, with EBITDA margins around 15-16% and capacity being expanded toward ~430,000 CBM plus new lines at Hoshiarpur, Chennai and UP.

parts.name: Laminate
parts.what: Decorative laminate sheets used as surfacing for furniture and interiors, including compact and larger-size laminates for export from the newer Andhra plant; revenue was INR 183 crores in the Dec-2025 quarter, and margins recovered to 8.5% for FY26 from 5.2% a year earlier after a weak couple of years.

parts.name: MDF (medium-density fibreboard)
parts.what: Engineered wood panels sold as a plywood alternative for furniture, made at Hoshiarpur and a large new South India plant at Badvel (Andhra), costing about INR 730 crores; it is the fastest-growing segment with FY26 revenue up 25.5% and margins of 12.7%, running at 80-85% utilisation with capacity heading toward roughly 625,000 cubic metres a year.

parts.name: Particle board
parts.what: Lower-cost boards made from wood particles, largely sold as pre-laminated panels; the smallest board segment at INR 65 crores in the Dec-2025 quarter, it grew 38.2% in FY26 off a new continuous-process plant but is only just around breakeven on profits.

parts.name: PBC board (Andhra)
parts.what: A newer board line started at the Andhra location in May 2024 that management said would add close to INR 100 crores of revenue within a year.

parts.name: Century Ports
parts.what: A wholly owned subsidiary that began commercial operations in Q4 FY26 running the rejuvenated Khidderpore Docks (KPD-1 West) at Kolkata port — a diversification into port logistics and infrastructure that management expects to turn cash positive in Q1 FY27.

overview.what_it_does: Cera Sanitaryware is an Indian branded bathroom products company that sells toilets and other ceramic sanitaryware, taps and bathroom fittings (faucetware), tiles, and 'wellness' products such as higher-end bath fixtures. It sells mainly to household consumers doing new homes, renovation and upgradation — reaching them through a network of dealers and retailers (B2C was about 64% of revenue in Q1 FY25) — and also directly to real estate developers and institutions through a B2B projects channel, plus franchise and institutional tie-ups with names like McDonald's, JSW One Homes and Shalby Hospitals. It makes money by manufacturing sanitaryware and faucetware in its own plants in Gujarat (Kadi) and selling under its own brands at a markup, supplementing in-house output with outsourced and a small amount of imported product (imports from China were about 2% of sales in Q1 FY25); profitability swings with raw material costs (clay, brass), natural gas prices, trade discounts and advertising spend. Operations are entirely in India, spread across urban markets and Tier 2/Tier 3 towns, with named focus states including the Northeast, West Bengal, Bihar, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha.

parts.name: Sanitaryware
parts.what: Ceramic bathroom fixtures (toilets, washbasins and similar) made in the company's own plant — the largest business at roughly 46%-54% of quarterly revenue across the calls, with plant capacity utilization ranging from about 76% to over 109%, and a greenfield expansion plant in progress since 2022.

parts.name: Faucetware
parts.what: Taps, showers and metal bathroom fittings, also made in-house — the second-largest business at roughly 35%-43% of revenue, with monthly output grown from 1.8 lakh pieces (FY22) to 3 lakh, then 4 lakh after expansion, and 4.3 lakh in March 2026, with a further expansion to 5 lakh pieces planned by Q4 FY27 for about INR 5 crore.

parts.name: Tiles
parts.what: Floor and wall tiles sold under the Cera brand, a smaller side category at roughly 9%-12% of revenue.

parts.name: Wellness
parts.what: The smallest category at about 1%-2% of revenue, though growing fast in some quarters (up 29.4% year-on-year in Q3 FY26).

parts.name: Cera (flagship brand)
parts.what: The main mass and mid-segment brand that management calls the primary driver of volumes and overall business performance.

parts.name: Cera Luxe / Lustre
parts.what: Premium and contemporary sub-brands used to push into higher-priced bathroom products; in Q1 FY25, 44% of sales were premium, 32% mid and 24% entry-level.

parts.name: Senator
parts.what: A luxury brand sold through a separate flagship-store retail format — 32 stores operational as of Q3 FY26 and 40 by end-FY26, targeting 60 by FY27 — still in the investment and brand-building phase with pre-operating costs weighing on margins.

parts.name: POLIPLUZ
parts.what: A newer value-focused brand aimed at price-sensitive markets, distributed through 102 distributors and 1,120 dealers as of FY26 with a target of 200 distributors and 2,000 dealers by end-FY27; like Senator, it is still in buildup phase and not yet a meaningful revenue contributor.

parts.name: B2B / project sales
parts.what: Direct supply to real estate developers for residential projects, described as an important support pillar during weak retail demand, with management being selective about projects to protect margins.

parts.name: Retailer loyalty and dealer management programs
parts.what: Not a revenue line but a core distribution tool — an app-based retailer rewards scheme with over 28,000 enrolled retailers by Q3 FY26, being linked to a new dealer management system to track secondary sales and channel inventory.

overview.what_it_does: Capri Global Capital (CGCL) is an Indian non-bank lender — it borrows money (from banks and the debt market) and lends it out at higher rates, keeping the difference. Every loan it makes is backed by collateral: gold jewellery, a house, a shop or other property, or a residential project under construction. Its customers are mostly small, self-employed retail borrowers and small businesses, plus mid-sized property developers, served through a branch network that reached 1,429 locations and roughly 6.9 lakh (690,000) customers by March 2026, spread across India with heavy recent expansion into the south and east (Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Odisha). Alongside interest income (yields around 16.3% and a spread of about 7% in Q4 FY26), it earns fee income from distributing car loans and insurance for other institutions and from co-lending arrangements with banks; total loan book (AUM) was INR36,623 crores in March 2026, up 60% year-on-year, with full-year profit of INR949 crores.

parts.name: Gold Loan
parts.what: Small loans against household gold jewellery, made through dedicated branches; launched around 2022 and now the biggest business at INR16,965 crores AUM (grew 111% in FY26), with very low bad loans (0.3% gross NPA) and about INR17 crores of loans per branch.

parts.name: Housing Finance (affordable home loans)
parts.what: Home loans in the affordable segment, increasingly to self-employed borrowers (74% of the book), at INR7,447 crores AUM and growing 43% year-on-year.

parts.name: MSME lending (including Micro LAP)
parts.what: Secured business loans to micro, small and medium enterprises — INR6,465 crores AUM, up 23% — including a newer 'Micro LAP' sub-vertical of smaller-ticket loans to emerging self-employed borrowers (INR824 crores across 151+ branches).

parts.name: Construction Finance
parts.what: Project loans to mid-sized and small residential developers in metro and Tier-1 cities, run with escrow-controlled cash flows; INR5,708 crores across 282 active projects, and management deliberately caps this at or below about 20% of the total book.

parts.name: Co-lending (with partner banks)
parts.what: Loans originated by Capri but funded jointly with banks, so Capri earns fees and keeps only part of the loan on its own balance sheet — a capital-light growth route that had reached INR7,138 crores, about 23.5% of AUM, by December 2025.

parts.name: Car loan distribution
parts.what: A fee-only business where Capri sources and originates car loans for other lenders rather than lending itself — an early and steady contributor to non-interest income (e.g. INR11 billion of originations and INR186 million of net fees in a single quarter of FY23).

parts.name: Insurance distribution
parts.what: Selling insurance to customers for fee income; described as a newer stream expected to contribute from FY25 onward.

parts.name: Indirect / wholesale lending
parts.what: A smaller legacy wholesale book grouped with construction finance in reporting (together about 20% of AUM in FY24), historically with near-nil bad loans.

overview.what_it_does: CG Power and Industrial Solutions makes heavy electrical equipment in India — electric motors, drives, railway propulsion and signalling systems, power transformers, and switchgear such as circuit breakers, instrument transformers and lightning arrestors. It sells mainly to industrial customers, power utilities and grid operators (for example Power Grid Corporation and Techno Electric), Indian Railways, and increasingly to overseas buyers, including a US data-centre project that placed a roughly INR 900 crore (about $99 million) transformer export order in January 2026. Revenue comes from winning equipment orders, largely through tenders, and executing them over months or years, so the company reports an order intake and an unexecuted order backlog alongside sales; contracts in the power business typically carry price variation clauses that pass commodity cost changes on to customers, while industrial products rely on periodic price increases. It is based in India (standalone FY26 sales of INR 11,331 crores) and also runs subsidiaries in Sweden, Germany and the Netherlands plus semiconductor ventures, taking consolidated FY26 sales to INR 12,418 crores with PAT before exceptional items of INR 1,232 crores and a closing backlog of INR 17,107 crores.

parts.name: Power Systems
parts.what: Makes and services transformers (up to 765 kV) and switchgear/EHV products for utilities, grid projects and data centres; FY26 sales were INR 5,138 crores, up 46%, at a 21.9% PBIT margin, and it is the company's fastest-growing and most profitable segment with a backlog of INR 12,644 crores, up 91% year-over-year.

parts.name: Transformers business
parts.what: The transformer half of Power Systems, which won the largest-ever domestic order of INR 641 crores for 765 kV transformer packages from Power Grid and the largest-ever single order overall, roughly INR 900 crores of power transformers exported to a US hyperscale data-centre project.

parts.name: Switchgears & EPD / EHV business
parts.what: The other half of Power Systems, supplying medium-voltage and extra-high-voltage circuit breakers, instrument transformers and gas-insulated switchgear; management said it is running neck-and-neck with transformers on orders and the board approved a INR 748 crore greenfield expansion in October 2025 for domestic and export demand.

parts.name: Industrial Systems
