parts.what: Covers motors, railways and drives; FY26 sales were INR 6,197 crores, up only 6%, with PBIT margin slipping to 9.9% from 12.1% because of commodity inflation the company could not fully pass on and competitive pricing and mix changes in railways.

parts.name: Motors business (India subcontinent)
parts.what: Sells low-tension and high-tension electric motors to industrial customers; a soft market forced a roughly 5% price increase from July 2025, and by Q4 FY26 management said motors had stabilised and were growing at double digits.

parts.name: Railway business
parts.what: Supplies propulsion systems for locomotives and Vande Bharat trains (including an order from an RVNL joint venture) and KAVACH train collision avoidance systems; it grew fast enough to shift the Industrial mix, but its tender pricing and a restrictive price variation clause dragged segment margins down.

parts.name: Drives & Automation (and international motors)
parts.what: Overseas operating subsidiaries in Sweden, Germany and the Netherlands whose weak sales in Q1 FY26 hurt consolidated margins through poor fixed-cost absorption, though management pointed to recovering bookings and healthy order growth by year-end.

parts.name: CG Semi Private Limited
parts.what: A subsidiary building India's semiconductor packaging (OSAT) capacity at Sanand, Gujarat — the G1 plant opened in August 2025 at a peak half a million units a day and G2 is due by end-2026 at about 14.5 million chips a day — a INR 7,584 crore project with roughly INR 3,501 crores of central and INR 1,400 crores of state government support that is currently a cost, not a profit contributor.

parts.name: Axiro Semiconductor Group
parts.what: A radio-frequency semiconductor components business bought from Renesas and affiliates, first consolidated in Q1 FY26; together with CG Semi it cut consolidated FY26 profit by INR 111 crores (89 basis points of margin).

parts.name: G.G. Tronics
parts.what: A subsidiary in railway signalling that won a roughly INR 148 crore order for station KAVACH supply, installation and commissioning in North Western Railways, executable over two years.

parts.name: Consumer Products business
parts.what: A separate business headed by its own EVP who joined the FY26 earnings calls, though the excerpts give no sales, margin or product detail for it.

parts.name: CG Adhesive Products
parts.what: A consolidated operating subsidiary listed in the group results, with no size or activity detail given in the calls.

overview.what_it_does: Chalet Hotels is an Indian company that owns and develops hotels, plus some office and residential real estate, mainly in and around big cities like Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Delhi NCR and Goa/Udaipur. Its main business is selling hotel rooms and food and beverage to business travellers, wedding and conference (MICE) groups, airline crew and, increasingly, leisure guests — the hotels carry outside brands such as JW Marriott, Westin, Novotel, Hyatt, Taj and Ritz-Carlton, with Chalet owning the buildings and the brands running/marketing them, plus its own new resort brand 'Athiva'. Alongside the hotels it earns steady rental income from office towers it owns (the 'CIGNUS' buildings at Powai and Whitefield) and one-off cash from selling flats in a residential project in Bengaluru. By FY26 the group did about INR25 billion of consolidated revenue and roughly INR10 billion of EBITDA, with 3,389 hotel rooms operating and about 1,655 more in the pipeline.

parts.name: Hospitality
parts.what: Owning and operating branded hotels and resorts (rooms plus restaurants, bars and banquets), which management calls the core of the platform — roughly 88% of revenue in Q1 FY23 and still the bulk of the INR20.7 billion ex-residential FY26 revenue, at margins of about 41-46%.

parts.name: Rental and annuity / Commercial real estate
parts.what: Leasing out office space it owns (about 2.4 million sq ft leasable as of 2024, branded CIGNUS at Powai and Whitefield), described as a deliberate move into a different asset class to smooth out the hotel cycle — small but growing, at roughly INR355 million of quarterly revenue in FY25 rising to an INR280 million monthly run-rate by March 2026, with high margins around 75-80%.

parts.name: Residential
parts.what: Selling apartments in a project at Koramangala, Bengaluru — a finite, one-time cash generator rather than an ongoing business; 138 units had been sold since relaunch by mid-2024, and by FY26 it added only about INR166 million on top of the ex-residential revenue.

parts.name: Development / pipeline
parts.what: Building new hotels and towers and buying land or existing properties to convert — e.g. the Taj hotel at Delhi International Airport, Hyatt Regency at Airoli, CIGNUS Powai Tower II, a Goa resort, the acquired Udaipur resort (INR1,710 million for 144 keys) and a 330-key Ritz-Carlton in Hyderabad — the main use of capital and the source of future growth in both segments above.

overview.what_it_does: Chambal Fertilisers and Chemicals is an Indian company that makes and sells farm inputs, chiefly fertilizer, to farmers across India through a dealer network. Its core business is urea, which it manufactures at its own plants at Gadepan in Kota district, Rajasthan (Gadepan-I, II and III); management calls itself India's largest private-sector urea producer, supplying close to 10% of the country's urea. Alongside its own urea it buys in and sells other bulk fertilizers — DAP, NPK and MOP (roughly 5%, 5% and 6% national share) — and a growing, higher-margin range of crop protection chemicals, specialty nutrients, biological products and, more recently, seeds. Because fertilizer prices to farmers are government-controlled, a large part of its revenue comes as subsidy from the Government of India (about INR 10,228 crore received in the first nine months of FY26), and delays in those payments swing its working capital and interest costs; it also earns from a phosphoric acid joint venture, IMACID, and is building a Technical Ammonium Nitrate plant.

parts.name: Urea
parts.what: Manufactures urea at its Gadepan plants in Rajasthan using imported gas, running about 9.23 lakh tonnes a quarter and contributing close to 10% of India's urea supply; management describes urea as what 'anchors volumes and cash flows', and it is sold at a government-set price with the balance recovered as subsidy.

parts.name: P&K / bulk fertilizers (DAP, NPK, MOP)
parts.what: Sources phosphatic and potassic fertilizers — largely imported — and sells them to Indian farmers under a 'portfolio approach' tuned to each region; it is a big revenue contributor and the more volatile one, since import prices, the rupee and NBS subsidy rates can produce one-time hits such as the loss taken in the September 2022 quarter.

parts.name: Crop Protection Chemicals and Speciality Nutrients (CPC-SN)
parts.what: Sells pesticides, weedicides, fungicides, insecticides and specialty plant nutrients aimed at high-value crops like fruits and vegetables; smaller than fertilizer at about 3% of the national market, but the main growth and margin engine, with contribution up roughly 27-30% year-on-year in FY26 and 17 new products launched that year.

parts.name: Biologicals
parts.what: A sub-set of the CPC-SN push selling bio-based inputs such as UTTAM PRANAAM (bio-nano phosphorus, developed with TERI) and UTTAM SUPERRHIZA; small but fast-growing — volumes up about 30% and revenue about 57% in FY26, roughly 6% of that market, with the two lead products covering close to 3 million acres since launch.

parts.name: Seeds
parts.what: A newly entered line in hybrid and research-variety seeds — wheat, maize, mustard and bajra — described as completing the agri-input product profile; still at the early, portfolio-building stage with no size given.

parts.name: Technical Ammonium Nitrate (TAN) project
parts.what: A new plant being built to convert the company's surplus ammonia into technical ammonium nitrate, with total estimated cost of INR 1,645 crore (INR 1,184 crore spent by December 2025) and completion scheduled for April 2026; management calls it a very important focus area and is already exploring further expansion.

parts.name: Surplus ammonia
parts.what: Ammonia made in-house beyond what the urea plants consume — in the range of 90,000 tonnes a year as of 2022 — sold on or, going forward, fed into the TAN plant; management claims to be the country's most efficient ammonia complex.

parts.name: IMACID (joint venture)
parts.what: A joint venture producing phosphoric acid and sulphuric acid, most of its output directed to the Indian market; it contributes to consolidated profit and is expanding P2O5 capacity from 5 to 7 lakh tonnes by December 2026.

overview.what_it_does: Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) is a government-owned oil refiner based at Manali, Chennai, and a group company of Indian Oil Corporation (IOCL). It buys crude oil — roughly 55%-60% under long-term term contracts priced off suppliers' monthly Official Selling Price (Basrah heavy/medium from Iraq, Arab grades from Saudi Aramco), the rest bought spot as opportunity cargoes, including Russian crude in FY23 — runs it through its three crude units, and sells the resulting fuels: diesel (HSD), petrol (MS), LPG, ATF, naphtha and a range of speciality products. It makes money on the gross refining margin, the per-barrel spread between what the crude costs and what the products fetch, which management tracks against the Singapore benchmark ($9.2/bbl vs $5.83 in FY26); profit therefore depends on running the plant hard (throughput was 11.71 MMT, or 112% of installed capacity, in FY26) and on keeping fuel-and-loss and energy use low. Products go mainly into the Indian market, with export used as an option to optimise realisations rather than a compulsion, and a large greenfield refinery is being built through a joint venture at Nagapattinam.

parts.name: Refinery operations / crude throughput (the Manali refinery)
parts.what: The core business — three crude units processing about 10.5-11.7 million tonnes of crude a year at 99%-113% of rated capacity, producing petrol, diesel, LPG and other fuels; this is essentially the whole of the company's revenue and profit.

parts.name: Gross Refining Margin (GRM) and crude sourcing
parts.what: How the money is actually made: management picks the crude mix (52%-66% high-sulphur depending on the year, term vs spot balanced for economics) and sells the product slate to earn a per-barrel margin that has consistently beaten the Singapore benchmark over the past five to six years.

parts.name: Value-added and niche products
parts.what: Speciality streams sold alongside bulk fuels — food-grade and pharma-grade hexane, MTO, lean butane, LS naphtha, NATO-grade diesel, with pentane and textile-grade MTO in trial runs; volumes are small relative to fuels but management flags them repeatedly as record-setting and as the route into new, higher-margin markets.

parts.name: Energy efficiency / fuel-and-loss reduction
parts.what: An in-house programme to cut the share of crude burned as refinery fuel (fuel and loss down from 9.71% to 7.73% over the period, Energy Intensity Index down to 84) partly by substituting purchased RLNG gas; management says this contributed a significant part of profits and is a main reason its margin beats the benchmark.

parts.name: Cauvery Basin Refinery (CBR) joint venture, Nagapattinam
parts.what: A new 9 million-tonne greenfield refinery with about 6% polypropylene integration, built as a separate JV with Indian Oil at a revised cost of Rs. 36,354 crore and 25:75 equity — CPCL puts in equity (around Rs. 2,570 crore, spread over years) but no capex of its own, so it is an investment rather than an operating business today.

parts.name: Growth and capex projects (Group II/III LOBS, retail outlets)
parts.what: Standalone spending is mostly maintenance capex of Rs. 200-250 crore a year (total capex Rs. 856 crore in FY26), on top of which the approved Group II/III lube base oil project is now under execution and about 300 retail outlet licences have been taken with commissioning expected from FY27.

overview.what_it_does: Choice International is an India-based financial services group that sells investing, lending and advisory services to ordinary retail savers, small businesses (MSMEs) and government bodies, with a deliberate push into Tier-2/Tier-3, semi-urban and rural markets. It makes money three ways: fees and commissions from stock broking, mutual-fund/wealth distribution and insurance sales; interest on small secured loans it lends off its own book through its NBFC arm; and fee income from consulting mandates for state and central government projects plus investment-banking fees for managing IPOs. Distribution runs through a network of over 67,000 self-employed 'Choice Business Associates', roughly 200+ branches, and in-house apps (Choice FinX, Choice Money, Choice Connect), with a new tie-up giving it access to India Post Payments Bank's postal network. It operates only in India; FY26 consolidated revenue was Rs 1,145 Cr with profit after tax of Rs 238 Cr, up 24% and 46% respectively.

parts.name: Broking and Distribution
parts.what: The biggest piece at roughly 58-62% of revenue (Rs 179 Cr in Q4 FY26 with Rs 55 Cr pre-tax profit), it runs the retail stock-broking business — about 13 lakh demat accounts and Rs 52,482 Cr of client assets — and earns commissions on top by distributing mutual funds and wealth products to those same clients.

parts.name: Wealth Product Distribution (within Broking and Distribution)
parts.what: Sells mutual funds and other investment products to retail clients, with AUM of about Rs 4,268 Cr in Q4 FY26; it grew largely through acquisitions (Arete Capital, and the wealth-distribution businesses of Fintoo and Glory), and the recent India Post Payments Bank mandate is meant to scale it further.

parts.name: Insurance Distribution
parts.what: Sells life, health and motor policies for 40+ insurance partners through a 'POSP' agent model, collecting around Rs 84 Cr of premium and about 50,000 policies in Q4 FY26 — a small but steady cross-selling business rather than a main profit driver.

parts.name: Asset Management (Choice AMC / Choice Mutual Fund)
parts.what: A newly built, wholly owned fund house that got final SEBI approval in FY26 and launched its first products — a Gold ETF, then the Nifty 50 and Nifty Next 50 index funds — so it is still at start-up scale with index and commodity products planned next.

parts.name: NBFC (Choice Finserv)
parts.what: The lending arm, contributing about 13-15% of revenue (Rs 43 Cr revenue and only Rs 2 Cr pre-tax profit in Q4 FY26), which lends roughly Rs 800 Cr to MSMEs and individuals in semi-urban and rural areas — mostly secured loans such as micro-LAP, vehicle and rooftop-solar financing — at healthy margins (11-12% NIM) with net bad loans at 1.86%.

parts.name: Advisory — Government Consulting (Choice Consultancy Services)
parts.what: Consults for state and central governments on infrastructure and development programmes (Jal Jeevan Mission, MSME awareness drives, digital PACS computerisation, World Bank-backed governance work), and is the most profitable part per rupee of revenue — with the whole advisory segment at 28% of revenue, Rs 330 Cr FY26 revenue, Rs 120 Cr pre-tax profit, and a Rs 698 Cr order book giving two-to-three years of visibility.

parts.name: Advisory — Investment Banking
parts.what: Advises companies on raising money, having completed 15 IPOs so far with 37 live mandates and a tentative pipeline of about Rs 9,700 Cr; it is reported inside the advisory segment and is fee-driven and deal-dependent.

parts.name: Choice Business Associate (CBA) network and technology platforms
parts.what: Not a revenue segment itself but the group's delivery engine — 67,000-plus associates plus in-house apps (FinX, Money, Connect), 200-plus branches and 49 project offices — described as what lets every other vertical reach and cross-sell to small-town customers.

overview.what_it_does: Cholamandalam Investment and Finance Company Limited (CHOLAFIN) is an Indian non-banking finance company (NBFC) that lends money to retail and small-business borrowers across India, with most loans backed by collateral such as a vehicle or property. Its biggest business is financing the purchase of vehicles — commercial vehicles, passenger vehicles, two-wheelers, tractors and construction equipment, both new and used — mainly for retail customers and small operators rather than the large fleet owners that banks typically fund. Alongside that it lends against property, gives home loans, funds small and medium enterprises, and offers consumer, personal and gold loans. It earns money on the spread between the interest it charges borrowers and its own cost of funds, so its profits depend on loan growth (assets under management), that net interest margin, and how much it loses to bad loans; management tracks AUM (INR 2,42,630 crores as of March 2026, growing about 21% a year), net interest margin, credit cost (~1.5-1.6%) and returns (ROA ~3-4%, ROE ~19-23%).

parts.name: Vehicle Finance
parts.what: Loans to buy new and used commercial vehicles, passenger vehicles, two-wheelers, tractors and construction equipment, aimed at retail customers and smaller operators; it is by far the largest business, with 'Auto' AUM of INR 1,19,558 crores in March 2026 (roughly half the total book) and INR 14,390 crores of disbursements in a single quarter as far back as Q3 FY25.

parts.name: Loan Against Property (LAP), including Affordable LAP
parts.what: Loans given against a borrower's property as collateral, largely to small businesses and self-employed customers; it is the second-largest business with AUM of INR 52,295 crores in March 2026, growing 26% year-on-year, and management describes it as a low-loss book (steady-state credit cost around 0.5%) where recoveries come through SARFAESI property auctions.

parts.name: Home Loans
parts.what: Mortgage loans for buying or building homes, including self-occupied residential property; a mid-sized, steadily growing business — disbursements went from INR 478 crores a quarter in mid-2022 to INR 1,820 crores in Q3 FY25, with AUM up 23% year-on-year in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: SME (small and medium enterprise loans)
parts.what: Business loans to small and medium companies — term loans, equipment finance and (until management deliberately slowed it) supply-chain finance; a smaller book at INR 9,338 crores AUM in March 2026, but growing fast at 41% year-on-year, and behaving much like LAP because loans are collateral-backed.

parts.name: CSEL (Consumer and Small Enterprise Loans)
parts.what: Mostly unsecured personal and small-business loans, launched as a 'new business' in 2022; it grew quickly (INR 3,149 crores disbursed in Q3 FY25) but ran higher losses through fintech/partnership tie-ups, so management wound that channel down — from 10 partners to 3 and then a full exit from Q1 FY26 — leaving CSEL AUM up only 4% in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: SBPL (Secured Business and Personal Loans)
parts.what: Small collateral-backed business and personal loans, also started as a new business in 2022; still the smallest of the lending lines at INR 3,537 crores AUM in March 2026, but the fastest-growing, up 46-52% year-on-year.

parts.name: Gold Loans
parts.what: The newest business, lending against gold as security out of 118 dedicated branches in south and east India; still small but ramping quickly — INR 772 crores disbursed in Q3 FY26 and INR 1,130 crores in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: MSME segment (grouping: LAP + SME + SBPL)
parts.what: Management's umbrella label for its property- and business-backed small-enterprise lending, distributed through branches; combined AUM grew 29% year-on-year in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: Consumer segment (grouping: Home Loans + CSEL + Gold Loans)
parts.what: Management's umbrella label for its household-facing lending; combined AUM grew 20% year-on-year in Q4 FY26 with disbursements up 45%.

overview.what_it_does: Cholamandalam Financial Holdings Limited (formerly TI Financial Holdings) is a Chennai-based listed holding company that does not run an operating business of its own — on a standalone basis its total income was only about Rs.2.10 crores in a quarter, with a small loss — and instead owns stakes in financial-services companies whose results it consolidates. Its two consolidated subsidiaries are Cholamandalam Investment and Finance Company (lending) and Cholamandalam MS General Insurance, with Chola MS Risk held as a joint venture; consolidated total income was Rs.3,963 crores in the June 2022 quarter with profit after tax of Rs.582 crores. So its earnings come from interest and fees on loans made by the finance arm, plus insurance premiums, claims experience and investment income at the general insurance arm. Almost all of the discussion on these calls is about the Indian market — customers are vehicle owners, businesses and farmers across India, with the insurer particularly strong in Tamil Nadu, Chhattisgarh, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.

parts.name: Cholamandalam Investment and Finance Company (Chola Finance)
parts.what: The lending subsidiary, whose loan book and impairment charges drive most of the consolidated income line (a fall in loan impairment charges was cited as the main reason consolidated profit rose 63% in Q1 FY23); management notes it is covered in its own separate earnings call, so these calls give it little airtime.

parts.name: Cholamandalam MS General Insurance (Chola MS)
parts.what: The general (non-life) insurance subsidiary and the main focus of every call, selling motor, health/accident/travel, commercial, property/fire and crop policies through agents, OEM and financial channels — full-year FY26 direct premium (GDPI) was Rs.7,762 crores and gross written premium Rs.8,904 crores, with a combined ratio of 115.2% and profit before tax of Rs.454 crores.

parts.name: Motor insurance (within Chola MS)
parts.what: Described by management as "the principal line of business" — roughly 49% cars, 40% commercial vehicles and 10.5% two-wheelers in FY26, with about a 5.25% market share and around a quarter of motor premium coming from new vehicles; it splits into own-damage (OD) cover, where loss ratios have risen with competition, and third-party (TP) cover, where the company reserves about 10–14% more conservatively than peers because premiums have not been raised in four years.

parts.name: Health, accident and travel (within Chola MS)
parts.what: About 11% of the insurance portfolio in Q1 FY23 and growing 67% that quarter, but management deliberately writes very little employer/employee group health (only about Rs.36 crores of Rs.1,290 crores of premium) as a board policy, because of volatile and adverse claims.

parts.name: Commercial and property/fire (within Chola MS)
parts.what: Cover for businesses, about 17% of the portfolio in Q1 FY23 and growing 44%; a few large fire claims alone pushed the group claims ratio up by 1.78% in one quarter, so it is small but lumpy.

parts.name: Crop insurance (within Chola MS)
parts.what: Government-tender-based farm cover that the company lost on a re-tender, costing about Rs.590–598 crores of premium in FY26; it ran at roughly a 95% combined ratio (i.e. profitable), and management plans to bid again in the next three-year national tender to win it back.

parts.name: Reinsurance inward (accepted) business
parts.what: Taking on slices of other insurers' risks across all lines; it jumped from about 2% of gross premium to 8–10%, done both for profit opportunities and to help meet the regulator's expense-of-management limits, and it accounted for most of FY26's gross premium growth.

parts.name: Insurance investment portfolio
parts.what: The pool of premium money invested in debt and equity, standing at about Rs.19,050 crores at end-FY26 (up from Rs.18,140 crores in mid-2025); its yields and mark-to-market swings — such as Rs.137 crores of equity gains against a Rs.112 crores debt deficit — feed directly into reported profit.

parts.name: Chola MS Risk (joint venture)
parts.what: A jointly controlled company listed alongside the two subsidiaries in the consolidated results; the calls name it but give no revenue or business detail, implying it is immaterial to group earnings.

parts.name: Holding company (standalone)
parts.what: The listed parent itself, with essentially no operations — quarterly standalone income of around Rs.2.1 crores and a small loss — existing to hold and consolidate the finance and insurance stakes.

overview.what_it_does: CIE Automotive India (formerly Mahindra CIE, majority-owned by its Spanish parent CIE Automotive) makes metal and composite parts that go into vehicles — it does not make vehicles itself. It supplies these components to vehicle manufacturers (OEMs) and their suppliers across passenger cars and light vehicles, two- and three-wheelers, tractors, heavy trucks, and off-highway/construction equipment, winning multi-year orders for specific parts on specific vehicle platforms and then earning revenue on the volumes the customer actually builds; steel and energy cost swings are passed on to customers through negotiated price adjustments, so profitability depends on volumes, cost pass-through and plant efficiency. Roughly 65% of sales come from its plants in India and about 35% from Europe and a small Mexican operation, with consolidated quarterly sales around INR 23–25 billion and EBITDA margins in the 16–18% range in recent quarters. Management describes the company as a large, deliberately diversified auto-component group spanning many manufacturing processes, product lines, plants and customers, and it is adding a growing portfolio of parts for electric vehicles (about 11% of new orders won in Q1 CY26).

parts.name: India operations
parts.what: The plants located in India, making a wide spread of components across technologies; about 65% of group sales, with the India end-market mix in CY25 being light vehicles 53%, two- and three-wheelers 23%, tractors 13% and heavy trucks 11%, and EBITDA margins around 17–18%.

parts.name: European operations (incl. Mexico)
parts.what: Plants in Europe plus a small Mexican forging unit, contributing about 35% of sales; roughly 80% of European sales are forgings and more than half go into light vehicles, with margins recovering to about 15.7% in Q1 CY26 after restructuring in CY25.

parts.name: Forgings
parts.what: Hot-forged steel parts such as crankshafts and other engine and driveline components — the company's biggest vertical in Europe (about 80% of European sales, through units like CIE Galfor and CIE Legazpi) and a major India business too, though the European forgings market has been weak lately on Chinese and Indian competition and the shift to EVs.

parts.name: Bill Forge
parts.what: A forging business supplying two-wheeler parts including crankshafts and bearing races; management calls the two-wheeler crankshaft project one of its most exciting growth drivers and is adding capacity for it.

parts.name: Iron castings
parts.what: Cast-iron components; a growth area where the company has won sizeable export orders as well as other new domestic projects.

parts.name: Stampings
parts.what: Sheet-metal pressed parts, made at units such as Zaheerabad, with several new orders tied to customer Mahindra; the Zaheerabad unit has also received state subsidies that occasionally flatter reported margins.

parts.name: Composites
parts.what: Non-metal composite parts, a smaller vertical, again with new order wins linked to Mahindra.

parts.name: Aluminium
parts.what: Aluminium components (including the Aurangabad Electric operation); a smaller vertical currently being restructured, and from Q4 CY25 only the value-add portion of sales is recognised for some categories, which trimmed reported growth.

parts.name: Magnetics
parts.what: A small vertical whose business portfolio management was restructuring during CY25, which held back overall India sales growth.

parts.name: Metalcastello
parts.what: An Italian gear business selling into off-highway/off-road, earth-moving and mining equipment, heavily exposed to the US construction-equipment cycle; sales fell from roughly EUR 75–80 million a year to about EUR 50–60 million in CY24 and it carried one-off restructuring costs in CY25.

overview.what_it_does: Cipla is a 90-year-old Indian pharmaceutical company that makes and sells medicines — branded prescription drugs, cheaper generic copies of off-patent drugs, over-the-counter consumer health products, and active pharmaceutical ingredients (the bulk chemicals other drugmakers use). It sells to doctors, chemists, distributors, hospitals and retail consumers in India, and to wholesalers, pharmacy chains and business partners in the United States, South Africa, and a group of Europe/Middle East/emerging markets it calls EMEU. It earns money by manufacturing drugs in its own plants (in India, the US, Goa, Bangalore, Mumbai, China and elsewhere) and selling them at a gross margin of roughly 62%–67% after raw-material cost, with respiratory/inhalation drugs, complex peptide injections and other hard-to-copy products carrying the best economics. Quarterly revenue was about INR 7,119 crores in the June 2026 quarter, with India the largest single market followed by North America; its plants are regularly inspected by the US FDA, and inspection outcomes are a recurring business risk management discusses.

parts.name: One-India (branded prescription)
parts.what: Doctor-prescribed branded medicines sold in India, concentrated in long-term 'chronic' therapies such as respiratory, diabetes, cardiac and urology; it is the biggest piece of the company's largest market, with 33 brands each above INR 100 crores of sales, flagship inhaler brand Foracort alone above INR 1,000 crores, and chronic drugs making up about 60% of the India mix.

parts.name: One-India (trade generics)
parts.what: Unbranded/low-cost generic medicines sold in India through a distributor-and-chemist network reaching over 1.5 lakh chemists; it was re-plumbed into a direct distribution model in FY25 (which briefly dented growth) and has since delivered double-digit growth on the back of new launches.

parts.name: Consumer Health (Cipla Health)
parts.what: Over-the-counter wellness and self-care products people buy without a prescription — Nicotex, Omnigel, Cipladine and similar brands, each number one in its segment; described as roughly an INR 600 crore annualised franchise in 2022 growing since via acquisitions (Endura Mass, Astaberry, Inzpera), with operating margins in the mid-teens.

parts.name: North America
parts.what: Generic and 505(b)(2) specialty medicines sold in the US, led by inhalers (albuterol MDI, where Cipla is the number one player at about 21% market share, plus the newly approved generic Ventolin) and peptide injections like Lanreotide and Liraglutide; annual revenue was about $780 million in FY26 and it is the second-largest market after India.

parts.name: One Africa / South Africa
parts.what: Prescription medicines and over-the-counter brands sold in South Africa and other African markets, where Cipla holds the number one ranking in prescription drugs and consistently grows faster than the local market; it grew 14% year-on-year in the March 2026 quarter and 7% for the full year in dollar terms.

parts.name: EMEU (Europe, Middle East and emerging markets)
parts.what: A collection of smaller international markets served through both 'DTM' (Cipla's own front-end selling directly to those markets) and B2B (supplying other companies who sell under their own labels); it crossed $400 million of annual revenue in FY26 despite war-related disruption.

parts.name: API
parts.what: Sale of active pharmaceutical ingredients — the raw drug substances — to outside partners, sometimes with profit-sharing on commercial supply; it is a small, lumpy contributor whose swings management has had to explain away in quarterly comparisons.

parts.name: R&D and pipeline
parts.what: In-house development plus in-licensing deals (Eli Lilly for obesity drug Yurpeak, MannKind for inhaled insulin Afrezza, rights to Pfizer's established brands) that feed future launches; R&D runs about 5%–7% of revenue (INR 486 crores in the June 2026 quarter) and the US pipeline alone covers roughly 40–50 filings planned over three years, including respiratory, peptides, oligonucleotides and two biosimilars.

overview.what_it_does: Clean Science and Technology is an India-based specialty chemicals manufacturer (registered in Pune, with plants at units including Unit-3 and a subsidiary Clean Fino-Chem) that makes small-volume, high-value chemical molecules used as ingredients by other manufacturers — things like MEHQ, Guaiacol, para-benzoquinone (PBQ), TBHQ, BHA, 4-MAP, Veratrole and a range of Hindered Amine Light Stabilizers (HALS). It does not sell to consumers; its customers are industrial buyers in polymers/plastics, coatings, agrochemicals, pharmaceuticals, food and cosmetics, who blend these molecules into their own products. It makes money by producing these chemicals in-house using processes it develops itself (management stresses 'differentiated technology', better yields and backward integration into its own raw materials such as hydroquinone and catechol) and selling at high margins — standalone EBITDA margins in the 40-46% range, with a debt-free balance sheet. It is heavily export-oriented — roughly two-thirds of sales overseas versus a third domestic in FY23 — shipping to Europe, the US, China and India, with consolidated revenue of about INR 945 crore in FY26.

parts.name: Performance Chemicals
parts.what: The core and largest business, at roughly 66-72% of revenue across the period, built on flagship products MEHQ (a polymerisation inhibitor) and Guaiacol plus BHA, with two new 'Performance Chemical 1 and 2' plants (about INR 150 crore capex each) added — one targeting ~15% of global capacity for its product with expected revenue of roughly INR 260-350 crore.

parts.name: Pharma and Agro Intermediates
parts.what: Building-block chemicals sold to drugmakers and crop-chemical makers, about 18-23% of revenue, including para-benzoquinone (PBQ) — an agrochemical input previously made only in China where Clean expanded capacity from 500 to 1,000 tonnes — and a pharma intermediate called DHDT still in customer testing as of early 2026.

parts.name: FMCG Chemicals
parts.what: The smallest segment at roughly 5-13% of revenue, covering food and personal-care ingredients such as TBHQ (a food antioxidant) and 4-MAP for cosmetics; it shrank sharply in FY26 after losing a key 4-MAP customer in China.

parts.name: HALS (via subsidiary Clean Fino-Chem Limited)
parts.what: The newest growth engine — Hindered Amine Light Stabilizers (grades 770, 622, 944, 783, 119, 701, plus higher-value NOR-HALS) that stop plastics, masterbatches, agricultural films and coatings from degrading in sunlight; started commercial production in FY25, scaled from ~80-125 tonnes a month to about 2,000 tonnes over nine months of FY26, grew 55% year-on-year in Q3 FY26 at a blended realisation of INR 425/kg, and reached its first positive EBITDA (INR 7 crore) in Q4 FY26 after cumulative investment of about INR 750 crore.

parts.name: Backward integration / captive raw materials
parts.what: Not a sales segment but an important cost lever — a hydroquinone and catechol plant commercialised in December 2025 that now fully replaces imports and feeds its own TBHQ and Veratrole production, plus planned in-house production of key HALS starting materials, both aimed at lowering raw-material cost and lifting margins.

overview.what_it_does: CMS Info Systems is an India-only outsourcing company that banks, ATM operators and retailers hire to move, count and look after their physical cash, and to build and run the machines and technology around it. Its people and armoured-van network collect cash from shops, petrol pumps and NBFC branches, transport it between bank branches and vaults, and refill roughly 140,000 service touch points across more than 16,000 pin codes; alongside this it deploys and manages ATMs for banks, and sells camera/sensor-based remote monitoring, AI surveillance and payment-technology services. It earns money mainly as recurring annuity service fees — historically per-transaction or per-ATM charges, though management says it has now shifted deliberately to fixed-price contracts — plus some one-time revenue from selling hardware. FY2026 revenue was Rs 2,487 crore, of which Rs 2,312 crore was recurring service revenue, with the largest single customer at 18% of revenue.

parts.name: Cash Management / Cash Logistics
parts.what: Physically handles currency for clients through three lines — ATM cash replenishment, retail cash pickup from shops and outlets, and currency-in-transit between bank branches and vaults; it is the older and larger half of the company (about 70% of revenue at IPO, roughly 55% by FY2026) and management says it gained 200 bps of market share in FY2026.

parts.name: Managed Services & Technology Solutions
parts.what: Builds, deploys and runs ATMs and technology for banks — including brown-label ATMs (BLA) owned and operated by CMS, remote monitoring and AI/IoT surveillance systems, and software — grown internally from nothing to about Rs 800 crore by FY2024 and roughly 45% of revenue by FY2026, with CMS moving from the industry's number five to number three position.

parts.name: ATM Management Solutions (platform, post-FY2026 restructure)
parts.what: The combined ATM-facing business — cash filling plus machine deployment and upkeep — now run as one platform focused on higher-yield, fixed-price contracts; its biggest single win is the SBI cash outsourcing deal for about 10,000 ATMs, worth Rs 1,000 crore over ten years (Rs 500 crore of it new revenue).

parts.name: Retail and Currency Logistics (platform, post-FY2026 restructure)
parts.what: Direct-to-retail cash collection and reconciliation for organised retail, fuel outlets, airlines, NBFCs, travel and hospitality clients, now being expanded into tier-3 and tier-4 towns using a 'gig' partner model of 2,000-plus partners covering 20% of retail points.

parts.name: Tech and Payment Solutions (platform, post-FY2026 restructure)
parts.what: The software, remote-monitoring SaaS and payments piece, described as growing from Rs 235 crore to Rs 330 crore of revenue in one year and targeted at Rs 400 crore in FY2027 — roughly a 30% annual growth rate, the fastest-growing part of the company.

parts.name: Remote Monitoring / AIoT RMS
parts.what: A subscription service that watches ATM sites, bank branches, vaults and gold-loan vaults remotely using cameras, sensors and AI models; started during COVID as the smallest business (15,000 ATM sites live by mid-2022) and has since scaled to large mandates such as a 2,000-location integrated surveillance build-and-operate project for a leading bank.

parts.name: Acquisitions (FY2026)
parts.what: Two deals were signed: Securens, to scale the vision-AI monitoring business (closed, integrated, expected to add to profit in FY2027), and FSS's managed services business, to consolidate the ATM managed-services market and open cross-selling into midsized private banks.

parts.name: Bullion management (incubation)
parts.what: A very small new venture being incubated internally, repeatedly described by management as early-stage with no meaningful revenue yet.

overview.what_it_does: Coal India Limited (CIL) is a government-owned mining company — a "Maharatna" Government of India enterprise, registered in Kolkata and listed on the BSE and NSE — that digs thermal (power-grade) coal out of the ground in India and sells it domestically. Most of its coal goes to electricity generators under tied-up long-term supply contracts at government-notified prices (in 9M FY24 it dispatched 454 million tonnes to the power sector out of 531.9 million tonnes produced), with the rest going to non-power industrial buyers such as sponge iron makers and to spot buyers through e-auctions. Management says roughly 90% of volume is sold under tied-up contracts where there is "hardly any profit," while the 10-15% sold by e-auction — at a premium over notified prices that has ranged from ~35-50% in normal years to 250-300% in tight years — is where most of the profit comes from. It mines through seven regional subsidiary companies (South Eastern/SECL, Central/CCL, Mahanadi/MCL, Northern/NCL, Western/WCL, Eastern/ECL and others), and its economics hinge on pushing volumes up — 700 million tonnes in FY23, ~770-780 in FY24, guidance of 875 in FY26 and 900-plus in FY27, against a long-standing 1-billion-tonne government target — because higher output spreads fixed costs and cuts cost per tonne.

parts.name: Tied-up / linkage supplies to the power sector (FSA/SSC coal)
parts.what: Coal sold to electricity utilities under long-term supply agreements at notified prices; it is by far the biggest part — about 90% of volume and 454 million tonnes of the 531.9 million tonnes produced in the first nine months of FY24 — but management says it carries hardly any profit.

parts.name: Long-term linkages to the non-power sector
parts.what: Long-term coal commitments to industrial buyers like sponge iron plants and other non-power consumers, grown about 28% in two years from 90 to 115 million tonnes, with management still scouting for another 30-40 million tonnes of such commitments.

parts.name: E-auction / spot sales
parts.what: Roughly 10-15% of volume auctioned on the open market at a premium over notified non-power prices (43% in Q4 FY25, over 100% in Q3 FY24, up to 250-300% in the tight 2022-23 years) — a small slice of tonnage that management describes as the source of essentially all its profit.

parts.name: Producing subsidiaries
parts.what: Seven regional mining companies (SECL, CCL, MCL/Mahanadi, NCL, WCL, ECL and others) that actually run the mines; performance varies by subsidiary — SECL and CCL missed targets on rainfall, land acquisition and environment/forest clearances, while coal grade also differs, with ECL producing good G6-G8 quality and Mahanadi coal running as high as ~42% ash.

parts.name: Coal evacuation and first mile connectivity (FMC) infrastructure
parts.what: Silos, rail sidings and railway lines (e.g. Tori-Shivpuri, Jharsuguda-Sardega doubling) built to get coal from pithead to customer; rake loading through FMC grew ~32% last year to 87.1 rakes per day in early FY26, with a target of at least 100 per day.

parts.name: Mine development and capex programme
parts.what: Buying land, obtaining environmental and forest clearances, and awarding Mine Developer-Operator (MDO) contracts — about 100 million tonnes of capacity awarded as of FY23 — funded by capex of about ₹16,500 crore in FY24, all aimed at lifting output toward 1 billion tonnes.

parts.name: Overburden removal
parts.what: The waste rock stripped away to reach the coal, tracked as a headline operating measure — 1,404.85 million cubic metres in 9M FY24, up 22% year on year.

parts.name: Diversification (early stage)
parts.what: Small ventures outside core mining mentioned only in passing: CIL won about 300 MW of solar projects from Gujarat Industrial Power Corporation at Khavda via e-auction in January 2024, and analysts asked about rare earth and lithium mining interests in India and Australia.

overview.what_it_does: Cochin Shipyard Limited is an Indian shipyard company that builds new ships and repairs existing ones, working to order under long contracts rather than selling off the shelf. Its customers are mainly the Indian Navy and other government arms (it built and delivered the indigenous aircraft carrier INS Vikrant, is building 8 anti-submarine warfare shallow water craft worth about INR 6,300 crores, and builds electric ferries for the Kochi Water Metro and the Inland Waterways Authority), plus commercial buyers in India and Europe such as German and Norwegian owners, tug operators like Ocean Sparkle and Polestar, and Dredging Corporation of India; it has also signed a Master Ship Repair Agreement letting it repair US Navy vessels. Money comes in as a contract is executed over several years — roughly a year of design, engineering and procurement first, then steel fabrication, outfitting, trials and delivery — with repair work billed on refits, drydocking and equipment upgrades. It operates from its main yard in Kochi (including a new 310-metre dry dock and an International Ship Repair Facility commissioned in January 2024 at a capex of about INR 2,769 crores), from ship repair units in Mumbai, the Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Kolkata, and through subsidiaries at Udupi and Hooghly; in Q1 FY26 it reported turnover of INR 1,068.59 crores and an order book of about INR 21,100 crores.

parts.name: Shipbuilding
parts.what: Designs and constructs new vessels — naval ships, ferries, dredgers, cargo ships and offshore wind service vessels — and is the larger half of the business, at 72% of operating income in FY24 and about INR 19,600 crores of the INR 21,100 crore order book across 75 vessels.

parts.name: Ship Repair
parts.what: Drydocks, refits, repairs and upgrades ships (including mid-life upgrades and repowering of naval platforms and maintenance on INS Vikrant), contributing 28% of FY24 operating income, crossing INR 1,000 crores of turnover for the first time that year, with an order book of roughly INR 1,500 crores.

parts.name: Indigenous Aircraft Carrier (IAC) work
parts.what: The INS Vikrant programme, delivered and commissioned in 2022, which still generated 46% of FY24 shipbuilding revenue and now also feeds repair and maintenance contracts, such as an INR 488.25 crore deal signed in December 2023.

parts.name: ASW-SWC corvettes for the Indian Navy
parts.what: A series of 8 anti-submarine warfare shallow water craft valued at about INR 6,300 crores — management calls it the biggest ongoing project after the carrier — with 3 launched in November 2023 and the rest in keel-laying or fabrication stages.

parts.name: Kochi Water Metro / inland passenger vessels
parts.what: Hybrid electric catamaran ferries for Kochi Metro Rail (23 under contract, 19 delivered by mid-2025) plus a follow-on 8-vessel order from the Inland Waterways Authority of India; small in rupee terms but described as high-visibility work that is being replicated in other regions.

parts.name: Commercial / export shipbuilding
parts.what: Merchant and specialised vessels for overseas owners — 8 numbers of 7,000 deadweight multi-purpose vessels for European clients, autonomous electric barges for ASKO in Norway, and Hybrid Service Operation Vessels for the European offshore wind market worth roughly INR 1,000–1,200 crores for two.

parts.name: Udupi Cochin Shipyard Limited (UCSL)
parts.what: A wholly-owned subsidiary yard acquired through insolvency proceedings that builds tugs and small dry cargo ships for clients like Ocean Sparkle, Polestar and Wilson of Norway; it turned profitable in FY24 with INR 186 crores of revenue and about INR 800 crores of orders.

parts.name: Hooghly Cochin Shipyard Limited (HCSL)
parts.what: The other wholly-owned subsidiary yard, newer and much smaller, building ASD tugs and a luxury river cruise vessel, with an order book of roughly INR 150 crores as of FY24.

parts.name: Regional ship repair units (CMSRU, CANSRU, CKSRU)
parts.what: Satellite repair yards in Mumbai, the Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Kolkata that supplement the Kochi yard, with Mumbai billing over INR 150 crores and Andaman about INR 100 crores in FY24.

parts.name: Green and new-technology vessels
parts.what: A small but strategically emphasised line covering India's first indigenously built hydrogen fuel cell vessel, hybrid-electric ferries and an autonomous underwater vehicle — management says these are not yet financially material but position the yard for future green shipbuilding work.

overview.what_it_does: Coforge is an India-headquartered IT services firm that builds, tests, runs and modernises software and technology systems for large companies, and lately sells AI-based work — what it calls AI-led engineering, data and integration, and cloud services, which made up 86% of revenue in the June 2026 quarter. Its customers are big enterprises concentrated in banking and financial services, insurance, travel and transportation, healthcare and hi-tech, and non-Indian government bodies; the top 10 clients were about 26-31% of revenue, with one client above $100 million a year. It earns money mainly through multi-year outsourcing and project contracts won as 'large deals' (21 signed in FY26, order intake $691 million in Q1 FY27) that convert into a rolling 12-month 'executable order book' of $2.23 billion, delivered largely by offshore staff in India (about 51% offshore back in 2023) plus onsite teams, so revenue tracks headcount, utilisation (~82.5%) and billing rates. Revenue was $1.445 billion in FY25, grew 29.2% in FY26, and Q1 FY27 was $592.2 million, with staff of 46,228; selling is concentrated in the Americas and EMEA, with a smaller Rest of the World business.

parts.name: Banking and Financial Services (BFS)
parts.what: Technology work for banks, payments and financial firms — historically the biggest vertical at around 31% of revenue in 2023 and still 24.7% in Q1 FY27, and the source of the company's earliest large deals such as a 5-year $300 million contract.

parts.name: Insurance
parts.what: Software, claims and policy-processing work for insurers, including AI tools that pull data out of policy and claims documents and plug into insurance platforms like Duck Creek and Guidewire; roughly 22.6% of revenue in 2023, trimmed to 13.6% by Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Travel, Transportation and Hospitality
parts.what: Systems and AI solutions for airlines, transport operators and air-transport communications firms (for example cutting weather alerts to pilots by 75%); about 18.5% of revenue in 2023 and 21.3% in Q1 FY27, and one of the fastest growers at 62% in FY26.

parts.name: Healthcare and Hi-Tech
parts.what: A newer, fast-expanding vertical serving healthcare and technology companies that grew 98% in FY26 and contributed 17.3% of revenue in Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Government outside India
parts.what: Public-sector technology contracts in markets other than India, growing 17.5% in FY26 and contributing about 6% of revenue in Q1 FY27; management separately announced it was exiting the India government business.

parts.name: Others / emerging verticals (retail, manufacturing)
parts.what: A catch-all group of remaining industries including retail and manufacturing that grew 27% in FY26 and was 17.1% of revenue in Q1 FY27, though it declined 8% after deliberate exits from unwanted business.

parts.name: AI-led Engineering
parts.what: The largest service line at 50% of revenue in Q1 FY27 — building and modernising software with AI embedded in the delivery process, supported by 11,000+ data and AI practitioners, 8 AI platforms and roughly $58 million of AI investment in FY26.

parts.name: Data and Integration
parts.what: Work on clients' data systems and connecting their applications together, at 21% of revenue in Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Cloud
parts.what: Moving and running client systems on cloud infrastructure, at 15% of revenue in Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Intelligent Automation and Business Process Management
parts.what: Automating and running back-office business processes for clients, each contributing about 7% of revenue in Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Nuuron (AI operationalisation platform)
parts.what: The company's own software layer, launched by FY27, meant to take clients from AI pilots to live AI operations by tying together enterprise knowledge, workflows, governance and AI agents — positioned as the centrepiece of its future growth story rather than a separately sized revenue line.

parts.name: Cigniti (acquired software testing business)
parts.what: A listed testing-services firm bought around 2024 that management says was fully absorbed, lifted from 12% to 19% EBITDA margin, and whose top two clients grew from $25-30 million to $75 million a year through cross-selling.

parts.name: Encora (acquired in FY27)
parts.what: An acquisition completed in mid-2026 that added 9,256 employees and about 25% more shares outstanding, contributed two months of Q1 FY27 revenue, and broadened the client base; earlier tuck-ins named on the calls include SLK Global and Incessant.

overview.what_it_does: Cohance Lifesciences (formerly Suven Pharmaceuticals, listed in India as COHANCE) is a contract manufacturer and developer of complex chemicals for other companies — it does not sell its own branded drugs. Its customers are global innovator pharmaceutical firms, biotech companies, other Western CDMOs, generic drug makers, and agrochemical and specialty-materials innovators, who pay it to develop and then manufacture drug ingredients, intermediates and specialised chemicals. It makes money by supplying these molecules under contract: development-stage programs that scale up into commercial supply once a customer's drug is approved, plus a steadier book of active pharmaceutical ingredients and finished formulations sold to many customers. Manufacturing and R&D are based in India (sites at Pashamylaram, Suryapet, Vizag, Nacharam and a Genome Valley R&D centre in the Hyderabad area), with a US operation via NJ Bio, serving export customers in the US, Europe and Japan; FY26 revenue was about INR 22.68 billion, down roughly 13% year on year.

parts.name: Pharma CDMO
parts.what: Contract development and manufacturing of drug intermediates and active ingredients for innovator pharma and biotech customers under patent, including advanced niche platforms — ADC payloads and payload-linkers (with NJ Bio in the US doing bioconjugation) and oligonucleotides/amidites via the Sapala platform; it brought in INR 8.89 billion in FY26 (commercial products over 70% of it), runs 140+ active projects and a 10-program Phase 3 pipeline, and management treats it as the strategic growth engine even though it declined sharply in FY26 on customer destocking.

parts.name: API Plus
parts.what: A broad portfolio of niche small-to-mid-volume active pharmaceutical ingredients plus finished-dosage formulations sold to generic and other pharma partners, backed by DMF/CEP and partner ANDA filings; at INR 10.88 billion in FY26 it is the single largest revenue segment, down 8% year on year after a warning letter and production disruption at the Nacharam formulation site.

parts.name: Specialty Chemicals
parts.what: Contract manufacture of active ingredients and advanced intermediates for large global agrochemical innovators, plus performance chemicals such as photochromic coating materials and OLED materials with early work in electronic/semiconductor chemistries; the smallest segment at INR 2.913 billion in FY26 (down 2.1%), with management calling FY27 a qualification year and growth expected only from FY28.

overview.what_it_does: Colgate-Palmolive (India) Limited is an Indian consumer-goods company that makes and sells everyday oral care products — mainly toothpaste and toothbrushes — under the Colgate brand, plus a small personal care range (such as body washes) under the Palmolive brand. It earns money by selling these low-priced, frequently repurchased products to households across India through roughly 1.7 million retail stores, along with modern trade and e-commerce channels, where management says its share is usually higher than in traditional trade. Management describes it as largely a single-category company in oral care: it is India's most penetrated brand, present in nine out of ten households, about three times the size of the number-two player in toothpaste, and the leading dentist-recommended brand after nearly nine decades in the country. The business is India-only, with full-year sales of Rs. 5,999 crores in FY2024-25, gross margins near 69-70% and EBITDA margins in the 32-34% range, and it spends heavily on advertising (Rs. 822 crores on the Colgate brand in FY25) to keep driving category consumption.

parts.name: Core toothpaste (leading toothpaste category growth)
parts.what: The largest part of the business — mass-market toothpaste sold under three core brands, Colgate Strong Teeth, Max Fresh and Colgate Active Salt, where the company's job is to grow the whole category by getting Indians to brush twice a day (only 20% of urban households do) and to brush daily at all (55% of rural households don't); management calls this its first and biggest strategic pillar.

parts.name: Premium oral care / premiumisation
parts.what: Higher-priced, science-backed toothpaste variants such as Colgate Visible White Purple (described as the most successful innovation in the last decade), Max Fresh Sensorials, the revamped Lemon Fresh and the relaunched Colgate Total — a smaller but fast-growing pillar the company has stepped up investment behind, and where it says advertising is producing strong response.

parts.name: Toothbrushes and devices
parts.what: Manual toothbrushes and devices, where 78% of brushes sold are under Rs. 40 and buyers replace them only every nine months instead of the recommended three — so the growth comes from selling pricier premium and super-premium handles and getting people to replace them more often.

parts.name: Personal Care (Palmolive)
parts.what: A relatively small business outside oral care — Palmolive-branded personal care including body washes — which management calls 'the little jewel in our crown' and treats as a big future opportunity rather than a big current contributor.

parts.name: Dentist and professional partnership (Dentist FIRST)
parts.what: Not a separate revenue line but a key support to the business: long-standing relationships with the Indian Dental Association and dentists, plus a 'Dentist FIRST' digital platform launched for dentists to access Colgate products and information, underpinning Colgate's position as the #1 dentist-prescribed brand.

parts.name: Consumption-driving programs (Bright Smiles Bright Future, Oral Health Movement)
parts.what: Nationwide habit-building and screening programs — a school program now in its fifth decade that reached over a crore children in 2025 and 190 million since inception, and a 2024-launched Oral Health Movement that screened 4.5 million consumers — used to expand how much toothpaste the country uses rather than to earn revenue directly.

overview.what_it_does: CONCOR (Container Corporation of India Ltd.) is a government-owned ("Navratna CPSE") multi-modal logistics company that moves freight packed in containers around India, mainly by rail. It buys haulage on the rail network and runs its own fleet of trains and containers — 423 high-speed rakes and about 57,746 owned containers as of FY26 — between seaports such as JNPT/Nhava Sheva, Mundra, Pipavav, Kandla, Chennai and Vishakhapatnam and its own network of inland terminals/ICDs (Dadri, Khatuwas, Nagpur, Raipur, Sonipat, Hyderabad and others), 26 of which sit on Indian Railways land for which it pays a land license fee of roughly Rs. 450 crores a year. Its customers are shipping lines (long-term volume-discount deals with the likes of Maersk and PSA), exporters and importers of goods like garments, rice, meat, auto parts, solar panel parts and polymers, and domestic shippers of cement, tiles and gunny bales. It earns money on rail freight plus terminal handling, warehousing and road pickup/delivery, and its volumes are measured in TEUs — an all-time-high 5.58 million TEUs in FY26, up 9.6% — with profitability driven by rail freight margin (27.16% in FY26), running double-stack trains, and cutting empty container/rake running.

parts.name: EXIM
parts.what: Carries import and export containers between seaports and inland terminals for shipping lines and traders; it is by far the bigger half — 4.21 million of the 5.58 million TEUs handled in FY26, and the first time revenue from this stream crossed Rs. 6,000 crores.

parts.name: Domestic
parts.what: Moves containerized cargo within India (cement, tiles, gunny bales, food and other goods, roughly 14-15 million tonnes of loading a year), growing faster in percentage terms — 14.6% in FY26 — but a much smaller share of total volumes than EXIM.

parts.name: Terminals / ICDs (Projects & Services)
parts.what: Owns and operates the inland container depots and terminals where containers are handled, stored and transferred between rail and road, including 26 built on Indian Railways land; new terminals and rakes are funded from an annual capex budget of about Rs. 945-1,085 crores.

parts.name: Double-stack and high-speed rake operations
parts.what: Runs trains with containers stacked two high on routes like Khatuwas and NCR to Mundra, Pipavav and (from June 2026, over the Western Dedicated Freight Corridor) JNPT — management calls this a main driver of both faster transit times and better margins, with 6,396 double-stack trains run in FY26.

parts.name: Tank containers / bulk cement (new domestic product)
parts.what: A newly launched service hauling bulk cement and liquids in tank containers; still small — a fleet of about 500 tanks growing by 200 a month, with 3,000 more approved — and management targets at least 1 million tonnes of loading from it.

parts.name: Warehousing and first-mile/last-mile (FMLM) road services
parts.what: Road pickup and delivery plus warehousing bolted onto the rail leg so customers get an end-to-end "total logistics solution"; described as a focus area rather than quantified, and supported by assets like 230 LNG trucks and electric handling equipment.

parts.name: Direct Port Delivery (DPD) and cabotage services
parts.what: Schemes that let containers move straight between the port and the customer under liberalized rules; a liberalized policy lifted DPD volumes 38% in FY26 and is flagged as a continuing growth driver.

parts.name: Bharat Container Shipping Line (30% stake)
parts.what: A shipping-line joint venture CONCOR signed an MOU for and holds 30% of, under which it has begun issuing its own bills of lading — about 700 containers moved to the Middle East before conflict halted the service.

overview.what_it_does: Concord Biotech is an Ahmedabad-based drug ingredient maker that grows active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) using fermentation — brewing microbes and purifying the output — rather than ordinary chemical synthesis. Its main products are immunosuppressant APIs (drugs used after organ transplants), where management says it is the world's only supplier with the complete fermentation-based portfolio, plus a growing range of oncology, anti-infective and antifungal APIs. It sells these bulk ingredients to other pharmaceutical companies in India and abroad (roughly half domestic, half export in FY26, with the US, Europe and the Middle East as key markets), and since 2016 it has also made finished medicines itself — tablets/capsules, and more recently injectables and soft gels — sold under its own brand in India and to customers overseas. Revenue is about 80% APIs and 20% finished formulations; FY26 revenue fell about 12% on tariff uncertainty, a regulatory approval delay that blocked European supplies for about three months, and a stalled Middle East tender, with reported EBITDA margin around 35%.

parts.name: API business (fermentation-based active pharmaceutical ingredients)
parts.what: Makes and sells bulk drug ingredients — immunosuppressants (its leadership area), oncology, anti-infectives and antifungals — to pharma manufacturers worldwide; it is the core of the company at roughly 80% of revenue, INR 829 crores in FY26.

parts.name: Formulations (oral solid dosage)
parts.what: The Valthera facility, started in 2016, makes finished tablets and capsules (capacity around 802 million units) sold in India — mainly critical care, nephrology and rheumatology through a field force of 175+ people — as well as in emerging and regulated markets; it is the smaller leg at roughly 20-26% of revenue depending on the quarter.

parts.name: Injectables facility
parts.what: A newer plant that started production in FY26 and has WHO-GMP certification, aimed at own-brand domestic sales, contract manufacturing and government supply contracts; management puts its peak revenue potential at about INR 600 crores, though start-up costs dented margins in FY26.

parts.name: CDMO / second-source supply
parts.what: Contract development and manufacturing for other drug companies, including acting as a backup ('second source') supplier — described as small today but in advanced discussions, with supplies begun to two innovator companies in FY26.

parts.name: Stellon Biotech (US subsidiary)
parts.what: A newly set-up American arm that gives Concord its own marketing, distribution and commercialisation presence in the US; still an early-stage cost rather than a revenue contributor.

parts.name: Concord Lifegen (India subsidiary)
parts.what: A wholly owned company incorporated to strengthen marketing, sales and distribution of Concord's products within India.

parts.name: Cell and gene therapy investment (Celliimune Biotech)
parts.what: An investment into a cell-and-gene-therapy venture described as a long-term growth platform; no revenue attributed to it in the calls.

parts.name: Soft gel facility
parts.what: A newly commercialised soft gelatin capsule line described as an additional avenue for revenue; no size disclosed.

overview.what_it_does: Coromandel International is an Indian company that makes and sells farm inputs — mainly phosphate-based fertilizers such as DAP, NPK complexes and single super phosphate (SSP), plus crop-protection chemicals — to farmers, largely through a dealer channel and its own retail centres. It earns money by buying raw materials (rock phosphate, phosphoric acid, ammonia, sulphur, mostly imported and dollar-priced), converting them into finished fertilizer at its own plants, and selling at government-controlled prices topped up by a government subsidy under the Nutrient Based Subsidy scheme, so profitability depends on the gap between raw-material costs and the subsidy rates New Delhi announces each season. Its home market is southern India (Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and neighbouring states), where the calls say it is the largest phosphatic player with roughly 17.5% national market share and record sales of about 4.3 million tons of DAP/NPK in FY26, and it is now pushing into north and central India. It is also buying its way backwards up the supply chain — a rock phosphate mine in Senegal (71.5% owned) and new phosphoric/sulphuric acid plants at Kakinada — and its results swing with the monsoon, since demand follows rainfall and sowing.

parts.name: Nutrition and allied business (fertilizers)
parts.what: The core and by far the largest business — manufacturing and selling DAP and NPK complex fertilizers (record 3.5 million tons produced and 4.3 million tons sold in FY26 across plants at Kakinada, Vizag and Ennore), which drives most of the revenue and is the segment management spends nearly all the call time on.

parts.name: Single super phosphate (SSP)
parts.what: A cheaper phosphate fertilizer where the company says it is the market leader, selling a record 8.4 lakh tons in FY26, increasingly in higher-priced 'differentiated' versions like GroPlus, GroAlpha and Urea-SSP that now make up over half the volume.

parts.name: Crop protection (agrochemicals)
parts.what: Pesticides and related chemicals sold both in India and exported; the calls treat it as the clear number-two business, and it has been volatile — hit by global destocking and weak domestic demand in muted seasons, with exports recovering by FY26.

parts.name: Specialty nutrients and organic products
parts.what: Higher-value plant nutrition products including water-soluble/specialty fertilizers and organic and seaweed-based inputs, described as a strong-growing but smaller business, with new plants (technical MAP, seaweed granulation) being built to expand it.

parts.name: Bio products
parts.what: Biological crop inputs, run under the same executive as crop protection and retail; management flags a global and Indian shift toward biologicals as a growth driver but gives no size.

parts.name: Nano fertilizers (Nano DAP)
parts.what: A newer liquid nano-nutrient line launched around November 2023 and described as well received, but still a small, emerging part of the mix.

parts.name: Retail and drone spraying services (Gromor Drive)
parts.what: Company-run farm retail centres plus a drone crop-spraying service using drones from group company Dhaksha, which covered about 3 lakh acres in FY26 — a small service business used mainly to build farmer relationships.

parts.name: Backward integration / mining
parts.what: Not a selling business but a cost lever: the Senegal rock phosphate mine (3.5 lakh tons output in FY26, stake raised to 71.5%), a majority stake in BMCC, and new sulphuric and phosphoric acid plants at Kakinada intended to cover 60%-70% of its own acid needs and secure raw material supply.

overview.what_it_does: CORONA Remedies is an India-focused branded pharmaceutical company, set up in 2004 and headquartered in Ahmedabad, that develops, manufactures and sells finished medicines (formulations) — tablets, capsules, sachets, bottles, topical sprays, ointments and injections — under its own brand names such as B29, Myoril, Tricium, Cortel and Obimet. It earns money by getting specialist and super-specialist doctors to prescribe these brands and selling the products through a pan-India network of distributors and medical representatives, with a deliberate focus on the 'middle of the pyramid' in metro, semi-metro, urban and semi-urban markets; roughly 70-72% of sales come from chronic and semi-chronic (long-term treatment) therapies, which management says gives repeat, sticky volume. About 96% of revenue comes from India, with only a small export/B2B business; FY26 revenue was INR 1,403 crore (up 17.3%) with EBITDA of INR 293 crore (20.9% margin) and adjusted PAT of INR 199 crore. It runs two manufacturing plants (Gujarat and Solan, Himachal Pradesh) with in-house R&D, is net cash surplus, and grows both organically and by buying or in-licensing brands from large multinationals.

parts.name: Women's healthcare
parts.what: Sells brands covering the full female life cycle — menarche to menopause, pregnancy, post-pregnancy and pre/post-menopause — and is described as one of the four key therapy areas, now reinforced by a dedicated IVF/infertility taskforce set up in Q4 FY26 (its 'fourth focus theme') to exploit the acquired Bayer-Zydus infertility brands.

parts.name: Cardio-Diabeto (cardio-metabolic)
parts.what: Brands spanning insulin resistance and pre-diabetes through diabetes and its complications, plus cardiac conditions like hypertension, dyslipidemia and ischemic heart disease — a core chronic therapy area (Obimet is named among its prominent brands).

parts.name: Pain management
parts.what: A diversified range across dosage forms — oral tablets and capsules, topical sprays, ointments and injections — for musculoskeletal spasm and neuropathic pain; one of the four key therapy areas, with Myoril among the flagship brands.

parts.name: Urology
parts.what: Products for benign prostatic hyperplasia, overactive bladder, urinary tract infection and stone management, the fourth of the key therapy areas and one where the company also sells in-licensed brands from Ferring.

parts.name: Other therapies (VMN, gastrointestinal, respiratory)
parts.what: A supporting basket of vitamins/minerals/nutrition, gastro and respiratory products that rounds out the portfolio; management notes CORONA today addresses only about one-third of the Indian pharma market and wants to add areas like infertility, nephrology, CNS, oncology and dermatology.

parts.name: Acquired brands and in-licensing
parts.what: A deliberate growth engine — seven brand trademarks bought from Bayer Zydus in July 2025 (Noklot and Noklot CV in the 1,500-crore-plus anti-platelet market, infertility brands Fostine, Menodac and Ovidac, and women's-health brands), the Wokadine povidone-iodine brand (No. 2 in a 630-crore-plus market) acquired in FY26, and in-licensed brands from Swiss firm Ferring; management guides to 25% growth from acquired brands in FY27.

parts.name: Biosimilars and biologics
parts.what: A newly entered area, with three biosimilar launches in FY26 (Fostine R, Tricium DnaB, Wyntide, Tyvenza named), positioned as a long-term diversification platform rather than a material earner today.

parts.name: Manufacturing and backward integration
parts.what: Two WHO-GMP plants (the Gujarat one also EU-GMP and now EAEU-GMP certified) with total capacity of about 1.65 billion tablets/capsules, 20 million sachets and 10 million bottles, two DSIR-approved R&D centres, a new 600-kg line and a dedicated hormone plant due in Q1-Q2 FY27, plus an investment in La Chandra Pharma Lab which supplies hormonal APIs under a right-of-first-refusal arrangement.

parts.name: International / export (B2B)
parts.what: The small remaining ~4% of revenue; EAEU GMP accreditation opens five Eurasian markets (Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Armenia, Kyrgyzstan) worth roughly USD 25 billion on a B2B model, but management says dossier approvals take 1-2 years and the India:international mix will stay around 90:10 even after 3-5 years.

overview.what_it_does: Aditya Infotech Limited (listed as CPPLUS) makes and sells video security and surveillance equipment in India under its own brand CP PLUS — CCTV cameras of every type (analog HD, IP network, Wi-Fi, 4G, thermal, explosion-proof, AI), the recorders that go with them (DVRs and NVRs), plus cables, power supplies and accessories so a customer can buy the whole kit from one place. It sells to four customer groups: small and medium businesses (about 60% of revenue), government and large enterprise projects (about 30%), and homes (about 10%), reaching them mainly through a wholesale channel of 1,000-plus distributors and 2,000-plus system integrators across 500-plus cities, plus 141 exclusive 'Galaxy' franchise stores and online marketplaces. It earns money largely by manufacturing hardware in India and selling it at a margin — helped by making more of the parts itself — with a smaller and newer layer of cloud-storage, AI video-analytics and monitoring services on top. The business is essentially India-only; FY26 revenue was Rs 4,220.8 crore with EBITDA of Rs 579 crore and adjusted PAT of Rs 368 crore, and management says its share of India's surveillance market reached roughly 45% by Q3 FY26.

parts.name: CP PLUS brand (own-brand products)
parts.what: The core own-brand range of cameras, recorders and allied security gear that management says contributed 86-87% of total company revenue in FY26, within which IP (network) products were about 73-75% of the mix as customers shift away from older analog HD.

parts.name: SMB segment
parts.what: Sales of cameras and recorders to small and medium businesses through distributors, system integrators and franchise stores — described as the largest slice at about 60% of revenue.

parts.name: Government and large enterprise projects
parts.what: Bigger tendered deployments for smart/safe city schemes, public safety and critical infrastructure plus large corporates, described as roughly 30% of revenue and an area where the company is adding vertical-focused salespeople.

parts.name: Consumer / home segment
parts.what: Retail products such as ezyKam smart Wi-Fi home cameras, 4G cameras for places without wired internet and CarKam dashcams, sold online and offline; about 10% of revenue but the place where the CP PLUS brand name matters most.

parts.name: Professional range
parts.what: Higher-end products for institutional buyers — AI network cameras with facial recognition and video analytics, number-plate recognition cameras for traffic, GPS-enabled mobile NVRs for trains and buses, police body-worn cameras and control-room displays.

parts.name: Services and solutions
parts.what: A software/services layer — CP PLUS Cloud Storage for backup video, CP PLUS AI for video analytics, and the OnVigil AI-IoT monitoring platform — small today but the direction management is pushing, including a Qualcomm partnership to move from 'hardware-led surveillance' to AI analytics.

parts.name: Manufacturing (AIL Dixon, Kadapa)
parts.what: The in-house factory in Kadapa, Andhra Pradesh — originally a 50:50 joint venture with Dixon Technologies, bought out in September 2024 to become a wholly owned subsidiary — which management calls India's largest single-location surveillance plant, with capacity grown from 1.5 million units a month at listing to 2.5 million by end-FY26.

parts.name: Backward integration / component localisation
parts.what: A push to make more of the input parts itself rather than import them — an enclosures and housing plant at Kadapa targeting 30 million units a year, a CCTV lens assembly line scaling toward 1 million lenses a month, and a cable joint venture with Orient Cables in Rajasthan due to start up in FY27.

parts.name: R&D centres
parts.what: In-house product design and engineering, originally in Noida and later Ahmedabad, with a Bangalore centre coming and a wholly owned Taiwan subsidiary set up for chip-level and embedded work; described as central to holding STQC certification leadership and building AI products.

parts.name: Multi-brand strategy (EYRA, NEXIVUE)
parts.what: Two new lower-priced brands launched at IFSEC in December 2025 aimed at the mass-market and unorganised end of the market, launching through Q4 FY26 and Q1 FY27 — a way to compete below the main CP PLUS price points.

parts.name: Non-CP PLUS business
parts.what: The remaining roughly 13-14% of revenue outside the CP PLUS brand; the calls trace this to the company's origins as a distributor of global IT brands from 1995 onward but give no further detail on its current size or composition.
